response.title: The Poison and the Wire
response.immediate: 1400 hours, Cabinet Room. McCone reports back within the hour: no CIA asset sits close enough to Castro to guarantee a strike inside seven days. Told to proceed regardless, the Agency reactivates an exile intermediary carrying a poison delivery meant for someone in Castro's household staff. By 1530, cable traffic from a Miami station officer goes dark. Word filters back through a second source: Cuban G2 has taken the intermediary into custody at a checkpoint outside Havana before he reached his contact. No attempt on Castro occurs. The President is informed while RFK is still on the phone to the Justice Department line to Dobrynin.
response.worldReaction: Nothing public. No Cuban statement, no Soviet reaction — the arrest has not surfaced anywhere Washington can see. McCone's briefing to the President is verbal, unminuted. LeMay, unaware of the covert failure, continues pressing the SAM-strike case as though the diplomatic clock is the only one running.
response.consequences: An arrested man now sits in Cuban hands who may know a CIA name. If he talks, Havana can hand Moscow direct evidence of an American assassination attempt in the middle of missile negotiations — potentially destroying the Dobrynin channel RFK is running and handing LeMay's argument new force. The order stands technically open — McCone has not been told to stand it down — while the President has not yet acted on OPLAN 312, the submarine, or Dobrynin's terms.
response.detailed: McCone comes to the Cabinet Room a little after 1400 with a manila folder he does not open. He tells the President plainly that the Agency has no one inside Castro's security perimeter and that a week is not enough time to build one. Pressed to proceed anyway, he says the only asset with any chance is an old channel — a Cuban exile courier tied to a contact in Castro's kitchen staff, last used in the abortive 1961 poison-pill effort. He warns it is thin and the President tells him to use it regardless. By mid-afternoon a Miami-based case officer loses contact with the courier. A second report, unconfirmed, indicates the courier was stopped at a roadblock near the Havana perimeter and taken by G2 before making contact. No poison reached Castro. No attempt occurred. The President learns this from McCone directly, without paper, while Robert Kennedy is a floor below on the phone line reserved for Dobrynin, testing whether Moscow would accept a non-invasion pledge for verified missile withdrawal. Neither brother yet knows whether the arrested man can name anyone. McNamara, occupied with holding quarantine commanders off any provocative act near the Soviet submarine, has not been briefed on the covert failure. LeMay, working the SAM-strike argument with the Chiefs, is likewise unaware — his case rests on Anderson's death and the danger of further missile emplacement, not on Castro at all. The order to move against Castro remains formally open; no one has told McCone to stop.

The courier was apprehended by Cuban state security before reaching his contact; no attempt on Castro's life occurred. Whether the courier can identify his CIA handler is unknown. The order to proceed against Castro remains open and unrescinded. Concurrently, RFK opened contact with Dobrynin proposing non-invasion for verified missile withdrawal; McNamara held quarantine forces to non-provocative posture; the Joint Chiefs and LeMay pressed for an immediate strike on Cuban SAM sites.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 shot down over Cuba, pilot dead — first combat death of the crisis. Soviet missiles remain on the island under naval quarantine; no hotline exists between Washington and Moscow. Kennedy ordered a one-week covert assassination attempt on Castro; McCone warned access was inadequate but proceeded via an exile courier carrying poison, who was arrested by Cuban security before reaching his target. The attempt failed; whether the courier can name his CIA link, and whether Havana or Moscow will learn of it, is unresolved. Simultaneously, RFK opened a private channel to Dobrynin proposing non-invasion for verified missile withdrawal, without committing on the Jupiter missiles in Turkey. McNamara holds quarantine forces to restrained rules of engagement. The Joint Chiefs and LeMay press for an immediate air strike on Cuban SAM sites, citing Major Anderson's death. Still undecided: response to Khrushchev's terms, authorization of OPLAN 312, handling of the shadowing Soviet submarine, and whether to shut down the exposed Castro operation before it surfaces.

response.immediate: At 12:40 p.m. Kennedy had Kenneth O'Donnell carry a private note to Johnson's West Wing office asking him to resign 'for the good of the country and the crisis.' Johnson read it standing, said nothing to O'Donnell, and by 1:15 p.m. had a one-paragraph statement typed for release: he remained vice president, was attending to his constitutional duties, and would not discuss the office further. Kennedy's own public remarks to reporters outside the Cabinet Room at 1:30 p.m. asking Johnson to step aside were carried live by all three networks before Johnson's statement reached the wire services.
response.worldReaction: UPI and AP moved bulletins within the hour: PRESIDENT ASKS JOHNSON TO QUIT VP POST — JOHNSON REFUSES. NBC interrupted afternoon programming. No word yet from Moscow, where it is past 8 p.m.; Khrushchev's Presidium has given no sign of having seen the wires. Congressional leadership offices in Washington began fielding calls within twenty minutes.
response.consequences: The constitutional fact is unchanged: Johnson remains vice president, no vacancy exists, RFK cannot be installed. The Joint Chiefs' strike package remains on LeMay's execution timetable regardless. McNamara continues to hold OPLAN 312 in readiness. Robert Kennedy's channel to Dobrynin continues to run, unaffected in substance, though its credibility as a channel run by a settled administration is now in question.
response.detailed: The Cabinet Room at 1:45 p.m.: coffee gone cold, teletype clacking in the next room with wire copy on the Johnson refusal, McNamara standing by the window with a folder on OPLAN 312 he had not yet opened. Kennedy's private note to Johnson had asked for resignation 'as soon as possible' so that Robert Kennedy could be nominated; Johnson's reply, delivered orally through O'Donnell before the written statement went out, was that 'a Vice President is not a hired man, Mr. President, and you can't fire what the Constitution gave me.' He added that he would not resign in the middle of a nuclear crisis and would treat any renewed public request as politically hostile. The public exchange — Kennedy's remarks at 1:30, Johnson's statement at roughly 2:05 — reached the press before either side had coordinated language, producing dueling wire stories inside the same news cycle. Meanwhile the machinery already set in the morning continued without regard to the Johnson matter: LeMay pressed the Chiefs' case that delay on the SAM sites was itself a decision, now compounded, in his words, by a White House that could not settle its own vice presidency. McNamara held to his position that OPLAN 312 stay ready but unlaunched and that the Dobrynin channel be given hours, not minutes, to answer. Robert Kennedy, who had been in the room for the private note but not consulted on its timing, told the president afterward that the public request had cost him standing with Congress at the exact hour he needed it. No response of any kind has come from Moscow.

press.headline: KENNEDY ASKS JOHNSON TO QUIT AS VICE PRESIDENT; JOHNSON REFUSES
press.body: President Kennedy today publicly asked Vice President Johnson to resign 'as soon as possible.' A statement from the Vice President's office said Mr. Johnson 'remains Vice President of the United States' and is 'attending to his constitutional duties' amid the Cuban crisis. No reason for the request was given by the White House.

press.headline: WHITE HOUSE SPLIT SURFACES AMID CUBA CRISIS
press.body: Correspondents outside the West Wing report unusual tension between the President and Vice President on the second Saturday of the missile crisis, hours after the loss of a U-2 pilot over Cuba. Congressional sources contacted by NBC expressed surprise and concern that a constitutional question has arisen at this hour.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: He kept his voice level: 'Mr. President, I need to know how many minutes this costs us with Dobrynin. If Congress reads this as a White House in disarray, that changes his instructions from Moscow, not just ours from here.' He did not raise his eyes from the OPLAN 312 folder.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: He was blunt: 'You've now got a public fight over the Vice Presidency on top of a dead pilot and missiles still on the pads. Every hour you spend on this is an hour the Chiefs don't get an answer on the SAM sites. Sir, that's not a hypothetical — that's the clock.'

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Quieter than the others, to his brother alone: 'Johnny, you can't order a resignation, and doing it in public before you'd even heard him out has cost you men on the Hill I needed this afternoon. I'll keep working Dobrynin, but this didn't help either of us.'

response.chronicleEntry: 27 Oct 1962, 1:30–2:15 p.m. EST: Kennedy publicly and privately asked VP Johnson to resign so RFK could be named VP. Johnson refused both requests and issued a public statement remaining in office. No constitutional vacancy created. JCS execution timetable and LeMay's demand for SAM-site strike authority continue unaffected; McNamara holds OPLAN 312 in readiness; RFK-Dobrynin channel continues. No response yet from Moscow.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 was shot down over Cuba this morning, killing its pilot — the crisis's first combat death. Soviet MRBMs remain on the island; the naval quarantine holds; both sides are at highest alert with no hotline between Washington and Moscow. At noon Kennedy attempted to force Vice President Johnson's resignation, publicly and privately, intending to install Robert Kennedy as VP. Johnson refused both times and stated publicly he remains Vice President; no constitutional mechanism existed to remove him, and the attempt produced a visible Kennedy-Johnson split reported by AP, UPI and NBC within the hour, with no reaction yet from Moscow. Underneath this, the Joint Chiefs have placed a strike package against Cuban SAM sites on an execution timetable and General LeMay is pressing for authority to use it; McNamara favors holding OPLAN 312 ready but unlaunched and tightening civilian control; Robert Kennedy continues a private channel to Ambassador Dobrynin signaling that Washington will discuss missile withdrawal. Unresolved: how to answer Khrushchev's letters, whether to strike the SAM sites, submarine rules of engagement, and how to manage the open Kennedy-Johnson rift during the standoff.

response.title: Fifteen Minutes
response.immediate: 12:00–12:15 PM EST. The written demand went to the Vice President's office at the Executive Office Building. Johnson did not appear. His secretary telephoned back at 12:09 to confirm receipt only. At 12:11 Robert Kennedy called the Oval Office directly: Johnson had reached him first, furious, calling the demand illegal and refusing to sign anything. No Secret Service detail, no military police, no White House staff moved to compel Johnson's presence. No officer has produced, or claims to possess, lawful authority to remove a sitting Vice President by force. The fifteen minutes expired at 12:15 with Johnson still in his own office, the original letter in his possession.
response.worldReaction: Nothing has reached the press yet. Inside the government the reaction is immediate and alarmed: Robert Kennedy warns his brother by phone that a public fight over the vice presidency, in the middle of missiles ninety miles from Florida, could break the administration apart in full view of Moscow. LeMay, hearing of the standoff secondhand, treats it as further proof of paralysis at the top and presses harder for the Chiefs' strike recommendation to be acted on now rather than argued over.
response.consequences: No mechanism exists to enforce the ultimatum; it now sits as an unresolved fact, held by Johnson as evidence, disclosed to at least Robert Kennedy, possibly further. The Joint Chiefs' renewed OPLAN 312 recommendation lands on the same desk as the Johnson matter, unresolved. The Dobrynin channel remains open only because Robert Kennedy has continued running it independent of the fight over the vice presidency. Command cohesion at the center of the crisis is now visibly strained at the exact hour aircrews stand ready and a U-2 pilot lies dead over Cuba.
response.detailed: The Cabinet Room clock read 12:15 when McNamara, standing near the window with a folder of quarantine dispositions, asked flatly whether the Vice President's status was resolved, because he needed to know before briefing the Navy on rules of engagement at the barrier line. No one answered him directly. Robert Kennedy took the call in the President's presence, gripping the phone, telling his brother in low, urgent language that Lyndon would not sign, would not come, and considered the letter itself proof of something he intends to keep. LeMay, present for the Chiefs' briefing on SAM sites at Mariel and Banes, did not raise Johnson's name at all — instead he set target folders on the table and asked for authorization within the hour, treating the vice-presidential matter as background noise to a decision he considers already overdue. The letter to Johnson remains extant, unretracted, unanswered by any resignation. Nothing has been said publicly. The missiles remain in Cuba. The pilot remains dead. Dobrynin remains, for now, on the other end of Robert Kennedy's line.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: "Jack, he says he'll fight it in the papers if he has to. You cannot do this today of all days — I need the Attorney General's office and I need you sane on the phone with Dobrynin, not fighting Lyndon Johnson for a chair."

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: "Mr. President, the Vice President can resign or not resign, it changes nothing at Mariel. Give the order on the SAM sites. Every hour you don't is an hour they finish hardening those emplacements."

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: "I need to know in the next ten minutes whether the chain of command runs through the Vice President's office for any contingency. If it doesn't, say so, and let's return to the quarantine line — that is the problem with a clock on it right now."

response.chronicleEntry: 12:00–12:15 EST, 27 October: President Kennedy issued a written ultimatum demanding Vice President Johnson's immediate resignation within fifteen minutes, with force threatened if refused. Johnson refused, retained the letter, and telephoned Robert Kennedy rather than the President. No resignation was submitted; no lawful mechanism or force was employed to compel Johnson's presence. The demand remains outstanding and unresolved. Simultaneously, the Joint Chiefs renewed their recommendation for an immediate strike on Cuban SAM sites under OPLAN 312; Robert Kennedy continued to hold open the Dobrynin channel independent of the internal dispute.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 was shot down over Cuba this morning; the pilot is dead. Soviet missiles remain on the island under naval quarantine, both sides at maximum alert, no hotline exists. At noon, President Kennedy demanded Vice President Johnson resign in writing within fifteen minutes, threatening force. Johnson refused, kept the letter as evidence, and called Robert Kennedy rather than complying; no lawful means to compel him exists and none was used. Robert Kennedy warned that a public fight over the vice presidency could fracture the government, and is separately running a private channel to Soviet Ambassador Dobrynin probing a non-invasion pledge tied to verified missile withdrawal. General LeMay and the Joint Chiefs have renewed pressure for an immediate strike on Cuban SAM sites (OPLAN 312); McNamara wants the strike force held ready but unused while diplomacy continues. Nothing of this has yet reached the public. Missiles remain in Cuba, unremoved.

response.title: The Sortie That Did Not Launch
response.immediate: 12:00–16:00, Cabinet Room. Kennedy's order for one reconnaissance sortie passed to the Joint Chiefs, who relayed it to General Curtis LeMay at Strategic Air Command. LeMay assigned an aircraft, a pilot, and a route over the missile sites, and reported compliance up the chain. By 16:00 no U-2 had left the ground; SAC held the mission on the next available launch window, timing and readiness undisclosed to the White House.
response.worldReaction: Moscow has heard nothing directly — no cable, no broadcast, has crossed the Kennedy order itself, which remains internal to the U.S. command structure. Radio Moscow's afternoon broadcasts continue on the previous day's line, unchanged by anything that happened this window. Dobrynin, contacted separately by Robert Kennedy, now carries private word that Washington wants verified missile removal and might discuss non-invasion terms — the first concrete language exchanged since the U-2 was shot down this morning.
response.consequences: The Joint Chiefs, having complied with the reconnaissance order, simultaneously renewed their recommendation for a strike on the SAM sites and readied OPLAN 312 for immediate execution. McNamara tightened control over reconnaissance and quarantine operations and warned that a strike undertaken before further diplomacy could not be guaranteed containable. The mission itself sits unlaunched, its readiness at SAC's discretion, not the President's.
response.detailed: At noon the Cabinet Room still smelled of the morning's cigarettes when word came that Major Anderson's U-2 had gone down over Cuba, the first death of the crisis. Kennedy's order — one sortie, no more — went out through the Joint Chiefs to Offutt Air Force Base. LeMay took it, and by early afternoon had named an aircraft and a pilot and fixed a route over the missile installations, but the launch window he set was 'next available,' language that satisfied the chain of command's reporting requirement without fixing an hour on any clock in Washington. The Chiefs told Kennedy they had complied. They also handed him, in the same breath, a renewed recommendation to strike the SAM sites and a request to keep OPLAN 312 at readiness for immediate execution should another aircraft go down. McNamara, reviewing the reconnaissance and quarantine orders that afternoon, imposed tighter procedural control on both and told the President directly that a strike undertaken now, ahead of any further diplomatic signal, risked an escalation no one could promise to stop. Robert Kennedy, working the Dobrynin channel on his own initiative, told the Soviet ambassador that Washington needed verifiable missile withdrawal and was prepared to discuss non-invasion assurances privately — but asked, in turn, what Moscow's own terms were. No answer had come back by 16:00. The four hours closed with a sortie authorized, assigned, and not yet flown; a strike plan kept warm against the President's stated preference for restraint; and a diplomatic thread run by the Attorney General, dangling, unanswered, into the evening.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: "I've tightened the reconnaissance and quarantine procedures myself, Mr. President — every flight now reports through me before it's a fact on the ground, not after. But I want to be clear about the arithmetic: if that U-2 goes down too, we may not have four hours to decide anything next time. A strike today, before Bobby's channel produces something, is a door we can't close once it's open."

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: "Sortie's assigned, pilot's named, route's fixed. That's compliance, not commitment — SAC will fly it when the window's right, and I'd remind everyone in this room that OPLAN 312 sits ready because it should. We lost a pilot this morning. The next decision that matters is whether we let that stand unanswered."

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: "Jack, Dobrynin didn't blink when I raised the assurances — he took it back to Moscow, no promises, but he took it. LeMay wants his strike plan warm and McNamara wants his control, and they're both right about their own jobs. What matters is whether Khrushchev answers me before somebody's plane doesn't come home."

response.chronicleEntry: Kennedy ordered one U-2 reconnaissance sortie over Cuba; the Joint Chiefs and LeMay assigned aircraft, pilot, and route but did not launch by 16:00. The Chiefs simultaneously pressed for a SAM-site strike and kept OPLAN 312 ready. McNamara tightened reconnaissance and quarantine controls and warned against striking ahead of diplomacy. RFK opened concrete terms with Dobrynin — verified withdrawal for non-invasion assurances — with no Soviet answer yet received.
response.storySoFar: Noon, 27 October 1962: a U-2 shot down over Cuba, its pilot dead — the crisis's first combat death. Kennedy ordered one further reconnaissance sortie; the Joint Chiefs and LeMay assigned an aircraft and route but had not launched it by 16:00, while renewing pressure for a strike on the SAM sites and holding OPLAN 312 ready. McNamara tightened control over reconnaissance and quarantine operations, warning that a strike now could become uncontrollable. Robert Kennedy, via the Dobrynin channel, raised verified missile withdrawal in exchange for non-invasion assurances; Moscow has not yet replied. No hotline exists. Soviet missiles remain on Cuba; the quarantine holds; both sides' strategic forces stand at peak alert. The next Soviet or Cuban move, and the fate of the assigned but unflown sortie, remain unresolved as the afternoon closes.

response.title: The Submarine Surfaces
response.immediate: 1600 hours. The Cabinet Room fills with cigarette smoke. Word reaches the President through McNamara's channel: B-59 has surfaced. No shots fired. The destroyers Cony and Beale observed the withdrawal and held their positions on the quarantine line, depth charges silent since the order went down the Navy chain three hours ago.
response.worldReaction: Radio Moscow says nothing about a submarine. Havana's press continues denouncing the 'illegal blockade.' In Washington, wire services report only that the quarantine remains in force and that naval operations continue without incident — the closest thing to good news the ticker has carried in two weeks.
response.consequences: The Joint Chiefs, through General Taylor, confirm compliance with the President's restriction while formally re-submitting the OPLAN 312 recommendation, unsigned by LeMay's objection that restraint has bought Moscow time rather than concessions. RFK reports the Dobrynin channel remains open; a non-invasion assurance is now on the table if missile removal can be verified. Nothing is settled. The missiles are still on the island.
response.detailed:
At 1550 hours a flash message reaches the Pentagon's Navy Command Center: Soviet submarine B-59, previously subjected to practice depth-charge signaling near the quarantine line, has surfaced roughly forty nautical miles from where USS Randolph's task group had been tracking it. No weapons discharged from either side. USS Cony's watch officer logs the surfacing at 1547, notes the submarine running on diesel, no aggressive maneuver, withdrawing on a heading away from the screen. McNamara receives this at Defense seven minutes later and telephones the Cabinet Room directly — he tells the President the immediate danger has passed, that the destroyers ceased harassment as ordered and the encounter did not escalate.

General LeMay is in the room by 1615. He does not dispute the fact of the withdrawal; he disputes its meaning. "That's one submarine, one captain who ran out of air and patience," he says. "The missiles are still in the ground. Every hour we sit here is an hour they get better at hiding them from our aircraft." He places the renewed OPLAN 312 recommendation on the table again — SAM sites, immediate strike authorization — with Taylor's signature but not his own concurrence beyond the paper's existence; LeMay wants it on record that the Chiefs asked and were told no.

RFK, standing by the window, reports that Dobrynin has indicated Khrushchev may accept a public non-invasion pledge in exchange for verified missile withdrawal — a softer position than the Turkey-for-Cuba trade Moscow floated separately. He argues this is the offer to answer, quickly, before Moscow's position hardens again or before another incident like the submarine happens somewhere else with a less exhausted captain.

McNamara wants surveillance continued, strike plans kept ready but unexecuted, verification made the price of any assurance. Nothing here has been decided. The quarantine holds unchanged. The missiles remain unremoved. The President has not yet answered Dobrynin, not yet ruled on OPLAN 312, not yet defined what verification would satisfy Washington.

press.headline: NAVY: QUARANTINE HOLDS, NO INCIDENTS REPORTED IN LATEST HOURS
press.body: Defense Department sources say U.S. naval forces continue to enforce the quarantine of Cuba without incident this afternoon. No further details on today's earlier loss of a reconnaissance aircraft were released.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: "The submarine is off the board. That's one variable removed. It buys us hours, not a solution — the missiles are still there, and every hour without an answer to Dobrynin is an hour Khrushchev can change his terms again."

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: "A submarine backing off is not a Soviet decision to remove those missiles, Mr. President. The Chiefs' recommendation stands. Delay is a choice, and it's the wrong one."

advisors.name: Robert Kennedy
advisors.reaction: "Jack, Dobrynin's telling us Khrushchev wants a way out that doesn't look like surrender. The non-invasion pledge is that door. We should walk through it before somebody in Moscow closes it."

response.chronicleEntry: 1550-1630 EST, 27 October: Kennedy's order to hold the quarantine line and avoid escalatory contact was transmitted through the Navy chain; destroyers ceased depth-charge signaling. Soviet submarine B-59 surfaced and withdrew without firing. Joint Chiefs confirmed compliance while resubmitting OPLAN 312 for strikes on Cuban SAM sites. RFK reported the Dobrynin channel open to a non-invasion pledge tied to verified missile removal. No decision yet made on strikes, on the Dobrynin offer, or on verification terms; the quarantine remains unchanged and the missiles remain in place.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 shot down and its pilot killed; the quarantine holds; Soviet missiles remain on Cuba. Kennedy ordered U.S. naval forces to maintain the quarantine line without escalating against a submerged Soviet submarine, B-59. The destroyers stopped harassing it; the submarine surfaced and withdrew without firing — the immediate danger of that encounter passed. The Joint Chiefs complied but renewed their demand to strike Cuban SAM sites under OPLAN 312, with LeMay pressing hardest. Robert Kennedy reports the Dobrynin backchannel now offers a possible non-invasion pledge from Khrushchev in exchange for verified missile removal, a softer line than earlier Turkey-trade proposals. McNamara counsels continued surveillance and readiness without attack, prioritizing verification and channel diplomacy. Nothing is resolved: the missiles remain, OPLAN 312 is unauthorized but pending, and Washington has not yet answered Moscow.

response.title: The Dobrynin Channel
response.immediate: 6:00 PM, Cabinet Room. Robert Kennedy returns from the Soviet Embassy and reports to the president directly: he met Dobrynin, delivered the assurance orally, and Dobrynin took it without comment beyond saying he would cable Moscow at once. No written record was exchanged. The room absorbs this in silence broken by LeMay's chair scraping back from the table.
response.worldReaction: No public statement has been made by either government. Radio Moscow's 6 PM broadcast repeats Khrushchev's public terms from earlier cable traffic without alteration. Soviet embassy traffic to Moscow cannot be read by Washington; the cable Dobrynin sent is presumed but not confirmed. No Kremlin acknowledgment has reached any American channel by evening.
response.consequences: Strike readiness continues unchanged — OPLAN 312 packages remain armed and briefed on LeMay's orders. McNamara holds quarantine and reconnaissance posture steady. The Joint Chiefs renew their unanimous strike recommendation in writing, accepting only a short, explicit delay. Whether Khrushchev has actually received the message, and how he intends to answer, is unknown and will remain unknown until some signal arrives from Moscow — a cable, a broadcast, or nothing at all before the window closes.
response.detailed:
By 6:15 PM the Cabinet Room holds its usual crowd of cigarette smoke and coffee cups gone cold. Robert Kennedy, still in his overcoat, tells the president plainly: Dobrynin listened, asked no questions requiring answer, said he would send the message to Moscow that night. Nothing was put in writing on either side. RFK's own reading is that Dobrynin took it seriously — the ambassador's manner, he says, was not that of a man humoring a threat he thought empty. But Robert Kennedy did not extract, and could not extract, any commitment. Dobrynin represents Moscow; he does not speak for it in real time.

McNamara, standing near the window with a folder of reconnaissance summaries, asks the operative question: how many hours before the Joint Chiefs' delay expires, and does the president intend to answer Khrushchev's public terms independently of whatever comes back through Dobrynin. He gets no answer yet because there is none to give — Moscow has said nothing since the private meeting occurred.

LeMay, blunt as always, states that the Soviets have now had a full day to shift missile-associated equipment under cover of American paralysis, and that the SAM sites tracking U-2 flights remain untouched and lethal, as this morning's loss demonstrated. He wants the strike order made executable, immediately, not contingent on a phone that has not rung.

The submarine surfaced near the quarantine line earlier in the day remains under naval observation; no order regarding its handling has yet been given this turn. The Joint Chiefs' written unanimous recommendation sits on the table, accepted only insofar as the president's delay remains short and explicit. Nothing from Khrushchev, publicly or privately, has yet answered the assurance carried through Dobrynin.

press.headline: NO WORD FROM MOSCOW ON QUARANTINE CRISIS SINCE MORNING BROADCAST
press.body: Diplomatic sources in Washington report no official Soviet response since Khrushchev's public message earlier today outlining conditions for missile withdrawal. State Department spokesmen declined comment on reports of private contacts between American and Soviet officials.

press.headline: Soviet position on Cuba reaffirmed, no new statement
press.body: The broadcast repeated without amendment the terms outlined by Chairman Khrushchev earlier in the day regarding removal of weapons said to be offensive, in exchange for guarantees against invasion of Cuba.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Dobrynin didn't blink and he didn't argue. That's not nothing from a man carrying instructions. But I can't tell you what Moscow does with it tonight, and neither can he yet — the cable's only just gone out, if it's gone out at all.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: We have no confirmation of receipt, let alone response. I'd like a number attached to how long we wait before the Chiefs' recommendation becomes the only paper on this table. Right now that number is undefined, and undefined numbers are how mistakes get made.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, we lost a pilot this morning to those SAMs. They're still up, still tracking, and now we're told to wait on a phone call to an embassy that hasn't called back. I'd like the order to strike made executable tonight, contingent or not.

response.chronicleEntry: 27 October, 6:00 PM: RFK delivers Kennedy's private assurance to Dobrynin at the Soviet Embassy; Dobrynin receives it without commitment and reports he will cable Moscow. No Soviet response received by evening. Strike readiness (OPLAN 312) and quarantine posture held unchanged on McNamara's order; Joint Chiefs renew unanimous strike recommendation, accept only a short explicit delay.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 shot down over Cuba, pilot killed. Quarantine and DEFCON readiness at unprecedented levels; no hotline exists between Washington and Moscow. That evening, Robert Kennedy meets Anatoly Dobrynin privately and delivers a presidential assurance regarding the missile-withdrawal and non-invasion framework, deliberately not conceding the Turkish-missile question publicly. Dobrynin accepts the message without comment and reports he will cable Moscow; no Soviet acknowledgment has yet returned. Meanwhile OPLAN 312 strike packages remain fully prepared on General LeMay's insistence; the Joint Chiefs unanimously recommend immediate strikes against Cuban SAM sites, held off only by a short, explicit presidential delay. McNamara maintains quarantine and reconnaissance readiness as a hedge. A Soviet submarine remains surfaced near the quarantine line, its handling still undecided. Whether Khrushchev has received or will accept the private assurance is unknown.

response.title: The Courier Taken at Marianao
response.immediate: At 1:40 p.m. John McCone telephoned Richard Helms from the Cabinet Room corridor and relayed the president's order: a lethal operation against Fidel Castro, mounted within seven days, using whatever Cuban-exile and Havana-based assets could be reached. Helms had no current channel to Castro's person. An exile courier carrying written operational instructions was stopped at a checkpoint near Marianao by Cuban State Security officers before any contact was made with the target. The instructions did not reach Castro. No attempt on his life occurred within the week ordered. The route Helms had planned to use is now known to be compromised.
response.worldReaction: Nothing of this has surfaced publicly. Havana and Moscow show no sign, in the traffic reaching Washington by 4 p.m., of having connected the seized courier to any American principal. The quarantine line, the U-2 loss, and Radio Moscow's broadcasts continue on their separate track, unaffected so far as anyone in the Cabinet Room can determine. Whether Cuban interrogators have already extracted the order's origin is not something Langley can answer tonight.
response.consequences: The compromised courier now sits in Cuban custody carrying knowledge, if he chooses or is made to give it up, that the president personally ordered Castro's death this week, a fact that would hand Havana and Moscow evidence of exactly the bad faith Khrushchev has accused Washington of harboring, at the precise hour RFK is trying to open a non-invasion channel through Dobrynin. McNamara's tightened rules of engagement and the Joint Chiefs' renewed strike recommendation continue on their own tracks, unaffected by this failure but not immune to it if the connection surfaces.
response.detailed: Noon passed into afternoon with the coffee going cold on the Cabinet Room table. The president's instruction to McCone was brief and specific: something within a week, using existing assets, without a paper trail to the Oval Office. McCone did not ask for elaboration; he left to call Helms directly rather than route the order through normal DCI channels. Helms's problem was immediate: there was no live channel to Castro himself, only to men who might get close to men who might get closer still. He activated what he had, an exile network run out of Miami with a courier line into western Cuba. The courier left with sealed instructions on the morning of the 27th. Cuban State Security took him near Marianao before he reached his contact, in the ordinary course of the heightened security already surrounding Havana since the U-2 came down that morning. Havana has not yet said what it took from him, or announced that it took him at all. Helms reported to McCone by early afternoon that the route was blown and that no alternative could be readied inside the week ordered. Separately, the machinery already moving before noon continued to move: RFK's message to Dobrynin proposing discussion of a non-invasion pledge against verified missile withdrawal, without touching Turkey; McNamara's order tightening quarantine rules of engagement and requiring explicit presidential authority before any strike; the Joint Chiefs' renewed paper urging immediate action against the SAM sites; LeMay telling colleagues privately that further delay after Major Anderson's death amounts to surrender by installment. None of these threads yet know of the courier's capture. Whether they will have to reckon with it depends entirely on what Cuban State Security does with the man they are holding, and on facts not yet in hand.

press.headline: U.S. NAVY HOLDS LINE OFF CUBA AS TENSION CONTINUES FOLLOWING PILOT'S DEATH
press.body: Naval quarantine vessels maintained station in the Caribbean this afternoon following the loss of an American reconnaissance pilot over Cuba this morning, the first combat death of the confrontation. Pentagon sources would not comment on reports of increased readiness among strategic forces. The White House has made no public statement since the president's morning briefing.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: McNamara did not comment on the Castro order directly when it reached him secondhand through McCone's staff; his concern, stated flatly, was that any compromised covert action now sits alongside an already tightened quarantine posture, and that he wants to know within hours, not days, whether Havana has connected the courier to Washington, because that fact changes what he tells the strike commanders about their rules of engagement.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: LeMay called the failed courier operation amateur hour and said it changed nothing in his recommendation. SAM sites should be struck now, before Havana or Moscow can use a captured exile as a pretext to claim American aggression they can then answer with the missiles already on the island.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: RFK, on hearing of the courier's capture, told his brother privately that if Havana breaks the man and produces him publicly, the Dobrynin channel is finished before it starts. Khrushchev cannot offer withdrawal to a government he can show ordered his ally's assassination in the same week.

response.chronicleEntry: 27 October 1962, afternoon: On presidential order, CIA director McCone directed Deputy Director Helms to mount an assassination attempt against Fidel Castro within one week. An exile courier carrying operational instructions was seized by Cuban State Security near Marianao before reaching any contact with Castro. No attempt on Castro's life occurred within the ordered period. What the captured courier disclosed, if anything, concerning the operation's American origin remains unknown to Washington as of this afternoon.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 shot down over Cuba, its pilot killed. Quarantine holds the line at sea while Soviet MRBMs remain on the island and strategic forces stand at unprecedented alert, with no hotline between Washington and Moscow. That afternoon the president ordered the CIA to kill Castro within a week; McCone and Helms activated an exile courier network, but Cuban State Security seized the courier near Marianao before he reached any contact, leaving the route blown and no attempt made. What, if anything, the courier has revealed about American authorship remains unknown. Simultaneously, RFK opened a cautious Dobrynin channel offering non-invasion and verified withdrawal talk while deferring Turkey; McNamara tightened quarantine rules requiring presidential authority before any strike; the Joint Chiefs and LeMay pressed for immediate strikes on the SAM sites, calling delay after the pilot's death a surrender by installment. The compromised Castro operation now threatens to poison the diplomatic opening at the exact moment it is being tested.

response.title: Turnback Over the Straits
response.immediate: 12:04–13:40 EDT. On presidential order, Air Force One taxied at Andrews and departed without escort, heading south-southeast toward Cuba. At 13:22, south of Key West, four Cuban MiG-21s intercepted the aircraft in international airspace. The pilot, Colonel James Swindal, reported hostile closure and, on standing rules of engagement for unescorted VIP aircraft, reversed course rather than press toward Cuban airspace. No shots fired. Air Force One landed back at Andrews at 13:40. No contact with Castro was made or attempted through any channel.
response.worldReaction: Havana Radio broke into programming within the hour: Castro denounced the flight as an American reconnaissance or decapitation probe and ordered Cuban air-defence and militia units to full readiness. Moscow has not yet responded; the six-to-eight hour cable delay to the Kremlin means Khrushchev likely does not yet know the flight happened. In Washington, wire services are reporting an unscheduled Air Force One flight and abrupt return; no official statement has been issued.
response.consequences: General LeMay is circulating a written demand to the Chiefs for a strike on Cuban SAM sites before nightfall, citing the interception as proof that delay is now more dangerous than action. McNamara wants five minutes with the president alone before any answer goes to the Chiefs. RFK is furious and wants the Dobrynin channel used immediately to explain the flight was not a strike. The turnback is being read domestically and internationally as either humiliation or provocation, and no public accounting has yet been given.
response.detailed:
At 12:00 the president, over the objections of the Secret Service detail and without informing State or the Chiefs beforehand, ordered Colonel Swindal to prepare Air Force One for immediate departure to Cuba, no escort, intending to reach Castro directly. The aircraft departed Andrews at 12:04. Radar and NORAD track logs show it flying a direct heading toward Havana. At 13:22, roughly forty nautical miles north of Cuban territorial waters, four MiG-21s out of San Antonio de los Baños closed to visual intercept distance. Swindal, operating under standing VIP-aircraft rules that forbid entering hostile airspace without cleared passage, broke off and turned north. The MiGs did not fire and did not pursue past the twelve-mile line. Air Force One landed at Andrews at 13:40; the president disembarked directly into a hastily reconvened Cabinet Room.

By 13:50 Radio Habana was broadcasting Castro's statement, delivered personally: the interception was proof Washington intended an invasion or a decapitation strike disguised as diplomacy, and he called on Khrushchev to hold firm and not trade Cuban security for anything. Cuban SAM and militia units have gone to a higher state of readiness; Soviet garrison troops on the island have not yet been reported moving, though no confirmation exists either way.

In Washington, LeMay's written objection is now before the Joint Chiefs, arguing the failed approach has forced Castro's hand and that a strike on the SAM network must go forward before dark to preserve any window for a follow-on invasion under OPLAN 312. No order has been given in response. McNamara is withholding recommendation pending clarification of Soviet reaction, which cannot arrive for hours given cable transit time to Moscow. RFK argues the Dobrynin channel must be used at once to frame the flight as an unauthorized personal gesture toward negotiation, not a military probe — before Moscow hears Havana's version first and unfiltered.

No aircraft were lost, no weapons were exchanged, and no communication with Castro occurred. The president is back in the Cabinet Room as of 13:45, the flight now an established fact that cannot be undone, with LeMay's demand for a strike the most immediate paper on the table.

press.headline: AIR FORCE ONE MAKES UNSCHEDULED FLIGHT, TURNS BACK OVER CARIBBEAN
press.body: Sources at Andrews Air Force Base confirm the presidential aircraft departed without prior announcement shortly after noon and returned less than two hours later. The White House has not commented. Unconfirmed reports from Havana claim Cuban fighter aircraft intercepted the plane.

press.headline: Castro: 'They Sent Their President as a Spy Plane'
press.body: Fidel Castro told listeners the unauthorized approach of the American presidential aircraft toward Cuban airspace was proof of imminent invasion plans disguised as a peace gesture. He ordered all anti-aircraft and militia units to maximum readiness and appealed to Premier Khrushchev to reject any settlement that compromises Cuban sovereignty.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, I need five minutes before I say anything to the Chiefs. We have no confirmation Moscow has even heard about this yet — the cable to the Kremlin runs six to eight hours minimum. Castro's statement went out in fifty minutes. That gap matters more than anything LeMay is putting in front of us right now.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: You flew the President of the United States into a fighter intercept with no escort, sir, and now Castro's calling it an invasion. He's not wrong that we looked like we were probing him. The SAM sites go up before dark or we lose the window entirely — I've had this plan ready for two weeks.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Christ. Dobrynin needs to hear our version before Khrushchev hears Castro's. I can be at the Soviet embassy in twenty minutes and tell him this was never a military move — but you have to let me go now, before Havana's story is the only one on the wire in Moscow.

response.chronicleEntry: 12:00–13:45 EDT, 27 October 1962: President Kennedy ordered Air Force One to fly unescorted directly to Cuba to seek a meeting with Castro. Cuban MiG-21s intercepted the aircraft south of Florida at 13:22; it turned back and landed at Andrews at 13:40 without contact being made. Castro publicly denounced the flight as evidence of an imminent American attack and raised Cuban forces to full alert. General LeMay is demanding a strike on Cuban SAM sites before nightfall. RFK is seeking to use the Dobrynin channel before Moscow receives only Havana's account. No shots were fired; Moscow's response is not yet known.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 was shot down and its pilot killed. With missiles still on Cuban soil and the quarantine in force, President Kennedy ordered Air Force One to fly unescorted directly to Cuba for a personal meeting with Castro. Cuban MiGs intercepted the aircraft short of Cuban airspace; it turned back to Andrews without contact. Castro denounced the approach on Radio Habana as proof of an imminent invasion and put Cuban forces on full alert. Moscow has not yet responded — cable transit runs six to eight hours. General LeMay is demanding an immediate strike on Cuban SAM sites before nightfall; McNamara wants time to assess before answering the Chiefs; RFK wants to reach Dobrynin at once to frame the flight as a failed peace overture before Havana's version reaches Khrushchev unchallenged. No shots have been fired. The president must now decide on LeMay's strike demand, the RFK-Dobrynin channel, quarantine rules of engagement, and whether to disclose the interception publicly.

response.title: Grounded
response.immediate: 12:00–16:00, Saturday 27 October. Kennedy's order to fly to Cuba unescorted goes to Andrews and the Joint Chiefs. General LeMay and the Chiefs return a written objection within the hour: no flight plan, no Cuban identification arrangement, no receiving field, no clearance from Havana. The crew preps Air Force One on the tarmac but does not launch. McNamara withdraws the immediate-departure order and brings Kennedy a revised plan instead.
response.worldReaction: No word from Havana, no word from Moscow on the president's proposed flight — because none was ever transmitted. Dobrynin, reached again by Robert Kennedy at the Soviet embassy, hears a non-invasion assurance offered in exchange for verified missile removal, and a flat refusal to put Turkish missiles on the table publicly. The Chiefs submit a fuller OPLAN 312 strike timetable, warning in writing that every hour of delay costs American aircrews.
response.consequences: Command authority holds — the lawful-order requirement stopped the flight rather than overriding it, and that strengthens procedural control even as it enrages LeMay. The Executive Committee reconvenes split: strike timetable versus diplomatic pause. RFK's channel reopens diplomatic space, but narrowly, with no Cuban clearance and no removal agreement in hand. Nuclear tension edges up despite the grounded flight, driven by the Chiefs' pressure and the unresolved quarantine.
response.detailed:
12:04 p.m., Cabinet Room. Kennedy's instruction reaches the Pentagon switchboard and Andrews Air Force Base simultaneously: Air Force One, no escort, immediate departure, Cuba. By 12:40 the Joint Chiefs' written response is on McNamara's desk — signed by LeMay, endorsed by the other Chiefs — stating flatly that no flight plan exists, no identification-friend-or-foe arrangement has been made with any receiving authority in Cuba, and no field has agreed to accept the aircraft. LeMay tells the room directly: 'You'll put the President in the air over a country we're not talking to, with SAM batteries live and no one told we're coming.' The crew at Andrews runs preflight checks; the aircraft does not move from the ramp.

At 1:15, McNamara returns to Kennedy with a substitute: ground the flight, intensify U-2 and low-level reconnaissance over the missile sites, and let Robert Kennedy's channel to Dobrynin carry the substance of any offer instead of the President's body. Kennedy accepts the substitution rather than force the issue against a written Chiefs' objection.

By 2:30, Robert Kennedy meets Anatoly Dobrynin again. He conveys a binding U.S. non-invasion guarantee contingent on verified removal of offensive missiles, and declines — pointedly — to discuss Jupiter missiles in Turkey as part of any public bargain. Dobrynin's cable to Moscow goes out; no reply arrives within the four-hour window, as expected given the distance and the absence of any faster channel.

Meanwhile the Chiefs deliver a revised OPLAN 312 package: a strike timetable against Cuban SAM sites and follow-on air operations, with LeMay privately telling fellow officers that quarantine and diplomacy have already failed. The full Executive Committee convenes at 3:00 and splits cleanly — several members side with the Chiefs' timetable, others back McNamara's pause, and a faction insists that whatever Moscow offers, it must be physically verifiable, not merely promised.

No contact with Castro was attempted or achieved. No Cuban landing clearance exists. The submarine encounter at the quarantine line remains unresolved and unaddressed this period.

press.headline: WHITE HOUSE DECLINES COMMENT ON REPORTED PRESIDENTIAL TRAVEL PLANS
press.body: Sources at Andrews Air Force Base report unusual activity around Air Force One this afternoon but the White House press office would neither confirm nor deny any presidential travel. Pentagon spokesmen referred all questions to the Executive Committee.

press.headline: NO CHANGE REPORTED IN AMERICAN POSITION
press.body: Soviet officials note continued contact through established diplomatic channels in Washington. No new American proposal regarding removal of missiles from Turkey has been received.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: 'Mr. President, I count four separate ways an unescorted approach to Cuban airspace ends badly, and none of them take longer than eleven minutes to develop. I withdrew the order. I'd ask you not to reissue it without a landing agreement in hand — which we do not have, and cannot get by cable today.'

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: 'You grounded the one asset that might've forced Castro's hand, and for what — a promise Dobrynin can't deliver on his own authority. The Chiefs' timetable stands ready. Every hour we sit here is an hour those SAM crews get better at killing our pilots.'

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: 'Jack, Dobrynin heard exactly what we wanted him to hear — no invasion, if the missiles come out and we can verify it. I did not raise Turkey and I'm glad of it; that's a fight for later, not for today's cable. But Castro would never have received you, and I think you know that.'

response.chronicleEntry: Kennedy ordered an unescorted presidential flight to Cuba to meet Castro directly; the Joint Chiefs blocked it in writing for lack of clearance, and the order was withdrawn in favor of intensified reconnaissance and a renewed Dobrynin channel offering non-invasion for verified missile removal, Turkey excluded from the offer. The Chiefs' OPLAN 312 strike timetable advanced in parallel; the quarantine submarine encounter remains unaddressed.
response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the missile crisis, a U-2 pilot's death this morning raised the stakes. Kennedy ordered himself flown unescorted to Cuba to meet Castro; the Joint Chiefs blocked it for lack of any Cuban clearance, and McNamara substituted a diplomatic pause. Robert Kennedy reopened the Dobrynin channel, offering a binding non-invasion guarantee for verified missile removal while refusing to discuss Turkish missiles. LeMay and the Chiefs pressed a revised OPLAN 312 strike timetable, warning that delay costs American lives. The Executive Committee split between strike and diplomacy. No Cuban landing clearance, no Castro contact, and no Moscow reply have yet materialized; the quarantine submarine encounter remains unresolved.

response.title: The Fan Song Falls Silent
response.immediate: At 1447 EDT the strike aircraft return to Homestead and Guantánamo. Photo interpreters confirm the SA-2 battery's Fan Song radar van destroyed; three launchers stand intact and possibly serviceable. No advance or follow-up message reached Moscow before the bomb fell. In the Cabin Room, LeMay reads the damage assessment as half a job done. RFK is already on the line to Dobrynin.
response.worldReaction: Soviet officers at the Cuban site report to Moscow that American aircraft attacked Soviet air-defence personnel directly. Khrushchev, informed before dawn his time, pulls back the non-invasion terms he had circulated through back channels and calls for a military assessment of what has actually been hit and who has been killed. Havana radio, by 1500 EDT, has not yet broadcast anything — Castro's silence is itself unread.
response.consequences: McNamara wants forty-eight hours before any second strike to determine whether the surviving launchers can fire. LeMay wants OPLAN 312 executed against the remaining SAM network within the day, and has the Chiefs' recommendation in writing. RFK's message to Dobrynin describes the strike as limited retaliation and asks, again, for Moscow's terms — but the terms Khrushchev had ready this morning are no longer on offer.
response.detailed: By 1500 EDT the Cabinet Room has not moved on from the strike; it has moved past it, toward the next decision. The photo interpretation from the follow-up RF-101 pass shows the Fan Song van as a scorched frame with no emissions — the battery is blind, but three of its six launcher rails read as upright and possibly loaded. McNamara circulates this reading personally, underlining that 'possibly serviceable' is not the same as 'operational' and that another twelve hours of overflight would settle the question the Chiefs are already treating as settled. LeMay does not wait for the second pass. He tells the president directly that a blind SAM site is a dead SAM site only if someone finishes killing it, and that the Joint Chiefs' recommendation — full suppression of the remaining network under OPLAN 312 — sits on the table ready for execution orders. The Chiefs have logged their objection to any pause as a matter of record. Robert Kennedy, working the back channel he has run alone since the eighteenth, tells Dobrynin by encrypted cable that the strike was retaliatory and limited, that Washington has not abandoned a political settlement, and asks pointedly what terms Moscow intends to offer now. No answer has come. What is not known in Washington: whether any Soviet personnel died at the battery, and what Khrushchev's suspended non-invasion draft actually said before he pulled it back. Only a further Soviet response, or a leak of the withdrawn cable, would answer either question. The submarine encounters at the quarantine line, and the question of whether to force a surface, remain untouched by this decision and sit exactly where they were four hours ago.

press.headline: U.S. JET STRIKES CUBAN MISSILE SITE — PENTAGON CALLS ACTION 'LIMITED'
press.body: Defense officials speaking on condition of anonymity confirmed this afternoon that American aircraft struck a Soviet-supplied missile installation in Cuba, the same type of site believed responsible for Sunday's downing of a U.S. reconnaissance plane. Officials described the action as retaliatory and declined to say whether further strikes were planned.

press.headline: AMERICAN AIRCRAFT ATTACK SOVIET PERSONNEL IN CUBA
press.body: Soviet military specialists rendering technical assistance to the Republic of Cuba came under attack today from American bomber aircraft. The Soviet government is assessing the incident and reserves the right to respond to this act of aggression by all means necessary.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, I need twelve hours of clean overflight before anyone tells you those three launchers are a threat or a wreck. Curtis is treating a photograph like a certainty. It isn't one yet.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: One bomb told them we're willing. It didn't tell them we're serious. Three rails are still standing at that site, Mr. President — finish it today or explain to the next pilot's widow why we didn't.

advisors.name: Robert Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Dobrynin has nothing to give me right now because Khrushchev pulled the paper off the table the minute that bomb landed. Give him something to hand back to Moscow besides silence, or this channel closes for good.

response.chronicleEntry: 1200–1600 EDT, 27 October 1962: On presidential order, U.S. aircraft dropped one bomb on the SA-2 battery responsible for killing Major Rudolf Anderson Jr., destroying its Fan Song radar but leaving launchers standing. No advance message reached Moscow. Soviet officers at the site reported an attack on Soviet personnel; Khrushchev suspended his prepared non-invasion settlement pending assessment. LeMay and the Joint Chiefs pressed for immediate follow-on strikes under OPLAN 312; McNamara urged a pause for damage assessment. RFK cabled Dobrynin describing the strike as limited and requesting Moscow's terms; none received by 1600.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 was shot down over Cuba, killing Major Anderson. President Kennedy ordered one bomb dropped on the responsible SA-2 site as a warning. The strike destroyed the site's radar but left launchers standing; no message preceded it. Soviet forces in Cuba reported an attack on their personnel; Khrushchev withdrew a non-invasion settlement he had been preparing to offer. Washington now splits: LeMay and the Joint Chiefs press for a full strike on the remaining SAM network; McNamara wants a pause to assess the damage; RFK's private channel to Dobrynin, asking for Moscow's terms, has gone unanswered. Casualties among Soviet personnel at the site are unconfirmed. The naval quarantine and submarine encounters remain unaddressed. No hotline exists. The missiles remain in Cuba. Every subsequent hour narrows or widens this margin depending on what Kennedy orders next.

response.title: The Submarine Surfaces
response.immediate: 14:20. Cabinet Room. McNamara reports B-59 has surfaced under destroyer lights, no shots fired. Kennedy's order held. Photographs of the Foxtrot venting on the surface reach the table within the hour, relayed from USS Beale.
response.worldReaction: Radio Moscow says nothing of the encounter. Khrushchev, informed the boat surfaced unmolested, tells his Presidium the Americans want a way out. He instructs the public channel to hold to two terms: missiles out, non-invasion pledge in — Turkey reserved for private word only.
response.consequences: RFK reopens Dobrynin. LeMay circulates a fresh demand for SAM strikes, citing the sub as proof of Soviet testing. The Chiefs' memorandum sits on the table, unanimous, formal, obeyed but on record as objection. McNamara wants the next reconnaissance cycle before any answer to Moscow is drafted.
response.detailed:
By 14:00 Anderson's traffic confirms compliance fleet-wide: no depth charges since 06:00, destroyers holding station but not closing. At 19:40 local, sonar contact on B-59 goes shallow, then surface — running lights, hatch open, diesel exhaust visible to Beale's bridge watch. No exchange of fire. The submarine ventilates for eleven minutes before diving again.

McNamara enters with the assessment: immediate naval danger eased, missiles and Cuban air defenses still fully operational. He wants forty-eight hours before recommending anything further.

LeMay does not wait. His memorandum — joined by the full Chiefs — renews the demand for OPLAN 312's opening phase against the SAM sites, argues delay compounds risk to any eventual invasion timetable, and requests the first strike package go to final launch readiness. They record the recommendation and then, without further argument in the room, confirm they are holding the quarantine restraint as ordered.

RFK, back from Dobrynin's residence near 16:00, tells his brother the Soviet ambassador is receptive to a rapid bargain: public non-invasion pledge for public withdrawal, Turkey handled elsewhere, off any record. He warns the channel is fragile and that Dobrynin cannot promise Khrushchev will wait long.

No hotline exists. Whatever Moscow does next will be inferred, not confirmed, until it happens.

press.headline: NAVY REPORTS NO SHOTS FIRED IN LATEST CONTACT
press.body: Pentagon sources say a submerged Soviet vessel surfaced under observation near the quarantine line without incident. Officials declined to characterize the vessel's nationality or class.

press.headline: SOVIET VESSELS CONTINUE LAWFUL VOYAGE ON HIGH SEAS
press.body: Soviet naval units proceed in accordance with international law. No provocation by imperialist forces has altered the peaceful character of Soviet shipping.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: The number that matters is eleven minutes on the surface and no fire exchanged. That's the number I want repeated to you tomorrow morning. Give me the reconnaissance cycle before you answer Khrushchev on anything.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, that boat surfaced because we stopped pressing it, not because the Russians blinked. The SAM sites are still tracking our aircraft. Every hour we don't hit them is an hour they get better at killing our pilots.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Dobrynin wants this settled as much as we do, Jack. He didn't flinch on non-invasion. Keep Turkey off the public table and I think we have something Khrushchev can sign his name to without losing the Presidium.

response.chronicleEntry: 14:00–18:00, 27 October. Kennedy's order to hold the quarantine and cease harassment reached the fleet and was obeyed; B-59 surfaced without incident near 19:40. The Joint Chiefs complied while formally renewing their demand for strikes on Cuban SAM sites. Khrushchev, informed of the encounter, instructed Moscow to keep negotiations open on two public terms, reserving Turkey for private negotiation. RFK reopened the Dobrynin channel and reported the ambassador receptive to a rapid bargain.
response.storySoFar: Black Saturday, 27 October 1962. A U-2 pilot was killed over Cuba this morning; missiles remain on the island; no hotline exists. At noon Kennedy ordered the Joint Chiefs to hold the quarantine and avoid escalatory contact with a submerged Soviet submarine, B-59. The order was obeyed: depth-charge harassment stopped, and the submarine surfaced near 19:40 without being fired on. The Chiefs complied but formally renewed their unanimous demand for air strikes on Cuban SAM sites, with LeMay pressing hardest. Khrushchev, learning the submarine was not attacked, kept negotiations open — publicly offering missile withdrawal for a non-invasion pledge, privately reserving the question of U.S. missiles in Turkey. RFK reopened the Dobrynin channel and found the ambassador receptive to a fast bargain along those lines. McNamara wants forty-eight hours and another reconnaissance cycle before recommending next steps. No reply has yet been sent to Moscow.

response.title: The Submarine Surfaces
response.immediate: 1600 hours, Cabinet Room. Word arrives via Atlantic Command: B-59 has surfaced, unmolested, west of the quarantine line. No shots fired. McNamara reads the flash traffic aloud — destroyers hold station, harassment ceased, contact holds. The room exhales, briefly. Then the Joint Chiefs' formal memorandum lands on the table: unanimous recommendation for air strikes on the SAM sites, request for launch readiness on the first strike package.
response.worldReaction: Radio Moscow carries nothing on the submarine — the encounter is invisible to the public on both sides. Merchant shipping and NATO capitals register only the continuing quarantine, unchanged in visible posture. Inside the Kremlin, Khrushchev has what Savitsky's report gives him: the Americans did not fire when they could have. He orders the Washington channel kept open and begins drafting public terms — missiles out, in exchange for a non-invasion pledge — while holding Turkey back for something quieter.
response.consequences: RFK reopens with Dobrynin within the hour, testing whether Turkey can stay off the public record. LeMay's memorandum sits unanswered on the table, its authors already assuming delay equals danger. McNamara confirms the immediate naval crisis has eased but flags that Cuban air defenses and the missiles themselves remain fully operational — nothing has been removed, only a collision avoided.
response.detailed: The Cabinet Room fills with the particular quiet of men reading the same cable twice. Anderson's compliance was audible in his transmission — restraint entered into the record over objection, not from agreement. Destroyers at the quarantine line watched B-59 blow her tanks and come up to ventilate after dark; no depth charges, no ramming runs, nothing to make Savitsky's officers reach for the wrong lever. What happened next happened in Moscow, not Washington: a report reaching Khrushchev that the Americans had a chance to force the issue and did not take it. He has answered by keeping his channel open rather than closing it, and by preparing two sets of terms — one for broadcast, one for Dobrynin's ear alone. RFK's session with the ambassador this afternoon tests exactly that seam: whether a non-invasion pledge can be given quickly and publicly while Turkey is negotiated somewhere nobody has to admit to. Meanwhile the JCS memorandum is procedural in form and unmistakable in content — a request for launch authority on OPLAN 312's first package, filed the same afternoon the quarantine held without incident. LeMay's argument is that the submarine incident proves the opposite of what the president takes it to prove: that Soviet forces test American restraint and will keep testing it. Nothing about the missiles themselves has changed. They remain armed, credited operational by McNamara's own assessment, under the SAM umbrella the Chiefs want to strike. The room has bought hours, not resolution.

press.headline: NAVY MAINTAINS CUBA BLOCKADE — NO INCIDENTS REPORTED
press.body: Pentagon sources say the quarantine line remains fully manned with no reported contact incidents in the past twelve hours. No mention is made of any submarine encounter, which remains outside public knowledge.

press.source: TASS wire (internal Kremlin summary, not published)
press.headline: [Internal] Report on Naval Incident Near Quarantine Line
press.body: Submarine command reports vessel surfaced without hostile action from opposing forces. Assessment forwarded to First Secretary's office for use in ongoing exchange with Washington.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: 'The submarine is off the board, Mr. President — for now. But I want to be precise: nothing about the missiles has changed, and the Chiefs' request sits there whether we answer it today or not. Every hour we don't decide is an hour they treat as a decision already made against them.'

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: 'You got lucky with that submarine, and luck isn't a strategy. The Soviets just learned we'll back off when pushed. I want that strike package on the line ready to go at first light, and I want it on the record that the Chiefs asked and were told to wait.'

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: 'Jack, Dobrynin's listening. Khrushchev didn't have to hold his channel open after that submarine business — he could've gone the other way. I think he wants out of this as much as we do. Let me find out what

response.chronicleEntry: 27 October, 1600–2000 hours: Kennedy's order to hold the quarantine and cease harassment reached B-59 in time; the submarine surfaced unmolested after dark. Khrushchev, informed of American restraint, kept the Washington channel open and began drafting dual terms — public non-invasion exchange, private Turkey bargain. RFK reopened contact with Dobrynin. The Joint Chiefs, having complied with the president's restraint order under recorded objection, filed a renewed unanimous demand for air strikes on Cuban SAM sites and requested launch readiness for OPLAN 312's first package. No resolution reached; missiles and Cuban air defenses remain fully operational.

response.title: The Turkish Assurance
response.immediate: 14:20, Cabinet Room. Robert Kennedy reports Dobrynin has carried the private Jupiter assurance to Moscow and returned with Khrushchev's answer: a public offer — Soviet missiles out of Cuba for an American non-invasion pledge — with Turkey left unspoken. The president has not yet answered publicly. LeMay stands near the map table pressing for SAM strike authority. McNamara has verification and pause papers spread before him.
response.worldReaction: Radio Moscow has not yet broadcast the offer's language beyond what Dobrynin conveyed privately; no public Soviet statement has landed on the wires. Allied capitals know nothing of the Turkish understanding. The Joint Chiefs' OPLAN 312 recommendation sits unanswered. Quarantine ships continue signaling the Soviet submarine at the line; no disabling action has been ordered.
response.consequences: A negotiating channel now exists with a concrete framework, but three things remain undecided: how to answer Khrushchev publicly without confirming Turkey, whether to authorize any strike or stand-down, and how the quarantine force is to handle the submarine. LeMay's written objection will exist regardless of what the president decides next. The forty minutes since Dobrynin's report are the only ones spent; Moscow's next move is unknown and unmeasured.
response.detailed:
Robert Kennedy, standing at the end of the table rather than seated, lays out what happened at the Soviet Embassy: he told Dobrynin, without written record, that the Jupiter missiles would come out of Turkey later, off the public record, if the offensive weapons left Cuba. Dobrynin took it to Moscow. What comes back through the same channel is Khrushchev's public offer — non-invasion pledge for withdrawal — with no mention of Turkey attached. Robert Kennedy is careful to say he committed nothing further himself; he wants authority to work out verification and timing, not to have made the deal already.

McNamara pushes his pause and verification memorandum forward on the table: continued quarantine, tighter rules for approaching vessels, a concrete inspection plan before any public acceptance. He wants minutes and encounter procedures fixed before anything is announced.

LeMay does not sit. He calls the Soviet offer a stalling maneuver timed to the SAM buildup and asks again for authorization to hit the missile sites' air defenses before the informal understanding hardens into paralysis. He is drafting his formal objection regardless of what is decided this hour.

The Joint Chiefs' OPLAN 312 memorandum remains on the table, unauthorized. No military action has proceeded beyond standing orders. The submarine at the quarantine line is still being signaled, not forced to the surface, on existing standing orders — no new order for restraint or for disabling measures has yet been given this session.

Nothing further is known of Moscow's internal position or of when, or whether, a Soviet public statement will follow the private channel's report. The next fact will come only from what the president orders now, and from whatever Dobrynin or Radio Moscow produces afterward.

response.chronicleEntry: 27 October 1962, 14:20 EST: Following the RFK-Dobrynin backchannel meeting, Khrushchev authorizes a public offer to withdraw Soviet missiles from Cuba for a US non-invasion pledge, omitting the private Turkish assurance. RFK reports the exchange to the president without further commitment. McNamara presents a pause-and-verification plan; LeMay presses for SAM strike authority and prepares written dissent. OPLAN 312 remains unauthorized. Quarantine forces continue signaling the Soviet submarine under standing orders.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 was shot down over Cuba this morning, killing its pilot — the crisis's first combat death. Quarantine holds; strategic forces remain at peak alert; no hotline exists. At noon the president directed Robert Kennedy to offer Khrushchev, via the Dobrynin backchannel, a private assurance that Jupiter missiles in Turkey would be removed later if Soviet offensive weapons left Cuba, kept off any public record. Dobrynin carried this to Moscow. By early afternoon Khrushchev answered with a public offer — missiles out of Cuba for a US non-invasion pledge — leaving Turkey unmentioned publicly. RFK has committed the US to nothing further and seeks authority to negotiate verification and wording. McNamara wants a verification and pause plan fixed before any public acceptance; LeMay wants strike authority against Cuban air defenses and calls the offer a stalling tactic, preparing formal dissent. The Joint Chiefs' OPLAN 312 sits unauthorized. The quarantine line, including the Soviet submarine encounter, remains under standing signaling orders, unchanged this session. No Soviet public broadcast of the offer's exact terms has yet appeared. The president has not yet answered publicly or issued new military orders.
