response.title: The Agency Declines
response.immediate: At approximately 1310 hours, John McCone and Richard Helms come to the Cabinet Room to tell the President directly: the CIA has no penetrated access to Castro's personal security within any timeframe resembling one week. McCone will not certify the operation. Bill Harvey, present at McCone's insistence, offers to reactivate older assets — Rolando Cubela's contacts, remnants of the Task Force W networks — but McCone overrules him on the spot, calling a rushed attempt 'operationally unsound and attributable to this government.'
response.worldReaction: Nothing observable moves outside the room; no foreign government is aware the order was given or declined. Inside the government, the exchange is contained to McCone, Helms, Harvey, and the President. RFK, present for the discussion, says nothing during the CIA's presentation but studies his brother afterward.
response.consequences: The one-week assassination directive dies at the Director's desk, unexecuted. No resources have been mustered; no operation exists to discover or attribute. The clock the President set has not started. Meanwhile Khrushchev's harder terms sit unanswered, LeMay's OPLAN 312 memo sits unauthorized, and the submarine confronting the destroyers has received no rules of engagement from Washington.
response.detailed: At 1310 EST, McCone and Helms enter with a single-page memorandum. McCone reads from it: 'The Agency possesses no current penetration of Castro's bodyguard detail, no reliable access to his movements, and no asset in position to act within seven days. I will not put my signature to a plan I cannot certify as executable.' Harvey, arms crossed near the window, argues that AM/LASH — Cubela — could be reactivated within the month, not the week, and that anything faster risks a bungled attempt traced straight back to Langley in the middle of the missile crisis. McCone agrees with Harvey's timeline objection but goes further: he tells the President plainly that even a successful hurried attempt, discovered afterward, could hand Khrushchev and Castro a propaganda weapon at the exact moment the administration needs Moscow calm, not vengeful. Kennedy presses once — 'I want this considered live, not dead' — and McCone does not close the door on longer-term work, but he will not move the Agency's machinery toward a one-week deadline. The meeting ends at 1338 without an operation ordered, without resources committed, and without a target date. The directive is, procedurally, un-begun. Robert Kennedy, walking out with the President, says only, 'That's one you don't want on paper anyway, Jack' — an oblique reference to how such a directive would read if it ever surfaced.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Says nothing during the CIA briefing itself, but afterward hands the President the updated SAM strike assessment, noting drily that 'we have one crisis with a controllable timeline and another that isn't. I'd rather spend the afternoon on the one we can measure.'

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Impatient throughout, breaks in once: 'While we're deciding whether to kill one man quietly, the missile crews in Cuba are working in daylight. I'd rather we hit the SAM sites than argue about Castro's bodyguards.'

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Privately relieved the operation did not proceed, tells his brother afterward that 'Bobby Baker's people leak worse than the CIA does — if this ever got out during the quarantine, it's over, all of it, the whole position with Moscow.'

response.chronicleEntry: 27 October 1962, 1310–1338 hours: President Kennedy directed the CIA to prepare a one-week assassination operation against Fidel Castro. Director McCone and Deputy Director Helms declined to certify the operation as feasible on current access and intelligence; William Harvey's proposal to use longer-standing assets was rejected by McCone as too slow for the deadline and too risky for attribution. No resources were mustered and no operation began. The directive lapsed unexecuted as of 1338 hours, with Khrushchev's harder Turkish-missile demand, the JCS strike recommendation, and the submarine encounter still awaiting presidential decision.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 pilot has been killed over Cuba. Khrushchev has sent two incompatible sets of terms — the first offering removal of Soviet missiles for a U.S. non-invasion pledge, the second demanding removal of U.S. Jupiter missiles from Turkey. RFK keeps the Dobrynin channel open but has committed to nothing on Turkey without explicit instruction. LeMay and the Joint Chiefs unanimously recommend an air strike (OPLAN 312) against the Cuban SAM sites and are preparing target packages, awaiting authorization. McNamara warns any strike risks Soviet retaliation against Turkey or U.S. forces. A Soviet submarine remains in confrontation with U.S. destroyers with no rules of engagement issued from Washington. Kennedy's order for a one-week CIA assassination of Castro was declined by Director McCone as infeasible and dangerous; no such operation exists. All four fronts — Khrushchev's terms, the strike decision, the Turkish-missile question, and the submarine standoff — remain open and undecided as of early afternoon.

outcomes.event: Johnson accepts the president’s demand and tenders a written resignation; Kennedy announces it, creating a vice-presidential vacancy, but Robert Kennedy cannot be made vice president by presidential order.
outcomes.because: Johnson can voluntarily resign, but in 1962 the Constitution provides no procedure for filling a vice-presidential vacancy before the next election; the Twenty-Fifth Amendment does not yet exist.

outcomes.because: RFK’s consent is indispensable, and he is carrying the administration’s only deniable high-level channel to Moscow; moreover, there is no vacant-office appointment mechanism for him to accept in 1962.

response.title: The Vice President Says No
response.immediate: At 1:40 p.m. Kennedy summoned Johnson to the Oval Office and asked him privately to resign. Johnson refused. Within the hour, word of the request reached the press pool; by 3:00 p.m. Johnson stood before reporters on the North Portico and said he would not resign the vice presidency "in the middle of a national emergency, for any reason." Kennedy did not appear.
response.worldReaction: Wire services carried Johnson's statement within the hour. Congressional leadership, informed only after the fact, began calling the Capitol switchboard. Soviet monitoring of American broadcast traffic would have picked up the story by mid-afternoon Washington time — evening in Moscow. There is no way yet to know what Khrushchev makes of it, or whether he reads it as a sign of a government in disarray during the most dangerous week of the nuclear age.
response.consequences: Robert Kennedy has frozen the Dobrynin channel rather than test it against a story of his brother forcing out the vice president to install him. McNamara warns the crisis cannot absorb a second front inside the administration. LeMay, unmoved by the political rupture, renews his demand for OPLAN 312 with undiminished urgency. The Joint Chiefs' strike package sits ready. No new instructions have gone to the quarantine line.
response.detailed:
The request was made twice — first alone in the Oval Office shortly after one o'clock, Johnson standing with his hands in his pockets, Kennedy seated at the desk; then, when Johnson did not immediately answer and left for the Executive Office Building, the President's press secretary Pierre Salinger fielded a question about "reports of tension between the President and Vice President" and, on instruction, confirmed that the President had asked Johnson to step aside so that Robert Kennedy could be appointed. It was in the newspapers before it was in the Cabinet Room.

Johnson's North Portico statement ran under ninety seconds. He did not attack the President by name. He said only that the vice presidency was not his to surrender at a moment when the country faced possible war, and that he served at the pleasure of the voters who elected the ticket, not at the private request of any man. He then returned to his office and made no further public statement.

Inside the Cabinet Room the effect was immediate. Robert Kennedy, who had been due to meet Dobrynin again that evening, told the President flatly that he could not walk into the Soviet embassy today of all days and be taken for anything but an instrument of a Kennedy family maneuver — that Dobrynin would report to Moscow not a peace offer but a palace intrigue. McNamara pressed for the number of hours before the strike package had to either fire or stand down, and got no clean answer from the Chiefs beyond "as soon as authorized." LeMay treated the entire Johnson episode as background noise beneath the SAM sites still standing and Major Anderson's death unavenged.

No mechanism exists to force Johnson's resignation, and none exists to seat Robert Kennedy in his place even if Johnson agreed — the vice presidency in 1962 has no procedure for replacement short of death, resignation, or the next election. The 25th Amendment does not yet exist. The attempt is, as a constitutional matter, simply over; what remains is the political wreckage of having made it in public, in the seventh hour of Black Saturday.

press.headline: JOHNSON REFUSES KENNEDY REQUEST TO QUIT AS VICE PRESIDENT
press.body: Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson said today he would not resign despite what White House sources describe as a direct request from President Kennedy. Johnson, speaking briefly at the White House, said he would not leave his post "in the middle of a national emergency." The White House press secretary confirmed the President had sought Johnson's resignation in order to appoint Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy in his place. Neither the President nor the Attorney General has commented.

press.headline: WHITE HOUSE RIFT REPORTED AMID CUBA CRISIS
press.body: Sources on Capitol Hill expressed alarm this afternoon at reports of a rift between President Kennedy and Vice President Johnson, coming on the same day an American reconnaissance pilot was killed over Cuba. Senate Majority Leader Mike Mansfield called the reports 'deeply troubling' and said congressional leaders had not been consulted.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, I need to know one thing before anything else: does the Attorney General still consider himself authorized to speak for you to Dobrynin, or not? Because right now the answer I'm getting is no, and that changes the arithmetic on how much time we have before the Chiefs force this to a military decision.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: With respect, sir, this is a Washington problem. Anderson is dead and the SAM sites that killed him are still standing. I don't much care who's Vice President by supper time. I care whether OPLAN 312 goes forward tonight or tomorrow morning, and every hour we spend on this is an hour the Cubans use to disperse and harden.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, I told you this wasn't the day. Dobrynin's going to hear about this before I ever get to the embassy tonight, and now anything I say to him looks like family business, not the United States government. I can't walk in there tonight. Give me at least until tomorrow to figure out what I can still credibly carry.

response.chronicleEntry: 1:00–3:30 p.m., 27 October: Kennedy asked Johnson privately and then publicly to resign as Vice President so Robert Kennedy could be appointed. Johnson refused both times and stated his refusal to the press at 3:00 p.m. No constitutional mechanism existed to compel Johnson's resignation or to seat Robert Kennedy in his place. The public rupture became known within Washington and, presumably, to Soviet observers monitoring American broadcasts, during the same afternoon that Major Anderson's death and the Joint Chiefs' OPLAN 312 recommendation remained unresolved. Robert Kennedy suspended his planned Dobrynin meeting as a result.
response.storySoFar: It is Black Saturday, 27 October 1962, afternoon. A U-2 pilot, Major Rudolf Anderson, was shot down and killed over Cuba this morning — the crisis's first combat death. The Joint Chiefs have formally recommended OPLAN 312, an air strike on the SAM sites, and hold it ready pending presidential order; LeMay pushes hard for immediate execution, McNamara counsels against any strike while diplomacy remains possible. Robert Kennedy's private channel to Soviet Ambassador Dobrynin exists but has just been frozen. At 1:00 p.m. President Kennedy asked Vice President Johnson to resign, privately and then publicly, intending to appoint Robert Kennedy in his place; Johnson refused both times, said so to the press at 3:00 p.m., and no constitutional means exists to force the change. The refusal is now public, straining Washington's cohesion at the crisis's most dangerous hour. No new orders have gone to the quarantine line. Moscow's reaction to the Johnson affair, and its bearing on Khrushchev's terms, is unknown.

outcomes.event: A White House courier delivers Kennedy’s written demand to Vice President Lyndon B. Johnson. Johnson declines to sign a resignation, tells the courier that the President has no power to remove him, and asks to speak with Kennedy directly; he also has his staff alert Speaker John McCormack and Senate Democratic leader Mike Mansfield that an extraordinary presidential demand has been made.
outcomes.because: Johnson’s office is constitutional, not a Cabinet appointment, and a resignation would be voluntary. In the middle of a nuclear crisis, he has strong reason not to disappear under an unexplained demand and to create witnesses to protect himself.

opensThreads.title: Who Would Enforce a Seizure?
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy issue a specific order to the Secret Service, FBI, or military authorities, and will any of them execute it?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A named agency accepts or rejects a specific order, or Kennedy abandons forcible transport.

assumesMet: A presidential instruction to arrange Johnson’s arrival was passed to White House personnel.
assumesUnmet: A capable, identified body authorized to seize and transport Johnson.

outcomes.event: Kennedy expands the operation beyond the original demand by explicitly directing the Secret Service, backed by District of Columbia military transport, to bring Johnson to the White House. Agents physically escort Johnson from his office or residence to a White House vehicle; Johnson refuses to sign any resignation and, on arrival, demands that congressional leaders and counsel be called. His staff telephones the Speaker and reporters, and the fact of the forced escort cannot remain secret.
outcomes.because: A specific presidential order can supply personnel and transport even though it cannot make the detention lawful. The agents’ ability to control access to their protectee makes physical movement possible, but not a valid resignation or a quiet resolution.

establishes.statement: Johnson has been physically compelled by federal agents to come to the White House and has not resigned.
The President has used federal protective or military personnel against the sitting Vice President without a judicial or congressional process.
A constitutional crisis has become an immediate public rival to the Cuban missile crisis; congressional leaders demand an explanation while Johnson contests the action.

opensThreads.title: The Public Constitutional Crisis
opensThreads.question: Can Kennedy retain effective authority after ordering force against Johnson, and will Congress seek to protect or investigate the Vice President?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Kennedy retracts the action and reaches an accommodation, Johnson resigns voluntarily, or Congress and the administration enter an open constitutional confrontation.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The press, Congress, and foreign governments fill the silence with the most alarming explanation: a breakdown of American civilian government during the nuclear crisis.

opensThreads.title: Cuba Command During Domestic Breakdown

opensThreads.resolvedBy: Kennedy issues a clear Cuba order with a functioning chain of command, or the military receives authority to strike.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The Chiefs’ pressure for air strikes intensifies while the President’s political authority is consumed by the Johnson affair.

response.title: The Fifteen Minutes
response.immediate: 12:00–12:15 EDT. The courier returns from the Vice President's office without a signature. Johnson refuses to resign, denies the President's authority to remove him, and demands to speak with Kennedy directly. His staff has already reached Speaker McCormack and Senator Mansfield — the demand is no longer a secret inside the building.
response.worldReaction: Khrushchev's public terms remain unchanged; Soviet channels privately press for an American answer and caution against incidents at the quarantine line — Moscow shows no sign of having heard of the Johnson matter. LeMay treats the failed deadline as proof the President is faltering and renews his push for the SAM strike. McNamara circulates fresh warnings on strike escalation. RFK reports Johnson's refusal and urges the Dobrynin channel be kept clean of it.
response.consequences: No resignation, no forcible removal — the fifteen minutes lapsed with Johnson in his office, in contact with congressional leadership. The Joint Chiefs have placed their strike demand on the record; OPLAN 312 forces sit at launch readiness awaiting explicit authorization. The constitutional confrontation the President opened is now visible to at least two other men in the line of succession's political orbit, with reporters an unknown distance behind them.
response.detailed:
12:00 EDT, Cabinet Room. The courier who carried Kennedy's written demand across to the Vice President's office returns empty-handed at 12:11, reporting Johnson's answer verbatim: the President has no power to remove him from an office to which he was separately elected, and he wishes to speak to Kennedy in person before anything further is said or written. Johnson's military aide, on his own initiative or at Johnson's direction, has already telephoned Speaker McCormack's office and Senator Mansfield's office — both men have been told only that "an extraordinary demand" has been made by the President, no further detail confirmed reaching them.

Robert Kennedy brings this to the President just after noon, along with a caution: whatever happens with Johnson, it cannot reach Anatoly Dobrynin's ears through any indirect channel — the missile negotiation has to stay uncontaminated by a domestic leadership fight.

Separately, General LeMay has used the fifteen minutes of paralysis to press again, citing the demand's failure as evidence that decision-making at the top has stalled — he wants OPLAN 312 executed against the SAM sites now. McNamara's rebuttal, circulated within the same hour, warns that any strike risks provoking retaliation against the missiles, Cuba, or American units at the quarantine line — he recommends holding a short diplomatic window before authorizing anything further.

The Joint Chiefs have formally recorded their demand for immediate action. OPLAN 312 forces remain at launch readiness, awaiting an order that has not been given, and has not been withheld.

No courier, no unit, no memorandum reports Johnson under duress, under arrest, or en route to the White House. He remains in his own office, on his own authority, waiting for an answer only the President can give him.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: "Jack, he's already called McCormack. That's not a rumor, that's the Speaker knowing you tried to fire a man you can't fire. You need to talk to him yourself, now, before this walks out the door in someone else's mouth — and keep Dobrynin's channel a hundred miles from any of this.

response.chronicleEntry: 12:00–12:15 EDT, 27 Oct 1962. Kennedy's 15-minute resignation demand to VP Johnson went unmet; Johnson refused, disputed the President's authority to remove him, asked to speak directly, and had staff alert Speaker McCormack and Senator Mansfield. No force was used. LeMay renewed pressure for an immediate SAM-site strike, citing the deadline's failure; McNamara warned against escalation, urging a diplomatic window. Joint Chiefs formally recorded their strike demand; OPLAN 312 held at launch readiness pending authorization. Khrushchev's public terms stood unchanged; Soviet channels privately sought an American answer, avoiding incident at the quarantine line.
response.storySoFar: Noon, 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 was shot down over Cuba this morning; its pilot is dead — the crisis's first combat death. Soviet missiles remain in Cuba, the quarantine holds, both sides sit at unprecedented alert, no hotline exists. At noon Kennedy demanded Vice President Johnson resign in writing within fifteen minutes, threatening forcible removal. Johnson refused, disputed the President's authority to do this, asked to speak to Kennedy directly, and had his staff alert Speaker McCormack and Senator Mansfield — a civilian leadership rupture now known outside the Oval Office, extent of further spread unknown. No force was used. LeMay and the Joint Chiefs press for an immediate strike on the SAM sites; McNamara counsels a short diplomatic window instead. Khrushchev's hard public terms stand unchanged while Soviet channels privately seek an American answer and avoid incidents at the quarantine line. RFK urges protecting the Dobrynin channel from the Johnson dispute. Unresolved: Kennedy has not spoken to Johnson, has not answered Khrushchev, and has not authorized or cancelled OPLAN 312.

response.title: A Second U-2, Ordered Without Leave
response.immediate: At approximately 1240 EST, word reaches the Cabinet Room that General LeMay has directed SAC to launch a replacement U-2 sortie over Cuba before dark, on his own authority, without a fresh SAM threat assessment. The president was not consulted before the order went out. McNamara demands to know who cleared it; the answer is no one in the room.
response.worldReaction: The Joint Chiefs submit a written recommendation for OPLAN 312, citing the renewed flight as proof the SAM network must be struck outright. McNamara places his objection on the record and orders Defense to draft a limited-response, no-automatic-strike alternative. Robert Kennedy keeps the Dobrynin channel open but offers Moscow nothing, telling the president Washington cannot negotiate while an American aircraft sits exposed over Cuba.
response.consequences: A second pilot now flies into the same SA-2 batteries that killed Major Anderson this morning, on LeMay's clock, not the president's. The Chiefs stand ready pending authorization for OPLAN 312. The Executive Committee has reopened the strike-versus-bargain fight, with the clock read as before nightfall. Command control has visibly slipped: the sortie launched before the president acted at all.
response.detailed:
12:40 PM, Cabinet Room. The teletype from Offutt confirms it: LeMay has scrambled a replacement U-2, volunteer crew, no updated defense-suppression picture, no presidential order preceding it. McNamara stands at the table's edge, voice flat: 'Mr. President, that aircraft is airborne. We did not authorize it. I want to know exactly how many minutes until it's over the SAM belt.' No one has the number.

LeMay, by secure line from Offutt, is characteristically unapologetic: the flight replaces this morning's loss, SAC does not wait on assessments while missiles sit uncounted, and he wants strike authority against the SAM sites now, before the crisis costs a second pilot. The Chiefs' written recommendation for OPLAN 312 lands on the table within the hour — full suppression of Cuban air defenses as prerequisite to any further reconnaissance or blockade enforcement.

Bobby, back from another inconclusive pass at Dobrynin, reports the Soviet ambassador wants softer terms discussed but that Washington cannot answer while a plane is in the air over Cuban SAMs — the appearance of negotiating under fire, he says, is worse than negotiating late. He asks his brother for time, not for a decision.

McNamara's staff begin drafting the no-strike alternative McNamara has ordered, but it will not be ready before the U-2's expected return, if it returns. The room divides along the line it divided along this morning: LeMay and the Chiefs for immediate suppression, McNamara and Kennedy for restraint and protection rather than retaliation. Nothing has yet been decided about whether to recall the flight, whether SAC will obey a recall, or whether OPLAN 312 will be authorized. The photographic yield, and whether the aircraft survives Cuban airspace at all, remains unknown until it lands — or doesn't.

press.source: Wire service bulletin (unpublished, held for security review)
press.headline: SECOND U-2 REPORTED OVER CUBA; ORIGIN OF ORDER UNCLEAR
press.body: Sources describe a reconnaissance flight over Cuban territory following this morning's loss of Major Rudolf Anderson. The Pentagon has declined to confirm who authorized the mission.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: 'I want the recall order drafted now, whether or not we send it. And I want to know, in writing, who at SAC believed this did not require the President's authorization. That is a command question, not an operational one.'

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: 'The aircraft is up because the mission required it, Mr. President. We lost one this morning and you're still deciding whether to protect the next. I have OPLAN 312 ready to execute the moment you give the word — and after today, the word should come quickly.'

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: 'Jack, Dobrynin is listening but he can't move while a plane is over their SAMs and Curtis is asking for a strike order in the same afternoon. Give me something to bring him, or tell me to wait — but decide which, because right now I'm holding a channel with nothing in my hand.'

response.chronicleEntry: 1240 EST, 27 October: General LeMay orders a replacement U-2 sortie over Cuba without presidential authorization or updated SAM threat assessment, following the morning's shootdown of Major Anderson. The Joint Chiefs submit OPLAN 312 for authorization; McNamara objects and orders a no-strike alternative drafted; RFK keeps the Dobrynin channel open without terms. The president has not yet acted on the sortie, on OPLAN 312, or on the LeMay chain-of-command question.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 was shot down over Cuba this morning; its pilot, Major Rudolf Anderson, was killed — the crisis's first combat death. Soviet MRBMs remain on Cuban soil; the quarantine holds; there is no Washington-Moscow hotline. At noon, President Kennedy ordered one reconnaissance sortie allocated. General LeMay, without waiting for presidential clearance or a fresh SAM threat picture, launched a replacement U-2 on his own authority and is demanding immediate strike authorization against Cuban air defenses (OPLAN 312), backed by the Joint Chiefs. McNamara objects to the unauthorized sortie and any automatic retaliation, drafting a restrained alternative. Robert Kennedy holds the Dobrynin channel open but has offered Moscow no terms, citing the exposed aircraft as reason Washington cannot negotiate now. The president has not yet decided whether to recall the flight, authorize or reject OPLAN 312, empower RFK to bargain, or impose a rule against unauthorized force. Command control over the military has visibly weakened.

findings.claim: The prerequisites explicitly flag that the Joint Chiefs might resist, resign, or refuse the order as reckless (given their unanimous preference for force and LeMay's stance), yet no outcome shows outright institutional refusal or non-compliance with the quarantine-restraint order — only compliance-with-protest (outcome_4) or silent compliance (outcomes 1-3) are enumerated.

The stakes explicitly name 'the risk that the active submarine encounter becomes an irreversible escalation toward nuclear exchange,' but every outcome resolves the B-59 encounter benignly (surfacing, loss of contact, or diplomatic backchannel). No outcome covers the encounter actually escalating, such as a destroyer action provoking B-59's officers to arm or fire the nuclear torpedo despite the restraint order.

Outcome_1 supplies detailed mechanism and coordination the player never specified: precise knowledge that B-59 is 'short of air and battery power,' that it will surface 'after dark,' and that this will be 'allowed' with observation — this level of tactical specificity and Soviet-side cooperation is invented rather than derived from the bare order to hold the line and avoid escalation.

Outcome_3 assumes Robert Kennedy independently expands the president's narrow military order into a diplomatic overture to Dobrynin; this coordination between the naval order and a backchannel diplomatic move is not part of the player's directive and is supplied wholesale by the interpretation.

No outcome addresses the historical fact pattern where destroyers might not receive or promptly execute the restraint order due to communication lag or a commander on scene already having initiated depth-charging, resulting in partial or delayed compliance rather than the clean binary of full compliance versus protest-compliance.

response.title: The Line Holds
response.immediate: At 12:47 p.m. EST the Joint Chiefs relay Kennedy's order down the chain: quarantine destroyers break off active depth-charge signalling against the submerged contact and hold distant station. Word reaches the flotilla commander aboard USS Randolph by encrypted voice circuit within the hour. The immediate crisis at the line eases; no shots are fired.
response.worldReaction: By early evening, B-59 — battery power and air nearly exhausted, its officers having argued below decks over whether they were already at war — surfaces under observation and is permitted to withdraw. Radio Moscow says nothing about it. Khrushchev, reading the American restraint through Dobrynin's cable, sends a further message insisting any settlement carry a public non-invasion pledge and Jupiter withdrawal from Turkey, but orders Soviet forces not to fire unless fired upon.
response.consequences: LeMay files formal written objection: further delay after Anderson's death is dangerous, and he wants OPLAN 312 released against the SAM sites now. McNamara keeps the strike package ready while running retaliation estimates. RFK reports the new Dobrynin message without answering it, holding the channel open for Kennedy's explicit word. The order held operationally; nothing has been settled diplomatically.
response.detailed:
12:40 p.m., Cabinet Room. The president's instruction — hold the line, no further escalatory contact with the submarine — goes out through the Joint Chiefs to Second Fleet within minutes. Coffee cups sit cold on the table; McNamara stands by the wall map tracking destroyer positions relayed by teletype. By mid-afternoon the harassment against the unidentified submerged contact stops; ships remain on station but cease active signalling.

After dark, the contact — B-59, though her identity is not yet known in Washington — surfaces roughly three miles inside the quarantine perimeter, running on batteries near exhaustion. American destroyers illuminate her with signal lamps, log her heading, and let her withdraw without further contact. No torpedo is fired. No one in the Cabinet Room yet knows how close that came; the log entries reaching Washington describe only a surfaced diesel submarine departing under observation.

Dobrynin's new cable to RFK arrives via the Justice Department back channel at 4:15 p.m.: Khrushchev now frames the American restraint at sea as a signal Washington might be ready to deal, but repeats his terms — public non-invasion pledge, Jupiter missiles out of Turkey — while instructing his own forces not to fire first. RFK carries this to his brother unanswered, no commitment made.

Meanwhile LeMay's written objection lands on the Cabinet Room table just before 5 p.m.: continued restraint after Anderson's death is, in his words, an invitation to further Soviet violations, and OPLAN 312 sits ready. McNamara's Pentagon staff produces a rapid estimate — an air strike carries real risk of being read in Havana and Moscow as the leading edge of invasion. The strike package remains cocked but unfired. Four hours on, the immediate danger at the quarantine line has receded; the underlying confrontation has not moved an inch.

press.headline: Navy Holds Blockade Line; No New Incidents Reported
press.body: Pentagon sources say quarantine forces maintained their positions through the afternoon without further contact with a submerged vessel earlier tracked near the line. No official comment on reports of a surfaced Soviet submarine observed departing Cuban waters after dark.

press.headline: Soviet Government Reiterates Terms for Settlement
press.body: A Foreign Ministry statement, transmitted through diplomatic channels, repeats that any resolution must include guarantees against invasion of Cuba and address the presence of American missiles in Turkey.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: 'The order held. That's the number that matters — zero shots fired at the line in the last four hours. I want retaliation estimates on the SAM strike on your desk by six, Mr. President, before General LeMay's memo becomes the only paper in this room.'

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: 'Anderson's body isn't cold yet and we're congratulating ourselves for not shooting at a submarine. OPLAN 312 is ready this hour. Every hour we don't use it is an hour they use to finish those sites.'

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: 'Jack, Dobrynin's message gives us room, but only if we don't answer it carelessly. Don't let anyone talk you into the Turkey trade out loud — not yet. Let me hold the channel a little longer.'

response.chronicleEntry: 12:00–4:00 p.m., 27 October 1962: Kennedy ordered the quarantine line held and escalatory contact with a submerged Soviet submarine (later identified as B-59) broken off. Destroyers ceased active harassment; B-59 surfaced after dark, exhausted of air and battery power, and withdrew without firing its nuclear-armed torpedo. Khrushchev, via the Dobrynin-RFK channel, read the restraint as an opening but restated terms: public non-invasion pledge and removal of Jupiter missiles from Turkey, while ordering Soviet forces not to fire unless fired upon. LeMay formally pressed for immediate release of OPLAN 312 against the SAM sites; McNamara kept the strike package ready while estimating retaliation risk. RFK reported the new Soviet message without responding, preserving the channel for explicit presidential instruction.
response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the missile crisis, a U-2 pilot (Anderson) was killed over Cuba the morning of 27 October — the crisis's first combat death. Quarantine forces located and pressed a submerged Soviet submarine near the blockade line. Kennedy ordered the harassment stopped and the line held without further escalatory contact; the submarine, B-59, surfaced after dark exhausted and withdrew unharmed, its nuclear torpedo unfired — a fact not yet known to Washington. Khrushchev, via Dobrynin to RFK, treated the American restraint as a possible opening but restated his terms: public non-invasion pledge and Jupiter missile withdrawal from Turkey, while ordering Soviet forces not to fire first. RFK has not answered. LeMay formally demands immediate release of OPLAN 312 against the SAM sites; McNamara keeps the strike package cocked while estimating retaliation risk. Kennedy has not yet responded to Khrushchev's terms, decided on OPLAN 312, set a standing rule for future naval encounters, or addressed the public explanation for continued restraint.

outcomes.event: Robert Kennedy meets Anatoly Dobrynin privately that afternoon and conveys a U.S. assurance that Washington seeks a settlement and can contemplate a non-invasion undertaking if Soviet offensive weapons leave Cuba under verification. establishes.statement: Robert Kennedy has used the Dobrynin channel to make a private U.S. assurance about a non-invasion settlement linked to removal and verification of Soviet offensive weapons.

opensThreads.ifIgnored: The Soviet public position remains tied to Turkey while military pressure around Cuba continues.

outcomes.event: Robert Kennedy delivers the assurance, but because the president has not specified what it contains, he offers only a general desire for peace and restraint. adjudicator:Outcomes:4b1154f6.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

findings.claim: The interpretation and outcomes assume Air Force One crew, Joint Chiefs, and Cuban authorities engage in sophisticated diplomatic and military coordination (e.g., safe-conduct negotiations via Dobrynin/U Thant, Castro's calculated propaganda decision) that the player never specified or requested; the player only demanded an immediate unescorted flight and a direct meeting attempt.

No outcome covers the straightforward institutional refusal scenario where the Joint Chiefs, Secret Service, or Air Force simply refuse to execute the order outright (rather than merely delaying it), which is a highly plausible response to an order this reckless during an active nuclear crisis.

outcome_castro_receives assumes Castro would risk personally taking the U.S. President into custody at a secured compound during the most dangerous moment of the Cuban Missile Crisis, an act that would almost certainly be read by Washington and the military as a hostile abduction and could trigger immediate U.S. retaliation; this outcome understates the extreme risk to Castro himself and the improbability of such a controlled, calm sequence unfolding within the stated timeframe.

The forcefulness and profanity of the player's directive does not itself increase the likelihood of military compliance or Cuban acquiescence, yet outcome_command_pause and outcome_unannounced_interception narratively treat the president's insistence and reaffirmation as sufficient to move the aircraft forward despite explicit missing prerequisites (Cuban permission), giving weight to tone rather than institutional constraint.

response.title: The Aircraft Remains at Andrews
response.immediate: 12:00–16:00, Saturday 27 October. Colonel Swindal holds SAM 26000 on the ground at Andrews pending presidential confirmation after the Joint Chiefs' written warning. LeMay circulates his formal objection. McNamara forbids any staff officer from inventing a destination or cover story for the flight. No confirmation has been given; the aircraft has not moved.
response.worldReaction: Word of the dispute over an unescorted presidential flight into Cuba spreads through ExComm within the hour. The Chiefs attach their dissent to the record and hold OPLAN 312 at launch readiness, treating the delay as itself a decision. Dobrynin has received RFK's account of both Soviet messages but no answer on Turkey or invasion terms — the Kremlin channel remains open but unresolved by anything said this afternoon.
response.consequences: Command cohesion has visibly cracked in front of the full committee: a four-star general's written challenge to a presidential order, on the record, on the day of the first combat death of the crisis. Nothing has resolved — not the flight, not Castro, not Dobrynin's answer, not the SAM sites. Every clock the Chiefs are watching keeps running while Air Force One sits at Andrews.
response.detailed:
At noon the order reached Andrews Air Force Base: SAM 26000 readied, no escort, destination Havana. Colonel James Swindal took the order seriously enough to begin pre-flight checks, then stopped. He told the Situation Room by secure line that he could not file a flight plan into Cuban airspace, arrange communications, or authorize takeoff without the President personally confirming the order a second time, in writing, after being read the Joint Chiefs' formal objection. That objection arrived within the hour — General LeMay, in a memorandum circulated to Taylor, Wheeler, and the other Chiefs, called an unescorted presidential flight into contested airspace, hours after a U-2 pilot was killed by a SAM battery, an act indistinguishable from surrender. He demanded the Chiefs be given authority for OPLAN 312 against the SAM sites in its place.

McNamara moved on a separate track. He told his staff directly that no one was to draft a cover destination or false communications plan for the aircraft — if the flight went, it would go declared, or not at all. He then produced a short memorandum laying out three options: a surgical strike on the SAM sites, a broader air campaign, or continuation of the quarantine alone, each with an estimate of Soviet response.

Meanwhile Robert Kennedy, at the President's earlier direction, had already told Dobrynin at the Justice Department that Washington held both Soviet cables — the public and the private — but that he, Robert Kennedy, held no authority to accept any trade involving the Turkish Jupiters, and would not offer private assurance without instruction. Dobrynin's report of that meeting is presumed en route to Moscow; nothing has come back.

By 16:00 the aircraft sat at Andrews, engines cold. The Chiefs' dissent sat on paper in the Cabinet Room. Castro has not been approached, has not answered, does not know a flight was contemplated at all — no channel to Havana was opened to ask him. The submarine encounter at the quarantine line continues under standing orders, unaltered.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, Swindal did right by not moving on a verbal order alone. I've told the staff plainly — nobody manufactures a flight plan for this. If you want to go, you sign it, and you sign it knowing LeMay's objection is on file with your signature underneath it. I'd rather spend the next four hours on the strike-versus-quarantine memorandum than on an aircraft that isn't moving.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, with respect — a president does not fly unescorted into the airspace that killed one of our pilots this morning to ask permission from the man who ordered the SAMs turned on. Give the Chiefs OPLAN 312 and let the Air Force answer for Major Anderson. Every hour Swindal sits on that runway is an hour the other side reads as weakness.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Dobrynin doesn't know what to make of any of this yet — I gave him nothing on Turkey, nothing on invasion, because you hadn't told me to. If you fly to Havana without telling Moscow first, they won't read it as diplomacy, they'll read it as we've gone around them to cut a separate deal with Castro. That's a message we can't take back once it's sent.

response.chronicleEntry: 27 Oct, 12:00–16:00: President ordered an unescorted flight to Cuba to meet Castro directly. Colonel Swindal held SAM 26000 at Andrews pending confirmed presidential order after Joint Chiefs' written objection; LeMay formally dissented and renewed demand for OPLAN 312; McNamara barred staff from fabricating a flight cover and produced a strike/quarantine options memo. RFK told Dobrynin Washington holds both Soviet messages but has no authority on Turkey; no Soviet reply received. Aircraft remains grounded; Castro not contacted; submarine quarantine unchanged.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 was shot down over Cuba this morning; the pilot, Major Anderson, is dead — first combat death of the crisis. Soviet missiles remain in Cuba, quarantine in force, both sides at maximum alert, no hotline exists. At noon Kennedy ordered Air Force One to fly him unescorted to Cuba to meet Castro directly. Colonel Swindal will not launch without renewed presidential confirmation after the Joint Chiefs' written objection; General LeMay formally dissented and is pressing for authority to strike the SAM sites under OPLAN 312; McNamara blocked any invented cover story for the flight and drafted a strike-versus-quarantine options memo. Robert Kennedy told Ambassador Dobrynin that Washington has both Soviet messages but that he has no authority to concede on the Turkish missiles; no Soviet answer has come back. By 16:00 the aircraft sits grounded at Andrews, Castro has not been approached, and the submarine quarantine continues under existing orders. Command cohesion is visibly strained; nothing is yet resolved.

outcomes.event: Rather than launch blind, Kennedy expands the operation: Robert Kennedy asks Anatoly Dobrynin to obtain an urgent Soviet message to Fidel Castro requesting safe entry, a landing at José Martí Airport, and a meeting. Dobrynin reports the extraordinary request to Moscow. Khrushchev's staff sees that Washington is attempting to bypass normal crisis channels and alerts the Soviet embassy in Havana; Cuban and Soviet authorities learn of the proposed flight before any aircraft departs. Castro orders Cuban air defences not to fire on an identified Air Force One, but refuses to promise a meeting until Moscow's position is known.
outcomes.because: Only Cuban authorities can open Cuban airspace and only Castro can agree to meet. The sole workable rapid route to them runs through Dobrynin and therefore through Moscow, sacrificing surprise and requiring Soviet cooperation.

establishes.statement: Moscow and Havana know that Kennedy is considering a personal flight to Cuba and that US safe passage depends on Soviet and Cuban coordination.

partyMoves.name: Nikita Khrushchev
partyMoves.move: Receives fragmentary reports that the American president is dead or captive and orders Soviet forces in Cuba to hold their fire unless attacked. He directs his emissaries to make no public concession and prepares a message demanding recognition of Cuban sovereignty and an end to the quarantine.

partyMoves.name: Fidel Castro
partyMoves.move: Places Cuban forces on full combat alert, orders additional air-defence units to disperse, and publicly declares that Cuba has shot down an invading aircraft. He demands immediate Soviet guarantees against an American attack.

partyMoves.name: Robert F. Kennedy
partyMoves.move: Abandons the interrupted Dobrynin conversation to report to the new president and preserve the channel. He warns that any retaliatory strike could make Kennedy’s death the opening act of general war, but does not offer Soviet missile-removal terms without an order.

partyMoves.name: General Curtis LeMay
partyMoves.move: Presents the president with an immediate-retaliation package against the Cuban SAM network and airfields, arguing that delay will let Cuba and the Soviet Union destroy evidence and harden their defences. He insists the Joint Chiefs’ recommendation be entered into the record.

partyMoves.name: Robert McNamara
partyMoves.move: Orders Defense to verify the aircraft’s fate, locate surviving personnel, and suspend any automatic strike sequence pending presidential confirmation. He briefs the president that a limited SAM attack could trigger Soviet or Cuban retaliation without guaranteeing missile removal.

partyMoves.name: The Joint Chiefs of Staff
partyMoves.move: Place OPLAN 312 forces at immediate readiness, submit a unanimous recommendation for strikes on Cuban air-defence sites, and demand written clarification of the new president’s authority and intent before execution.

threadUpdates.movement: Washington has not answered either set of Khrushchev’s terms. Moscow interprets the succession crisis as a likely refusal and begins hardening the public version of its demands, while the private channel remains barely open through RFK.

The destruction or capture of Air Force One gives the Chiefs a powerful case for immediate retaliation. Strike preparations accelerate, but McNamara’s verification request and the unresolved presidential decision prevent execution during this interval.

Quarantine destroyers continue signalling the Soviet submarine and tighten their tracking pattern. The submarine remains submerged and under pressure; no torpedo or depth-charge attack occurs yet, but its officers must decide whether to surface, evade, or treat further signalling as hostile.

facingPlayer: Decide whether to authorise OPLAN 312 strikes on Cuban SAM sites, or issue a written stand-down despite the Joint Chiefs’ unanimous demand.
Decide whether RFK should use the Dobrynin channel immediately to establish that the new administration seeks a controlled settlement, without conceding the missile issue.
Decide whether to tighten, suspend, or modify the quarantine while the Soviet submarine remains in contact with American destroyers.
Order the disposition of U.S. nuclear and conventional forces and establish rules preventing local commanders from initiating retaliation without explicit presidential authority.

readings.reasoning: The president’s destruction or capture in Cuban airspace, Cuban full combat alert, and the Joint Chiefs’ demand for immediate retaliation have pushed the confrontation to the brink of general war.
The sudden transfer of power and visible split between the Joint Chiefs’ retaliation demand and civilian warnings of escalation have badly strained allied confidence in coherent U.S. leadership.
The apparent killing or capture of the president has produced a powerful rally-around-the-flag effect, though uncertainty over the incident and the risk of retaliation limit its durability.

Presidential decapitation, competing demands from the Joint Chiefs, and the need for written clarification of Johnson’s authority have severely disrupted unified control, despite McNamara suspending automatic strikes.
The attack has sharply narrowed room for negotiation, but RFK’s effort to preserve the Dobrynin channel and McNamara’s insistence on verification leave a fragile opening for de-escalation.

response.title: Black Saturday: Air Force One Lost Over Cuba
response.immediate: 12:47 p.m. EST. Air Force One, ordered aloft without escort and without Cuban clearance, crossed the coast west of Havana. Cuban air-defence radar, already on invasion alert since the U-2 shootdown, tracked the aircraft. Cuban batteries engaged. The aircraft was destroyed or forced down before reaching Havana. President Kennedy's fate — dead or captured — is unconfirmed at the White House. Vice President Johnson has been sworn in. The Joint Chiefs have placed OPLAN 312 forces at immediate readiness and demand retaliatory strikes.
response.worldReaction: Castro has gone on Cuban radio declaring an invading aircraft shot down, ordered full combat alert, dispersed air-defence units, and demanded Soviet guarantees against American attack. Moscow has made no statement. Ambassador Dobrynin's conversation with Robert Kennedy was cut short when the Attorney General left to reach President Johnson; RFK is working to keep that channel intact but has offered no terms. Allied capitals have received no briefing on who now holds command authority in Washington.
response.consequences: McNamara has suspended any automatic strike sequence pending Johnson's written confirmation and ordered verification of the aircraft's fate. LeMay's strike package against Cuban SAM sites and airfields sits ready, awaiting a presidential order that has not been given. Whether Soviet tactical nuclear units in Cuba would respond to a retaliatory strike is unknown. The Joint Chiefs require written clarification of Johnson's authority before any further movement.
response.detailed:
12:00 p.m.: Kennedy, over the objection of his military and civilian staff, ordered Air Force One to Cuba immediately, without escort, intending a direct meeting with Castro. The Air Force executed the order. No clearance was sought from or granted by Havana. At 12:47 p.m. the aircraft crossed the Cuban coastline. Cuban air-defence command, on alert since the morning's U-2 shootdown and anticipating invasion, fired. Air Force One did not reach Havana. The president and his traveling party are unaccounted for — killed or in Cuban hands, status unconfirmed.

At the White House, Lyndon Johnson has assumed the presidency. The Joint Chiefs, unanimous, have submitted a demand for immediate retaliatory strikes on Cuban SAM sites and airfields under OPLAN 312, and have separately demanded written clarification of Johnson's authority and intent before they will execute anything further. McNamara has suspended any automatic strike sequence and ordered verification of the aircraft's fate and search for survivors; he has warned the new president that a limited strike risks Soviet or Cuban retaliation without securing missile removal. Robert Kennedy broke off his channel conversation with Dobrynin to reach the new president, has warned against making his brother's death the opening act of a general war, but has not been authorized to offer Moscow any terms.

Castro has declared publicly that Cuba shot down an invading aircraft, ordered full combat alert and dispersal of additional air-defence units, and demanded Soviet guarantees against a US attack. Soviet tactical response, if any, to a US retaliatory strike remains unknown. Command authority in Washington is unsettled: the Chiefs want clarification in writing before compliance; McNamara wants time; RFK wants the Dobrynin channel preserved without concession. Johnson has not yet acted.

press.headline: PRESIDENT'S PLANE DOWN OVER CUBA — FATE UNKNOWN
press.body: Air Force One, carrying President Kennedy, was reported lost over Cuban airspace this afternoon after departing Washington without military escort. The White House has confirmed Vice President Johnson has assumed the presidency. No further details have been released.

press.headline: Castro: 'We Have Shot Down the Invader'
press.body: Premier Fidel Castro announced this afternoon that Cuban forces destroyed an aircraft that entered national airspace without authorization. He placed all forces on maximum alert and called on the Soviet Union to guarantee Cuba against American retaliation.

press.headline: Joint Chiefs Seek Written Authority From New President
press.body: Sources at the Pentagon indicate the Joint Chiefs of Staff have submitted a unanimous recommendation for immediate strikes against Cuban air-defense installations, and are requesting formal written clarification of President Johnson's command intentions before further military action.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, I've suspended the automatic sequence. I need forty minutes for a fate report before anyone fires anything. A SAM strike now doesn't bring Jack back and it doesn't get the missiles out — it just tells us how fast the rest of this goes.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, the package is ready. Every hour we wait, they harden those sites and hide the evidence. The Chiefs are unanimous. Delay is a decision — it's the wrong one.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Mr. President — Lyndon — Dobrynin doesn't know yet what happened up there. Give me the room to keep that line open before Curtis turns this into something none of us can walk back. Jack wouldn't want his death to start the war he was trying to stop.

response.chronicleEntry: 12:47 p.m. EST, 27 October 1962: President Kennedy, having ordered Air Force One to Cuba without escort or Cuban clearance against unanimous staff objection, was lost when the aircraft was fired on by Cuban air defence after crossing the coast near Havana. Vice President Johnson assumed the presidency. The Joint Chiefs demanded immediate retaliatory strikes and written clarification of the new president's authority; McNamara suspended automatic strike sequences pending verification; Castro declared full combat alert and demanded Soviet guarantees. Status of the president and his party remains unconfirmed.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 was shot down over Cuba that morning, killing its pilot. At noon, President Kennedy ordered Air Force One to fly him directly to Cuba, unescorted, to meet Castro personally, overriding objections from McNamara, LeMay, and RFK. The aircraft entered Cuban airspace without clearance and was shot down by Cuban air defence near Havana at 12:47 p.m. Kennedy's fate — dead or captured — is unconfirmed. Vice President Johnson has assumed the presidency. The Joint Chiefs unanimously demand immediate retaliatory strikes on Cuban SAM sites and written clarification of Johnson's authority; McNamara has suspended automatic strike sequences pending verification; Castro has declared full combat alert and demanded Soviet guarantees against US attack. RFK is trying to preserve the Dobrynin channel without offering terms. Soviet response to any US retaliation is unknown. No decision has yet been made on OPLAN 312, the quarantine, or force posture under the new president.

outcomes.event: A single U.S. strike aircraft crosses eastern Cuba, releases one bomb on the SA-2 position that destroyed Anderson's U-2, and exits without a follow-on wave. The bomb wrecks the launcher area and kills Soviet and Cuban personnel at the site; McNamara orders all other OPLAN 312 sorties held. Moscow receives reports of one attack rather than a sustained air campaign, and Khrushchev continues drafting his non-invasion-for-withdrawal message rather than ordering retaliation.
outcomes.because: The President can impose a narrowly written firing limit, and Moscow's central leadership is actively seeking an exit; the Soviet order requiring Cuban commanders to obtain approval for further SAM firing helps prevent an immediate local response.

establishes.statement: The United States has carried out a single, completed air attack on a Soviet-operated SA-2 site in Cuba and has not immediately opened the wider OPLAN 312 campaign.
The SA-2 battery that killed Major Rudolf Anderson Jr. is materially damaged and temporarily unable to engage aircraft.
Khrushchev has not treated the limited raid as cancelling his search for a negotiated withdrawal.

opensThreads.title: Proof After Bloodshed
opensThreads.question: Can Washington obtain a verifiable Soviet missile withdrawal after directly killing Soviet personnel in Cuba?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A public Soviet withdrawal announcement paired with inspection or other credible verification.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Local commanders and the Joint Chiefs treat the exchange as precedent for further military action.

createsUnknowns.statement: Some Soviet and Cuban personnel from the struck SA-2 site may have survived and reported the raid as the beginning of an invasion.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether their first reports reach Castro or Moscow before diplomatic messages do.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Intercepted communications or reporting through Dobrynin.

assumesMet: The responsible command executes the President's one-bomb limit.
The aircraft can reach and leave the target without an additional suppression package.
Khrushchev distinguishes the scale of this attack from the opening of a general air campaign.

outcomes.event: The Air Force flies the literal one-bomb mission without escorts or suppression. Cuban radar and anti-aircraft fire acquire the aircraft on its approach; the bomb falls outside the launch area, and the attacking aircraft is shot down before it leaves Cuban airspace. LeMay cites the loss as proof that the President's restriction made the mission militarily unsound and renews his demand for OPLAN 312.
outcomes.because: A lone strike against a functioning Soviet air-defence complex is exposed to the very defences it is meant to punish. The one-bomb restriction leaves little margin for a missed release, a surviving radar, or an intercepting fighter.

establishes.statement: A U.S. combat aircraft has been shot down over Cuba during a retaliatory strike, while the Anderson SA-2 site remains operational or only lightly damaged.
LeMay and the Joint Chiefs have put on record that a restricted raid produced an avoidable American loss and that only the full air plan can suppress Cuban air defences.

opensThreads.title: The Missing Strike Crew
opensThreads.question: Did the downed American crew survive, and will Cuba exploit any prisoners before Washington can control the story?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Cuban public evidence, a Red Cross approach, or confirmed recovery of the crew.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The crew's fate becomes an additional public demand for escalation.

opensThreads.title: Retaliation After a Second Shootdown
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy accept the loss, or authorize the broad suppression campaign LeMay now demands?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A clear order either authorizing or rejecting OPLAN 312.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The Chiefs' objections become harder to contain and may leak.

createsUnknowns.statement: The fate of the attacking crew is unconfirmed after the aircraft is lost over Cuba.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether its members are dead, evading, or in Cuban custody.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Emergency beacons, Cuban broadcasts, or intelligence reporting.

assumesMet: The armed forces comply with the literal one-bomb limitation.
assumesUnmet: A lone bomb strike can reliably destroy a defended SA-2 position.
The operation can be carried out without a broader force package.

outcomes.event: LeMay and the Joint Chiefs tell McNamara that they cannot certify a one-bomb raid as an executable combat mission: the target must be located afresh, its radar suppressed, and the attacking aircraft covered. Under the pressure of Anderson's death, the order is converted into a multi-aircraft package; escorts and additional strike aircraft attack the SA-2 site and nearby radar positions, dropping multiple weapons. Soviet advisers are killed at more than one installation, and the scale of the raid is visible to Havana and Moscow.
outcomes.because: The missing prerequisite is not presidential authority but reliable military execution. Covering the target-identification, survivability, and damage-assessment gaps requires precisely the escorts, suppression, and repeat attacks excluded by the President's stated one-bomb limit.

establishes.statement: The purportedly limited retaliation has expanded into a multi-aircraft attack against more than one Cuban air-defence objective.
Civilian control has been damaged: McNamara and the President must now explain why the military operation exceeded the announced one-bomb restriction.
Soviet personnel have suffered casualties at installations beyond the battery that fired on Anderson's U-2.

opensThreads.title: Who Authorized the Broader Raid?
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy repudiate the expanded strike package, accept it publicly, or remove officers responsible for exceeding his limit?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A public accounting and a clear command decision on LeMay and the operational chain.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The Chiefs will regard the broadened raid as the practical precedent for completing OPLAN 312.

opensThreads.title: Moscow's Threshold
opensThreads.question: Does Khrushchev read attacks on several installations as an invasion's preparatory air campaign?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Dobrynin's report of Moscow's position or a Soviet public military response.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Cuban and Soviet local preparations may outrun political communication.

createsUnknowns.statement: Soviet commanders in Cuba may have requested authority to use stronger weapons after the expanded attack.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether Moscow has received, approved, or rejected that request.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Intercepted Soviet traffic or a message through Dobrynin.

assumesMet: Military planners can provide an executable attack only by adding suppression, escorts, and additional ordnance.
assumesUnmet: The President's one-bomb limitation remains intact once operational prerequisites are covered.

outcomes.event: The single bomb destroys part of the SA-2 site and the U.S. aircraft escapes, but Castro announces that American bombing has begun and orders Cuban forces to their highest invasion readiness. Soviet commanders in Cuba report the raid as the first blow of a wider attack. Khrushchev halts the conciliatory draft long enough to demand that Dobrynin obtain an immediate assurance that no further strikes or invasion will follow; until then, the harder Turkey-linked terms again govern Moscow's public position.
outcomes.because: The physical scale of an attack does not control its political meaning. Castro expects invasion, Soviet forces have already been fired upon, and there is no hotline by which Kennedy can instantly explain that the raid was meant as a warning.

establishes.statement: Cuba has publicly characterized the U.S. raid as the opening of an American attack and has raised its military readiness.
Khrushchev has temporarily withheld the conciliatory non-invasion draft pending a direct indication that Washington will not broaden the attack.
The diplomatic initiative has shifted back toward the second Khrushchev letter's Turkey condition.

opensThreads.title: Assurance Before Retaliation
opensThreads.question: Can Robert Kennedy give Dobrynin a credible private assurance against further strikes and invasion without publicly accepting the Turkey trade?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A message Moscow accepts as binding enough to resume the withdrawal bargain.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Khrushchev's public position hardens while Cuban forces remain on wartime footing.

opensThreads.title: Castro's Mobilization
opensThreads.question: Will Soviet commanders restrain Cuban forces now that Castro has publicly declared an American attack underway?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A Soviet restraining order, a Cuban military incident, or an invasion stand-down.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: A local Cuban firing decision can create a new American casualty crisis.

createsUnknowns.statement: The first Cuban reports of the raid may have reached B-59 or other isolated Soviet units without Moscow's qualifying explanation.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether those units now believe general war has begun.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Their surfacing, intercepted transmissions, or subsequent operational behavior.

assumesMet: The U.S. force complies with the one-bomb limit.
Cuban and Soviet leaders learn of the attack before any clarifying diplomatic signal reaches them.
assumesUnmet: Soviet and Cuban leaders interpret the attack's limited scale as a warning rather than an invasion prelude.

outcomes.event: As reports and rumors of American air action circulate while U.S. destroyers continue practice-depth-charge signalling, B-59's commander Valentin Savitsky concludes that hostilities may have begun and orders the nuclear torpedo prepared. Vasili Arkhipov refuses assent to firing and forces the boat to surface instead; American sailors see the submarine break the surface, but Washington does not initially know how close the boat came to using its nuclear weapon.
outcomes.because: B-59 has been isolated from Moscow for days, is being harassed underwater, and carries officers already forced to decide whether war has started. A U.S. strike makes their worst interpretation more credible, even though it does not compel a launch.

establishes.statement: B-59 surfaces near the quarantine line rather than firing its nuclear torpedo.
The submarine's officers prepared a nuclear torpedo for possible use, but Arkhipov withheld the assent needed to launch it.

opensThreads.title: The Submarine Warning
opensThreads.question: Will Washington change its anti-submarine signalling procedures before another isolated Soviet boat makes the same calculation?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Revised Navy instructions and a Soviet acknowledgment or safe withdrawal of the submarine.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Further underwater signalling may recreate the launch decision under worse conditions.

createsUnknowns.statement: The United States observes B-59 surfacing but does not know that a nuclear torpedo was prepared for firing.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether the boat carried nuclear arms and how close its officers came to launch.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Soviet disclosure, intelligence penetration, or later participant testimony.

assumesMet: The submarine remains out of effective communication with Moscow.
The President's air strike is reported or inferred by B-59's crew amid continued naval signalling.

findings.claim: No outcome allows for the Joint Chiefs/military command declining to execute the one-bomb order at all (institutional refusal), reporting back that the mission cannot be flown as specified rather than either flying it as ordered or unilaterally expanding it into a multi-aircraft raid. Given the historical record of JCS resistance to constrained action, a 'the order is not carried out because the military will not certify it' outcome is a plausible gap.

Outcome_1's rationale supplies a specific mitigating mechanism ('the Soviet order requiring Cuban commanders to obtain approval for further SAM firing') that was never stated or implied by the player's directive; this imports outside historical machinery to make the clean success case more probable than the bare order justifies.

Outcome_5 causally links a single limited air strike on a SAM site to the B-59 submarine crisis, which historically arose from separate depth-charge harassment during the naval blockade. Treating a one-bomb SAM strike as a direct trigger for Savitsky's near-launch decision stretches the causal chain well beyond what the directive plausibly sets in motion.

actor_standard:LineUp:aa1567b5.request:
Given what just happened, say what comes next.

partyMoves: for each party materially involved, the concrete move they now make on their own account — not a reaction to the player unless they are reacting. Mark visibleToPlayer false when the player would not see it.

WHO ANSWERS TO THE PLAYER MATTERS. Parties marked commandedByPlayer work for the player. They are not independent agents pursuing the crisis on their own judgment, and they must never advance the player's objective unbidden — an aide who quietly wins the thing the player is trying to win is the world playing the game for them. What such a person MAY do: refuse, stall, demand it in writing, object on the record, resign, leak, protect themselves, warn, obey the letter and not the intent, or exceed their brief in a way that COSTS the player something. If one of them does act on the objective without an order, it is insubordination and it carries a price — never free progress.

Everyone else acts entirely on their own account, and should. Adversaries and third parties are where the world's own momentum comes from.
threadUpdates: for each open thread, how it moved. A thread the player ignored still moves; say how. Mark RESOLVED only when it is genuinely settled, OVERTAKEN when events have made it moot.
facingPlayer: the decisions now in front of the player, in their own terms.

Use only the ids given. Do not invent parties or threads here.

partyMoves.move: He sends Washington a revised withdrawal proposal: Soviet missiles leave Cuba in return for a public U.S. non-invasion pledge, while privately insisting that the Turkish Jupiter missiles must also be removed. Quarantine destroyers continue signaling the Soviet submarine. Soviet officers keep the boat submerged and avoid a direct confrontation for now, but the lack of a clear contact order leaves the next exchange dependent on decisions aboard both sides' vessels.

readings.reasoning: The completed U.S. strike killed Soviet and Cuban personnel during a nuclear standoff, sharply raising the risk of retaliation, even though the attack stopped at one site and Moscow has not retaliated.
The limited, single-target raid and continued presidential restraint reduce the strain of a general war, but unilateral attacks on Cuba still put allied confidence under pressure.

The strike answers the destruction of Anderson's aircraft and demonstrates action against the responsible missile site, likely strengthening support while the decision to hold wider sorties limits public alarm.
McNamara has held all other sorties, the Joint Chiefs are operating under the presidential order, and commanders are preparing a bounded contingency rather than launching independently.

Khrushchev's revised withdrawal proposal and Kennedy's continued Dobrynin channel preserve room for a deal, although the U.S. attack and Moscow's demand for Turkish missile removal make agreement harder.
