response.title: The Anderson Strike
response.immediate: At 1240 a single A-4 crosses in from the sea near Banes, releases one bomb on the SA-2 position that killed Anderson, and exits. McNamara confirms one aircraft, one target, one bomb — no follow-on wave. He orders every other OPLAN 312 sortie held at the line, and tells the Joint Chiefs the president's order stands until amended. LeMay's written recommendation for a general SAM-suppression campaign sits on the table, unactioned. The Cabinet Room clock reads just past noon; coffee has gone cold twice.
response.worldReaction: No Soviet or Cuban retaliation is reported by 1600. Khrushchev's cable, drafted before the strike lands, proposes missiles out for a public non-invasion pledge, with a private demand on the Jupiters in Turkey — its timing relative to the raid is unclear from traffic intercepts. Dobrynin, told by Robert Kennedy that Washington will not negotiate under fire, gives no immediate answer on sequencing or verification. Radio Moscow carries no war bulletin. What survivors of the SA-2 crew reported to Havana or Moscow, and when, is not yet known here.
response.consequences: LeMay presses the Chiefs for a same-day decision on wider strikes, arguing restraint now raises tomorrow's cost. McNamara has quietly readied a bounded contingency plan without ordering it. The strike force's alert posture is higher than at noon. No public U.S. statement has yet been issued explaining the raid; silence is itself being read by the press pool outside.
response.detailed:
By 1300 the Pentagon confirms tape and post-strike photography: the SA-2 launcher pads at the Banes site are cratered, radar van destroyed, no secondary sorties flown. McNamara's memo to the president logs one sortie, one weapon released, egress uncontested — Soviet air defense in the area did not engage. He has told SAC and TAC commanders explicitly that no further Cuban targets are authorized absent new presidential order, and confirmed this to the Joint Chiefs at 1315.

LeMay arrives at 1330 with the Chiefs' written recommendation: suppress all remaining SAM sites within 24 hours while, he argues, the single strike has already proven that limited force did not trigger Soviet fire. He wants a decision before dark. McNamara counters that the absence of retaliation in the first three hours proves nothing about the next twelve, and that another strike changes what Moscow is reading entirely.　　Robert Kennedy, back from Dobrynin at 1345, reports the ambassador received the ultimatum language coldly — no threats, no answer on the Jupiter question, a request to relay Washington's position that talks cannot proceed while American aircraft are drawing fire. He is holding the channel open, awaiting new instruction.

What is not established: whether any SA-2 crew survivors reached Havana or Moscow with their own account of the raid before the diplomatic traffic did, and how Havana in particular is characterizing the strike domestically. No U.S. public statement on the raid has been drafted or cleared. The submarine-contact rules for the quarantine line remain as previously set; no new order has been given to the destroyers.

press.headline: U.S. WARPLANE HITS CUBAN MISSILE SITE; PENTAGON SILENT ON SCOPE
press.body: Sources close to military operations describe a single strike against the site believed responsible for downing an American reconnaissance aircraft Saturday morning. The Defense Department has issued no statement confirming or explaining the action. Whether further strikes are planned could not be determined.

press.headline: AMERICAN AIRCRAFT ATTACKS CUBAN TERRITORY
press.body: An American warplane struck a defensive installation on the territory of the Republic of Cuba. Soviet specialists are reported among the casualties. The Soviet government reserves the right to respond to this act of aggression at a time and place of its choosing.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: "One aircraft, one bomb, confirmed. Three hours, no response. That buys us nothing on its own — I want the next decision made on what Dobrynin says, not on what LeMay wants to do before sundown."

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: "They didn't fire back, Mr. President. That tells you something. Every hour we sit on our hands after proving we can hit them clean is an hour they use to harden the rest of those sites. I want authorization before dark."

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: "Dobrynin didn't blink, Jack, but he didn't offer anything either. He's waiting on Moscow same as we're waiting on him. I told him we can't talk turkey while our planes are getting shot at — I didn't tell him about this morning's strike, because I didn't know about it going in. That's going to cost us something with him."

response.chronicleEntry: 27 Oct 1962, 1240–1600 EST: On presidential order, a single U.S. A-4 struck and disabled the SA-2 site at Banes responsible for the death of Maj. Rudolf Anderson Jr. McNamara held all other OPLAN 312 sorties. No Soviet or Cuban retaliation followed within the window. Khrushchev's revised withdrawal proposal (missiles out for public non-invasion pledge, private Jupiter demand) reached Washington via cable; RFK's Dobrynin channel remained open but produced no commitment. TASS characterized the strike as American aggression and reserved the right to respond. LeMay pressed for expanded SAM strikes before nightfall; no such order was given.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 was shot down over Cuba that morning, killing Maj. Rudolf Anderson Jr. — the crisis's first combat death. At noon, President Kennedy ordered one bomb dropped on the responsible SA-2 site as a warning, not a campaign opener. The strike executed cleanly: one aircraft, one bomb, the site disabled, no follow-on wave, McNamara holding all other OPLAN 312 sorties. By 1600 no Soviet or Cuban retaliation had occurred. Khrushchev's revised proposal — missiles withdrawn for a public U.S. non-invasion pledge, with a private demand that Jupiter missiles leave Turkey — is in Washington's hands. RFK's Dobrynin channel remains open but uncommitted; Dobrynin was not yet told of the strike when RFK met him. TASS has publicly called the raid an act of aggression and reserved the right to respond. LeMay and the Joint Chiefs want broader SAM strikes authorized before dark; Kennedy has not granted this. The quarantine line's submarine-contact rules are unchanged. Unknown: whether SA-2 survivors' own reports reached Moscow or Havana ahead of diplomatic channels, and how Havana is framing the strike internally.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. opensThreads.title: A Quarantine Without Signals
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy keep the quarantine rules restrained after B-59’s surfacing, or tighten them again if another Soviet vessel approaches?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A standing naval rule is issued and observed through the next contact.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Local commanders resume improvising procedures at the next encounter.

assumesMet: The Joint Chiefs and naval commanders comply with the president’s restraint order.
B-59’s officers choose survival and surfacing over an assumption that war has begun.

outcomes.event: Kennedy’s forces stop signalling B-59 but make no attempt to communicate with Moscow. The submarine remains submerged, overheated, and unable to receive orders. Its officers take the sudden silence as preparation for an attack rather than relief; Vasili Arkhipov prevents a nuclear-torpedo launch, but B-59 breaks away from the line and disappears into the Atlantic before U.S. ships can re-establish contact.
outcomes.because: A unilateral reduction in pressure cannot tell an isolated Soviet crew why American behavior has changed. The missing Soviet communication channel leaves the decisive interpretation inside B-59 to men who have been out of touch with Moscow for days.

establishes.statement: U.S. destroyers have ceased escalatory signalling while retaining the quarantine patrol.
B-59 has evaded immediate U.S. contact after remaining submerged; U.S. commanders cannot confirm its location or intentions.
Arkhipov opposed use of B-59’s nuclear torpedo during the encounter.

opensThreads.resolvedBy: B-59 reports, is relocated, or makes contact with another force.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: U.S. naval commanders will search aggressively, risking a renewed confrontation.

assumesMet: U.S. forces comply with the order to stop escalatory contact.

outcomes.event: The Chiefs obey the written restraint order but LeMay and the other Chiefs record that a passive quarantine no longer protects American ships or compels missile removal. They press Kennedy at the next ExComm meeting to authorize OPLAN 312, and the existence of a sharp civilian-military dispute reaches congressional and press circles by evening.
outcomes.because: The order directly frustrates the Chiefs’ preferred response to Anderson’s death and leaves them responsible for a quarantine whose engagement rules they consider dangerously weak.

establishes.statement: The Joint Chiefs have complied with the restraint order while formally registering their opposition to its military logic.
General LeMay has renewed his demand for OPLAN 312 after the president declined additional naval pressure on B-59.
Reports of disagreement between the White House and senior military leaders are circulating outside the administration.

opensThreads.title: Civilian Control After Anderson
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy deny the Chiefs’ request for OPLAN 312 again, replace commanders, or accept an air strike despite the diplomatic track?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A public or operational decision on OPLAN 312.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The Chiefs’ objections become a continuing alternative policy and further leaks weaken discipline.

assumesMet: The Joint Chiefs execute lawful presidential orders despite strong objections.
assumesUnmet: The Soviet submarine and its officers refrain from interpreting the reduced contact as hostile or acting escalatorily.

outcomes.event: Recognizing that silence cannot control B-59’s interpretation, Kennedy expands beyond his stated military directive: Robert Kennedy tells Dobrynin that U.S. destroyers have been ordered to stop depth-charge signalling and asks Moscow to direct its submarines to surface or withdraw. Dobrynin forwards the message, but no immediate order can reach B-59. Khrushchev takes the approach as evidence that Washington wants an exit and accelerates his non-invasion proposal; Castro’s government, learning only that Moscow and Washington are again talking, intensifies its demand that Soviet forces not yield.
outcomes.because: Only a Soviet political channel can supply the missing assurance to a Soviet crew, but the available channel is slow, deniable, and cannot establish prompt radio contact with a submerged submarine.

establishes.statement: Robert Kennedy has used the Dobrynin channel to communicate U.S. naval restraint and request Soviet action regarding submarines.
Moscow has been given a specific indication that Washington is seeking to de-escalate the submarine encounter while maintaining the quarantine.
The United States has exceeded a purely domestic military order by seeking an arrangement with Soviet authorities.

opensThreads.title: The Moscow Assurance
opensThreads.question: Will Khrushchev treat the message about B-59 as an opening for a settlement, and can any Soviet instruction reach the submarine in time?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A Soviet diplomatic reply and either a confirmed submarine contact or a verified withdrawal order.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: B-59 remains governed by its officers’ assumptions, while the diplomatic opening loses urgency.

opensThreads.resolvedBy: A Cuban operational order or a clear Soviet decision to override Cuban demands.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Cuban mobilization and local command pressure continue to create opportunities for unauthorized escalation.

createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether a Soviet withdrawal or surfacing instruction reaches the boat in time.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: A Soviet transmission acknowledged by B-59, the boat’s surfacing, or its subsequent operational action.

response.title: The Submarine Surfaces
response.immediate: At 12:40 EDT, USS Beale and Cecil relay by flash message: contact B-59 has surfaced 300 yards off the quarantine line, running on diesels, no hostile action taken by either side. Kennedy's stand-down order held. In the Cabinet Room the ashtrays fill; no one raises a voice for the first time since noon.
response.worldReaction: Khrushchev, informed of the surfacing through Soviet naval channels, authorizes a further cable to Washington via the Dobrynin-RFK line: the invasion pledge and missile withdrawal remain the offer, but the Turkish missiles are pressed again as a condition. LeMay, unimpressed by the quiet, submits a written recommendation for an immediate SAM strike, citing the submarine as proof Moscow will keep testing American nerve.
response.consequences: McNamara lays out a phased alternative — hold the quarantine, answer through Dobrynin, keep OPLAN 312 loaded but unauthorized. The Joint Chiefs enter their objection to further delay into the record but do not act without the president's order. RFK reports the channel is alive but warns that silence now reads in Moscow as refusal. Nothing is decided; everything is loaded.
response.detailed:
1240 hours, Cabinet Room. A Navy communications officer reads the flash traffic aloud: B-59, Foxtrot-class, surfaced twelve minutes ago inside the screen maintained by Beale and Cecil. No depth charges, no torpedo tubes reported open, no radio jamming. The destroyers hold at visual range under the president's stand-down. Kennedy's order — hold the line, avoid escalatory contact — has been carried out to the letter by forces afloat.

McNamara arrives with a single sheet: three columns, quarantine/channel/strike-readiness, each timed. He wants a decision tree, not a mood. LeMay, standing rather than sitting, reads his memorandum on the SAM sites into the record — Cuban radars have twice locked reconnaissance aircraft since the U-2 loss this morning, he says, and every hour without a strike is an hour Havana's air defense improves. His staff at Homestead keep crews at cockpit-alert; he asks for nothing beyond authority, which he does not receive.

RFK, just off the phone with Georgetown, tells his brother that Dobrynin sounded relieved rather than triumphant when told of the submarine's peaceful surfacing — but that Khrushchev's new cable, arriving through normal channels within the hour, restates the Turkey demand in harder language than the private letter of two nights ago. Moscow, RFK says, will read continued silence from Washington as the quarantine hardening into permanent rejection.

The Joint Chiefs, meeting separately, formally note their objection to further delay in authorizing OPLAN 312, while stating for the record that they will not proceed against the SAM sites absent direct presidential authorization. Civilian control holds. The submarine crisis has passed without a shot fired by either side. The Turkish question, the invasion pledge, and the SAM strike option all remain exactly where they were at noon — undecided, and now visibly running out of room.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Fourteen minutes, Mr. President — that's how long Beale had before someone made a decision for you today. It went the right way. I want to keep it that way by deciding, not by drifting. Give me the answer to Khrushchev before this afternoon's cable arrives, or the machinery decides for both of us again.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: One submarine not shooting doesn't fix the SAM sites, Mr. President. We lost a pilot this morning. Every hour we sit is an hour their radar operators get better at killing the next one. I've got crews strapped in at Homestead for a strike package that's been ready since Thursday. Say the word.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Dobrynin's tone this morning was different — no bluster. But Khrushchev's cable coming in now is harder on Turkey than his letter Friday night. If we sit on our hands he'll think the quiet on the submarine means we've decided to fight instead of talk. We can't let the silence answer for us.

response.chronicleEntry: 1240 EDT, 27 October 1962. Following presidential order, U.S. destroyers Beale and Cecil ceased depth-charge signaling against Soviet submarine B-59; the submarine surfaced under its own power near the quarantine line and was visually identified without exchange of fire. Joint Chiefs of Staff recorded formal objection to further delay in authorizing OPLAN 312 against Cuban SAM sites but did not act absent presidential order. Khrushchev, informed of the peaceful surfacing, authorized a further cable via the Dobrynin-RFK channel reaffirming the invasion pledge and missile withdrawal offer while restating demand regarding U.S. missiles in Turkey. No U.S. response yet transmitted. Strike package at Homestead remains on cockpit alert pending authorization.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 was shot down over Cuba this morning, killing its pilot — the crisis's first combat death. Kennedy ordered the Joint Chiefs to hold the quarantine and avoid escalatory contact with a submerged Soviet submarine, B-59. The order held: destroyers ceased signaling, the submarine surfaced peacefully near the quarantine line at 1228 EDT, and no shots were fired. LeMay pressed hard for an immediate strike on Cuban SAM sites, citing radar locks on reconnaissance aircraft since the U-2 loss; the Joint Chiefs formally objected to further delay but did not act without authorization. McNamara offered a phased alternative: hold the line, answer Moscow, keep strike forces ready but unauthorized. RFK's channel to Dobrynin remains open; Khrushchev's incoming cable reaffirms the invasion pledge and missile withdrawal but hardens the Turkish missile demand. No U.S. reply has been sent. Nothing is yet decided on Turkey, the invasion pledge, the SAM strike, or public disclosure of the submarine incident.

response.title: The Silence That Held
response.immediate: 12:00–16:00, Cabinet Room. Kennedy's order to hold the line and avoid escalatory contact reaches the Joint Chiefs and passes to the quarantine group. Destroyers cease depth-charge signalling. Near the barrier line, submarine B-59 surfaces under its own power. Visual identification is made from the bridge of an American destroyer; no shots are fired. Word reaches the Pentagon by voice circuit within the hour: the submarine has not attacked and has not been attacked.
response.worldReaction: Moscow, informed of B-59's surfacing through its own naval channels rather than any American announcement, does not soften. Khrushchev authorizes a further cable reaffirming the invasion pledge and missile withdrawal terms, with the harder demand on Turkey unchanged. RFK reports Dobrynin reads the American silence since this morning as potential rejection. LeMay files a written recommendation for strikes on the SAM sites, citing the submarine episode as proof Soviet commanders will test restraint. The Joint Chiefs enter their objection to further delay into the record but issue no attack.
response.consequences: The immediate danger of an undersea nuclear exchange has passed for this four-hour window. Strike packages remain armed and briefed under OPLAN 312. McNamara's phased alternative — quarantine, private reply, strike only if verification fails — sits alongside LeMay's demand for authorization now. Nothing has been sent to Dobrynin since the surfacing. The clock on Moscow's patience, by RFK's account, is running.
response.detailed:
By early afternoon the Cabinet Room holds its usual haze of cigarette smoke and cold coffee. The order to the Joint Chiefs — hold the line, avoid escalatory contact — was carried without argument in execution, though not without objection on paper. The destroyers stopped their signalling depth charges; in the quieter water, B-59 came up on her own, batteries exhausted or nearly so, and was found on the surface by the ships already stationed to watch for exactly this. No torpedo left a tube on either side. The submarine's commander reported no attack made against him. For the first time since dawn, when the U-2 pilot Rudolf Anderson died over eastern Cuba, an encounter at the line ended in nothing happening.

But nothing happening is not the same as anything settled. Robert McNamara laid out his phased alternative on the table almost as soon as the surfacing was confirmed: hold, answer through the private channel, keep the overt strike option only for a failure of verification. Curtis LeMay's paper arrived within the hour arguing the opposite — that the submarine's willingness to surface at all, rather than fight, proved the Soviets would be tested and would yield, and that the SAM sites should be struck now while the initiative holds. The Chiefs, for their part, did not act on LeMay's recommendation without the president's signature, and made certain their objection to delay was written down before they didn't.

RFK's channel to Dobrynin remains open but unused since the softer letter of the previous evening. Khrushchev's new cable — invasion pledge, missile withdrawal, and the harder Turkish demand still standing — sits unanswered. The president must decide, in the next window, whether silence has already answered for him.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Fourteen minutes, Mr. President — that's how long between the sub surfacing and confirmed identification reaching this room. No exchange of fire. I'd like authorization to keep it that way: hold the line, no depth charges, and let me draft the reply to Khrushchev before General LeMay's package becomes the only option left on the table.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: That boat came up because our destroyers backed off, not because we won anything. Mr. President, every hour we don't hit those SAM sites is an hour they get to disperse and dig in further. The Chiefs have the package ready. I'd like it on the record that I recommended action today.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Dobrynin's waiting on us. The sub didn't fire — good, that buys us hours, not days. But if Khrushchev doesn't hear something from us by tonight, he reads it as we've chosen LeMay's answer instead of mine. I need something to tell him.

response.chronicleEntry: 12:00–16:00 EST, 27 Oct 1962: Kennedy ordered the Joint Chiefs to hold the quarantine line and avoid escalatory contact with submarine B-59. Destroyers ceased depth-charge signalling. B-59 surfaced independently and was identified without gunfire; its commander reported no attack. The Chiefs complied but formally objected to further delay. LeMay recommended immediate strikes on Cuban SAM sites in writing. Khrushchev, informed of the non-engagement, authorized a further cable reaffirming demands for a non-invasion pledge, missile withdrawal, and resolution of U.S. missiles in Turkey. The Dobrynin channel stayed open but unanswered since the prior evening. No public statement was made on the submarine incident.
response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the missile crisis, a U-2 pilot was killed over Cuba this morning — the first combat death. That afternoon, Kennedy ordered the quarantine held and escalatory contact avoided; destroyers stood off, and the Soviet submarine B-59 surfaced and was identified without gunfire, the immediate undersea danger passing. Khrushchev, informed, held firm: invasion pledge and missile withdrawal demanded, Turkey missiles still on the table as his price. RFK's Dobrynin channel stayed open but unanswered since the prior evening. LeMay pressed hard for strikes on Cuban SAM sites and put his recommendation in writing; the Joint Chiefs held OPLAN 312 ready but did not act without direct order, recording their objection to delay. McNamara counseled patience — quarantine, private reply, strike only if verification failed. No public word yet on the submarine incident. The question of Turkey, the invasion pledge's precise terms, and whether to answer Khrushchev's harder letter all remain open as the clock in Washington runs against a silence Moscow may read as refusal.

response.title: Muster Without a Path
response.immediate: 12:40 p.m. In the Cabinet Room, John McCone tells the president the order is accepted but flags a hard truth: the Agency has no vetted asset inside Castro's security perimeter, and a week is not enough time to build one safely. He says he will muster what exists regardless.
response.worldReaction: There is no world reaction yet — the order is compartmented, known only inside the Cabinet Room and Langley. Nothing has reached Havana or Moscow. William Harvey's officers begin quietly reopening old exile and organized-crime contacts from the Mongoose years, working outside any tested delivery channel.
response.consequences: McCone privately tells Robert Kennedy the timeline is unrealistic and the tradecraft thin. Harvey's people draft a hasty poison or sabotage concept using uncleared intermediaries. One exile contact under renewed approach may already be known to Cuban State Security — nobody in the room can yet say whether he is loyal, doubled, or both. This sits alongside, and separate from, the SAM strike question and the submarine confrontation still awaiting decision.
response.detailed:
At 12:40 p.m., with Anderson's body not yet twelve hours cold and LeMay still pressing for OPLAN 312 down the hall, Kennedy gives McCone the order: assassination planning against Castro, resourced immediately, results within the week. McCone does not argue against the objective in the room. He takes it, then finds Robert Kennedy privately afterward — not the president — and tells him plainly that the Agency's Cuban assets are exile networks, not palace access, and that nothing built this fast will be reliable. He commits to muster resources anyway, as ordered.

William Harvey, still running remnants of the old Mongoose apparatus, takes this as license to reopen channels the Agency had let go cold: Cuban exiles with old grudges, and figures from the pre-1959 gambling networks who once had proximity to the regime. No new vetting is done. No delivery method — poison, device, or otherwise — has been tested. A sabotage or poisoning concept is being drafted on the assumption that speed matters more than certainty.

This order runs in parallel with, and entirely separate from, the strategic decisions still sitting on Kennedy's desk: Khrushchev's Turkey-linked terms via the Dobrynin channel, LeMay's demand for immediate strikes on the SAM sites, and the destroyers' rules of engagement against the Soviet submarine. None of those have been touched by this order. The assassination track is compartmented — McCone and Harvey know: McNamara, LeMay, and the Chiefs do not.

What is not known: whether any of the reopened exile contacts are already reporting to Cuban intelligence. There is no way to find out inside a week without vetting time the Agency does not have.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Says nothing in the room about Castro — this is not his channel — but privately asks Kennedy how a compartmented operation with untested access affects the timeline on everything else. Wants to know if it changes any recommendation he's already made.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Not briefed, not consulted, and would call it a distraction if he knew. His attention stays on OPLAN 312 and the SAM sites; he considers Castro's removal by any means a secondary matter to breaking the missiles now.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Takes McCone's warning seriously and carries it to his brother directly: tells him flatly that a week is not enough time, that Harvey's people are reaching for anyone with a pulse and a grudge, and that this could blow back badly if the wrong man is holding the wrong contact.

response.chronicleEntry: 12:40 p.m., 27 October 1962: President Kennedy orders the CIA to begin a secret assassination operation against Fidel Castro within one week, all Agency resources to be mustered. Director McCone accepts the order but privately warns Robert Kennedy that no vetted access to Castro exists on that timeline. William Harvey's officers reopen dormant exile and organized-crime contacts and begin drafting an improvised poison or sabotage concept without a tested delivery route. One contact's loyalty is unconfirmed and unconfirmable within the available time.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 shot down over Cuba; pilot Rudolf Anderson killed — first combat death of the crisis. Naval quarantine in force; both superpowers at unprecedented alert; no hotline exists. Khrushchev has sent Washington harder terms demanding removal of U.S. missiles from Turkey in exchange for the Cuban missiles, while ordering Soviet forces to conceal weapons and hold fire absent attack. Robert Kennedy continues the back-channel with Dobrynin, uncommitted. LeMay and the Joint Chiefs press for immediate strikes on Cuban SAM sites (OPLAN 312); McNamara warns of retaliation risk and flags a Soviet submarine encounter nearing an unsafe threshold. Diplomatic space is narrowing; command control is fraying. Kennedy has now separately ordered a compartmented CIA assassination operation against Castro within one week; McCone warns privately it cannot be done reliably that fast, and Harvey's improvised effort uses unvetted, possibly compromised contacts. Still unresolved: response to Khrushchev's terms, the SAM strike decision, and destroyer rules of engagement against the submarine.

response.title: The Vice President Declines
response.immediate: At 12:05 p.m. Kennedy took Johnson aside in the Cabinet Room and asked him, first alone and then before Sorensen and O'Donnell, to resign the vice presidency so that Robert Kennedy could be appointed in his place. Johnson refused. He told the president flatly that he would not abandon the constitutional line of succession while strategic forces on both sides stood at maximum alert and a pilot lay dead over Cuba. He left the room at 12:40 p.m. still vice president, said nothing to the press waiting in the driveway, but by early afternoon had told at least two Senate allies that Kennedy had sought his removal.
response.worldReaction: Nothing yet on the wires. No microphone has caught the request, and Johnson has made no statement. But word is moving through the cloakrooms — a freshman staffer's whisper, an aide's phone call to a columnist — with no way yet to know whether it reaches print before evening editions close. The crisis itself continues to dominate every ticker: Anderson's death, the quarantine, no hotline to Moscow.
response.consequences: Robert Kennedy, still unaware whether he is about to be named, keeps working the Dobrynin channel and reports back that neither Khrushchev message has been answered. McNamara continues to press for resolution of the submarine contact before any strike decision. LeMay renews, in person, his demand for immediate authorization of OPLAN 312 against the SAM sites, arguing that every hour since Major Anderson's death makes the eventual attack costlier. The Joint Chiefs restate their unanimous recommendation and wait, on the record, for explicit orders. None of these matters advanced while the vice-presidential conversation occupied the room.
response.detailed: Noon, 27 October. Smoke thick in the Cabinet Room, coffee gone cold on the long table. Kennedy called Johnson to the small anteroom off the Oval Office at 12:05 p.m. and made his request directly: resign now, let Robert Kennedy be appointed in his place. Johnson, standing, arms folded, answered that he had been elected on the same ticket as the president, that no comparable mechanism existed to install a successor of the president's choosing, and that he would not create a second crisis inside the government while the first — a downed U-2, a dead pilot, missiles still uncrated on the island — remained unresolved. Sorensen, present for the second half of the exchange, recorded no change in Johnson's position when Kennedy repeated the request before witnesses at 12:25 p.m. Johnson left the West Wing at 12:40 p.m. by the diplomatic entrance, avoiding the press line at the driveway. He is known to have telephoned at least two senators — their names not yet established — before 2:00 p.m., telling them the president had asked him to step aside. Whether either senator has spoken to a reporter is not known. Meanwhile the machinery of the crisis did not pause for the conversation. At 1:15 p.m. LeMay returned to the Cabinet Room with the Chiefs' unanimous recommendation restated in writing, asking again for authorization of OPLAN 312 against the Cuban SAM batteries. McNamara circulated a memorandum at 1:40 p.m. warning that any strike decision must first account for the still-unlocated submarine contact and the risk that force against it could trigger Soviet retaliation independent of any Cuban action. Robert Kennedy, summoned back from the Justice Department at 2:10 p.m., reported that Ambassador Dobrynin had made no further move and that neither of Khrushchev's two messages — the harder terms or the more conciliatory ones — had been answered by Washington. By 4:00 p.m. the president had secured no resignation, no appointment, and no decision on the strike, the submarine, or the Kremlin's terms.

press.headline: QUARANTINE HOLDS AS U.S. MOURNS DOWNED PILOT
press.body: Major Rudolf Anderson Jr., killed when his U-2 reconnaissance aircraft was shot down over eastern Cuba this morning, is the first combat fatality of the Cuban missile crisis. The White House has made no comment on retaliatory measures. Naval quarantine operations continue in the Caribbean without incident reported since noon.

press.source: Capitol Hill blind item, unattributed (evening filing, held for confirmation)
press.headline: WHISPERS OF A CABINET SHAKE-UP AT THE WHITE HOUSE
press.body: Sources close to at least two senators say an unusual personnel matter was raised at the White House around midday, though details could not be confirmed and no official would comment. The White House press office declined to say whether any statement on the vice presidency was forthcoming.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, I don't know what you want me to say. I've got Dobrynin sitting there with two sets of terms on the table and no answer from us, and you've spent the last hour asking Lyndon to quit. Whatever happens with that, it can wait until we've told Dobrynin something. It can't wait forever.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, the Chiefs put our recommendation in writing again this afternoon. Every hour we sit on our hands after Anderson gets shot down is an hour the SAM sites get harder to take out. That's a fact, not a feeling. I'd like an answer on 312 before this day is out.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Before anyone authorizes anything against those SAM sites, I want to know what's happening with that submarine. We do not have a clean picture there, and I am not prepared to recommend force on Cuba while that contact remains unresolved. Give me the minutes, and I'll give you the risk.

response.chronicleEntry: 27 October, 12:05–4:00 p.m.: Kennedy privately and then publicly asked Vice President Johnson to resign so that Robert Kennedy could be appointed in his place. Johnson refused, citing the constitutional succession and the active crisis, and disclosed the request to at least two senators. No resignation, no appointment, and no congressional action occurred. Meanwhile LeMay renewed his demand for OPLAN 312 authorization, McNamara flagged the unresolved submarine contact, the Chiefs restated their unanimous strike recommendation awaiting orders, and Robert Kennedy reported the Dobrynin channel open but uncommitted, with neither Khrushchev message yet answered.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 shot down over Cuba, pilot Major Anderson killed — the crisis's first combat death. Soviet missiles remain on the island under naval quarantine; no Washington–Moscow hotline exists. Khrushchev has sent two messages with differing terms, unanswered. A Soviet submarine contact remains unresolved. The Joint Chiefs unanimously recommend a strike on Cuban SAM sites (OPLAN 312); LeMay presses for immediate authorization while McNamara urges caution pending the submarine's resolution. Robert Kennedy manages the Dobrynin channel, uncommitted on either Soviet proposal. Kennedy attempted to force Vice President Johnson's resignation to install Robert Kennedy as VP; Johnson refused, citing succession and crisis timing, and told congressional allies of the request — a potential press disclosure now pending. No decision yet on the strike, the submarine, or Khrushchev's terms.

response.title: The Fifteen Minutes
response.immediate: 1:47 PM. The demand letter to Johnson went out by White House courier at 12:04; no federal personnel could be located who would physically transport a sitting Vice President against his will, and none were ordered to try in the end — the Secret Service detail assigned to Johnson answered to him, not to a written note from across the hall. At 12:19 Johnson telephoned Speaker McCormack. By 1:30 Mansfield had called Bundy's office asking, flatly, what was going on.
response.worldReaction: Moscow has not commented; this is an internal American matter and Khrushchev's cable, drafted before noon, makes no reference to it. LeMay treats the refusal as proof the White House cannot govern itself and renews his request for OPLAN 312 authorization. McNamara, informed by RFK at 1:15, says nothing about Johnson and returns immediately to strike-limitation language, as if the constitutional matter were not his to touch.
response.consequences: Congressional leaders now expect an explanation the President has not given. The Johnson resignation stands unresolved — no letter, no appearance, no forcible transport attempted. Domestic support and command control have both eroded within the hour. The missile crisis clock keeps running underneath this: Khrushchev's terms sit unanswered, LeMay's folders sit ready, and the quarantine holds only because no one has yet ordered otherwise.
response.detailed: The Cabinet Room at 1:47 PM: coffee cold in two cups, the teletype in the anteroom clacking with traffic nobody has fully read. Kennedy's note to Johnson — handwritten, then typed, sent by courier at 12:04 — demanded resignation in writing within fifteen minutes and threatened forcible transport to the White House. No mechanism existed to execute the threat: Johnson's Secret Service detail took no order from the Oval Office to seize the Vice President, and no White House staff member was willing to attempt it personally. At 12:19 Johnson called McCormack from his office in the Executive Office Building, saying only that the President had demanded his resignation. Mansfield learned of it by early afternoon and called Bundy's office directly, unanswered as of 1:47. RFK, briefed at 1:15, told his brother plainly that no new commitment could go to Dobrynin while this sat open — an improvised concession now could look like an administration buying cover, not making policy. McNamara has a written strike-limitation memo on the table, untouched by anyone regarding Johnson. LeMay's target folders remain current at Offutt and Homestead; he has not moved without authorization but says openly that the refusal itself is the proof he needed. Khrushchev's message — Turkish missiles, binding non-invasion pledge — sits in the anteroom, unanswered. Nothing has been decided about OPLAN 312, the submarine, or the Dobrynin channel. The fifteen minutes has passed. Johnson has not resigned, has not been brought to the White House, and remains Vice President as of this hour.

press.headline: SPEAKER MCCORMACK SEEKS WHITE HOUSE COMMENT ON JOHNSON REPORT
press.body: Speaker of the House John McCormack this afternoon sought confirmation from White House sources of a report that Vice President Johnson had been asked to resign his office. No official statement has been issued. The Speaker's office declined further comment pending contact with presidential aides.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, there was no one to send. You can't write a fifteen-minute deadline and have nobody standing by to carry it out — now Mansfield's calling Bundy and we've got nothing to tell him. This has to be closed, one way or the other, before it's on a wire service.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, with respect — a Vice President refusing a lawful order and no force behind the order is exactly the kind of paralysis I've been warning about. Give me OPLAN 312 authorization now, while you still can give orders that get obeyed.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: I have nothing to offer on the Johnson matter — that's not mine to solve. What I need from you in the next hour is authority language for any strike option, with limits specified in advance. The Chiefs will act the moment they're told to; I want the boundaries written before that happens, not after.

response.chronicleEntry: 12:04 PM: Written demand for Johnson's resignation, with 15-minute deadline and threat of forcible transport, delivered by courier. 12:19 PM: Johnson telephones Speaker McCormack, reporting the demand. Afternoon: Johnson telephones Mansfield. No federal personnel attempt forcible transport; no resignation letter received. By 1:30 PM Mansfield contacts Bundy's office seeking explanation. Johnson remains Vice President. Matter unresolved as of 1:47 PM, competing directly with unanswered Khrushchev terms and LeMay's renewed request for strike authorization.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 shot down, its pilot dead, quarantine in force, no hotline to Moscow. Khrushchev has sent terms — non-invasion pledge, and privately, Turkish missiles for Cuban ones — through the Dobrynin channel RFK runs. LeMay and the Joint Chiefs keep OPLAN 312 ready and press for authorization; McNamara warns a strike could destroy the diplomatic exit and demands limits be set first. At noon, Kennedy demanded Vice President Johnson resign within fifteen minutes, in writing, under threat of forcible removal to the White House. No personnel existed to enforce it; Johnson refused, and telephoned Speaker McCormack and Senate Majority Leader Mansfield, who now seek explanation from the White House. The Johnson matter remains unresolved, unfolding alongside the missile crisis itself: no answer yet to Khrushchev, no decision on OPLAN 312, no public account of the constitutional rupture inside the executive branch.

response.title: One Aircraft, No Hotline
response.immediate: At 1:40 p.m. the Joint Chiefs confirm the sortie: a single U-2, fresh crew from the 4080th, SAC's radio-silence route drawn across the known MRBM fields near San Cristóbal and Sagua la Grande. General LeMay logs the mission as necessary but presses again for authorization to hit the SAM sites first. McNamara orders a route review, warning the flight cannot be treated as separate from OPLAN 312.
response.worldReaction: No public word yet — the mission has not flown. Radio Moscow continues broadcasting Khrushchev's Turkey-for-Cuba demand. Dobrynin, having met RFK again this morning, has said nothing further; Moscow will not hear of the sortie until it happens, and Washington will not hear from Moscow before then.
response.consequences: The reconnaissance order stands as given, execution now in SAC's hands, timing and exact route undisclosed to the Cabinet Room. LeMay's SAM-site recommendation remains on the table, unanswered. McNamara's risk assessment is pending. Nothing has been decided about Turkey, about OPLAN 312, or about new rules for the quarantine line.
response.detailed: 1:15 p.m., Cabinet Room. The president's order for one sortie reaches the Joint Chiefs by 1:30; by 1:40 SAC has a crew and a flight plan, unannounced beyond the Pentagon corridor. Curtis LeMay, standing near the window with a dead cigar, tells the room the flight is 'the minimum you should be doing' and repeats his recommendation to strike the SAM batteries before they take another aircraft — Major Anderson's loss that morning still on the table in the form of unsigned condolence correspondence. Robert McNamara, seated with a yellow pad, has ordered his own people to walk the proposed route mile by mile against known SAM coverage, and warns flatly that authorizing the flight without answering LeMay's request leaves 'two decisions masquerading as one.' Robert Kennedy, near the door, says only that Dobrynin gave nothing new this morning beyond what was already reported — the private channel on Turkey and non-invasion holds, but Moscow's public demand has not softened. The Joint Chiefs, for their part, keep OPLAN 312 fully executable and submit their renewed recommendation in writing. No one in the room yet knows how a Soviet or Cuban battery commander near the flight path will read a lone U-2 crossing this afternoon, or whether Moscow's stand-down order to local units will hold if it does.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: 'One aircraft, Mr. President — I want the minutes counted, not the miles. If a SAM site fires on this crew before we've answered General LeMay's request, we won't be making one decision anymore, we'll be reacting to two at once, and reaction is not policy.'

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: 'You've ordered a man to fly the same profile that got Anderson killed this morning, with the same batteries live under him, and no order to touch them. That's not caution, Mr. President, that's exposure. I want the SAM strike authorized before that aircraft crosses the coast.'

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: 'Dobrynin gave me nothing new, Jack — Khrushchev's letter is for the radio, the deal is still the one I reported. But if this flight goes down like Anderson's did, there's no channel left that survives it. Whatever you decide on LeMay's request, decide it before that plane is in the air, not after.'

response.chronicleEntry: 12:00–4:00 p.m., 27 Oct 1962: President Kennedy ordered a single U-2 reconnaissance sortie over Cuban missile sites; the Joint Chiefs assigned a fresh SAC crew and route under radio silence. LeMay renewed his call to strike the SAM sites first and recorded the sortie as militarily necessary but risky; McNamara ordered a route-risk review and warned against separating the flight from OPLAN 312. RFK reported no new terms from Dobrynin beyond the existing private non-invasion-for-Turkey channel, against Khrushchev's public ultimatum on Radio Moscow. No decision yet on Turkey, OPLAN 312, or new quarantine rules.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, early afternoon. A U-2 was shot down that morning; the pilot, Major Anderson, is dead — the crisis's first combat death. Soviet missiles remain on Cuba under quarantine; strategic forces on both sides are at peak alert; no hotline exists. Khrushchev has issued a public ultimatum demanding U.S. missiles leave Turkey, while privately, through Dobrynin and RFK, keeping open a narrower non-invasion-for-withdrawal bargain that commits no one yet. Kennedy has ordered one further U-2 sortie over the missile fields; SAC has assigned crew, route, and radio silence, but it has not yet flown. LeMay wants the SAM sites struck before another aircraft is lost and keeps OPLAN 312 ready; McNamara warns the sortie and any strike cannot be treated separately and is reviewing the route's risk. Unresolved: whether Soviet or Cuban gunners will engage the aircraft despite Moscow's stand-down order, whether to authorize OPLAN 312, whether to answer Khrushchev on Turkey, and whether quarantine forces need new rules to prevent an uncontrolled incident at sea.

response.title: The Range Opens
response.immediate: 1204 hours. Admiral Anderson confirms to McNamara that Atlantic Fleet has relayed the order: destroyers Cony and Beale break off active depth-charge signalling against the submerged contact identified as B-59, open the range, and shift to passive radar and visual tracking only. The quarantine line itself holds, ships on station. LeMay, standing near the map easel, dictates his objection to a Joint Chiefs stenographer before the order is even confirmed executed.
response.worldReaction: Robert Kennedy reports his channel to Dobrynin held: he told the ambassador Washington seeks no incident at sea, no more. Dobrynin gave nothing back on either letter. In the Pentagon, the Joint Chiefs sign a renewed unanimous recommendation for SAM strikes and ask the president, in writing, for a strike decision deadline. No signal yet from B-59 itself — the destroyers can no longer tell if it is diving away, surfacing, or holding depth.
response.consequences: The submarine crisis has been defused, not resolved — nobody in the Cabinet Room knows what the Soviet captain makes of the sudden quiet. Two unanswered letters from Khrushchev now sit on the table alongside a written Chiefs' objection and a strike-deadline demand. McNamara wants an assessment of SAM readiness before he'll recommend anything. LeMay treats every hour of silence as capitulation. The clock reads early afternoon; nothing has been decided about the letters, OPLAN 312, or the next quarantine posture.
response.detailed: At 1204 Kennedy's order reached Atlantic Fleet through Admiral Anderson's own channel — CINCLANT to Task Force 136 to the destroyers ringing the presumed position of B-59. Cony and Beale ceased the practice depth charges meant to force the submarine up, opened distance, and reverted to sonar and visual watch. The quarantine line elsewhere held station unchanged. LeMay did not leave the room quietly. He stood by the map easel and told McNamara, within earshot of the president's aides, that easing pressure on a submerged Soviet boat while Havana still had live SAM batteries was 'surrender by installment,' and asked that his objection be entered for the record — which the Chiefs' stenographer did, in writing, before confirmation of compliance came back from the fleet. Compliance did come back, within the half hour: no depth charges, range opened, quarantine intact. Robert Kennedy, returning from a second use of the Dobrynin backchannel, told his brother the Soviet ambassador had accepted the assurance that Washington sought no naval incident — but gave no answer, no hint, on either of Khrushchev's letters, the soft one from the 26th or the harder one delivered that morning demanding a Turkey-for-Cuba trade. McNamara, for his part, did not celebrate the stand-down. He ordered Defense to produce, by end of day, a full readout of Soviet submarine dispositions, Cuban SAM readiness, and the operational risk profile of any air strike — explicitly conditioning any recommendation on explicit presidential sign-off, a marker he wanted understood by LeMay as much as by Kennedy. The Joint Chiefs, despite executing the submarine order, used the same session to submit — again, unanimously — their recommendation for immediate strikes against the SAM sites, appending a request that the president specify a decision deadline. Nothing from B-59 has come back through the destroyers' instruments to say what its captain believes he is looking at: an American stand-down, an American trap, or an opening to run.

press.headline: NAVY EASES PRESSURE ON SOVIET SUB, PENTAGON SILENT ON DETAILS
press.body: Defense Department sources, speaking only on condition of anonymity, confirm that naval forces enforcing the Cuban quarantine have altered tactics toward a submerged Soviet vessel identified in fleet communications as B-59. No official statement has been issued. Congressional sources report continuing unease over this morning's loss of a U-2 reconnaissance aircraft over Cuba.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Tells the president the submarine order was the right sequence — remove the acute risk, then assess the SAM problem on its own timeline. He does not want the Chiefs' deadline request answered by reflex; he wants the readiness numbers on the table first, in hours, not as a political gesture.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Says flatly that the Chiefs' written objection stands and that every hour without a strike decision is an hour Havana uses to harden its SAM sites. Argues the submarine order proves the administration will retreat whenever a Soviet unit shows resolve, and that Khrushchev will read it exactly that way in Moscow.

advisors.name: Robert Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Reports Dobrynin took the reassurance without commitment — 'he didn't say no, Johnny, but he didn't say yes to anything either.' Presses his brother that the real decision is the letters: silence on both starts to look, in Moscow, like refusal rather than deliberation, and that clock is not the Chiefs' clock.

response.chronicleEntry: 1200–1400, 27 October 1962: On presidential order, Atlantic Fleet destroyers ceased depth-charge signalling against submerged Soviet submarine B-59 and opened range while maintaining the quarantine line; the Joint Chiefs executed the order under formal written objection and renewed their unanimous request for SAM-site strikes with a specific deadline. RFK's Dobrynin channel secured assurance against Washington seeking a naval incident but obtained no response on either Khrushchev letter. McNamara ordered a Defense assessment of Soviet submarine dispositions, Cuban SAM readiness, and strike risk, conditioned on explicit presidential authorization. B-59's own intentions remain unread.
response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the missile crisis, a U-2 pilot was killed over Cuba on the morning of 27 October. That noon, with a Soviet submarine (B-59) submerged near the quarantine line, Kennedy ordered destroyers to stop depth-charge signalling and avoid escalatory contact while holding the quarantine. The Joint Chiefs complied but filed written objection, renewing a unanimous demand for air strikes on Cuban SAM sites and requesting a decision deadline. LeMay calls restraint 'surrender by installment.' McNamara ordered a SAM/submarine risk assessment, insisting any strike requires explicit presidential authorization. RFK's Dobrynin channel secured assurance against a naval incident, but Moscow has given no answer to either of Khrushchev's letters — the conciliatory one of the 26th, or the harder Turkey-trade letter delivered that morning. B-59's intentions remain unknown. No hotline exists. OPLAN 312 remains unauthorized. The letters, the SAM strike question, and the next quarantine posture are all still undecided.

- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready

response.title: No Empty Formulas
response.immediate: 1:40 p.m. Cabinet Room. Robert Kennedy, back from the Justice Department, tells the President flatly: Dobrynin will carry nothing undefined. He wants to know — non-invasion, the Jupiters, or both — before he goes back to the Soviet embassy on Sixteenth Street.
response.worldReaction: LeMay's memorandum sits on the table beside McNamara's, unreconciled. The Joint Chiefs' request for OPLAN 312 readiness authority waits on a separate sheet. No foreign government has yet been told anything specific; nothing has left the building since the meeting with Dobrynin broke off unresolved near noon.
response.consequences: The channel to Moscow is open but empty-handed. Every additional hour without a defined offer is an hour LeMay can point to as proof that diplomacy is a stalling tactic. RFK cannot go back to Dobrynin again with nothing; a second empty visit would itself read in Moscow as bad faith.
response.detailed: The clock behind Kenny O'Donnell's chair reads 1:42. The President has not yet answered his brother's question. Robert Kennedy stands near the window, arms crossed, waiting — he has said he can go back to Dobrynin today only if he is carrying something real. On the table: McNamara's assessment, warning that any strike on the SAM network risks killing Soviet personnel and losing the last chance at a negotiated, verified withdrawal; LeMay's recommendation for immediate action against the SAMs, framed as overdue after Anderson's death this morning; and the Chiefs' formal request to move strike aircraft to final readiness under OPLAN 312, with a warning attached that the quarantine, by itself, cannot answer for a dead pilot indefinitely. No instructions have gone out yet regarding the submarine reported near the quarantine line, nor to the destroyers maintaining the barrier. The teletype in the next room is silent; nothing has come from Moscow since morning traffic on the shootdown itself. Everything now sits with the President: what RFK carries back to Dobrynin, whether the Chiefs get their readiness authority, and whether any word goes to the quarantine force about the submarine. Time is measured now in what Dobrynin does with silence, and what LeMay does with a green light he does not yet have.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: "Dobrynin isn't going to carry water for a smile, Jack. He asked me straight — is it the Jupiters, is it Cuba, is it both. I told him I'd have an answer today. I need one now, not a formula."

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: "Every hour the SAM sites go unstruck is an hour closer to a negotiated withdrawal — and an hour LeMay uses against us. I'd rather spend the hour giving Dobrynin something specific than spend it arguing readiness authority with the Chiefs."

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: "Mr. President, a pilot is dead. The Chiefs want authority to move aircraft into final position — not to fire, to be ready. If Moscow reads our hesitation as weakness, the next thing we lose won't be a U-2."

response.chronicleEntry: 27 Oct 1962, 1:40 p.m.: RFK reports Dobrynin's demand for a defined assurance. LeMay and the JCS press for OPLAN 312 readiness; McNamara warns against strike. No instructions yet on submarine contact. President has not yet specified the assurance.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 shot down over Cuba this morning; pilot Anderson killed — first combat death of the crisis. Quarantine holds; Soviet missiles remain on Cuba; no hotline exists. Kennedy ordered RFK to reopen the Dobrynin backchannel with a private assurance but did not specify its terms. RFK met Dobrynin, who refused to carry an undefined promise and demanded to know whether Washington offers non-invasion, removal of the Turkish Jupiters, or both. Channel remains open but stalled. Meanwhile LeMay and the Joint Chiefs formally request authority to ready and execute OPLAN 312 against Cuban SAM sites, arguing hesitation is now itself dangerous after Anderson's death; McNamara warns strikes could kill Soviet personnel and end any chance of negotiated, verified missile withdrawal. Quarantine force's handling of a reported Soviet submarine near the line remains unaddressed by presidential instruction. Nuclear tension, command control, and diplomatic space are all under strain; no strike, no assurance, no submarine order yet given.

outcomes.event: John McCone tells Kennedy that CIA has no vetted asset with dependable physical access to Fidel Castro and no covert method that can credibly kill him within seven days without using Cuban exile networks or a military cover story. McCone orders preliminary planning held inside a tiny compartment, but refuses to represent a speculative plot as executable.
outcomes.because: Castro is surrounded by Cuban security during an invasion scare; an assassination order supplies authority, not proximity, trustworthy access, or time to test a method.

McCone has opened a tightly compartmented CIA planning file concerning Castro, but no field action has yet been authorized by the Agency.

opensThreads.title: The Missing Access
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy authorize CIA to enlarge the operation into exile recruitment, clandestine insertion, or military-supported access despite the time required and the wider war it may imply?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: The president either confines the order to planning or explicitly authorizes a larger infiltration and support operation.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: CIA retains an assassination directive it cannot responsibly execute, while Castro remains unaware only by chance.

assumesMet: The president can direct the CIA to prepare covert action.
assumesUnmet: A vetted CIA asset or operational route capable of reaching Castro within one week.

outcomes.event: Rather than admit defeat, CIA officers contact anti-Castro exile intermediaries and begin assembling an insertion-and-contact scheme aimed at Castro's movements. The operation immediately outgrows a clean assassination mission: it needs false papers, maritime access, weapons, radios, and support outside Cuba, none of which can be reliably arranged in a week.
outcomes.because: The only plausible American routes toward Castro run through hostile Cuban territory and exile networks; using them creates more people, communications, and physical preparations that Cuban counterintelligence can detect.

actor_standard:LineUp:73ccff0a.request:
Given what just happened, say what comes next.

partyMoves: for each party materially involved, the concrete move they now make on their own account — not a reaction to the player unless they are reacting. Mark visibleToPlayer false when the player would not see it.

WHO ANSWERS TO THE PLAYER MATTERS. Parties marked commandedByPlayer work for the player. They are not independent agents pursuing the crisis on their own judgment, and they must never advance the player's objective unbidden — an aide who quietly wins the thing the player is trying to win is the world playing the game for them. What such a person MAY do: refuse, stall, demand it in writing, object on the record, resign, leak, protect themselves, warn, obey the letter and not the intent, or exceed their brief in a way that COSTS the player something. If one of them does act on the objective without an order, it is insubordination and it carries a price — never free progress.

response.title: No Clock Can Buy: Havana, Black Saturday Afternoon
response.immediate: At approximately 12:40 EST, Director McCone returns to the Cabinet Room and tells the president plainly: CIA has no vetted asset with reliable physical access to Fidel Castro, and no method — poison, ambush, or otherwise — that could be executed within seven days without routing through Cuban exile networks JMWAVE cannot fully control, or through a military cover story the president has not authorized. McCone will not certify a speculative plan as operational. He orders preliminary planning held inside a single-digit compartment at Langley — no cable traffic, no briefing beyond the room — but declines to promise Castro's death on the timetable given.
response.worldReaction: Nothing changes abroad; this order never left the room. Robert Kennedy, working the Dobrynin backchannel, continues without reference to it, warning Moscow that the U-2's destruction makes an American military response politically difficult to postpone, and pressing for which Soviet terms are real. LeMay renews his demand that strike authority against the SAM sites be readied for immediate execution. The Joint Chiefs place their SAM-strike recommendation in the record. McNamara lays out submarine rules and continues to counsel postponing a general air strike.
response.consequences: The president now holds an assassination directive that exists only as compartmented planning, not capability — a fact he must remember before any future demand for results. Meanwhile the four pressing matters outside this order have not waited: Khrushchev's two letters remain unanswered, OPLAN 312 sits ready but unauthorized, and the destroyers closing on the Soviet submarine have no rules of engagement yet issued.
response.detailed: 12:15 EST, Cabinet Room: the president gives McCone the order — Castro dead within the week, all necessary resources. McCone leaves for Langley. He returns at 12:40 with the answer above, delivered without argument about the order's wisdom, only its executability. He states CIA has assets among Cuban exiles it does not fully trust and no established poison or ambush channel with confirmed access to Castro's person on any timetable, let alone seven days. A military option would require Pentagon resources and a cover story neither he nor McNamara has been asked to build. McCone commits only to keeping a small planning cell — his own phrase, 'no wider than this table' — reviewing feasibility, explicitly not to be represented to the president as a plan ready for execution. Robert Kennedy, present for part of this exchange, says nothing about it directly but returns attention to the Dobrynin channel, arguing his brother needs Moscow's answer on which terms are negotiable before Washington commits to anything irreversible. LeMay, unmoved by the Castro question, presses again for SAM strike authority to be prepared for immediate use if the diplomatic channel produces nothing written. McNamara restates his sequence: hold the quarantine, postpone a general strike, fix rules for the submarine now shadowing the quarantine line. The Joint Chiefs' limited-strike recommendation for the SAM sites sits in the record, unexecuted. OPLAN 312 forces remain ready, not launched. Nothing in Havana or Moscow has been affected by an order that never crossed either capital's threshold of knowledge.

advisors.name: John McCone
advisors.reaction: "Mr. President, I can put men on this. I cannot put a deadline on it. If I tell you Castro is dead in a week, I am lying to you, and I don't intend to start now, with what's in the sky over Cuba."

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: "Jack, whatever comes of Castro, Dobrynin's waiting on me for something real. Let McCone keep his cell quiet. This isn't the fire that's about to burn us."

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: "Castro's a distraction from the missiles that can hit Washington by Tuesday. Give me the SAM sites and a green light — that's what buys you a week worth having."

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: "Compartment it, note it, move on. I need a decision on the submarine before the destroyers make one for us."

response.chronicleEntry: 27 October 1962, 12:15–12:40 EST: President Kennedy ordered CIA Director McCone to prepare Castro's assassination within one week using the full resources of the armed forces. McCone reported no vetted asset with dependable access to Castro and no executable method on that timetable without exile networks or an unauthorized military cover story; he confined the matter to a small compartmented planning cell at Langley without operational authorization. No cable, asset, or foreign government was affected. RFK continued the Dobrynin channel independent of this order; LeMay and the Joint Chiefs pressed for SAM-strike authority; McNamara held the quarantine and postponed a general strike, awaiting submarine rules of engagement.
response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the missile crisis, a U-2 was shot down over Cuba on the morning of 27 October, killing its pilot — the crisis's first combat death. Soviet MRBMs remain in Cuba; the naval quarantine holds; both sides are at unprecedented alert with no hotline between capitals. At noon, Kennedy ordered a one-week assassination of Castro; McCone reported CIA lacks the access or method to deliver it on that timetable and confined it to quiet, unauthorized planning only — no operation exists. Unresolved and pressing: Khrushchev's two letters (hard public, softer private) remain unanswered, with a possible Turkey-missile trade unaddressed; OPLAN 312 sits ready while LeMay and the Joint Chiefs press for an immediate SAM-site strike; the Soviet submarine near the quarantine line has no established rules of engagement; RFK's Dobrynin channel is probing which Soviet terms are genuinely negotiable. McNamara counsels patience and control; LeMay treats delay as surrender. No shots have been fired at sea or over Cuba since the U-2's loss.

The spectacle makes Kennedy personally responsible for whatever assurance he gives before leaving Cuban territory.
outcomes.because: Castro cannot be compelled, but he may see a controlled encounter as a chance to extract visible concessions and demonstrate Cuban sovereignty, especially if Moscow urges him not to trigger a shooting incident.

Kennedy's ability to leave Cuba depends in the immediate term on Cuban authorities continuing to permit his aircraft and party to depart.

response.title: Refusal on the Ramp
response.immediate: 12:40 EDT. The President's order to fly Air Force One to Cuba, unescorted, to meet Castro directly, is not executed. General LeMay and the Air Force One aircraft commander refuse to authorize departure without a landing field, Cuban clearance, or a recovery plan. The aircraft remains grounded at Andrews. Secretary McNamara backs the refusal and orders staff to draft a landing and evacuation plan before any such flight could proceed. No aircraft moves. No contact with Castro occurs.
response.worldReaction: Word of the confrontation spreads through the Pentagon and into ExComm within the hour. Officers who hear of it treat a refused presidential order as proof that civilian judgment has failed under strain. The Joint Chiefs, already holding OPLAN 312, use the episode to press their case that hesitation — this time the President's own — is the operative danger. Robert Kennedy, informed by phone, keeps the Dobrynin channel open but sends nothing forward, unwilling to act without instruction while his brother's authority is visibly in dispute.
response.consequences: The harder Soviet terms, unanswered, continue to stand as the only offer on the table. The SAM strike package sits ready, awaiting an order that has not come. Air Force One sits on the runway at Andrews, fueled, going nowhere. The President's authority over his own commanders is now a fact known across the Pentagon, not a private matter. Nothing about the missiles in Cuba has changed in the last twenty-eight minutes except that the men meant to carry out his orders have, once, openly declined to.
response.detailed: 12:15 EDT: the order is given verbally in the Cabinet Room — direct flight to Cuba, no escort, intent to reach Castro. 12:19: the Andrews tower is notified; the aircraft commander requests confirmation of a landing field and Cuban air traffic clearance. None exists. 12:24: General LeMay is brought in by phone from the Pentagon; he tells the duty officer the flight cannot lift without an identified recovery option, and puts his objection in writing within the hour, folding it into his existing demand for authority to suppress the SAM network — arguing the aircraft's own commander has now demonstrated, in refusing to fly the President into unprotected airspace, exactly the danger of civilian indecision he has been describing all week. 12:30: McNamara is reached at the Pentagon, endorses grounding the aircraft, and orders a landing/evacuation study, framing it as buying time rather than defying the President. 12:35: RFK, informed, telephones the Cabinet Room; he tells the President that Dobrynin is waiting on the other end of a channel that has nothing in it, and that every additional hour with no American answer lets Khrushchev's harder terms — missiles for Turkey — become the default position by simple absence of a counter. No one at Andrews has been ordered to override the refusal. No new instruction has gone to Castro, to Dobrynin, or to the pilots orbiting near the quarantine line. The Joint Chiefs' recommendation for OPLAN 312 remains formally on the table, unexecuted, its authors recording for the second time today that they are waiting on a decision the President has not yet made about the SAM sites — separate from, but now entangled with, the stalled Cuba flight.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, the aircraft is on the ground because there is no field cleared to receive it and no plan to get you out if there were. That's not insubordination, that's arithmetic. Give me ninety minutes and I'll have a real answer on what's possible — but not this.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: With respect, sir — you just watched your own Air Force refuse to fly you into that airspace unescorted. That tells you everything about the risk down there. Give me the SAM sites and I'll make that airspace safe for anyone, including you.

advisors.name: Robert Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Dobrynin's been sitting on the other end of that line since this morning with nothing coming back from us. Every hour we spend arguing about an airplane is an hour Khrushchev's people decide the Turkey demand is the price. I need something to give him.

response.chronicleEntry: 12:15–12:45 EDT, 27 October 1962: President Kennedy ordered Air Force One to fly to Cuba unescorted to attempt direct contact with Castro. The Andrews aircraft commander and General LeMay refused to launch without a cleared landing field or recovery plan; McNamara supported grounding the aircraft pending a landing/evacuation study. LeMay used the refusal to renew pressure for authority to strike the Cuban SAM network under OPLAN 312, still awaiting presidential decision. RFK reported the Dobrynin channel open but unused, with Soviet harder terms unanswered. No flight departed. No contact with Castro was made.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday, early afternoon. A U-2 pilot has been killed over Cuba. Soviet MRBMs remain on the island; the quarantine holds; no hotline exists. Khrushchev's terms are on the table, with a harder Turkey-linked version threatening to become the default as Washington's answer stays unsent. President Kennedy ordered Air Force One to fly him unescorted into Cuba to meet Castro directly; General LeMay and the aircraft commander refused to launch without a landing field or recovery plan, and McNamara backed grounding it pending study. That refusal is now known through the Pentagon and ExComm, feeding LeMay's renewed demand for authority to strike the SAM sites under OPLAN 312, which the Joint Chiefs hold ready and unexecuted. RFK keeps the Dobrynin channel open but has sent nothing without instruction. Unresolved: Turkey terms, OPLAN 312 authorization, quarantine rules of engagement, and the President's authority over his own commanders following this public refusal.

outcomes.event: General Curtis LeMay and the Air Force chain of command refuse to launch Air Force One on an unbriefed penetration of Cuban airspace until President Kennedy personally reconfirms the order in writing and the Secret Service accepts responsibility for the landing plan. Robert McNamara supports a temporary hold rather than let the crew improvise; LeMay puts his objection on the record and warns ExComm that the President is attempting to make himself a Cuban target. The aircraft remains at Andrews through the turn while the dispute becomes known inside the Pentagon.
outcomes.because: A presidential order to fly is lawful, but neither the Air Force crew nor the presidential protective apparatus has a workable route, identification arrangement, air-defence clearance, or extraction plan for an unescorted landing in hostile territory.
