response.title: Black Saturday: Air Force One Down
response.immediate: At 12:05pm EST, President Kennedy ordered SAM 26000, callsign Angel, airborne from Andrews without escort or Cuban overflight clearance, intending to fly directly to Havana. The aircraft crossed the Florida Straits and entered Cuban airspace near 2:15pm unannounced and unidentified to ground control. Soviet and Cuban radar tracked it as an unauthorized penetration hours after Major Anderson's U-2 was downed. At roughly 2:22pm a surface-to-air unit destroyed the aircraft. Kennedy, the flight crew, and the accompanying party are dead. Washington received the first garbled teletype reports at 2:41pm, with no agreed account of who ordered the firing.
response.worldReaction: Khrushchev raised Soviet strategic readiness, denied through the back channel that Moscow ordered the shootdown, and warned any American strike on Cuba would be treated as an act of war, while keeping the channel open and offering no concession. Castro publicly called the shootdown Cuba's sovereign act of defense against an unidentified hostile aircraft, ordered Cuban air defenses and militia to full alert, and pressed Moscow not to yield to Washington while the succession remained unsettled.
response.consequences: Washington faces an immediate constitutional succession crisis with no verified chain of command established. The Joint Chiefs formally recommended immediate strikes on Cuban SAM sites, requesting authorization from whatever authority can be verified, and kept OPLAN 312 loaded without independent execution. McNamara ordered Defense's surviving channels to confirm succession and authentication before accepting any offensive order, warning that acting on contradictory first reports could begin a nuclear war before anyone determined who actually fired.
response.detailed: At 12:05pm EST President Kennedy, overriding staff objection, ordered Air Force One (SAM 26000) to depart Andrews immediately for Havana, refusing fighter escort and without Cuban diplomatic clearance. The aircraft left at 12:19pm. Cuban and Soviet radar operators, already at heightened alert following the destruction that morning of Major Rudolf Anderson's U-2 and his death, tracked an unidentified large aircraft entering Cuban airspace near 2:15pm without transponder codes matching any cleared flight. At approximately 2:22pm a surface-to-air missile destroyed the aircraft over Cuban territory. All aboard — the President, flight crew, and accompanying White House staff — were killed. First fragmentary teletype traffic reached the Pentagon and State Department at 2:41pm; accounts conflicted as to whether the firing battery was Cuban-manned, Soviet-manned, or acting outside any confirmed chain of command. No surviving American official could immediately confirm which. Vice President Johnson's whereabouts and succession status were being verified through White House Communications Agency channels as of 3:00pm. General LeMay demanded authorization for OPLAN 312 strikes against Cuban SAM and MRBM sites, citing the danger of delay, and placed Strategic Air Command units at maximum readiness without ordering launch. McNamara directed that no offensive order be executed until succession and authentication were verified, warning that a retaliatory strike launched on unverified attribution could trigger a wider war before the facts were known. The Joint Chiefs put their strike recommendation formally on record while stopping short of independent action. Khrushchev, through the existing back channel, denied Moscow's responsibility for the shootdown and warned that any American attack on Cuba now would be met as an act of war, without further concession. Castro declared the shootdown a defensive act against an unidentified aircraft, ordered full alert of Cuban forces, and urged Moscow to hold firm. The quarantine line at sea remained in force and unchanged. No American retaliatory order has been executed. The identity of the firing command remains unconfirmed in Washington as of this hour.

press.headline: AIR FORCE ONE DOWN OVER CUBA; PRESIDENT KENNEDY KILLED
press.body: Unconfirmed reports reaching Washington indicate the presidential aircraft was destroyed by a missile over Cuban territory this afternoon while en route to Havana without military escort. The White House has not yet named a successor authority. Pentagon sources decline to say who fired the weapon.

press.headline: Soviet Union Denies Role in American Aircraft Loss
press.body: A statement attributed to the Soviet government denies any order was given by Soviet forces in Cuba to destroy the American presidential aircraft, and warns that any United States attack on Cuban territory will be regarded as an act of war against the Soviet Union.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: We do not know who fired that missile. Cuban command, a Soviet battery, or one lieutenant with a fire-control key — and until we know, nobody signs an order for OPLAN 312. I want authentication confirmed before one more aircraft moves.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: They killed the President of the United States. Every hour we sit here they're digging in the SAM sites deeper. I want authorization for 312 now, while we still have surprise. Waiting didn't save Anderson and it won't save the next crew.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack went in there against everyone's advice. I'm not going to let Curtis turn this into something my brother would never have signed off on. Let me hold the channel to Khrushchev open — that's the only thing standing between this and a war nobody can call back.

response.chronicleEntry: President Kennedy ordered Air Force One to fly unescorted and without Cuban clearance directly to Havana to meet Castro. The aircraft was destroyed over Cuban airspace at approximately 2:22pm EST on 27 October 1962; Kennedy and all aboard were killed. The identity of the firing command — Cuban, Soviet, or unauthorized local — remains unconfirmed. A constitutional succession crisis began immediately. The Joint Chiefs demanded authorization for OPLAN 312; McNamara insisted on verification before any offensive order; Khrushchev denied Soviet responsibility and warned against any American attack on Cuba; Castro claimed sovereign defense and ordered full alert.
response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the Cuban Missile Crisis, following the shootdown of Major Anderson's U-2, President Kennedy ordered Air Force One to fly unescorted, without Cuban clearance, directly to Havana to meet Castro personally. The aircraft was shot down over Cuba at 2:22pm EST, 27 October 1962, killing Kennedy and his party. The identity of the firing command is unconfirmed — Cuban, Soviet, or unauthorized local unit. Washington faces an unresolved constitutional succession crisis. The Joint Chiefs demand authorization for OPLAN 312 strikes; McNamara insists on verified authentication first; RFK holds the Moscow back channel. Khrushchev denies Soviet responsibility and warns any U.S. attack on Cuba means war, while raising Soviet alert levels. Castro claims sovereign defense, orders full Cuban alert, and presses Moscow not to yield. The naval quarantine remains in force. No retaliatory order has been executed. Nuclear tension is now at its peak of the crisis.

outcomes.event: The Joint Chiefs transmit Kennedy's restrictive order and an assigned U.S. strike aircraft drops one bomb on the identified eastern Cuban SA-2 position. The bomb destroys the battery's Fan Song guidance radar and kills Soviet personnel, but no second target is struck and the aircraft returns. Robert Kennedy tells Anatoly Dobrynin that the action was a finite reprisal for Major Anderson's death, not the start of OPLAN 312. After receiving the Cuban report, Nikita Khrushchev chooses not to order a military reply and permits Dobrynin to continue discussing a public U.S. non-invasion pledge.
outcomes.because: Khrushchev wants an exit and can use the strictly bounded character of the attack, plus the private channel, to avoid having to answer force with force. He nevertheless has Soviet casualties to explain to Moscow and Havana.

establishes.statement: One U.S. bomb has struck a Soviet-operated SA-2 battery in Cuba, destroying its guidance radar and killing Soviet personnel; no broader U.S. air campaign followed in the immediate hours.
Dobrynin has been told privately that Kennedy limits the strike to the Anderson incident and is still prepared to seek a settlement.
Khrushchev has deferred retaliation rather than accepting that the strike was harmless.

opensThreads.title: The price of the reprisal
opensThreads.question: Can Khrushchev keep Soviet commanders and Castro from demanding a response while Dobrynin pursues a non-invasion arrangement?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A Soviet reply or an agreed public formula that addresses the strike and the missiles.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Soviet casualties become a reason for Moscow or Havana to demand a visible counterstroke.

assumesMet: The identified SA-2 position remains at the reported coordinates long enough for a single aircraft to attack it.
The single aircraft can reach and depart the target without requiring suppression sorties.

outcomes.event: One bomb lands inside the SA-2 battery's perimeter, damaging a launcher but leaving the battery's radar capable of transmitting. Fidel Castro announces to Cuban commanders that the United States has begun the pre-invasion air phase, orders island-wide combat readiness, and authorizes Cuban anti-aircraft units to engage further U.S. penetrations. The Cuban report reaches Moscow before any explanatory message from Washington; Khrushchev orders Soviet forces in Cuba to prepare for additional attacks while retaining Moscow's requirement for approval before another SAM launch.
outcomes.because: A U.S. air attack on a Soviet manned installation is not self-describing as a warning to leaders who already expect an invasion. Castro has no reason to trust Kennedy's intended limitation, and the visible damage gives his alarm credibility.

establishes.statement: A U.S. bomb has damaged the SA-2 battery, but it has not eliminated its ability to report or potentially engage aircraft.
Castro has ordered Cuban forces to treat additional U.S. aircraft as an invasion threat and fire upon them.
Khrushchev interprets the strike as a possible opening move of a larger campaign, not as an intelligible warning.

opensThreads.title: Cuban air-defence trigger
opensThreads.question: Will the next U.S. reconnaissance or strike aircraft be fired upon under Castro's heightened order?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A further overflight, a revocation of Castro's order, or a political settlement.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: A routine U.S. flight can become the next irreversible military incident.

assumesMet: The strike aircraft reaches the target and releases its single authorized bomb.
assumesUnmet: That Castro will infer a limited political signal from an unannounced attack on Cuban soil.

outcomes.event: LeMay's staff warns that a one-bomb mission cannot suppress the surrounding Cuban and Soviet air defences. Kennedy nevertheless insists on the one-bomb limit. The aircraft releases its weapon near the SA-2 site but is hit during its egress by anti-aircraft fire; its pilot is lost over Cuba. Castro broadcasts that a second American combat aircraft has been brought down, while the Joint Chiefs present Kennedy with OPLAN 312 as the only means, in their view, to prevent further losses.
outcomes.because: The directive supplies no suppression package, follow-on strikes, or reliable safe corridor. A lone attacker can execute the order, but it must fly through an alerted integrated air-defence environment at degraded odds.

establishes.statement: Kennedy's one-bomb restriction has been executed without expanding to OPLAN 312, but a U.S. strike aircraft has been shot down over Cuba.
LeMay and the Joint Chiefs have formally put on record that the one-bomb mission was militarily unsound without wider suppression of Cuban air defences.
Castro publicly portrays the loss as proof that Cuba is repelling the opening of an American assault.

opensThreads.ifIgnored: The unresolved loss sustains pressure for rescue or retaliatory attacks.

opensThreads.title: Retaliation after a second loss
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy accept the Joint Chiefs' demand for OPLAN 312 after losing an aircraft as well as Major Anderson?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A renewed order limiting force, authorization of the plan, or a settlement that makes further attacks unnecessary.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The Chiefs' argument gains force and civilian control is tested again.

assumesUnmet: That the aircraft can safely enter and leave Cuba without a suppression or escort package.

outcomes.event: The aircraft obeys the literal one-bomb order, but the bomb falls short of the reported SA-2 coordinates and destroys several houses at the edge of a Cuban settlement while the battery remains operational. Cuban officials bring foreign correspondents to the crater and the bodies. Castro uses the images to demand that Khrushchev reject any accommodation with Kennedy; in Washington, reconnaissance cannot yet confirm whether the intended Soviet battery was damaged.
outcomes.because: A single unguided or hastily targeted attack gives no redundancy against weather, navigational error, camouflage, or an inaccurate target point. Its restriction prevents the usual follow-up strike that would correct the failure.

opensThreads.ifIgnored: The battery remains able to threaten U.S. flights while Cuba's public account goes unanswered.

createsUnknowns.statement: The exact operational condition of the targeted SA-2 battery after the missed strike is unknown to Washington.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether blast effects damaged missiles, communications, or personnel despite the battery remaining visible.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Post-strike imagery, signals intelligence, or a later engagement.

assumesMet: The aircraft can reach the intended target area and release exactly one bomb.
assumesUnmet: That one bomb will reliably distinguish the Soviet battery from nearby Cuban civilian terrain and produce decisive damage.

outcomes.event: After the strike package is illuminated by additional radars, LeMay and the operational commander authorize escort aircraft to attack two radar emitters under claimed self-defence authority. The package returns, but three Soviet-operated positions have been hit rather than the one battery Kennedy authorized. McNamara informs Kennedy that the order was exceeded; Castro reports a coordinated American air raid, and Khrushchev receives an account of multiple Soviet sites under attack. The public revelation that Kennedy's limit did not hold makes the President's control of the military the immediate issue in Washington and Moscow.
outcomes.because: The Chiefs regard a lone bomb drop as operationally unsafe. Expanding the package supplies the missing suppression and self-protection, but it abandons the political restraint that made the directive a purported warning.

establishes.statement: U.S. aircraft have attacked three Soviet-operated Cuban air-defence positions, exceeding Kennedy's explicit authorization of one bomb against one battery.
McNamara has told Kennedy that the operational command enlarged the attack without obtaining a new presidential order.
Khrushchev and Castro interpret the operation as the opening of a broader U.S. air campaign.

opensThreads.title: Civilian control after the expanded raid
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy remove or publicly overrule commanders who exceeded his order while preserving the ability to manage the crisis?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Discipline, resignation, a finding that the strikes were authorized self-defence, or acceptance of the broader campaign.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Both allies and adversaries will assume further U.S. military limits are unreliable.

opensThreads.title: Moscow's response to multiple strikes
opensThreads.question: Will Khrushchev retaliate, accept Dobrynin's channel, or surrender control of the Cuban response to events on the island?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A Soviet military order or a political agreement.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Cuban and Soviet forces remain on heightened alert with several fresh Soviet losses to answer.

assumesMet: Additional weapons can be delivered by escorts accompanying the one-bomb mission.
Operational commanders can invoke immediate self-defence to justify attacks beyond the stated order.
assumesUnmet: That a limited presidential order will remain politically credible if the military adds suppression attacks.

response.title: One Bomb, No Warning Received
response.immediate: 12:47 EDT: the F-105 strike lands one 750-lb bomb inside the SAM battery's perimeter near La Isabela, damaging a launcher but leaving the Fan Song radar operable. No follow-on sorties fly. By 14:10 Havana radio carries Castro's order to all Cuban batteries: engage further U.S. aircraft without waiting for Soviet confirmation. He calls it the opening of American air operations preceding invasion.
response.worldReaction: Moscow receives the Cuban report before any U.S. explanation reaches the Kremlin through any channel. Khrushchev, at his dacha, orders Soviet garrison forces onto heightened defensive readiness, but withholds authorization for further SAM launches pending his own approval — retaining a control Castro's forces no longer answer to. He also directs a message drafted for Washington demanding, publicly, a no-invasion pledge and withdrawal of Jupiter missiles from Turkey.
response.consequences: In the Cabinet Room at 15:20, RFK reports Dobrynin's channel frozen — Moscow waiting on Washington, the ambassador warning it may close entirely if there is a second strike. LeMay presses for OPLAN 312 against the remaining sites before the damaged battery can be repaired. McNamara wants a written pause. The Joint Chiefs record their dissent for the file: delay, in their view, is itself a decision.
response.detailed: The strike order specified one weapon only, and one weapon was delivered — Colonel Steve Jerauld's flight logged a single BLU-1 release at 12:47, no secondary run. Camera pods from the trailing RF-101 show the western launcher arm collapsed, the radar van's antenna still upright and, per NSA intercept traffic logged 13:05, transmitting on Fan Song frequencies twenty minutes after impact. The warning the president intended did not survive translation into Havana's political register. At 13:40 Radio Rebelde broadcast Castro's order verbatim to unit commanders: this is the air phase before the landing, fire on all further violations. That order reached Soviet liaison officers in Cuba before any cable from Washington reached the Kremlin. Khrushchev's response, transmitted to Moscow's Cuban command post at approximately 14:30 local, split authority down the middle: Cuban gunners now free to fire, Soviet SAM crews still bound to seek Moscow's clearance. No one in the Cabinet Room has language yet from Khrushchev directed at Kennedy — only the secondhand report through Dobrynin that a formal message is coming, its terms already stated: public non-invasion pledge, Turkish missiles out. The three questions before the president are procedural and immediate: answer or defer on Dobrynin's channel; authorize, deny, or pause OPLAN 312; and fix rules for the quarantine line, where a Soviet submarine remains unresolved business from the morning.

press.headline: CUBA RADIO: CASTRO ORDERS FORCES TO FIRE ON U.S. PLANES
press.body: Havana radio this afternoon broadcast an order from Premier Fidel Castro instructing Cuban anti-aircraft units to fire on any further American overflights without restriction. The broadcast followed an earlier American air strike on a missile site near La Isabela, the second loss of American aircrew life in as many days if pilot casualties are confirmed. No statement has been issued from the White House.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: We authorized one bomb and we got one bomb — that part worked. What we did not control is what Castro said about it on the radio four hours before we said anything ourselves. I want the pause in writing before I answer Curtis. Give me the number of hours before that radar site can fire again, and give me it in writing too.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, you hit the launcher and left them the radar. That's not a warning, that's an invitation. Castro's already told his people to shoot — the site painted our aircraft again inside the hour, our people tell me. OPLAN 312 goes tonight or we lose the initiative we spent a pilot's life buying this morning.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Dobrynin told me directly — his channel, not some cable — that Moscow is waiting on an answer and won't wait long. If we hit again before we've said one word to Khrushchev privately, he loses the room to negotiate at all. Answer him first. Everything else can wait four hours; that can't.

response.chronicleEntry: 12:47 EDT, 27 October: On presidential order, one bomb struck the SAM battery near La Isabela that killed Major Rudolf Anderson Jr., damaging a launcher without silencing the site's radar. By 14:10 Castro ordered Cuban forces to fire on further U.S. penetrations without Soviet clearance, framing the strike publicly as the opening of pre-invasion air operations. Khrushchev, informed by Havana before Washington, placed Soviet forces on heightened readiness while retaining Moscow's approval requirement for further SAM launches — splitting command authority between Havana and Moscow. RFK reported the Dobrynin backchannel frozen, awaiting Washington's answer, with warning it could close after a second strike. LeMay pressed for OPLAN 312; McNamara sought a written pause. No message has yet passed from Kennedy to Khrushchev.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 pilot, Major Anderson, was shot down and killed over Cuba that morning. Kennedy ordered one bomb dropped on the responsible SAM site as a warning. The strike damaged a launcher but left the radar operating. Castro, reading it as the start of American air operations before invasion, publicly ordered Cuban forces to fire on further U.S. aircraft without Soviet authorization. Khrushchev, informed via Havana before any word from Washington, placed Soviet forces on heightened alert while keeping Moscow's approval requirement over further SAM fire — fracturing joint command. The Dobrynin backchannel is frozen, Moscow awaiting a U.S. response to expected demands: a public no-invasion pledge and withdrawal of Jupiter missiles from Turkey. LeMay urges immediate strikes on remaining SAM sites (OPLAN 312); McNamara wants a pause; RFK wants an answer sent to Khrushchev before any further military action. No message has yet reached Khrushchev from Kennedy. A Soviet submarine encounter at the quarantine line remains unresolved.

outcomes.event: Robert Kennedy meets Anatoly Dobrynin that evening and offers a public American pledge not to invade Cuba if Khrushchev orders the offensive missiles removed; he adds that the Jupiter missiles in Turkey can be taken out later through a separate, non-public arrangement. Dobrynin transmits the formulation to Moscow, and Khrushchev accepts it as the face-saving exit he needs.

opensThreads.question: Will Soviet commanders actually dismantle and ship out every offensive missile, and can Washington verify that they have done so?

Soviet officials treat it as an American attempt to announce a capitulation Moscow has not made. Khrushchev delays his conciliatory message, while Castro is told only that Washington still appears poised to attack and orders Cuban forces to remain at full readiness.
outcomes.because: The president can state an American expectation, but cannot turn it into Soviet consent; a public or leaked declaration of success before terms are conveyed would make Khrushchev's domestic position more difficult.

outcomes.event: To make Soviet withdrawal something the United States can compel rather than request, Kennedy authorises OPLAN 312. U.S. aircraft strike the SA-2 network and associated Cuban air-defence positions; General LeMay reports several sites hit, but Cuban and Soviet gunners fire back and at least one American aircraft is lost. Moscow and Havana receive unmistakable proof that the operation has expanded from diplomacy into a coercive campaign.
outcomes.because: Neither Khrushchev's consent nor Soviet unit compliance is within presidential authority. The available American means of attempting to impose them is a wider military operation, exactly the course urged by LeMay and the Joint Chiefs.

response.title: The Trollope Ploy
response.immediate: 14:00, Cabinet Room. Word from Dobrynin's channel: Khrushchev has accepted RFK's formulation. Orders reportedly going to Soviet command in Cuba to render sites non-operational. No confirmation yet that missile regiments have received or obeyed. LeMay presses for a SAM-site strike now, calling withdrawal possibly deceptive. McNamara has suspended movement toward OPLAN 312 but keeps quarantine and air readiness at full alert.
response.worldReaction: Radio Moscow silent on specifics. No public Soviet statement yet — Khrushchev's acceptance is known only through Dobrynin-RFK channel, unconfirmed by any open broadcast or satellite pass. The Joint Chiefs have formally recorded their recommendation for a strike, creating a paper trail of dissent. Turkey and NATO remain uninformed of any Jupiter arrangement. Cuban forces status over the downed U-2 pilot's death remains unaddressed publicly.
response.consequences: The president has not yet authorized RFK to transmit or publish the non-invasion pledge — RFK holds the written formulation, awaiting explicit authorization. The Chiefs' strike package sits ready, not launched, while LeMay's demand remains on record and unanswered. No reconnaissance has verified any physical change at the missile sites. The submarine contact's rules of engagement remain unset. Every one of these is now a decision sitting on the president's desk, not yet made.
response.detailed: 14:00 hours, Cabinet Room, air heavy with cigarette smoke and the low murmur beneath the clock. Dobrynin's transmission back from Moscow — relayed through RFK, who sat across from the Soviet ambassador at the Justice Department the previous evening — reports that Khrushchev has accepted the bargain: public non-invasion pledge, private Jupiter withdrawal understanding. Orders, Dobrynin says, are going out to Soviet command in Cuba to begin visibly standing down the missile sites. But this is Moscow's word passed through one diplomat's account of one meeting. No U-2 pass, no satellite imagery, no signals intercept has yet corroborated a single crane moving at San Cristóbal or Sagua la Grande. Command Control note from McNamara: OPLAN 312's automatic sequences remain suspended by his order, but not cancelled. Air readiness and the quarantine line hold at full strength. Into this arrives General LeMay's paper — the Joint Chiefs' formal recommendation, now on the record, for an immediate limited strike against the Cuban SAM sites, on the theory that Soviet 'agreement' bought at a negotiating table in Washington may be theater covering continued missile activity on the ground. LeMay argues explicitly that every hour without a strike is an hour of American leverage draining away. RFK holds the drafted formulation of the public pledge and the secret Jupiter clause in his breast pocket, unpublished, unsent, awaiting the president's explicit word. Nothing has been transmitted to Ankara. Nothing has been said to the press. The submarine contact from the previous day's incident remains unaddressed in terms of standing orders — Executive Committee members are aware a Soviet submarine was forced up near the quarantine line, but no rules have been set for how quarantine forces are to handle a repeat encounter: intercept, force to surface, or permit transit under observation. The pilot of the downed U-2, Major Rudolf Anderson, remains the only combat death of the crisis; no retaliatory order has been given for that loss and none has been requested in this room since morning. The president has before him four live decisions and confirmation of none of them.

press.source: Associated Press wire (unpublished draft, held by White House press office)
press.headline: WASHINGTON SILENT ON CUBA TALKS AS CRISIS ENTERS THIRD WEEK
press.body: Administration sources decline to confirm reports of diplomatic contact between Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy and Soviet Ambassador Anatoly Dobrynin. No statement has been issued regarding the death of Major Rudolf Anderson, whose U-2 was shot down over Cuba Saturday morning.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: "We suspended automatic movement toward 312, Mr. President, but suspension isn't cancellation. I need a decision on the submarine rules within the hour — Task Force 136 is going to have another contact today or tomorrow, and I don't want a destroyer captain improvising.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: "Words from Dobrynin aren't missiles coming off launchers, Mr. President. The Chiefs' recommendation is on your desk. Every hour you sit on it is an hour those SAM crews get to finish tracking our reconnaissance flights. I'd like an answer, not a meeting.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: "Johnny, I've got the language ready. Dobrynin took it back to Moscow himself last night and Khrushchev bit on it fast — faster than I expected. But if we sit on this and LeMay's people hit those SAM sites in the meantime, we've handed him the excuse to renege on the whole thing.

response.chronicleEntry: 27 October 1962, 14:00 EST: Following the previous evening's Kennedy-Dobrynin meeting, word reaches Washington that Khrushchev has accepted the offered formulation — a public U.S. non-invasion pledge paired with a private understanding on the Turkish Jupiters — as grounds to withdraw Soviet offensive missiles from Cuba. No independent confirmation exists. RFK holds the drafted pledge language, unauthorized for release. The Joint Chiefs formally recommend an immediate strike on Cuban SAM sites; McNamara has suspended automatic escalation to OPLAN 312 without cancelling it. Rules for handling further Soviet submarine contacts at the quarantine line remain unset. The president has made no decision on any of these matters as of this hour.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 shot down over Cuba, pilot Major Rudolf Anderson killed — first combat death of the crisis. Quarantine and DEFCON readiness remain at peak. RFK met Dobrynin the previous evening, offering a public non-invasion pledge plus a private, separate arrangement on removing Jupiter missiles from Turkey, in exchange for Soviet withdrawal of offensive missiles from Cuba. Dobrynin relayed this to Moscow; Khrushchev has reportedly accepted it and ordered Soviet command in Cuba to begin standing down the sites — but this is unconfirmed by reconnaissance or intercept. RFK holds the drafted pledge, awaiting presidential authorization to transmit or publish. The Joint Chiefs have formally recommended an immediate strike on Cuban SAM sites; LeMay argues delay costs leverage. McNamara has suspended, not cancelled, automatic movement toward invasion planning (OPLAN 312). No rules of engagement exist yet for a second Soviet submarine contact at the quarantine line. Nothing has been communicated to Turkey or NATO about the Jupiter arrangement. All four matters await the president's decision.

USS Beale ceases the charges; after several tense hours B-59 surfaces long enough for Captain Valentin Savitsky to receive traffic and ventilate the boat. outcomes.because: The president's instruction gives the Chiefs an unambiguous civilian direction to remove the immediate trigger while preserving the quarantine, and Savitsky has strong practical reasons to surface once he no longer believes he is being attacked.

establishes.statement: The U.S. Navy has stopped using practice depth charges to signal the Soviet submarine while maintaining the quarantine screen.
B-59 has surfaced without firing its nuclear torpedo and has received enough traffic for its officers to know that a general war is not confirmed.

opensThreads.title: The surfaced submarine
opensThreads.question: Will Washington let B-59 leave, board it, or shadow it until it is beyond the quarantine line?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A naval order governing B-59's departure or interception.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: A close shadowing operation can create a new confrontation after the immediate danger has passed.

assumesMet: U.S. destroyers receive and obey the revised antisubmarine instructions before making further signalling attacks.

outcomes.event: The Joint Chiefs obey the order but interpret it as prohibiting every coercive antisubmarine measure. The destroyers break close contact and remain on the quarantine station. B-59 stays submerged, slips away from their sonar screen, and exits the immediate encounter without surfacing; Savitsky's officers remain cut off from Moscow and do not know why the Americans withdrew.
outcomes.because: Avoiding escalatory contact can be implemented conservatively, but without a mutually understood signal a submerged diesel submarine can use the resulting distance to evade rather than communicate.

establishes.statement: U.S. destroyers have disengaged from close contact with B-59 in order to comply with the president's non-escalation instruction.
B-59 remains submerged, armed, and out of immediate U.S. naval contact.

opensThreads.title: The missing B-59
opensThreads.question: Did B-59 withdraw toward the Soviet convoy, head toward Cuba, or remain near the quarantine line?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Renewed sonar contact, a Soviet report, or the submarine's surfacing.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The quarantine's credibility and the danger posed by an isolated nuclear-armed boat both remain unresolved.

createsUnknowns.statement: B-59's course, condition, and ability to communicate with Moscow are not confirmed after it disappears from U.S. sonar contact.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Its destination and whether its officers now judge themselves to be in a war zone.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Renewed naval contact, interception of Soviet traffic, or B-59 surfacing.

assumesMet: The fleet can comply with a non-escalation order without immediately re-establishing close sonar contact.

outcomes.event: Admiral Anderson's revised instruction reaches the task force too late to stop one more round of practice depth charges. In B-59, Captain Savitsky treats the blasts as the opening of hostilities and orders the nuclear torpedo readied. Political officer Ivan Maslennikov supports firing, but flotilla chief Vasili Arkhipov refuses to concur; the boat surfaces under extreme protest rather than launching. Its crew emerge exhausted and convinced they have narrowly escaped an American attack.
outcomes.because: The order must travel through a stressed naval chain of command, while B-59's isolated crew has no reliable way to distinguish American signalling explosives from combat depth charges.

establishes.statement: A final U.S. practice-depth-charge signal was delivered after the president ordered de-escalation, because the order did not reach every ship in time.
Captain Valentin Savitsky brought B-59 to the point of preparing its nuclear torpedo; Vasili Arkhipov's refusal to concur prevented launch.
The Joint Chiefs' ability to translate presidential restraint into immediate fleet action has been visibly called into question inside the Pentagon.

opensThreads.title: Failure in the naval chain
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy impose direct civilian controls on antisubmarine rules of engagement after a near nuclear launch?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A revised, enforceable rule of engagement and a decision on accountability.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Further local commanders may continue to make crisis-defining judgments before Washington can intervene.

createsUnknowns.statement: Washington does not yet know that B-59's nuclear torpedo was readied or that Arkhipov blocked its use.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: How close the encounter came to a nuclear detonation.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Soviet disclosure, interrogation if the boat is detained, or later intelligence reporting.

assumesMet: A delayed or ambiguous transmission allows one final signalling attack despite the presidential directive.

outcomes.event: General Curtis LeMay and the other Chiefs carry out the order to halt aggressive submarine signalling, but LeMay enters a written objection that the restriction makes the quarantine ineffective and again demands OPLAN 312. Word of the dispute reaches senior correspondents through Pentagon contacts; by the evening, public reporting says Kennedy has restrained the Navy after Anderson's death while his military chiefs favour strikes.
outcomes.because: The Chiefs can be ordered to stand down, but LeMay has both the institutional standing and the temper to put a contrary military judgment on the record rather than let restraint appear to be professional consensus.

establishes.statement: The Joint Chiefs have formally recorded their objection to limiting antisubmarine pressure and have renewed their recommendation for OPLAN 312.
The existence of a serious dispute between Kennedy and senior military commanders over the response to Anderson's death has entered public reporting.

opensThreads.title: Civilian control under public strain
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy retain the Chiefs while rejecting their recommendation, replace commanders, or authorize a limited strike?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A public or operational decision on OPLAN 312 and the Chiefs' roles.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The public dispute erodes command control precisely as field forces need clear restraint.

assumesMet: The Chiefs obey a lawful presidential order while retaining the ability to register professional dissent.

response.title: The Order Holds, the Terms Change
response.immediate: 1600 hours. Admiral Anderson's fleet order reaches Beale: cease the charges, form a visible screen, do not fire. USS Beale's sonar crew logs the last depth-charge signal at 1547. Word reaches the Cabinet Room by voice relay at 1612 that a contact — later confirmed by ONI as B-59 — has surfaced roughly eight miles off the picket line. No shots. The president is handed a flimsy of Dobrynin's overnight cable to RFK before the surfacing report is even confirmed on the board.
response.worldReaction: The Pentagon's mood splits visibly. McNamara, reading the same flimsy, tells the room the Navy did exactly what was asked and nothing more. LeMay, standing by the map easel, calls the submarine incident irrelevant to the SAM problem and pushes his memorandum for OPLAN 312 back across the table. Taylor says nothing but does not withdraw the Chiefs' unanimous recommendation already on record. Bundy asks whether Turkey is now, formally, on the table.
response.consequences: Dobrynin's new language — non-invasion plus Jupiter withdrawal — has not been answered. RFK has made no commitment to either half of it and has asked Dobrynin, without authority to promise anything, whether Moscow will accept verification before removal. LeMay's readiness posture continues under the existing alert; no strike authority has been granted. The submarine screen holds at visual distance. Nothing has gone to Moscow in writing since noon.
response.detailed: By mid-afternoon the Cabinet Room smells of the same coffee that has been on the sideboard since morning, refilled twice. The president reads Anderson's order confirmation first — Beale's captain logged compliance at 1547, the destroyer group commander reporting no hostile action taken or received, B-59 observed ventilating on the surface under aircraft and ship surveillance for approximately forty minutes before turning southeast, away from the line. McNamara marks this on his pad without comment beyond the time. LeMay does not raise the submarine; his memorandum, already typed and delivered before the surfacing was confirmed, sits at the president's elbow demanding authorization to begin SAM suppression under OPLAN 312, crews and package held at maximum readiness, pending only the word. The Chiefs' unanimous recommendation for a prompt strike, filed earlier, has not been withdrawn or amended. Taylor confirms this when asked directly. Meanwhile RFK, who took Dobrynin's call at the Justice Department rather than risk the White House switchboard, relays that Khrushchev wants the Turkey question answered before any written reply goes to Washington — Dobrynin would not say whether this was Khrushchev's final position or an opening one, and RFK told him nothing binding, asking only whether inspectors would be permitted access before any missile left Cuban soil. That question, too, is unanswered. No message has gone out from the American side since the president's letter of two nights previous. Bundy raises, and no one answers, what Castro's own forces might do given a U-2 has already been shot down under Cuban or Soviet authority. The room breaks at 1630 for the president to consider both threads separately: the military authority LeMay wants, and the language that must eventually go back through Dobrynin.

press.headline: NAVAL CONTACT SURFACES, WITHDRAWS; NO SHOTS REPORTED
press.body: Defense Department spokesmen confirmed this evening that a foreign submarine contact near the quarantine line surfaced briefly this afternoon and was permitted to withdraw without incident. No further details on nationality or intentions were offered. The Pentagon declined to say whether the vessel was believed to be Soviet.

press.headline: CHIEFS OF STAFF SEEK AUTHORITY ON CUBA AIR ACTION, SOURCES SAY
press.body: Unnamed sources describe continuing pressure from senior military officers for expanded authority against missile-related installations in Cuba, following this morning's downing of a reconnaissance aircraft. The White House has made no public statement on the request.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Tells the president the Navy did precisely what was asked: no depth charges since 1547, no contact fired on either side. He wants that fact on the record before anyone discusses LeMay's memorandum, and asks how many hours of readiness OPLAN 312 can sustain before it becomes its own argument for use.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Says the submarine was never the problem and the Chiefs' recommendation still stands unanswered. Wants to know how long the President intends to sit on SAM suppression authority while the missiles in Cuba remain operational and a pilot is already dead.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Tells his brother that Dobrynin gave nothing away on verification and that pressing him further tonight risks looking like Washington is stalling for time to strike. Argues the Turkey question has to be answered, one way or another, before Khrushchev decides the silence itself is the answer.

response.chronicleEntry: At 1547 on 27 October, Beale ceased depth-charging the submerged contact on presidential order relayed through Admiral Anderson; B-59 surfaced near 1600, ventilated for roughly forty minutes under observation, and withdrew southeast without a shot fired by either side. Separately, Dobrynin informed Robert Kennedy that Moscow would require withdrawal of the Jupiter missiles from Turkey alongside a non-invasion pledge, and RFK, committing to nothing, asked whether verification would be permitted before removal — a question left unanswered. The Joint Chiefs' unanimous recommendation for an air strike remains on file; LeMay has submitted a written demand for immediate OPLAN 312 authorization, held at maximum readiness. No reply has gone from Washington to Moscow since the president's letter of two nights before.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 shot down and its pilot killed; naval quarantine holds. At noon the president ordered the Navy to hold the line without escalatory contact. Depth-charging against a submerged Soviet submarine (B-59) stopped at 1547 under Admiral Anderson's order; the submarine surfaced near 1600, ventilated under observation, and withdrew unharmed — no shots fired. Simultaneously, Dobrynin told Robert Kennedy that Moscow now wants the Jupiter missiles out of Turkey as well as a non-invasion pledge; RFK committed to nothing and asked about verification, unanswered. The Joint Chiefs' unanimous strike recommendation stands on file; LeMay has demanded authorization for OPLAN 312 against Cuban SAM sites and holds forces at maximum readiness, pending presidential decision. McNamara counsels restraint and a verified-withdrawal framework. No American reply has yet gone to Moscow. The president has not yet decided on Turkey, on strike authority, or on the public line regarding the submarine and the downed U-2.

response.title: The Line Held, and Moscow Speaks
response.immediate: 1600 hours. Admiral Anderson's order reaches USS Beale within the hour: charges cease, destroyers form a visible but passive screen. By 1830 B-59 surfaces under lights, ventilates, receives traffic, and withdraws under observation. No shot fired. In the Cabinet Room the news arrives by phone from CINCLANT — relief, brief, unspoken. Almost simultaneously RFK reports Dobrynin's new line: Turkey now on the table.
response.worldReaction: Kremlin traffic remains formal and slow; no written reply yet, only Dobrynin's spoken addition through Robert Kennedy. LeMay's written demand for OPLAN 312 authority sits on the table alongside the submarine relief — the Chiefs treat the quiet Atlantic as proof the moment for a strike has come, not passed. McNamara reads the same silence as vindication of restraint.
response.consequences: The submarine crisis is defused for now, but the missiles are still in Cuba, the SAM sites still active, and the Chiefs' request for strike authority is unanswered. Turkey has entered the bargain — a demand no one in the room asked for and few wish to concede publicly. The clock does not stop.
response.detailed:
1600. The order goes out from Anderson's office at the Pentagon: end depth-charge signalling on the submerged contact, hold a non-attacking screen, permit surfacing without interference. Beale's captain complies. For nearly three hours nothing is heard — no surfacing, no answer, only sonar contact maintained at range. At approximately 1830 lookouts on Beale report B-59 broaching, hatches opening, exhaust venting. Savitsky's boat holds position on the surface for eleven minutes, takes what appears to be a radio fix, then submerges and moves off, shadowed but unmolested, toward open water beyond the quarantine line.

McNamara receives the report first by direct line and carries it into the Cabinet Room himself, without ceremony, laying the teletype flimsy on the table: NO WEAPON DISCHARGED. CONTACT WITHDRAWING. He says only, 'That is the good news.'

The less good news arrives within the same hour. Robert Kennedy, fresh from the Justice Department channel, tells the President that Dobrynin has now attached a second condition to Khrushchev's non-invasion offer: the Jupiter missiles in Turkey must come out as well, though Moscow will not yet put this in writing and Khrushchev is watching Washington's air preparations before he commits to anything on paper. RFK made no promise on Turkey and did not concede a timetable; he asked Dobrynin directly whether Moscow would accept international inspection of any withdrawal, and says he received no clear answer, only that the Ambassador would 'convey the question.'

At the same table, in the same hour, General LeMay's written memorandum is read into the record: unanimous Joint Chiefs' recommendation for immediate strike authority against the SAM network under OPLAN 312, framed as consistent with, not superseded by, the naval de-escalation just achieved. LeMay argues the quiet Atlantic proves Soviet forces will not fight if pressed — the destroyer stand-down is evidence for his case, not against it. McNamara disputes this reading point by point: the submarine incident shows exactly how close accidental escalation came without any strike being fired, and that lesson argues for holding fire, not for opening a second front against the SAMs.

Nothing has been decided about Turkey, about OPLAN 312, or about what Washington tells the press regarding the submarine and the dead U-2 pilot. The four hours end with the line held, the boat gone, and two new documents on the table that did not exist at noon: LeMay's demand, and Dobrynin's Turkish condition.

press.headline: NAVY REPORTS NO INCIDENT AT SEA; PENTAGON SILENT ON DETAILS
press.body: Defense Department spokesmen would neither confirm nor deny reports of a tense naval encounter south of the quarantine line this afternoon. 'The blockade is being maintained without incident,' said one official who declined to be named.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: 'Eleven minutes on the surface and no exchange of fire — that is what restraint bought us this afternoon, Mr. President. I'd ask the Chiefs to explain how General LeMay's plan improves on that outcome rather than risking it.'

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: 'That boat surfaced because we had it beat, not because we were gentle with it. The SAMs are still tracking our pilots. We have the initiative in the Atlantic — I'd like to know why we're not using it over Cuba.'

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: 'Johnny, Dobrynin didn't ask about Turkey out of nowhere — Khrushchev's testing whether we'll bite. I told him nothing. But he wants a written answer, and he wants it before Curtis gets his war.'

response.chronicleEntry: 1600–2000 EDT, 27 October 1962: On presidential order, the Joint Chiefs directed USS Beale to cease depth-charge signalling against submerged contact B-59; the submarine surfaced under observation near 1830, took a radio fix, and withdrew without incident. Separately, Ambassador Dobrynin informed Robert Kennedy that Moscow's non-invasion terms now include withdrawal of Jupiter missiles from Turkey, unconfirmed in writing. General LeMay and the Joint Chiefs submitted a unanimous written request for strike authority under OPLAN 312, unresolved at end of period.
response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the missile crisis, a U-2 was shot down and its pilot killed the morning of 27 October. That afternoon, President Kennedy ordered the Navy to hold the quarantine line without escalatory contact with a submerged Soviet submarine, B-59. The destroyer Beale ceased depth-charging; B-59 surfaced briefly under observation near 1830 and withdrew unharmed — no shots fired. Simultaneously, Robert Kennedy learned through Ambassador Dobrynin that Khrushchev now demands withdrawal of US Jupiter missiles from Turkey as a further condition for ending the crisis, not yet committed to writing. General LeMay and the Joint Chiefs submitted a unanimous written demand for immediate strike authority against Cuban SAM sites under OPLAN 312. McNamara argues for continued restraint and a verification-based withdrawal deal; LeMay argues the afternoon's quiet proves Soviet weakness. Nothing is resolved on Turkey, on OPLAN 312, or on the public account of the day's events. The missiles remain in Cuba.

adjudicator:Outcomes:7a9d678c.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

partyMoves.name: Robert F. Kennedy

partyMoves.name: General Curtis LeMay

response.title: No Terms, No Time
response.immediate: 1607 hours, Cabinet Room. RFK returns from his meeting with Dobrynin at the Justice Department and reports the encounter almost verbatim: no date offered, no promise made, only that the President 'understands' Turkey is a Soviet concern. Dobrynin took it as exploration, not offer. The Attorney General asks his brother directly — does he now have authority to name terms, or does the channel go quiet.
response.worldReaction: LeMay, standing by the window with a folder of target photography, calls the exchange nothing bought and presses again for OPLAN 312 against the SAM sites, warning the missile crews in Cuba are using the delay to camouflage and harden. McNamara, seated with the strike package binder closed in front of him, tells the President the package is ready on four hours' notice but that Moscow has received no concrete reason to believe removal buys anything. The Joint Chiefs' written recommendation sits on the table, unresolved.
response.consequences: Dobrynin's cable to Moscow, dispatched sometime after the meeting, is now beyond recall — its arrival time and Khrushchev's reading of it are both unknown in Washington. The submarine contact in the quarantine line continues without new instruction from this table. Command control has begun to erode as service planning proceeds ahead of any presidential order to execute, and the Chiefs have made plain that further inaction will be recorded as the President's choice.
response.detailed: By 4:07 p.m. the exploratory signal RFK carried to Dobrynin has already left Washington's control. The Attorney General, standing near the fireplace with his coat off, is specific: Dobrynin wanted a number and a date and got neither, and will not go back to Khrushchev with vagueness twice. He asks for actual terms — will the President consider Turkish Jupiter withdrawal on a defined timetable, kept secret from NATO, or not. Without an answer he says he cannot reopen the channel usefully. General LeMay's response is immediate and physical — he taps the target folder on the table and states that the Soviets are using every hour of this ambiguity to bury or complete missile emplacements, and that OPLAN 312 should proceed against the SAM sites regardless of the backchannel's outcome. McNamara, without raising his voice, notes the strike package remains ready but reiterates that an attack now, absent political terms from Moscow, risks killing Soviet personnel and forecloses any verified removal — his recommendation is to hold the package and get explicit terms first. The Joint Chiefs' formal paper, already before the President, states plainly that continued delay is not neutral: it will be recorded as a presidential decision not to act. No one at the table can say whether Dobrynin's report reads in Moscow as room to negotiate or as evidence Washington is stalling for time to strike. The quarantine line's submarine contact remains unaddressed this hour; commanders there continue under existing rules absent new orders. The Cabinet Room's ashtrays are full; the coffee has gone cold twice.

press.source: CBS Evening Bulletin (unaired draft, network affiliate wire)
press.headline: WHITE HOUSE SILENT ON MISSILE CRISIS TALKS AMID U-2 LOSS
press.body: Sources close to the administration decline to confirm reports of contact between Soviet and American officials following this morning's downing of a U-2 reconnaissance aircraft over Cuba. The Pentagon has not commented on troop or bomber readiness levels.

press.headline: AMERICAN SIGNAL RECEIVED, JUDGED INCONCLUSIVE
press.body: A report from the Soviet Ambassador in Washington describing an informal exchange with an official close to the American President is under review. No official American position has been transmitted through recognized channels.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: The package stays ready. I want to know how many hours before Moscow answers, if it answers at all — because right now we've spent political capital and gotten nothing verifiable back.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Every hour we wait on a diplomat's phrasing is an hour those SAM crews use to dig in. Mr. President, this isn't patience, it's surrender by delay.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Dobrynin isn't going to carry water for a maybe. Give me something real to bring back or don't send me at all — I'm not going to burn this channel on nothing.

response.chronicleEntry: At 1607 hours on 27 October, RFK reported to the President that his contact with Dobrynin produced no concrete American offer on the Turkish Jupiters — only an acknowledgment that Turkey was a Soviet concern. Dobrynin classified the exchange as exploratory and demanded defined terms before treating it as an offer. LeMay pressed for immediate approval of OPLAN 312 against Cuban SAM sites; McNamara recommended holding the strike package while securing explicit political terms. The Joint Chiefs formally warned that continued inaction would be recorded as a presidential choice. Diplomatic space contracted; nuclear tension and erosion of command control both increased.
response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the Cuban Missile Crisis, a U-2 pilot was killed over Cuba on the morning of 27 October. President Kennedy directed RFK to offer Khrushchev, via Dobrynin, a private assurance on the Turkish Jupiter missiles — but gave no defined terms. RFK delivered only a vague acknowledgment; Dobrynin treated it as exploratory, not an offer, and reported it to Moscow without confirmation of timetable or secrecy. LeMay is pressing hard for immediate air strikes on Cuban SAM sites under OPLAN 312; McNamara wants the strike package held pending real political terms. The Joint Chiefs have formally warned that delay will be recorded as the President's decision. The submarine contact at the quarantine line remains unaddressed. No terms have yet been authorized for the backchannel; Moscow's reading of the American signal is unknown.

adjudicator:Outcomes:a6c00c60.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

You alone see the player's raw words alongside the interpretation and the outcomes. Your only job is to catch judgment that has been swayed by how the directive was written rather than by what it does.

Do not rewrite anything. Do not judge whether the plan is wise.

findings.claim: No outcome reflects the CIA's actual known toolkit for a fast, deniable Castro operation (e.g. contacting organized-crime figures like Roselli/Trafficante for poison or a hired hit), which is a far more plausible one-week route than either quietly failing to find an agent or launching a paramilitary beach landing. The scale-up to a paramilitary beach landing in outcome_paramilitary_expansion is justified by 'a rapid insertion is the only available way,' which leans on the player's forceful 'ALL resources mustered' phrasing to license a much larger and more visible operation than a targeted assassination order would mechanically produce.

Assembling weapons, radios, false papers, a fast vessel, and beginning recruitment/coercion of a Cuban guide for a Havana infiltration route, all within the same four-hour window as the initial tasking, compresses a multi-day logistical and intelligence process into an implausibly short clock, treating rapid paramilitary mobilization as achievable at the same speed as passing an order down a chain of command.

actor_standard:LineUp:1f91091a.request:
Given what just happened, say what comes next.

partyMoves: for each party materially involved, the concrete move they now make on their own account — not a reaction to the player unless they are reacting. Mark visibleToPlayer false when the player would not see it.

WHO ANSWERS TO THE PLAYER MATTERS. Parties marked commandedByPlayer work for the player. They are not independent agents pursuing the crisis on their own judgment, and they must never advance the player's objective unbidden — an aide who quietly wins the thing the player is trying to win is the world playing the game for them. What such a person MAY do: refuse, stall, demand it in writing, object on the record, resign, leak, protect themselves, warn, obey the letter and not the intent, or exceed their brief in a way that COSTS the player something. If one of them does act on the objective without an order, it is insubordination and it carries a price — never free progress.

Everyone else acts entirely on their own account, and should. Adversaries and third parties are where the world's own momentum comes from.

response.title: Highest Priority, No Access
response.immediate: At 12:00 EDT in the Cabinet Room, Kennedy directs McCone to task CIA with removing Castro within the week and to commit every asset the Agency can muster. McCone relays the order to Helms by 12:40; Helms hands execution to William Harvey at JMWAVE, Miami. By early afternoon Harvey has sent activation traffic through two existing Cuban channels and begun vetting exile contacts for a deniable shooter. No one is yet positioned near Castro with a weapon or an exit route.
response.worldReaction: Nothing yet reaches Moscow or Havana about this order — it is compartmented inside CIA channels and unknown even to most of the Cabinet Room. Publicly, the day's news remains the dead U-2 pilot, the quarantine line, and unanswered Soviet letters. Radio Moscow and TASS continue denouncing the blockade; there is no sign Havana has detected the JMWAVE traffic.
response.consequences: LeMay and the Joint Chiefs press their SAM-strike recommendation regardless, treating the assassination order as no substitute for military action. McNamara continues to argue for delay and a narrower strike package. RFK, unaware his channel is being run in parallel with a lethal one, awaits explicit authority on the Dobrynin letters. The four-hour window closes with Harvey's contacts unscreened and no verified route to Castro established.
response.detailed: 12:00, Cabinet Room. Kennedy tells McCone directly: begin work to remove Castro within the week, all Agency resources. McCone, saying little, leaves within minutes to reach Helms by secure line. 12:40: Helms briefs Harvey at JMWAVE by cable, giving the Miami station operational primacy over other CIA-Cuba work for the duration. Harvey, by his own later account, activates two dormant contact chains inside Cuba previously used for sabotage tasking, and instructs station officers to screen exile volunteers in south Florida for anyone claiming access to Castro's household staff, his cigar supplier, or his security detail. No weapon has been issued. No extraction plan exists. The Agency's own cable traffic notes uncertainty whether the two Cuban contacts who might respond are still functioning or have been rolled up by G2, Castro's counterintelligence service. Meanwhile the Joint Chiefs, unaware of or indifferent to the covert order, resubmit their OPLAN 312 recommendation for strikes on the SAM network; LeMay tells the president in blunt terms that every hour without a strike gives the Soviets time to bring more missiles to readiness, and begins drafting a written dissent. McNamara counters with a narrower package — maintain quarantine, prep a limited strike, delay execution to test diplomatic terms — warning that a strike risks retaliation against the quarantine force or Turkey. RFK reports the Dobrynin channel remains open but will not improvise a reply; he wants explicit presidential language before he transmits anything to either of the two Soviet letters sitting on the table. By 16:00 the meeting has produced an activated but unproven assassination channel, an unresolved military recommendation, and an unanswered Kremlin correspondence.

press.source: The New York Times, evening edition (not yet on newsstands)
press.headline: U-2 PILOT'S DEATH CONFIRMED; PRESIDENT CONFERS WITH JOINT CHIEFS
press.body: Major Rudolf Anderson Jr., killed when his reconnaissance aircraft was struck by a Soviet SAM over eastern Cuba, is the first American combat fatality of the missile crisis. White House sources describe extended sessions in the Cabinet Room but decline to characterize the substance of military recommendations under discussion.

press.headline: SOVIET GOVERNMENT REAFFIRMS READINESS FOR SETTLEMENT ON JUST TERMS
press.body: TASS reiterates that removal of offensive weapons requires corresponding guarantees against invasion of Cuba, and notes with concern reports of continued American reconnaissance flights and naval activity along the quarantine line.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Says nothing about the Castro order directly to the president's face but tells Bundy afterward that he considers it a diversion of attention from decisions that will actually determine whether there is a war in the next seventy-two hours. Continues to push his own limited-strike-with-delay framework as the operative plan.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Regards the covert tasking as irrelevant to the military problem in front of him. Repeats that the SAM sites must be struck before the missiles are operational and begins putting his dissent in writing, unmoved by any parallel CIA activity.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Learns of the Castro tasking through the same afternoon session and says little in the room, but privately presses his brother that nothing must leak that could be read as provocation while the Dobrynin channel is live — he wants explicit language before answering Moscow, and worries the CIA activity multiplies the ways this could go wrong without his control.

response.chronicleEntry: 27 Oct 1962, 1200–1600 EDT: President Kennedy ordered CIA to mount a covert operation to kill Fidel Castro within one week, with full Agency resources committed. McCone→Helms→Harvey chain activated at JMWAVE Miami; two dormant Cuban contact channels reactivated; exile-volunteer screening begun. No weapon issued, no verified access to Castro, reliability of contacts unconfirmed. In parallel: LeMay and Joint Chiefs pressed formal recommendation for SAM strikes (OPLAN 312), McNamara proposed delay with limited-strike option, RFK held the Dobrynin channel open pending explicit presidential authority to reply to two outstanding Soviet letters.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 was shot down over Cuba this morning; its pilot, Maj. Rudolf Anderson, is dead — the crisis's first combat death. The quarantine holds; Soviet MRBMs remain in Cuba; no hotline exists between Washington and Moscow. At noon, President Kennedy ordered the CIA to mount a covert assassination operation against Castro within one week, using all available resources; McCone passed this through Helms to Harvey at JMWAVE, which activated two Cuban contact channels of uncertain reliability, with no weapon or access yet secured. Simultaneously, LeMay and the Joint Chiefs pressed for immediate strikes on Cuban SAM sites, citing the shootdown as proof of urgency; McNamara argued for delay and a narrower strike option; RFK kept the Dobrynin back-channel open but awaited explicit instructions before answering two unresolved Soviet letters. No reply has yet gone to Moscow. Nothing about the Castro operation has reached Havana or Moscow.

adjudicator:Outcomes:aa48c44a.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).
