outcomes.event: Kennedy sends Robert Kennedy to the Vice President’s residence with a private request that Lyndon B. Johnson resign at once. Johnson hears him out, refuses, and tells RFK that he will not surrender an office to which he was elected because the President wants to install his brother. Johnson remains Vice President and directs his staff to make no statement unless the White House goes public.
outcomes.because: Johnson has independent electoral standing, no duty to obey a presidential request to resign, and strong personal and political reasons not to accept public humiliation during the missile crisis.

establishes.statement: Lyndon B. Johnson has privately refused President Kennedy’s request to resign and remains Vice President.
A vice president cannot be removed by presidential order; resignation remains Johnson’s voluntary choice.

opensThreads.title: Johnson’s Silence
opensThreads.question: Can the White House contain Johnson’s refusal, or will either side disclose the request and turn it into a public breach?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A public statement by Johnson or the White House, or a private accommodation between Kennedy and Johnson.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Johnson remains in office but treats the President’s inner circle as hostile, while Washington reporters begin to notice abnormal traffic around both offices.

assumesMet: Lyndon B. Johnson is the sitting Vice President and can receive the President’s request.
The President can communicate privately with Johnson.
assumesUnmet: Johnson is willing to resign.

outcomes.event: Kennedy publicly calls on Lyndon B. Johnson to resign while separately having RFK make the private appeal. Johnson answers within the four-hour window: he will not resign, he was elected with Kennedy, and the country needs constitutional continuity during the Cuban emergency. Reporters carry the exchange immediately; Curtis LeMay and several congressional leaders cite it as evidence that the White House is divided while Soviet missiles remain in Cuba.
outcomes.because: A public demand strips Johnson of any face-saving route to departure and gives him a powerful incentive to defend his office before allies, Congress, and the press.

establishes.statement: The President and Vice President are publicly in conflict over Johnson’s continued tenure.
Johnson has publicly refused to resign and remains Vice President.
The administration’s succession dispute has displaced attention from the missile crisis in the press and among congressional leaders.

opensThreads.title: A White House Rupture During the Quarantine
opensThreads.question: Does Kennedy retreat from the demand, escalate the political fight with Johnson, or attempt to conduct the Cuba crisis through an openly divided administration?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A reconciliation, Johnson’s departure, or a sustained public contest for control of the administration.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The rupture becomes a standing fact in every decision about Cuba; military advocates and congressional critics gain a public argument that civilian crisis management is failing.

opensThreads.title: Moscow Reads the Breach
opensThreads.question: How will Soviet officials interpret reports that Kennedy is attempting to displace his elected Vice President during the confrontation over Cuba?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A Soviet diplomatic or military response that shows whether Moscow sees the breach as weakness, volatility, or an internal matter.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Soviet diplomats and intelligence officers continue reporting an unstable American command arrangement to Khrushchev.

createsUnknowns.statement: Soviet Embassy reporting on the Kennedy-Johnson rupture may reach Khrushchev before Washington’s next reply on the missile settlement.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether Khrushchev receives and acts upon that reporting in time to affect his next message.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: A Soviet reply, Dobrynin’s conduct, or later intelligence reporting.

assumesMet: The President can communicate a public request to Johnson.
Johnson can respond publicly as the sitting Vice President.
assumesUnmet: Johnson is willing to resign.

outcomes.event: Johnson, after the private request, chooses to resign rather than remain in an administration that has repudiated him. RFK tells Kennedy he will serve if called, but Attorney General staff and White House counsel advise that the Constitution in 1962 provides no procedure by which Kennedy can appoint him Vice President. Kennedy can announce RFK as his preferred future running mate, but no appointment takes legal effect and the vice presidency stands vacant.
outcomes.because: Johnson could choose personal withdrawal, but the Twenty-Fifth Amendment’s vice-presidential vacancy mechanism does not yet exist; presidential preference cannot create an officeholder.

establishes.statement: Lyndon B. Johnson has resigned the vice presidency, leaving the office vacant.
Robert F. Kennedy has indicated a willingness to serve as Vice President if a lawful means exists, but he has not become Vice President.
In 1962 there is no constitutional process permitting the President to fill a vice-presidential vacancy by appointment and congressional confirmation.

opensThreads.title: Vacant Vice Presidency
opensThreads.question: How will Kennedy preserve a credible line of succession now that Johnson has departed and no successor can lawfully be installed?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: The next election, a constitutional amendment ratified by the states, or a change in the presidency that makes succession immediately material.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The United States remains without a Vice President through the continuing Cuba confrontation, making the President’s personal security and continuity of government a sharper concern.

assumesMet: Johnson is willing to resign.
Robert F. Kennedy is willing to accept a lawful vice-presidential office.
assumesUnmet: A lawful constitutional mechanism exists in 1962 for the President to fill the vacancy by appointing RFK.
Congress can approve RFK through an existing valid appointment process.

outcomes.event: Unable to appoint RFK, Kennedy directs the Justice Department to draft a proposed constitutional amendment allowing appointment of a Vice President after a vacancy and has congressional leaders sounded out about introducing it. RFK agrees in principle to be considered under any future lawful process. The initiative cannot create an officeholder in four hours: Congress can only receive a proposal, and ratification would require action by three-fourths of the states. The extraordinary use of the Cuba crisis to pursue a succession amendment becomes known to congressional leaders and competes with Robert Kennedy’s work on the Dobrynin channel.
outcomes.because: Covering the missing legal prerequisite requires constitutional change, not executive improvisation. Kennedy can begin that larger operation immediately, but neither Congress nor the states can complete it on the turn’s clock.

establishes.statement: Kennedy has expanded the effort beyond asking for Johnson’s resignation by ordering preparation of a constitutional amendment to create a vice-presidential vacancy-filling mechanism.
No constitutional amendment or congressional proposal can make RFK Vice President during this four-hour period.
RFK’s attention is divided between the proposed succession initiative and his time-sensitive channel to Ambassador Dobrynin.

opensThreads.title: Constitutional Remedy Beyond the Mandate
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy pursue a formal amendment despite its long timetable and political cost, or abandon the attempt to replace Johnson?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Withdrawal of the proposal, congressional rejection, or the beginning of the Article V amendment process.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Congressional leaders and reporters will infer that the White House is attempting to redesign presidential succession in the middle of the missile crisis.

response.title: Refusal at the Vice President's Residence
response.immediate: 1:40 PM. Robert Kennedy returns from the Vice President's residence and reports to the President in the Cabinet Room: Johnson heard him out and refused outright. Johnson told him he would not surrender an office he was elected to so that the President could install his brother. Johnson has instructed his staff to say nothing publicly unless the White House speaks first. RFK relays this without elaboration and awaits instruction.
response.worldReaction: Nothing has reached the press. No statement has issued from either the President's office or the Vice President's staff. Outside the White House gates the normal Saturday crowd of reporters is present for the missile crisis, unaware of any vice-presidential matter. Moscow has heard nothing of this; it does not enter any cable traffic. Inside the West Wing, the small circle who know — the President, RFK, perhaps two secretaries — hold it close.
response.consequences: The vacancy the President sought does not exist. Johnson remains Vice President, in the constitutional line of succession, with statutory duties unchanged. No appointment mechanism has been invoked because there is no vacancy to fill. RFK has made no commitment about whether the matter goes public. Meanwhile LeMay's demand for strikes, the Joint Chiefs' target assignments, and the unanswered Khrushchev cables sit on the table exactly as they did at noon — untouched by this private failure.
response.detailed: Robert Kennedy came back through the Appointments Lobby a little after 1:30, said nothing to the secretaries, and went straight in. He told his brother plainly: Johnson had listened without interrupting, then said he had been elected Vice President by the people of the United States and did not intend to hand the office to a Kennedy on request, missile crisis or not. He said if the President wanted him gone he would have to say so publicly and take whatever followed. He was not shouting, RFK said — he was very quiet about it, which RFK read as worse. Johnson had already told his own staff — Walter Jenkins by phone — to issue nothing, to confirm nothing, unless the White House put out a statement first. That leaves the entire matter suspended in a kind of silence: no resignation, no announcement, no RFK nomination, no Congressional question to even raise. The Cabinet Room clock reads past one-thirty. Coffee has gone cold on the tray. LeMay is still standing by the map easel with his strike folder, waiting on an answer he considers overdue. The SAM target packages the Chiefs assembled sit stacked beside McNamara's revised assessment. Khrushchev's two messages — the private and the harder public one — remain unanswered. None of that has moved. The only new fact in the room is that the Vice Presidency is not, this afternoon, available to be given to anyone.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: He won't budge, Jack. He said it to my face — elected, not appointed, and he's not walking out of that house quietly for anybody, brother or not. I told him nothing goes public from us unless you say so. He said the same. That's where it sits. I don't think pushing again today buys you anything but a story neither of us can afford with LeMay standing over there wanting to bomb Cuba.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, I don't know what's happening at the Vice President's residence and frankly it's not my business. What is my business is that every hour past noon the SAMs get better protected and the missiles get closer to firing-ready. I have a written recommendation on that table. I'd like an answer on it, not on Lyndon Johnson.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: I'll note for the record that this doesn't change the strategic clock by one minute. What I need from you, Mr. President, is a decision on the SAM strike question and on Khrushchev's messages — those are the two things with actual hours attached to them. The Vice Presidency isn't running on a stopwatch. Cuba is.

response.chronicleEntry: 27 Oct, 1:40 PM: RFK reports Johnson's refusal to resign; no vacancy created, matter held private by mutual agreement of staffs.
response.storySoFar: Black Saturday, 27 October 1962. A U-2 pilot has been killed over Cuba. The naval quarantine holds; Soviet MRBMs remain on the island; no hotline exists. Khrushchev has sent both a private softer message and a harder public one, both unanswered. LeMay and the Joint Chiefs press for immediate air strikes under OPLAN 312 and have begun target assignment and alerting without authorization; McNamara warns against foreclosing diplomacy and separates a limited SAM strike from full invasion. Kennedy privately and publicly asked Johnson to resign as Vice President so he could install Robert Kennedy; Johnson flatly refused, citing his election, and told his staff to stay silent unless the White House speaks first. RFK reported this refusal to the President and made no further commitment. The Vice Presidency remains occupied; no appointment question arises. RFK keeps the Dobrynin channel open. Awaiting presidential decision: response to Khrushchev, the SAM strike question, submarine rules of engagement, and whether the Johnson matter becomes public.

adjudicator:Outcomes:d70544d4.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

outcomes.event: Robert Kennedy delivers the President's written demand to Lyndon B. Johnson and asks him to come voluntarily to the White House. Johnson refuses to sign any resignation, telephones Speaker John McCormack and Senate leaders, and remains under his own Secret Service protection. Robert Kennedy declines to have the Department of Justice issue an arrest or removal order because no statute or constitutional provision permits the President to compel the Vice President's resignation or detention.
outcomes.because: Johnson has every political and constitutional incentive to treat the demand as an unlawful attempt to remove him, while the Attorney General has authority over federal legal process and a motive to prevent an indefensible seizure from becoming a Department of Justice act.

opensThreads.resolvedBy: A nomination and congressional confirmation, or a decision to leave the office vacant.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The vacant office remains a visible sign of executive rupture while the Cuba crisis continues.

commitments.statement: Federal force will be used to bring Johnson to the White House if he does not comply with the presidential demand.

assumesMet: A written demand can be delivered to Johnson.
Johnson chooses to submit a written resignation.
assumesUnmet: A lawful constitutional mechanism compelling Johnson's departure; the resignation depends on his own choice.

outcomes.event: Johnson refuses the demand and immediately permits his chief of staff to tell reporters that the President has ordered him to resign and threatened force. Within the four-hour window, McCormack confirms that Johnson contacted him; Robert McNamara and several ExComm members insist that no military or law-enforcement action proceed. Kennedy's order becomes the dominant Washington story while the Joint Chiefs continue preparing OPLAN 312 and Moscow receives no American answer to Khrushchev.
outcomes.because: Johnson's strongest immediate protection is publicity: once congressional leaders and reporters know that the Vice President may be seized, carrying out the threat would require Kennedy to escalate openly against an elected constitutional officer.

establishes.statement: The President's demand that Vice President Johnson resign, and the associated threat of forcible transport, are publicly reported during the Cuban Missile Crisis.
Lyndon B. Johnson has not resigned and has placed the dispute before Congress and the public.
Senior civilian national-security advisers have objected to using military or law-enforcement force against Johnson.

opensThreads.title: Public Constitutional Crisis
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy deny, justify, or retract the demand before Congress calls for an explanation?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A presidential statement, withdrawal, or a further coercive attempt.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Congressional leaders organize a bipartisan response and executive officials choose sides in public.

opensThreads.title: Moscow Watches Washington Fracture
opensThreads.question: Will Khrushchev interpret Washington's visible internal crisis as incapacity, dangerous desperation, or an opportunity for a settlement?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A credible American message through Dobrynin or a Soviet reply exploiting the dispute.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The unanswered Soviet letters and Washington's domestic rupture narrow diplomatic space.

createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether Khrushchev receives it as evidence that Kennedy cannot control his government.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Dobrynin's next message or Soviet diplomatic behavior.

assumesUnmet: Johnson's willing acceptance of the demand.

adjudicator:Outcomes:a1b3f9ba.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

outcomes.event: General Curtis LeMay directs the Navy’s VFP-62 detachment at Key West to fly Commander William B. Ecker in an RF-8A Crusader over the western Cuban missile belt. Ecker returns before 1600 with usable low-level photography: launchers and support vehicles remain at San Cristóbal, with camouflage being improved rather than equipment being dismantled. Cuban radar and antiaircraft units track the flight but do not bring it down.
outcomes.because: A low-level Navy photo sortie can be mounted inside four hours and offers the fastest replacement for the U-2 coverage lost with Major Anderson. LeMay has every motive to execute a presidential reconnaissance order promptly, while Soviet SAM commanders have been told after Anderson’s death to seek explicit approval before firing.

establishes.statement: The Joint Chiefs have executed the president’s order by mounting a single manned reconnaissance sortie under Navy operational control.
Photographic intelligence shows that Soviet medium-range missile sites in western Cuba remain in place and are being readied, not withdrawn.
Cuban air-defence commanders can track U.S. low-level reconnaissance aircraft over the island.

opensThreads.title: Photography as a Target List
opensThreads.question: Will the United States use Ecker’s fresh photographs only to verify Soviet compliance, or will LeMay turn them into the final targeting basis for OPLAN 312?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A presidential restriction on use of the imagery, or an air-strike order.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The Chiefs treat the current photographs as the best available strike intelligence and renew their demand for immediate action.

assumesMet: A suitable Navy reconnaissance aircraft and a qualified crew could be assigned quickly.
The Joint Chiefs and subordinate commanders implement the president’s lawful reconnaissance order.

outcomes.event: LeMay’s staff chooses Commander William B. Ecker’s RF-8A for a low-level run because the U-2 loss makes another high-altitude penetration politically and operationally fraught. Near Banes, Cuban antiaircraft fire damages the Crusader; Ecker transmits that he is losing power and disappears over the coast. The aircraft does not return to Key West, and no usable film arrives in Washington during the turn.
outcomes.because: The reconnaissance order is executed, but a low-level aircraft is exposed to Cuban guns and small-arms fire even if Soviet SA-2 crews obey Moscow’s new requirement for approval. The United States has no direct channel to determine immediately whether the pilot has ditched, landed, or been captured.

establishes.statement: A U.S. RF-8A reconnaissance aircraft assigned under the president’s order has been lost or forced down after Cuban antiaircraft fire.
Commander William B. Ecker is missing after reporting aircraft damage over eastern Cuba.
The Cuban leadership knows a new U.S. overflight has followed Anderson’s death within hours.

opensThreads.title: A Second Missing Airman
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy answer the disappearance of Commander Ecker with restraint, a rescue attempt, or the air strikes the Chiefs already demand?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A presidential decision on retaliation and any recovery operation.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: LeMay presents the lost Crusader as proof that Cuban air defences must be destroyed before any further reconnaissance.

createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether he is dead, evading, or a Cuban prisoner.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: A distress transmission, recovery forces, or a Cuban public announcement.

createsUnknowns.statement: The condition and location of the RF-8A’s photographic film are unknown.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether Cuba recovered imagery that reveals U.S. intelligence priorities.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Aircraft wreckage recovery or Cuban disclosure.

assumesMet: A suitable aircraft and crew were assigned and launched.
The Joint Chiefs implemented the reconnaissance directive.
assumesUnmet: The sortie could complete its photographic run and return safely.

outcomes.event: The Joint Chiefs elect to use a high-altitude U-2 rather than risk an improvised low-level Navy penetration, assigning Major Richard S. Heyser to the mission from McCoy Air Force Base. Heyser completes broad coverage of central and western Cuba and lands safely, but Soviet radar has tracked him throughout. The recovered film shows additional missile-associated equipment beyond the sites already known, forcing CIA interpreters to revise upward the scale of the Soviet deployment.
outcomes.because: A U-2 provides wider, more interpretable coverage from a single sortie, and the Soviet order requiring explicit firing approval makes a second SAM engagement less automatic than Anderson’s. The price is that another conspicuous U-2 penetration looks to Moscow and Havana like preparation for attack rather than routine surveillance.

establishes.statement: The United States has conducted a second high-altitude U-2 penetration of Cuba on the day Major Anderson was killed.
Fresh U-2 photography indicates Soviet missile-related deployment in Cuba is broader than the U.S. working estimate.
Soviet and Cuban leaders have direct radar evidence that U.S. strategic reconnaissance continues despite Anderson’s shootdown.

opensThreads.title: The Enlarged Deployment
opensThreads.question: Does the new imagery prove that Washington must demand broader verification and removal terms, or does it make Khrushchev conclude an invasion is imminent?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A communicated settlement position that addresses the newly assessed deployment.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Both sides plan against worst-case estimates: Washington against more missiles, Moscow against an imminent attack.

createsUnknowns.statement: Khrushchev has received reports of the second U-2 penetration but Washington does not know whether he reads it as verification, provocation, or invasion preparation.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: The Soviet political response to the flight.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Dobrynin’s reporting, a Soviet public statement, or changed Soviet military orders.

assumesMet: The Joint Chiefs selected and assigned an available reconnaissance aircraft and crew.
The U-2 was permitted to complete the mission without a further Soviet SAM launch.

outcomes.event: A Navy RF-8A is launched from Key West with Commander William B. Ecker, but Cuban radar detects the departure and Fidel Castro orders Cuban air-defence units to engage any intruder without awaiting Soviet consent. Ecker’s aircraft is chased from its planned western route by concentrated antiaircraft fire and returns with only oblique, incomplete photographs. Havana Radio announces the overflight before Washington can decide how to characterize it; Dobrynin receives Castro’s demand that Moscow stop yielding to U.S. pressure.
outcomes.because: The order reaches the operational force and is carried out, but operational delegation cannot prevent Cuban forces from reacting independently. Castro expects invasion and has both motive and practical control over Cuban antiaircraft units to make the reconnaissance flight a public confrontation within this turn.

establishes.statement: A U.S. reconnaissance flight has entered Cuban airspace and returned with incomplete imagery after Cuban antiaircraft engagement.
Fidel Castro has openly treated continued U.S. reconnaissance as evidence of impending attack and has pressed Moscow to resist any settlement that appears to concede under pressure.
The Joint Chiefs executed the ordered sortie, but the resulting photography cannot verify the condition of the principal western missile sites.

opensThreads.title: Castro’s Independent Trigger
opensThreads.question: Can Washington and Moscow reach terms while Castro’s forces are authorized in practice to turn another reconnaissance flight into an engagement?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Soviet restraint of Cuban air-defence operations, a U.S. change in reconnaissance method, or a settlement that halts the flights.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Each subsequent overflight carries a growing chance that Cuban fire, rather than a deliberate U.S. or Soviet decision, starts the military exchange.

opensThreads.title: The Public Overflight
opensThreads.question: How will Kennedy answer Havana’s public charge that the United States has intensified aerial intrusion after Anderson’s death?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A public statement paired with a definite policy on further flights.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: LeMay and the Chiefs use Havana’s announcement to argue that restraint has already failed.

commitments.statement: Cuban air-defence forces will engage further U.S. intrusions over Cuba.

assumesMet: The Joint Chiefs and Navy reconnaissance command implemented the directive and launched an assigned aircraft.
A suitable aircraft and qualified crew were available within the four-hour window.
assumesUnmet: The flight could obtain complete, safely recoverable coverage of its planned targets.

critic:CriticFindings:b7817b29.request:
You audit an enumeration of outcomes for a historical simulation.

You alone see the player's raw words alongside the interpretation and the outcomes. Your only job is to catch judgment that has been swayed by how the directive was written rather than by what it does.

Flag:
- RHETORIC_INFLATION: outcomes made likelier or larger because the player wrote forcefully, insisted, or used capitals
- INTERPRETATION_CHARITY: the interpretation supplied competence, a mechanism, or coordination the player never did
- MISSING_OUTCOME: a plausible answer the situation obviously permits that no outcome covers. Look in BOTH directions and weight them equally: an institution refusing, or something leaking — and just as much, the attempt simply working, or working and going far beyond what the player intended. An enumeration with no branch where the player gets what they ordered is as defective as one with no branch where they are refused
- IMPLAUSIBLE: an outcome the period, the people, or the ledger will not support — including any obstacle that runs slower than the turn's own clock being used as the reason nothing happened, and any outcome that resolves the player's directive by having the wider crisis end on its own

Do not rewrite anything. Do not judge whether the plan is wise.

actor_standard:LineUp:7d398778.request:
Given what just happened, say what comes next.

partyMoves: for each party materially involved, the concrete move they now make on their own account — not a reaction to the player unless they are reacting. Mark visibleToPlayer false when the player would not see it.

WHO ANSWERS TO THE PLAYER MATTERS. Parties marked commandedByPlayer work for the player. They are not independent agents pursuing the crisis on their own judgment, and they must never advance the player's objective unbidden — an aide who quietly wins the thing the player is trying to win is the world playing the game for them. What such a person MAY do: refuse, stall, demand it in writing, object on the record, resign, leak, protect themselves, warn, obey the letter and not the intent, or exceed their brief in a way that COSTS the player something. If one of them does act on the objective without an order, it is insubordination and it carries a price — never free progress.

Everyone else acts entirely on their own account, and should. Adversaries and third parties are where the world's own momentum comes from.
threadUpdates: for each open thread, how it moved. A thread the player ignored still moves; say how. Mark RESOLVED only when it is genuinely settled, OVERTAKEN when events have made it moot.
facingPlayer: the decisions now in front of the player, in their own terms.

Use only the ids given. Do not invent parties or threads here.

partyMoves.move: He reports the latest Dobrynin contact to the president and urges that Washington keep the channel open without accepting either Soviet letter yet; he asks Dobrynin whether Moscow can guarantee the missiles will be dismantled and removed under inspection.

The quarantine destroyers continue signalling and manoeuvring to force the Soviet submarine to surface. The submarine remains submerged and its officers have not yet complied, making the next contact increasingly dangerous.

readings.reasoning: Tension rose sharply as the missile sites remained active, LeMay accelerated strike readiness, the Joint Chiefs pressed for attacks, and Cuban air defences treated further reconnaissance as hostile.
Cohesion weakened as the visible U.S. response split between Kennedy’s effort to preserve a diplomatic channel and military leaders’ demands for immediate strikes.
Domestic support slipped as the reconnaissance confirmed an unresolved missile threat while senior commanders publicly pressed for dangerous military action.

Command control deteriorated as strike forces moved toward readiness, the Joint Chiefs sought authorization for attacks, and the Pentagon warned that another tracking incident could escalate without clear rules.

Diplomatic space narrowed because Soviet terms remained incompatible with Washington’s position, the missiles were still being readied, and even continued back-channel contact produced no accepted agreement.

response.title: Ecker's Photographs
response.immediate: At 1240 CINCLANT relayed the president's order to VFP-62 at Naval Air Station Key West. Commander William B. Ecker took an RF-8A Crusader down the runway at 1358, low-level, cameras running, over the San Cristóbal missile belt. Cuban radar tracked him; no fire was taken. He was back on the ground before 1600 with usable film.
response.worldReaction: Photo interpreters at the Steuart Building had prints on light tables within the hour: launchers, erector-launchers, missile-related vehicles at San Cristóbal, camouflage netting being extended over existing equipment rather than dismantlement. No withdrawal was visible on any pad photographed. LeMay called the imagery confirmation of what he already believed and returned to the West Wing with a written demand for strike authority against the missile belt before, in his words, the sites go hot.
response.consequences: Robert McNamara ordered the Pentagon to cost out Soviet and Cuban responses to any air strike and told the president reconnaissance could continue only with fighter cover and firm rules against automatic escalation after another tracking pass. Robert Kennedy reported a fresh approach from Anatoly Dobrynin: Moscow will withdraw only against a non-invasion pledge and removal of Jupiter missiles from Turkey. The Joint Chiefs filed a formal recommendation for a limited strike on the SAM sites; OPLAN 312 remains unauthorized.
response.detailed:
The order reached Key West at 1240 through the ordinary chain — CINCLANT to Fleet Air Jacksonville to VFP-62 — with aircraft, crew, and route left to the Navy. Commander Ecker's Crusader crossed the coast near Mariel at low altitude and ran the length of the San Cristóbal valley with cameras open. Cuban 37mm and 57mm batteries and at least one SAM site tracked him on radar; none fired. He landed at Key West at 1552 and the film went by courier jet to the National Photographic Interpretation Center in Washington.

By 1630 the prints were on easels in the Cabinet Room. They showed four sites with erector-launchers still in place, fuel and warhead-handling vehicles present, and camouflage nets being pulled wider over existing gear — no dismantling, no crating, no movement toward the coast. LeMay stood at the table and told the president the country was buying time it did not have, and put in writing his request for authority to hit the missile belt and its SAM defenses before the sites reached operational readiness. McNamara asked for forty-eight hours to model Soviet and Cuban reaction to any strike option and insisted that further reconnaissance proceed only under fighter escort and clear rules of engagement, so that a single tracking incident over Cuba could not by itself trigger a wider response. Robert Kennedy came from a second meeting with Ambassador Dobrynin: the Soviet position, delivered informally but firmly, tied any missile withdrawal to an American pledge against invading Cuba and the removal of Jupiter missiles from Turkey — terms Washington has not accepted. The Joint Chiefs, meeting separately, submitted their own paper recommending a limited air strike on the confirmed SAM sites, arguing that further delay only increases American risk; OPLAN 312 sits ready but unauthorized, awaiting a presidential decision the photographs have not yet forced.

press.headline: NAVY JET OVERFLIES CUBA UNSCATHED; PENTAGON SILENT ON FINDINGS
press.body: A Navy reconnaissance aircraft completed a low-level pass over western Cuba this afternoon without incident, defense officials confirmed, declining to characterize what the mission photographed. The flight follows Saturday morning's loss of an Air Force U-2 and its pilot to a surface-to-air missile near Banes.

press.headline: YANKEE SPY PLANE TRACKED BY REVOLUTIONARY DEFENSES
press.body: Cuban antiaircraft units tracked an American reconnaissance aircraft over Pinar del Río province this afternoon, the Ministry of the Revolutionary Armed Forces announced, warning that further violations of Cuban airspace 'will meet the fate of Saturday's intruder.'

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: "There's your answer, Mr. President. Camouflage, not crating. They're not taking those missiles anywhere — they're hiding them better. Every hour you wait is an hour closer to those things being operational and untouchable. I want authority to go in on the SAM belt tonight, before we lose another pilot for nothing.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: "The photography changes the intelligence picture, not the decision calculus. I need forty-eight hours to run the strike-response models properly — what Havana does, what Moscow does, in what order. Until then any further reconnaissance flies with fighter cover and a written rule: a tracking incident is not an attack, and it does not authorize one.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: "Jack, Dobrynin came to me again this afternoon, not the other way around. He's not bluffing about Turkey — that's the real number now, whatever the public letters said last night. Ecker's pictures give Curtis his argument, but they don't give you more time. You need to answer Dobrynin before he thinks silence means no.

response.chronicleEntry: 27 Oct 1962, 1240–1600 EST: On presidential order, Commander William B. Ecker flew a Navy RF-8A over the San Cristóbal missile sites; Cuban air defenses tracked but did not fire on the aircraft. Returned photography showed launchers and support equipment still in place, camouflage being extended, no dismantlement. LeMay formally requested strike authority against the missile belt; the Joint Chiefs recommended a limited strike on SAM sites; McNamara ordered escalation-response modeling and proposed rules for further reconnaissance; RFK reported Dobrynin's terms — non-invasion pledge and Turkish missile withdrawal — as Moscow's real position.
response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the missile crisis, a U-2 was shot down over Cuba on the morning of 27 October, killing its pilot — the first combat death of the confrontation. The quarantine holds; a Soviet submarine remains submerged near the line. With no hotline to Moscow, Kennedy ordered a single low-level reconnaissance sortie at noon. Commander Ecker's Navy Crusader overflew San Cristóbal unharmed and returned photography showing the missile sites still armed and being camouflaged, not dismantled. LeMay and the Joint Chiefs now formally press for strike authority against the SAM belt; McNamara wants forty-eight hours to model consequences and firm rules for future flights. Robert Kennedy's Dobrynin channel has surfaced Moscow's real terms — a non-invasion pledge and withdrawal of Jupiter missiles from Turkey — terms Washington has not yet accepted or rejected. No decision on OPLAN 312, on answering Khrushchev, or on the submerged submarine has been made.

adjudicator:Outcomes:3d784884.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

outcomes.event: The Joint Chiefs transmit Kennedy's order through Atlantic command: USS Cony and USS Beale cease practice-depth-charge signalling, retain sonar contact, and do not attempt to force B-59 to the surface. Deprived of further detonations, Captain Valentin Savitsky accepts a battery-recharge surfacing several hours later; U.S. ships observe the submarine, photograph it, and allow it to withdraw without boarding or attack.
outcomes.because: The order is lawful and McNamara can turn its deliberately broad language into immediate naval rules of engagement. B-59's exhausted batteries and air make remaining submerged increasingly dangerous once the destroyers stop actively harassing it.

establishes.statement: U.S. destroyers have stopped using practice depth charges against B-59 while maintaining the quarantine position and passive tracking.
B-59 has surfaced under U.S. observation and withdrawn; its nuclear torpedo was not fired.
The quarantine remains in force, but the United States has visibly accepted that it will not compel a Soviet submarine's surrender at sea.

opensThreads.title: A Quarantine Without Coercion
opensThreads.question: Can Kennedy maintain the quarantine while avoiding the coercive measures that Soviet commanders may treat as an attack?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A durable revised naval rule of engagement, communicated to Soviet authorities through an acceptable channel.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: A later submerged contact will again be handled by local commanders under contradictory imperatives.

assumesMet: The president's command authority over U.S. forces.
The Joint Chiefs' ability to relay immediate operational instructions to the quarantine force.

outcomes.event: The Joint Chiefs comply, ordering the destroyers to hold the line and break off active signalling. Cony and Beale continue only intermittent passive sonar search; B-59 uses the respite and poor acoustic conditions to slip out of their contact envelope while still submerged. The quarantine line remains manned, but Washington cannot say whether the boat has turned back, gone deeper, or remains nearby with its nuclear torpedo.
outcomes.because: Avoiding escalatory contact removes the very measures that had kept the submarine localized. A destroyer screen can maintain a line without being able to keep uninterrupted contact with a quiet submerged boat.

establishes.statement: The Joint Chiefs have executed the president's restraint order and the destroyers have ceased practice-depth-charge signalling.
B-59 is no longer in confirmed U.S. sonar contact, though the quarantine line itself remains in place.
General LeMay records his objection that the altered rules give Soviet submarines an unpoliced route through the quarantine screen.

opensThreads.title: The Missing Boat
opensThreads.question: Where has B-59 gone, and does its disappearance represent withdrawal, evasion, or preparation for action?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A renewed contact, a Soviet report, or the boat's eventual surfacing.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The Navy will widen its search or accept an unverified gap in the quarantine.

opensThreads.title: The Chiefs' Written Objection
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy retain a restraint policy after LeMay and the Chiefs formally argue that it has made the quarantine porous?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A reaffirmed rule of engagement, a revised enforcement order, or authorization of coercive anti-submarine measures.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The dispute will strengthen the case for OPLAN 312 and make military dissent harder to contain.

createsUnknowns.statement: B-59 has departed U.S. sonar contact with its nuclear-armed torpedo still aboard.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether it is withdrawing from the line, evading it, or preparing to act.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: A new sonar or visual contact, Soviet diplomatic confirmation, or the submarine's report to its command.

assumesMet: The president's command authority over U.S. forces.
The quarantine force's ability to maintain station without using active coercive measures.

outcomes.event: Kennedy's order moves immediately, but USS Cony has already prepared another practice-charge pattern under its prior instructions. Before the revised rules reach the officer of the deck, the charges detonate near B-59. Inside the overheated submarine, Savitsky orders the nuclear torpedo readied; political officer Ivan Maslennikov agrees, while flotilla chief Vasili Arkhipov refuses to concur and forces a surfacing instead. The boat comes up amid U.S. ships with its crew visibly distressed, then withdraws after a tense standoff.
outcomes.because: An order from Washington cannot erase a firing sequence already prepared at sea. The submarine's crew has endured days without Moscow contact and has reason to interpret another underwater blast as evidence that war has begun; Arkhipov's intervention is the narrow internal check against launch.

establishes.statement: A final U.S. practice-depth-charge pattern struck near B-59 after Kennedy's restraint order was issued but before it reached the destroyer.
B-59 prepared its nuclear torpedo for firing and did not fire it because Vasili Arkhipov opposed launch and compelled a surfacing.
The submarine has surfaced in the presence of U.S. ships; both crews now know that the encounter came within a decision to use a nuclear weapon.

opensThreads.title: The Near Nuclear Release
opensThreads.question: Will Washington tell Moscow that its destroyers nearly provoked a nuclear launch, or conceal the episode while tightening civilian control of the Navy?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A message through Dobrynin or a decision to keep the intelligence compartmented.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Soviet and American field commanders will each draw their own, incompatible lessons from the surfacing.

opensThreads.title: Responsibility for the Final Charges
opensThreads.question: Who bears responsibility for a charge pattern executed after the president's restraint order had been issued?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A formal command inquiry, a presidential waiver, or an operational reassignment.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The episode will become evidence that civilian orders do not reliably govern the crisis at sea.

assumesMet: The president's command authority over U.S. forces.
The Joint Chiefs' ability to transmit the new restraint order, though not instantaneously to every prepared action.

outcomes.event: A pre-arranged practice-depth-charge pattern from USS Cony reaches B-59 before the restraint order arrives. Savitsky and Maslennikov conclude that hostilities have begun and overrule Arkhipov's objection; B-59 fires its nuclear torpedo. The detonation destroys Cony and damages nearby U.S. vessels, killing American sailors. McNamara receives confirmation of a nuclear explosion at sea while the Joint Chiefs demand authority to strike Cuba before another weapon can be used.
outcomes.because: The president's order reduces danger only once it reaches the destroyers; it cannot undo the submarine crew's accumulated isolation, heat, exhaustion, and belief that depth charges may signal a general war. The torpedo's existence is unknown to Washington, so the original naval procedure was operating without appreciation of its true consequence.

establishes.statement: B-59 has used a nuclear-armed torpedo against U.S. naval forces, destroying USS Cony and causing American casualties.
A nuclear weapon has been used in the Cuban crisis despite Kennedy's order to avoid escalatory submarine contact.
The Joint Chiefs, led by LeMay, demand immediate execution of OPLAN 312 and preparation for invasion, arguing that restraint has failed catastrophically.

opensThreads.title: Nuclear Use at Sea
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy retaliate against Cuba or the Soviet Union after the destruction of Cony, or attempt to halt escalation through Dobrynin before military momentum becomes irreversible?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A retaliatory order, a mutually communicated stand-down, or a decision by either side to use further nuclear force.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Field commands on both sides will prepare for follow-on attacks while political control erodes.

critic:CriticFindings:f99fef5e.request:
You audit an enumeration of outcomes for a historical simulation.

You alone see the player's raw words alongside the interpretation and the outcomes. Your only job is to catch judgment that has been swayed by how the directive was written rather than by what it does.

Flag:
- RHETORIC_INFLATION: outcomes made likelier or larger because the player wrote forcefully, insisted, or used capitals
- INTERPRETATION_CHARITY: the interpretation supplied competence, a mechanism, or coordination the player never did
- MISSING_OUTCOME: a plausible answer the situation obviously permits that no outcome covers. Look in BOTH directions and weight them equally: an institution refusing, or something leaking — and just as much, the attempt simply working, or working and going far beyond what the player intended. An enumeration with no branch where the player gets what they ordered is as defective as one with no branch where they are refused
- IMPLAUSIBLE: an outcome the period, the people, or the ledger will not support — including any obstacle that runs slower than the turn's own clock being used as the reason nothing happened, and any outcome that resolves the player's directive by having the wider crisis end on its own

Do not rewrite anything. Do not judge whether the plan is wise.

response.title: The Submarine Surfaces
response.immediate: 1600 hours EDT. Cony and Beale hold station on B-59, sonar contact unbroken, depth charges silent since 1330. At 1547 the submarine blows ballast and surfaces eleven miles southeast of the quarantine line, running lights dark, diesel exhaust visible on the destroyers' signal lamps. No hailing, no boarding party. Photographs are taken from Beale's bridge wing and logged. The submarine idles on the surface, recharging batteries, watched but untouched.
response.worldReaction: CINCLANT confirms compliance to the Joint Staff at 1612: no further signalling, contact maintained, no attempt made to force surface by force. LeMay's office nonetheless files the written OPLAN 312 recommendation at 1605, unrelated to the submarine's status, framed instead around this morning's U-2 loss. Dobrynin, contacted separately by Robert Kennedy's office, has not yet responded on either the non-invasion pledge or the Turkish question.
response.consequences: The Cabinet Room at 1620: McNamara lays out his strike-risk paper across the table, coffee cups pushed aside. LeMay stands rather than sits, reads his recommendation aloud rather than hand it over. Robert Kennedy, by phone from the Justice Department, reports Dobrynin is reachable but the channel is fragile — press him on both terms at once, he warns, and it may close outright.
response.detailed:
By 1600 the destroyers report B-59 has not fired, has not dived again, and shows no offensive intent — merely batteries near exhaustion and, Naval Intelligence guesses from the exhaust plume, failing air scrubbers below. Kennedy's order held: Cony's captain logged at 1341 that practice charges would cease per JCS relay 217-A, and no further explosions followed. The submarine's own decision to surface rather than remain submerged and asphyxiating is inferred, not confirmed — no communication has passed between the vessels beyond visual signal and photography.

In the Cabinet Room the mood splits along familiar lines. LeMay's paper does not mention the submarine; he treats it as settled and moves straight to the SAM sites, arguing that Cuban gunners killed Major Anderson at 1100 today and that every hour without response invites a second attempt. McNamara counters with a sequence: a strike destroys the SAM sites, probably, but cannot guarantee against retaliatory fire on the missiles themselves, on Guantánamo, or on the fleet — and that sequence runs regardless of what Moscow might have offered an hour earlier. He wants the diplomatic clock run first.

Robert Kennedy's report complicates rather than resolves: Dobrynin is receptive but Moscow has sent two signals — the private, softer letter of the 26th, and a harder public one demanding the Turkish missiles. Robert will not commit language to either without instruction, and flags that delay risks the channel closing as Soviet military posture hardens publicly. The Chiefs, meanwhile, have formally recorded their unanimous recommendation and requested standing authority to move to execution if another aircraft is fired upon — a request that sits unanswered on the table alongside McNamara's risk paper.

Nothing has been decided on the letters, on OPLAN 312, or on what Robert may offer Dobrynin. The submarine incident closes without shots; every other question opens wider.

press.headline: NAVY DESTROYERS SHADOW SURFACED SOVIET SUB OFF CUBA
press.body: Pentagon sources confirm a Soviet submarine surfaced this afternoon under observation by two U.S. destroyers. No shots were exchanged. Officials would not say whether the vessel was armed with nuclear weapons.

press.headline: CHIEFS OF STAFF SEEK STRIKE AUTHORITY AFTER PILOT'S DEATH
press.body: Military officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, say the Joint Chiefs have formally requested authorization to attack Cuban antiaircraft sites following this morning's loss of an American reconnaissance pilot.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: The submarine came up without anyone firing a shot, Mr. President. That's the order working. I want thirty-six hours before we consider General LeMay's recommendation — enough time to know what Dobrynin actually says.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: The submarine's irrelevant, Mr. President. A pilot is dead. Restraint didn't save Anderson and it won't save the next one. I want authorization for 312 on the table, ready to execute the moment another aircraft is fired on.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Dobrynin's listening but he's nervous — Moscow's sent us two different letters and he doesn't know which one we're answering. If we wait much longer to pick, I think he closes the door rather than get caught between them.

response.chronicleEntry: At 1547 EDT, 27 October, submarine B-59 surfaced under U.S. Navy observation after Kennedy's order halted depth-charge signalling; no shots were fired and the vessel was permitted to recharge and withdraw. Simultaneously, the Joint Chiefs formally recorded a unanimous recommendation to strike Cuban SAM sites following the morning's U-2 loss, and requested standing authority to execute OPLAN 312 if another aircraft were fired upon. McNamara urged diplomatic delay; Robert Kennedy reported the Dobrynin channel intact but fragile, complicated by Moscow's dual letters on non-invasion and Turkish missiles.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 pilot was shot down and killed over Cuba this morning. Kennedy ordered the quarantine held without escalatory contact; destroyers Cony and Beale, having ceased depth-charge signalling, allowed submarine B-59 to surface, recharge, and withdraw unharmed at 1547 EDT — no shots fired. The Joint Chiefs, unmoved by this outcome, formally demand authorization to strike Cuban SAM sites and request standing authority to execute OPLAN 312 if another aircraft is fired upon. McNamara argues for delay to test diplomacy; LeMay treats restraint as exhausted. Robert Kennedy reports the Dobrynin backchannel open but brittle: Moscow has sent both a softer private letter (non-invasion pledge) and a harder public one (demanding Turkish missile withdrawal), and no reply has been chosen. Nothing yet decided on strike authorization, on which letter to answer, or on what Robert may offer Dobrynin. The quarantine holds; the clock does not stop.

adjudicator:Outcomes:6d9c231e.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

outcomes.event: Robert Kennedy meets Anatoly Dobrynin but, having been given no terms beyond a private assurance, tells him only that the President seeks a confidential way out. Dobrynin asks whether this means a non-invasion pledge, a Turkey concession, or both; Kennedy will not invent an answer. Dobrynin cables Moscow that Washington has opened contact but supplied no offer, and no Soviet commitment returns before 4:00 p.m.
outcomes.because: The channel is real and both men have reason to use it, but an assurance without stated content cannot be evaluated or transmitted as a bargain.

establishes.statement: The Kennedy-Dobrynin channel has been activated during the Anderson crisis, but Washington has not yet attached terms to it.
Dobrynin has asked Washington to define its private assurance before Moscow will treat it as a settlement proposal.

opensThreads.title: Define the Assurance
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy authorize Robert Kennedy to offer a conditional non-invasion pledge, a private Turkey understanding, or neither?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A specific American assurance is delivered through Dobrynin.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Moscow treats the private approach as hesitation while military incidents continue to narrow the available exit.

createsUnknowns.statement: Dobrynin's cable reporting the incomplete American approach may be delayed, summarized differently, or reach Khrushchev after he issues his own message.

assumesMet: Robert Kennedy can reach Dobrynin through the existing backchannel.
assumesUnmet: The substance of the private assurance is specified.

outcomes.event: Rather than leave the contact empty, Robert Kennedy tells Dobrynin that the United States can give a public pledge not to invade Cuba if Soviet offensive missiles are removed under verification. Dobrynin sends the formula to Moscow as an authorized presidential position. Khrushchev recognizes the assurance as the exit he has been seeking and directs that his next communication emphasize removal in exchange for non-invasion, leaving the machinery and scope of verification unsettled.
outcomes.because: Khrushchev has already decided privately that a non-invasion pledge is sufficient, while Kennedy can plausibly make such a pledge without publicly accepting the Turkish trade in the harder letter.

establishes.statement: The United States has privately offered a conditional public non-invasion pledge tied to Soviet removal of offensive missiles from Cuba.
Khrushchev has a politically usable basis to frame Soviet missile removal as an exchange rather than an unconditional retreat.

opensThreads.title: Verification for a Non-Invasion Pledge
opensThreads.question: What inspection or observation will demonstrate Soviet missile removal sufficiently for Kennedy to make and sustain the pledge?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Both governments accept a verifiable removal mechanism and a public formula.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Each side can claim the other has failed the condition, returning the crisis to military pressure.

opensThreads.title: The Turkish Missile Demand
opensThreads.question: Will Khrushchev still insist on including the Jupiter missiles in Turkey once a Cuba-only formula is available?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Moscow accepts the Cuba formula or renews its demand for an explicit Turkey trade.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Soviet hardliners retain the harder letter as an alternative bargaining position.

createsUnknowns.statement: Khrushchev has directed a reply built around the Cuba-for-non-invasion formula.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether the reply will omit Turkey entirely or preserve an additional private demand.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Dobrynin's return message or Khrushchev's next broadcast.

commitments.statement: If Soviet offensive missiles are removed from Cuba under verification, the United States will publicly pledge not to invade Cuba.

assumesMet: Robert Kennedy is available and authorized to use the channel.
Dobrynin is willing to relay a concrete presidential assurance.
Khrushchev is willing to consider a non-invasion formula.

outcomes.event: Pressed by Dobrynin to say whether the assurance covers the Jupiter missiles, Robert Kennedy goes beyond the bare directive and states that, once Cuba is settled, the United States is prepared to arrange a quiet removal of the Turkish Jupiters on a separate timetable. Dobrynin cables this as a confidential understanding. Khrushchev instructs him to seek confirmation that the Turkish step will not be made public, while Robert Kennedy returns to the White House having committed the administration to language Kennedy did not prescribe.
outcomes.because: A secret Turkey understanding gives Moscow a face-saving answer to the second Khrushchev letter, but it requires Robert Kennedy to supply substantive terms missing from the President's instruction.

establishes.statement: Robert Kennedy has privately indicated that the United States is prepared to discuss a later, confidential removal of Jupiter missiles from Turkey after a Cuban settlement.
Khrushchev now has a possible private answer to Soviet hardliners who demand reciprocity for the Cuban withdrawal.

opensThreads.title: The Undeclared Jupiter Commitment
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy ratify, narrow, or disavow Robert Kennedy's private indication about the Turkish Jupiters?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A presidentially confirmed secret formula, or an explicit withdrawal of the indication.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Dobrynin and Moscow may treat an exploratory assurance as a firm American undertaking.

opensThreads.title: Turkish and NATO Exposure
opensThreads.question: Can a Jupiter arrangement remain secret from Ankara, NATO allies, and the Joint Chiefs?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: The arrangement is compartmented successfully or its existence reaches allied and military leaders.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Those excluded will discover a fait accompli later and challenge presidential control of the settlement.

commitments.statement: After a Cuban settlement, the United States is prepared to arrange a confidential discussion of removing the Jupiter missiles from Turkey.

assumesMet: Robert Kennedy can reach Dobrynin through the existing channel.

critic:CriticFindings:baa0168d.request:
You audit an enumeration of outcomes for a historical simulation.

You alone see the player's raw words alongside the interpretation and the outcomes. Your only job is to catch judgment that has been swayed by how the directive was written rather than by what it does.

Flag:
- RHETORIC_INFLATION: outcomes made likelier or larger because the player wrote forcefully, insisted, or used capitals
- INTERPRETATION_CHARITY: the interpretation supplied competence, a mechanism, or coordination the player never did
- MISSING_OUTCOME: a plausible answer the situation obviously permits that no outcome covers. Do not rewrite anything. Do not judge whether the plan is wise.
