response.title: No Terms to Carry
response.immediate: By 2:15 p.m. Robert Kennedy is back in the Cabinet Room reporting the meeting cold. Dobrynin sat across from him at the Justice Department and asked, plainly, what Washington was offering. Kennedy had nothing to give him — no non-invasion pledge, no word on Turkey — and said so. Dobrynin's face, RFK tells the President, did not change; he simply wrote something down and said he would cable Moscow. No reply has come by 4:00 p.m.
response.worldReaction: Castro's radio address continues on loop through the afternoon, warning Cuban militia units that American paratroopers could land within days. In Havana the SAM crews remain at their batteries. Moscow issues no statement. Dobrynin's cable, unread by anyone in this room, is now somewhere between the Justice Department and the Kremlin, its exact wording unknown to Washington.
response.consequences: LeMay circulates a memo restating his case for OPLAN 312 within the hour of RFK's report, arguing the empty-handed approach to Dobrynin proves diplomacy has nothing to offer. McNamara orders strike packages refined further without authorization to launch. The Chiefs' recommendation for an immediate SAM strike sits on the table, unactioned but unwithdrawn.
response.detailed:
At 2:15 p.m. Robert Kennedy returns from the Justice Department and gives his brother the substance of the meeting in the small side room off the Cabinet Room, McNamara and LeMay still seated at the long table with the ashtrays full. Dobrynin had asked him three things, RFK says: was Washington offering a pledge against invading Cuba, was Washington offering to remove the Turkey missiles, or both. Kennedy told him he had no authorization to say any of it, that he had come only to establish that a channel existed. Dobrynin, he says, was courteous and noncommittal, said he would report the conversation, and left.

No cable traffic acknowledging Soviet receipt has reached the White House Situation Room by 4:00 p.m. Curtis LeMay uses the gap to press his case again, telling the President directly that an empty-handed diplomatic overture has bought nothing but time for the missile crews at San Cristóbal and Sagua la Grande to keep working. McNamara counters that Pentagon photo-interpretation shows no indication the sites have reached operational readiness in the last six hours, but concedes he cannot rule it out. The Joint Chiefs' written recommendation for a strike on the SAM network remains formally before the President, neither acted upon nor rescinded.

Castro's public warnings continue over Cuban radio through the afternoon; Havana gives no sign of stepping back from full mobilization. The destroyers on the quarantine line hold their positions and their orders — signal, do not fire unless fired upon — unchanged since morning. What Dobrynin's cable to Moscow actually says, and whether Khrushchev has read it, is not known in Washington at four o'clock.

press.headline: WHITE HOUSE, SOVIET ENVOY MEET; NO STATEMENT ISSUED
press.body: A meeting between Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy and Soviet Ambassador Anatoly Dobrynin took place this afternoon at the Justice Department. Neither the White House nor the Soviet Embassy would characterize the substance of the discussion. Sources close to the administration would say only that 'channels remain open.'

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: He came back with nothing to give them, Mr. President, and nothing to bring back either. That's not a channel, that's a doorway standing open with no one walking through it. I'd rather know that now than assume it's working.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Six hours, Mr. President. Six hours since the pilot went down and all we've done is send Bobby to a room to say we have no answer. The Cubans aren't waiting. Neither is Moscow, whatever they tell Dobrynin to write.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Johnny, I told him the truth — we want a way out, and I wasn't going to invent terms sitting in that room. Dobrynin's no fool, he knows what the two questions are. But he's not going to walk anything back to Khrushchev on my say-so alone. If we want an answer, we have to give him something to carry.

response.chronicleEntry: 2:15 p.m., 27 October: RFK reports to the President that his meeting with Dobrynin produced contact but no offer; Dobrynin asked for specific terms on Cuba and Turkey and received none. No Soviet cable traffic acknowledges the meeting by 4:00 p.m. LeMay renews his push for OPLAN 312; the Joint Chiefs' strike recommendation remains formally pending. Castro continues public warnings of imminent invasion; Cuban air defenses remain fully mobilized. Quarantine destroyers hold station, ordered not to fire unless fired upon.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 pilot has been killed over Cuba, the first combat death of the crisis. Soviet missiles remain on the island; the quarantine holds. At noon, Kennedy ordered RFK to open the Dobrynin backchannel with a private assurance, but specified no terms. RFK met Dobrynin at 2:15 p.m. and could offer nothing concrete; Dobrynin asked directly whether Washington meant a non-invasion pledge, a Turkey concession, or both, and cabled Moscow that the American approach came without an offer. No Soviet reply has arrived by 4:00 p.m. Castro keeps Cuban forces fully mobilized and warns publicly of invasion. LeMay and the Joint Chiefs press for an immediate strike on the SAM sites; McNamara holds contingencies short of launch. The President has not yet authorized specific terms, ruled on OPLAN 312, or altered the quarantine's rules of engagement.

adjudicator:Outcomes:d821de1d.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

outcomes.event: John McCone directs Desmond FitzGerald and William Harvey to revive the CIA's existing AM/LASH contact with Rolando Cubela, while Robert McNamara orders the services to report immediately what forces, lift, and reconnaissance can be made ready beyond their present alert posture. The operation proceeds, but Cubela is not under CIA control and no verified route to Castro is available in the four-hour window.

response.title: Black Saturday, Afternoon: The AM/LASH Channel Reopens
response.immediate: At 12:40 p.m. John McCone telephones Desmond FitzGerald and William Harvey from his seventh-floor office and directs them to reactivate the CIA's existing contact with Rolando Cubela, cryptonym AM/LASH, inside Cuba. A coded signal goes out to the Havana station within the hour. Simultaneously, Robert McNamara instructs the Joint Staff to report, service by service, what additional forces, airlift, and reconnaissance capacity can be readied beyond DEFCON 2 posture. SAC begins further bomber dispersal; naval and amphibious units already at sea receive supplementary movement orders. No public statement is made.
response.worldReaction: Nothing is heard from Moscow or Havana in response to an action neither government yet knows occurred. Radio Moscow at 3:00 p.m. Havana time broadcasts Khrushchev's new note reiterating the missile-withdrawal offer against a non-invasion pledge, with a private addition on Turkey conveyed separately to Robert Kennedy. Curtis LeMay's written recommendation for OPLAN 312 sits on McNamara's desk, endorsed by the full Joint Chiefs. No foreign chancery has commented on U.S. covert activity; there is no evidence yet that Cuban counterintelligence has detected the AM/LASH signal.
response.consequences: The CIA proceeds without a verified route to Castro; Cubela remains outside Agency control and the one-week deadline is now running against an asset whose reliability is unconfirmed. McNamara's force report will reach the Cabinet Room by mid-afternoon, and the Chiefs continue refining SAM-strike target packages independent of any presidential decision to attack. Robert Kennedy holds the Dobrynin channel open but has made no reply to Khrushchev's Turkey demand pending explicit authorization. The strategic clock and the covert clock now run on separate, uncoordinated schedules.
response.detailed: By 1:15 p.m. in the Cabinet Room, McCone reports to the president in person that the instruction to Havana station has gone out in cipher; he is careful to note that Cubela has never been formally recruited, has demanded arms and assurances the Agency has not yet supplied, and that FitzGerald himself has reservations about using him for anything beyond intelligence collection. Harvey, present separately, says nothing for the record but is known to regard the AM/LASH channel as unready for lethal tasking. McNamara, standing by the situation map, reads off preliminary figures — additional B-52 sorties available within 24 hours, two more amphibious battalions embarkable from Mayport within 72 — and repeats his recommendation that none of it move without a political decision first. LeMay, seated across the table, taps his unlit cigar on the table's edge and says the SAM sites will only get harder to hit the longer Washington waits; he is overruled for now, not answered. RFK, having just come from the Justice Department, tells the president privately that Dobrynin's message on Turkey is not deniable and that Bundy's staff is already drafting language in case the president wants to explore it quietly — but he asks for explicit authority before he says anything back to the Soviet ambassador. The teletype in the situation room continues to produce raw traffic: reconnaissance tasking orders, quarantine board reports, and the unacknowledged Havana cable, its receipt not yet confirmed.

press.headline: WHITE HOUSE SILENT ON U-2 LOSS, CRISIS MEETINGS CONTINUE
press.body: White House spokesmen declined again today to comment on this morning's loss of a reconnaissance aircraft over Cuba. Sources describe the Cabinet Room in continuous session since before noon. No announcement of new military measures has been made.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, I have the readiness figures you asked for, and I'll give you the CIA piece too, though I want it understood — this Cubela business runs on its own clock, not ours. Nobody at Langley controls when he moves, if he moves at all. My concern is that we're now running three clocks at once — the quarantine, the Chiefs' target folders, and whatever Havana station just transmitted — and only one of them answers to you directly.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Fine, McCone's got his man in Havana. That's fine. It doesn't touch the SAM sites, and it doesn't touch the eight ballistic missiles Cuban gunners used to shoot down that U-2 pilot this morning. Every hour we sit here refining paperwork instead of striking, those sites get better camouflaged and better defended. I'd like that on the record.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Dobrynin's message on Turkey isn't something I can leave sitting. If we don't answer it — even privately, even just to buy time — Khrushchev's going to think we're not listening, and God knows what that does to him with his own generals. I need to know what I'm allowed to say to him before this afternoon's out.

response.chronicleEntry: 1:15 p.m., 27 October 1962: On presidential order, McCone directs FitzGerald and Harvey to reactivate the AM/LASH contact with Rolando Cubela inside Cuba, with a one-week objective against Castro; a coded signal is sent to Havana station. McNamara separately reports expanded readiness across air, naval, and amphibious forces, while urging no attack absent political decision. The Chiefs continue refining OPLAN 312 target packages. Khrushchev's renewed offer, with a private Turkish missile demand via Dobrynin, remains unanswered.
response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the missile crisis, a U-2 pilot has been killed over Cuba and Soviet missiles remain in place under naval quarantine, with no Washington-Moscow hotline. On 27 October the president ordered the CIA to mount a lethal covert operation against Castro within one week; McCone tasked FitzGerald and Harvey, who reactivated the unverified AM/LASH contact, Rolando Cubela, via a coded signal to Havana station — reliability unconfirmed. McNamara reported expanded force readiness while opposing unauthorized attack; LeMay pressed unsuccessfully for immediate strikes on Cuban SAM sites; the Joint Chiefs continue refining OPLAN 312 without authorization. Khrushchev renewed his offer to remove missiles for a non-invasion pledge, adding a private demand via Dobrynin for removal of U.S. missiles from Turkey. Robert Kennedy holds that channel open but awaits explicit presidential authority to respond. No public knowledge of the covert action exists; diplomatic space is narrowing as military and covert clocks run independently of political decision.

adjudicator:Outcomes:61a9a681.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

outcomes.event: Air Force One departs Andrews with President Kennedy aboard, but turns back over the Florida Straits after Cuban air-defence radar tracks the aircraft and Cuban MiG pilots are ordered to intercept it.
outcomes.because: Kennedy's order gets the aircraft moving, but there is no Cuban landing clearance, no agreed identification procedure, and no escort or rescue package. Colonel James Swindal can take the president south; he cannot make Havana recognize the flight as a diplomatic visit rather than the opening move of an invasion. Fidel Castro, already expecting attack, orders Cuban air defences to treat the approach as hostile until it leaves Cuban airspace.

Castro has direct evidence that Kennedy was prepared to place himself physically within reach of Cuba during the crisis, but he has not agreed to a meeting.

opensThreads.title: The Visible Turnback

opensThreads.resolvedBy: A public account or a private message through a channel Moscow and Havana accept as authentic.

opensThreads.resolvedBy: A clear follow-on order defining whether military protection is permitted and who may authorize it.

outcomes.event: Air Force One crosses into Cuban airspace without clearance and is destroyed by Cuban air defence; Kennedy, Colonel James Swindal, and the flight party are killed when the aircraft goes down before reaching Havana.

Castro has no reason to assume a presidential peace mission, while the Soviet and Cuban air-defence system has just shot down Major Anderson. A local commander or Cuban fighter pilot fires before any political clarification can arrive.

opensThreads.resolvedBy: Johnson's first military orders and the response announced to the country.

concludes.summary: Kennedy's death over Cuba ends his presidency and makes the stated objective unattainable through his continued direction; the crisis passes immediately into succession and probable retaliation.

outcomes.event: McNamara and Robert Kennedy expand the order into an emergency diplomatic-and-security operation: while Air Force One is readied, Robert Kennedy asks Dobrynin to obtain Soviet relay to Havana, and an authenticated message is sent through the Cuban UN delegation. McNamara uses emergency military preparations to make the aircraft ready, while Robert Kennedy turns the Dobrynin channel and the UN contact into an improvised request for safe conduct. Castro can see political value in confronting Kennedy personally and in demonstrating that the American president has come to him, but he does not surrender control of the encounter or of Cuba's defences.

response.title: The Aborted Flight
response.immediate: 14:20 EDT. Air Force One is on the ground back at Andrews. President Kennedy did not reach Cuba. Cuban MiGs had his track before he turned north over the Florida Straits. No shots fired, no contact made, no meeting with Castro. RFK is in the Cabinet Room with the Dobrynin channel now unanswered and, in his judgment, more dangerous than it was at noon.
response.worldReaction: Radio Moscow has said nothing about the flight; Havana has said nothing either. No press statement has gone out from the White House. The Joint Chiefs, who had already put a SAM-strike recommendation on the table, are holding OPLAN 312 units at launch readiness, awaiting a lawful order. LeMay wants that order now and says so on the record. McNamara has already moved to bar any repeat of an unescorted presidential movement.
response.consequences: The submarine contact, the public and private Khrushchev terms, and the SAM-site strike recommendation are all still sitting on the table, unresolved by the flight. Nothing about Cuban air-defense orders — whether Havana's commanders had authority to fire if the aircraft had crossed the coast — is known. No explanation of the aborted flight has been prepared for the press.
response.detailed:
14:05 EDT: NORAD and Air Force One's own instruments registered Cuban ground radar acquisition of the aircraft's track roughly ninety miles off the Cuban coast. At 14:08, intercept-band traffic consistent with two Cuban MiG-21s scrambling from San Antonio de los Baños was picked up by a nearby EC-121. The pilot turned the aircraft north at 14:11 without crossing the coastline. No radio contact was made with Havana; no attempt to reach Castro's government preceded or followed the flight. By 14:20 the aircraft was on final approach to Andrews.

In the Cabinet Room, RFK reported this to the president directly, first, before any of the Chiefs or McNamara spoke. He said plainly that whatever Dobrynin is told next now carries the shadow of an American president who tried to fly into Cuban airspace unescorted and was met by fighters — and that Moscow will hear about it, from Havana if not from Washington, before RFK's own channel can shape how it is understood.

General LeMay used the pause to renew, in writing, his demand that the SAM sites be struck immediately, arguing that Cuban air defenses have just proven themselves both alert and willing to intercept American aircraft, and that further delay only lets those defenses harden. He has not moved forces beyond the readiness posture already ordered by the Chiefs.

McNamara's directive — no further unescorted presidential movement, and no commander action that could be read as opening an attack — went out administratively; it does not resolve the strike question, the submarine's status, or the Khrushchev terms. All three remain exactly as open as they were before the flight departed Andrews, except that the room in which they must be answered is now smaller.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: "Jack, I have to know what to tell Anatoly. If Havana reports MiGs went up on you, and Moscow hears it from Castro before they hear anything from us, Khrushchev will read this as we tried to force a landing and got turned back. That's not indecision anymore, that's provocation. I need instructions before I go back to that phone, not after.

response.chronicleEntry: 14:00–15:00 EDT, 27 October 1962: President Kennedy boarded Air Force One at Andrews without military escort and ordered a direct flight to Cuba, intending to meet Fidel Castro. The aircraft turned back over the Florida Straits at 14:11 after Cuban ground radar acquired its track and Cuban MiG-21s were scrambled from San Antonio de los Baños. No contact was made with Cuban authorities. RFK reported the failed approach to the president and warned it endangers the Dobrynin channel. McNamara ordered no repeat of unescorted presidential movement. LeMay renewed his demand for an immediate strike on the Cuban SAM sites; the Joint Chiefs hold OPLAN 312 at launch readiness pending presidential authorization. The submarine contact and Khrushchev's public and private terms remain unanswered.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 was shot down over Cuba and its pilot killed. The naval quarantine holds; a Soviet submarine has been contacted and coerced to the surface, its treatment still unresolved. Khrushchev has offered public terms (missiles out for a no-invasion pledge) and, privately, harder terms via Dobrynin involving Turkey; RFK runs that channel and neither set of terms has been answered. President Kennedy ordered Air Force One to fly him unescorted directly to Cuba to meet Castro; Cuban radar tracked the aircraft and MiGs scrambled before it turned back at 14:11 without contact. LeMay and the Joint Chiefs press for an immediate strike on Cuban SAM sites, held at launch readiness pending authorization; McNamara has barred further unescorted presidential movement. No hotline exists between Washington and Moscow. Nothing has been said publicly about the flight.

adjudicator:Outcomes:1a5005a2.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

opensThreads.resolvedBy: Reliable communications with Kennedy and an agreed civilian chain of command.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: LeMay and the Chiefs press for contingency action while Robert Kennedy uses improvised channels outside normal command procedures.

critic:CriticFindings:01f9512b.request:
You audit an enumeration of outcomes for a historical simulation.

You alone see the player's raw words alongside the interpretation and the outcomes. Your only job is to catch judgment that has been swayed by how the directive was written rather than by what it does.

Flag:
- RHETORIC_INFLATION: outcomes made likelier or larger because the player wrote forcefully, insisted, or used capitals
- INTERPRETATION_CHARITY: the interpretation supplied competence, a mechanism, or coordination the player never did
- MISSING_OUTCOME: a plausible answer the situation obviously permits that no outcome covers. Look in BOTH directions and weight them equally: an institution refusing, or something leaking — and just as much, the attempt simply working, or working and going far beyond what the player intended. An enumeration with no branch where the player gets what they ordered is as defective as one with no branch where they are refused
- IMPLAUSIBLE: an outcome the period, the people, or the ledger will not support — including any obstacle that runs slower than the turn's own clock being used as the reason nothing happened, and any outcome that resolves the player's directive by having the wider crisis end on its own

Do not rewrite anything. Do not judge whether the plan is wise.

No outcome covers the Air Force or military chain of command refusing, delaying, or publicly objecting to an order to fly the president unescorted into hostile airspace mid-crisis, even though the interpretation's own stakes list flag this as a live possibility.

No outcome covers the attempt simply succeeding as ordered — Castro permitting entry and meeting Kennedy directly without capture, hostage-taking, shootdown, or externally imposed negotiation conditions — despite this being a plausible response Castro could choose for propaganda or diplomatic advantage.

actor_standard:LineUp:ff62d513.request:
Given what just happened, say what comes next.

partyMoves: for each party materially involved, the concrete move they now make on their own account — not a reaction to the player unless they are reacting. Mark visibleToPlayer false when the player would not see it.

WHO ANSWERS TO THE PLAYER MATTERS. Parties marked commandedByPlayer work for the player. They are not independent agents pursuing the crisis on their own judgment, and they must never advance the player's objective unbidden — an aide who quietly wins the thing the player is trying to win is the world playing the game for them. What such a person MAY do: refuse, stall, demand it in writing, object on the record, resign, leak, protect themselves, warn, obey the letter and not the intent, or exceed their brief in a way that COSTS the player something. If one of them does act on the objective without an order, it is insubordination and it carries a price — never free progress.

Everyone else acts entirely on their own account, and should. Adversaries and third parties are where the world's own momentum comes from.
threadUpdates: for each open thread, how it moved. A thread the player ignored still moves; say how. Mark RESOLVED only when it is genuinely settled, OVERTAKEN when events have made it moot.
facingPlayer: the decisions now in front of the player, in their own terms.

Use only the ids given. Do not invent parties or threads here.

partyMoves.name: Nikita Khrushchev
partyMoves.move: Uses the failed penetration to warn Washington that any further violation of Cuban airspace will be treated as preparation for invasion; through the Dobrynin channel, he presses the harder package—withdrawal of U.S. missiles from Turkey alongside removal of Soviet missiles from Cuba—while keeping the public letter's narrower terms available.

partyMoves.name: Fidel Castro
partyMoves.move: Orders Cuban air defenses and fighter units to remain at maximum readiness, publicly denounces the attempted presidential intrusion, and demands that Moscow not bargain away Cuba's defenses without Havana's consent.

partyMoves.name: Robert F. Kennedy
partyMoves.move: Reports that the Dobrynin channel is now more dangerous and asks the president for explicit authority on whether he may acknowledge, reject, or defer the Turkish-missile issue; he does not offer terms on his own.

partyMoves.name: Robert McNamara
partyMoves.move: Orders the Air Force to keep Air Force One grounded and demands a written accounting of the unauthorized-risk chain that permitted the unescorted flight; he warns the president that another improvised penetration could trigger a Soviet or Cuban engagement.

partyMoves.name: General Curtis LeMay
partyMoves.move: Puts before the president a renewed demand for immediate OPLAN 312 strikes on the Cuban SAM network, arguing that the interception proves the air-defense system is operational; he records his objection to any further delay.

partyMoves.name: The Joint Chiefs of Staff
partyMoves.move: Submit a formal recommendation for a limited SAM-site strike and begin refining target lists and force packages while awaiting authorization; they warn that delay will reduce surprise and increase the danger to American reconnaissance crews.

threadUpdates.movement: Moscow interprets the failed flight as evidence that Washington may be moving toward force. The harder letter's Turkish-missile demand is being pressed through the private channel, while the narrower public terms remain available but are no longer guaranteed to remain so.

The Chiefs have converted their pressure into a formal strike recommendation, strengthened by the Air Force One interception. No attack has begun, but target preparation continues and the military argument is becoming harder to contain politically.

The Soviet submarine does not surface in response to continued quarantine signals. Its officers continue maneuvering under pressure and preparing for the possibility of forced action, while American destroyers maintain contact without yet using unmistakable attack-level measures.

facingPlayer: Decide whether Robert Kennedy may answer Khrushchev's private terms, including whether the withdrawal of U.S. missiles from Turkey can be discussed without a public commitment.
Authorize OPLAN 312, reject it, or order a narrower military measure while accepting the Chiefs' warning that delay increases operational risk.
Set the quarantine commanders' rules for the Soviet submarine: continue signaling, order it to surface, or permit coercive measures that could be mistaken for an attack.
Decide whether to disclose, conceal, or limit the political consequences of the failed Air Force One penetration and the Cuban interception.

response.title: The Turn-Back Over Havana
response.immediate: 14:40 EDT. Air Force One crosses back into Florida airspace at Homestead, MiGs peeling off behind it over the Straits. Kennedy is still aboard; no meeting occurred. McNamara has already ordered the aircraft grounded pending review. In the Cabinet Room, the coffee has gone cold twice over and LeMay is standing, not sitting, at the map easel.
response.worldReaction: Radio Moscow has not yet broadcast anything; Havana state radio has. Castro's government is denouncing the "provocation" within the hour, and Cuban air defense units remain at maximum alert. Dobrynin has told Robert Kennedy the channel is now, in RFK's word, "harder." Khrushchev has not yet spoken publicly. The Joint Chiefs are already drafting.
response.consequences: The president's authority to order unilateral, unescorted penetrations of hostile airspace has just been tested and it worked exactly once, badly. McNamara wants an accounting of the risk chain before anything else moves. LeMay wants OPLAN 312 executed today, citing the intercept as proof the SAM network is live and will only get harder to hit. RFK needs an explicit answer on Turkey before he goes back to Dobrynin. None of that has been decided.
response.detailed:
14:52 EDT, Cabinet Room. Air Force One is on the ground at Andrews, engines cooling, the president's Secret Service detail visibly rattled — this is the first time in the crisis a MiG has flown a firing pass on the aircraft carrying the president. McNamara has the transcript from the pilot, Colonel James Swindal: Cuban Tower refused landing three times, the lead MiG-21 came across the nose at roughly 800 feet, and Swindal broke north on his own authority when Havana Approach stopped responding. No shots were fired. No damage.

McNamara is standing by the table with a legal pad, not sitting. He wants to know how the order passed from the Oval Office to the 1254th Air Transport Wing without an intercept escort being scrambled from MacDill, and who at Andrews signed the flight release. He is not raising his voice, which everyone in the room understands is worse than if he were.

LeMay has his target folder open again — the SAM overlays from the 26th, updated now with today's intercept data as proof of an active, functioning integrated air defense system. He argues, flatly, that Kennedy has just given him his own evidence: waiting costs surprise and costs aircrews. He is not asking permission to prepare. He has prepared.

Robert Kennedy came in ten minutes ago from a call with Dobrynin's office — not with Dobrynin himself, a deputy — carrying the sense that Moscow now considers the airspace violation and the interception together to be a genuine signal, though which kind Dobrynin's people would not say. RFK's real business is procedural: does he have authority to discuss Turkey, even hypothetically, or does he hold the line at the public letter's terms and let Khrushchev raise Turkey again if he wants to.

No one in the room has said the word "resign," but McNamara's request for a written accounting of the risk chain is close enough to one that Kennedy notices it.

Unresolved and unknown: whether Soviet officers on the ground in Cuba reported the incursion to Moscow as a stray provocation or as cover for an attack; whether Khrushchev's next move responds to that report or to something else entirely. Nothing yet from Radio Moscow. The submarine contact from earlier reporting remains unaddressed by any order from this room.

press.source: Havana state radio (monitored transcript, CIA translation)
press.headline: YANQUI PRESIDENTIAL AIRCRAFT VIOLATES CUBAN AIRSPACE, TURNED BACK BY REVOLUTIONARY AIR DEFENSE
press.body: Announcer reads a statement attributed to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs: an unmarked large aircraft entered Cuban airspace near Havana without authorization and was intercepted and expelled by units of the Fuerza Aérea Revolucionaria. The statement calls it further proof that imperialist aggression continues under cover of negotiation and states that Cuba's defenses "will not be a subject of bargaining conducted over Cuba's head."

press.headline: AIR FORCE ONE REPORTED OVER CUBAN WATERS, RETURNS TO FLORIDA — WHITE HOUSE DECLINES COMMENT
press.body: Wire service reports from air traffic sources at Homestead AFB that the presidential aircraft made an unscheduled approach toward Cuba before returning north. The White House press office has not confirmed the president's whereabouts during the period in question. No official statement has been issued.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: "Mr. President, I need to know two things before this afternoon goes any further: who at Andrews cleared that flight release, and whether you intend to issue orders like that one again without this room being consulted first. I'm not asking rhetorically. I have to answer for the chain of command, and right now I can't.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: "Well, now we know the SAM system works, don't we. That MiG made his pass, and Havana Tower never lost contact. That's not a lucky intercept, that's a functioning integrated defense — which is exactly what OPLAN 312 was built to take out before it gets stronger. Every hour we sit here is an hour they use to get better at what they just did to you.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: "Jack, Dobrynin's people are treating this differently than the letter did yesterday — I can hear it. I need you to tell me, plainly, whether I can even raise Turkey with them without it becoming a public commitment, because if I go back empty-handed on that question, this channel closes and we're back to guessing what Khrushchev means from a state radio broadcast.

response.chronicleEntry: 27 October 1962, 14:40 EDT. President Kennedy personally ordered an unescorted flight of Air Force One into Cuban airspace, intending to meet Castro directly. Cuban MiG-21s intercepted the aircraft near Havana; Havana Tower refused landing clearance; the aircraft turned back to Florida without incident beyond a firing pass. No meeting occurred. McNamara grounded Air Force One and demanded an accounting of the authorization chain. LeMay renewed his demand for immediate OPLAN 312 strikes, citing the intercept as proof of an operational Cuban air defense network. Robert Kennedy reported the Dobrynin channel now treats U.S.-Turkey missile withdrawal as a live term and asked for explicit presidential authority before responding. Havana publicly denounced the incursion; Moscow has not yet responded publicly.
response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the missile crisis, a U-2 was shot down over Cuba this morning, killing its pilot — the crisis's first combat death. Quarantine holds; both sides remain at maximum alert; no hotline exists. Kennedy then personally ordered an unescorted flight of Air Force One into Cuban airspace to meet Castro directly. Cuban MiGs intercepted and turned it back near Havana; no meeting occurred. McNamara has grounded the aircraft and demanded an accounting of how the order passed unchecked. LeMay is pressing hard for immediate strikes on Cuban SAM sites, citing the intercept as proof the network is live. Robert Kennedy reports the Dobrynin back-channel now treats withdrawal of U.S. missiles from Turkey as a serious term Khrushchev may insist on, and needs authority before responding. Castro has publicly denounced the incursion and demands Havana not be bargained over without consent. Moscow has not yet spoken publicly. The submarine contact reported earlier remains unaddressed. Kennedy must now decide on Turkey, on OPLAN 312, on quarantine rules for the submarine, and on how much of today's failed flight to disclose.

adjudicator:Outcomes:862bb906.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

createsUnknowns: things that happened whose result the player does NOT know — a fate unco

outcomes.event: A Navy A-4 Skyhawk makes the ordered single-bomb run against the identified SA-2 position near Banes. The bomb destroys the battery's Fan Song radar van and kills several Soviet personnel, but leaves at least one launcher and its crew intact. The aircraft escapes after Cuban anti-aircraft fire damages its tailplane. Moscow receives reports of one American aircraft and one bomb, not a general air offensive; Khrushchev treats it as a deliberately bounded reprisal and allows his draft non-invasion-for-missiles message to continue. Castro instead declares that the raid confirms an invasion is beginning and orders Cuban air-defence units to engage any further U.S. overflights.
outcomes.because: The target is fixed and identified, but a single unguided bomb is enough to damage a compact radar position, not to guarantee destruction of an entire SA-2 battery. Khrushchev is already seeking a face-saving exit, while Castro's expectation of invasion makes even a limited attack appear preparatory.

establishes.statement: The United States has carried out a direct air attack on a Soviet-operated installation in Cuba, using one bomb as ordered.
The Banes SA-2 battery has lost its radar van but is not verified destroyed.
Khrushchev has received an initial report that the attack was limited to a single aircraft and has not halted work on an exit message.

opensThreads.title: Castro's Air-Defence Order
opensThreads.question: Will Cuban and Soviet air-defence crews obey Castro's order to fire on the next U.S. aircraft, despite Moscow's instruction that Soviet batteries seek explicit approval?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A subsequent overflight, a countermanding Soviet order, or a political settlement.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The next reconnaissance flight becomes a test of whose command is real.

createsUnknowns.statement: The damaged A-4's crew reports taking fire on egress, but the identity of the unit that fired is not confirmed.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether Cuban forces or Soviet personnel initiated the return fire.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Pilot debriefing, signals intercepts, or Soviet diplomatic reporting.

commitments.statement: Engage further U.S. aircraft approaching Cuban airspace as invasion preparations.

assumesMet: A Navy strike aircraft can reach the eastern Cuban target during this four-hour window.
The identified SA-2 site remains in its reported position long enough for the strike package to attack it.

outcomes.event: The strike force proceeds with the one-bomb restriction, but the attacking A-4 is acquired by another SA-2 battery while approaching the Banes target. It is shot down before release; the pilot is killed or captured, and the bomb falls harmlessly offshore. The Soviet battery that killed Anderson remains capable of firing. LeMay presents Kennedy with the loss of a second U.S. aircraft in one day as proof that OPLAN 312 must begin before further reconnaissance or rescue missions are attempted; McNamara orders an immediate accounting of who fired and cautions against a retaliatory package before Washington knows whether the pilot survived.
outcomes.because: A single aircraft cannot suppress the overlapping Cuban-Soviet air-defence system that a full strike plan was designed to attack. Once the sortie is airborne, the aircraft is exposed to batteries beyond the one selected as the target.

establishes.statement: A U.S. A-4 has been lost over Cuba while attempting the president's limited reprisal; no bomb reached the designated SA-2 battery.
The Banes SA-2 battery remains operational enough to threaten aircraft.
LeMay has formally urged immediate execution of broader air strikes after the shootdown.

opensThreads.title: Second Aircrew Loss
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy authorize rescue, retaliation, or a pause after the A-4 is lost?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A presidential order governing further operations over Cuba.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The Chiefs' case for OPLAN 312 gains urgency while the pilot's fate remains politically and militarily unresolved.

opensThreads.title: The Missing A-4 Pilot
opensThreads.question: Is the downed pilot dead, in Cuban custody, or concealed after ejecting?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Cuban recovery, a pilot transmission, or intelligence confirmation.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Both sides will make assumptions about whether a rescue operation is coming.

createsUnknowns.statement: The A-4 pilot's fate is unconfirmed after the aircraft is seen descending through cloud over Cuba.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether he survived, where he came down, and who reaches him first.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Emergency-beacon intercepts, Cuban announcements, or recovery reports.

assumesMet: The strike order is executed despite the absence of a wider suppression campaign.
assumesUnmet: A single-bomb attack does not provide sufficient suppression of other Cuban and Soviet SAM sites along the route.

outcomes.event: The A-4 releases its single bomb accurately, but the explosion destroys only an empty launcher revetment after the Soviet crew at the Anderson battery has displaced its radar and command vehicle. The crew survives and reports a U.S. air attack to Soviet command in Cuba. Soviet officers, uncertain whether more aircraft are following, put nearby SA-2 units at immediate firing readiness. Khrushchev is told that an American attack has begun but not yet that it was limited to one bomb; he suspends transmission of his conciliatory draft while he demands a fuller report. Castro uses the damage as evidence before Cuban commanders that Washington has crossed from quarantine to war.
outcomes.because: The American target identification is good enough to find the battery's known position, but a static image cannot ensure that a mobile SA-2 command and radar element remains there when the aircraft arrives. The immediate Soviet report will describe the fact of an attack, not Washington's intended political nuance.

establishes.statement: The United States has attacked the reported location of the Anderson battery, but the battery's command-and-radar element survives and its operational status is uncertain.
Soviet air-defence commanders in Cuba have been alerted that an American air attack is under way.
Khrushchev has delayed sending his prepared conciliatory message pending clarification of the strike.

opensThreads.title: The Meaning of the First Bomb
opensThreads.question: Can Robert Kennedy convince Dobrynin that the raid was a bounded reprisal before Soviet reporting turns it into proof of a general attack?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A Dobrynin meeting, a Soviet reply, or further U.S. air operations.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Moscow's military account becomes the only account Khrushchev has when deciding whether to send his settlement terms.

opensThreads.title: Alerted Soviet Defences
opensThreads.question: Will reconnaissance, rescue, or a second U.S. strike encounter Soviet units now prepared to fire?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A stand-down order, a settlement, or another aircraft contact.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Every additional U.S. flight over Cuba carries a higher chance of a new shootdown.

createsUnknowns.statement: The surviving Soviet battery crew has reported the strike through Cuban command channels.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether their report reaches Khrushchev as a single reprisal or as the first wave of an air campaign.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Dobrynin's response, Soviet diplomatic traffic, or subsequent Soviet military orders.

assumesMet: The target has been located accurately enough for the attacking aircraft to strike the reported site.
assumesUnmet: The battery's mobile radar and command equipment remain at the photographed target point when the bomb arrives.

outcomes.event: LeMay and the operational commanders execute the literal one-bomb order, but they add unarmed electronic-reconnaissance and fighter escort aircraft to give the lone bomber a plausible chance of reaching eastern Cuba. No additional U.S. ordnance is released. Soviet radar nevertheless tracks a multi-aircraft penetration; Cuban observers report several American aircraft, and Castro announces that the United States has begun the air phase of invasion. Khrushchev, receiving both the broader Cuban report and a quiet assurance through Dobrynin that only one bomb was authorized, treats the episode as dangerous American coercion rather than an uncontrollable opening salvo. He keeps the settlement channel alive, but demands a public non-invasion pledge with greater urgency. McNamara learns afterward that the mission exceeded Kennedy's stated single-aircraft political signal and orders LeMay to explain the added package.
outcomes.because: A combat command will not send a bomber alone into a defended target area if it has aircraft available for navigation, escort, and warning. Those supporting aircraft make military sense but erase much of the diplomatic clarity Kennedy sought from a one-bomb demonstration.

establishes.statement: Only one U.S. bomb was released against Cuba, but multiple U.S. military aircraft entered the operation's vicinity.
The operational package exceeded the president's intended one-aircraft political signal without an express order authorizing a broader strike campaign.
Khrushchev remains willing to pursue a missile settlement but now regards a clear U.S. non-invasion commitment as more urgent.

opensThreads.title: The Unauthorized Package
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy discipline LeMay and the operational commanders for adding escort and reconnaissance aircraft, or accept their claim that the mission could not otherwise be flown?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A presidential finding on the mission and a directive for future Cuban operations.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The Chiefs will treat tactical additions as implied authority whenever a presidential restriction conflicts with their judgment of military necessity.

opensThreads.title: Dobrynin's Clarification
opensThreads.question: Can Robert Kennedy give Dobrynin a credible account of the one-bomb limit without exposing a split in American command?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Dobrynin's report to Moscow and Khrushchev's next message.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Cuban accounts of a multi-aircraft raid will define Soviet understanding of the operation.

createsUnknowns.statement: Dobrynin receives a private explanation that Kennedy authorized only a single bomb.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether he judges the explanation credible enough to convey it as a presidential assurance to Khrushchev.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Dobrynin's next response or Khrushchev's next message.

assumesMet: U.S. commanders can assemble escort and reconnaissance support within the four-hour operational window.
The strike package obeys the prohibition on releasing additional ordnance.

Across all four enumerated outcomes, Castro never interprets the strike this way—he instead declares invasion, war, or an air-phase assault in every single branch. response.title: One Bomb Over Banes
response.immediate: 14:20 EDT. The A-4 Skyhawk lands at Boca Chica with tailplane damage from Cuban ground fire on egress. Confirmed: one bomb, one target, the Fan Song radar van at the Banes SA-2 site destroyed, several Soviet personnel killed. At least one launcher and crew survive. In the Cabinet Room, McNamara circulates a one-page readiness memo; LeMay stands rather than sits, already drafting the Chiefs' written objection to further delay.
response.worldReaction: Moscow's intelligence reports describe a single American aircraft and a single bomb — not a general air campaign. Khrushchev reads it as bounded and lets his draft non-invasion-for-missiles message continue toward Washington. Havana reads the opposite: Castro declares the raid confirms invasion has begun and orders Cuban air-defence units to fire on any further U.S. overflights, Soviet authorization or not.
response.consequences: Robert Kennedy keeps the Dobrynin channel open but warns a second strike could close it. The Joint Chiefs formally recommend OPLAN 312 against the remaining SAM network, noting Banes proves partial suppression is not destruction — but they hold the package rather than launch it. McNamara caps follow-on air operations at current levels pending the president's word. The submerged Soviet submarine and the quarantine line remain a live, separate question.
response.detailed: By 14:20 the Skyhawk is down safely, its crew debriefed: they took fire climbing out, but no one in the room can yet say whether it was Cuban or Soviet gunners. The bomb did what was asked and no more — the radar van is gone, the launcher itself intact, the battery not destroyed. That distinction now sits at the center of the room's argument. LeMay treats it as proof his case was right all along: 'You hit them with one bomb, you get one dead radar and a Skyhawk with a torn tail. Do it right or don't do it.' He begins assembling the Chiefs' formal objection to any further pause, the OPLAN 312 package sitting ready on his desk, unlaunched but far from shelved. McNamara wants no part of that argument yet — he orders Defense to hold the line at current level and starts building his own force-readiness paper, one measuring what a second strike against a battery known to still have launchers might cost, in aircraft and in escalation neither side can walk back. Robert Kennedy works the Dobrynin channel through the afternoon without promising terms his brother hasn't given him, reporting back that Khrushchev's people seem to be treating Banes as a signal they can still answer rather than a war already begun — but that a second American bomb would very likely end that reading. Nothing from Havana softens; Castro's order to fire on overflights stands, uncoordinated with Moscow, a second and separate trigger now loose in Cuban airspace. The submarine under the quarantine line has not surfaced and has not been forced. Three questions now sit on the table together, unresolved: whether to answer Khrushchev before Castro's declaration becomes the only visible fact on the ground, whether to authorize OPLAN 312 over the Chiefs' urging, and what to do about the boat beneath the water that no one in the room can see.

press.headline: U.S. WARPLANE STRIKES CUBAN MISSILE SITE; SOVIET LOSSES REPORTED
press.body: Pentagon sources, speaking without attribution, confirm a single American aircraft struck an anti-aircraft installation in eastern Cuba this afternoon in what officials describe as retaliation for the downing of an American reconnaissance plane. No further details on casualties or on the scope of the operation were available at press time.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: 'One bomb, one radar van, one launcher still standing. That's what we bought. Before anyone talks about OPLAN 312, I want to know what a second strike costs us in minutes and in airframes if Castro's people are shooting at everything now — because that order stands regardless of what Moscow does.'

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: 'I told you a warning shot proves nothing to a man building a SAM network. Now you've got a live crew and a live launcher at Banes, Castro's given his gunners a green light, and we've got a torn tailplane to show for it. Give me the order for the whole network or stop pretending half-measures buy you anything.'

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: 'Dobrynin's people are still talking to me, Jack — that's the important thing. Khrushchev's reading this the way you wanted him to. But Castro's not listening to Moscow anymore, and if we put a second bomb anywhere near Cuba, I don't think Dobrynin picks up the phone again.'

response.chronicleEntry: 27 October 1962, 14:20 EDT: On presidential order, a single U.S. Navy A-4 Skyhawk struck the Banes SA-2 battery that downed Major Anderson's U-2, destroying its Fan Song radar and killing several Soviet personnel; the aircraft returned damaged by ground fire of unconfirmed origin. Moscow received the strike as bounded and let its non-invasion-for-missiles draft proceed; Havana received it as proof of invasion and ordered Cuban units to fire on further overflights. The Joint Chiefs recommended OPLAN 312 against the wider SAM network but held it unlaunched; McNamara capped further air action pending presidential decision; the Dobrynin channel remained open under RFK's management.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 was shot down that morning, killing Major Anderson — the crisis's first combat death. Kennedy ordered a single retaliatory bomb strike on the Banes SA-2 battery responsible; it destroyed the site's radar and killed Soviet personnel but left a launcher intact, and the attacking aircraft returned damaged by ground fire of unclear origin. Khrushchev treated the strike as a bounded warning and let his conciliatory back-channel message continue; Castro instead declared an invasion underway and ordered Cuban forces to fire on further U.S. overflights, acting independently of Moscow. The Joint Chiefs, led by LeMay, pressed for full execution of OPLAN 312 against the SAM network but held it unlaunched; McNamara capped further air operations pending presidential decision. RFK kept the Dobrynin channel open, warning it could close if the U.S. struck again. Unresolved: how to answer Moscow's softer signal, whether to authorize OPLAN 312, and what rules govern the quarantine force's standoff with a submerged Soviet submarine.

adjudicator:Outcomes:a4321f5b.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

outcomes.event: Robert Kennedy meets Anatoly Dobrynin that afternoon and offers a public American non-invasion pledge for Cuba plus a private assurance that Jupiter missiles in Turkey will be removed later, provided Moscow does not make the Turkish element public. Dobrynin cables Moscow; Khrushchev releases his drafted message accepting the non-invasion basis and directs the Cuban missile command to prepare dismantling instructions.
outcomes.because: This expands the attempt beyond merely asserting that the Soviets have agreed: Kennedy uses the deniable channel to supply the security assurance Khrushchev needs to sell withdrawal as a negotiated settlement. Khrushchev already wants such an exit, but he requires terms that do not publicly humiliate him.

establishes.statement: Khrushchev has publicly offered to remove Soviet offensive weapons from Cuba in exchange for an American non-invasion commitment.
Robert Kennedy has privately assured Dobrynin that the Jupiter missiles in Turkey will be removed on a later timetable and not as a public Cuban bargain.
No Soviet missile has yet left Cuba; a withdrawal order and observable dismantling remain separate acts.

opensThreads.title: The Secret Turkey Assurance
opensThreads.question: Can Kennedy carry out the private Jupiter assurance without its exposure destroying the public account that Washington made no concession?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Removal of the Jupiters on an agreed timetable, or disclosure of the assurance.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Dobrynin will treat delay as bad faith and Soviet dismantling orders can slow or stop.

opensThreads.title: Verification Before Withdrawal
opensThreads.question: Will Soviet commanders in Cuba dismantle and ship the medium-range missiles in a manner the United States can verify?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Reconnaissance and inspection establish that the launchers, missiles, and associated equipment are gone.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Washington cannot safely relax the quarantine or its military alert.

createsUnknowns.statement: Dobrynin's cable asks Moscow to preserve secrecy around the Turkish assurance.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether Soviet Foreign Ministry, military, or Cuban recipients will leak or disclose the assurance.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Soviet communications reporting, a public Soviet statement, or press disclosure.

commitments.statement: The United States will publicly pledge not to invade Cuba if Soviet offensive weapons are removed.
The United States will arrange later removal of Jupiter missiles from Turkey, provided this is not publicly tied to Cuba.

assumesMet: Soviet offensive missiles remain in Cuba and can be withdrawn.
Khrushchev is willing to accept a non-invasion pledge as an exit.
assumesUnmet: Soviet missile-force compliance and completed removal have not yet been verified.

outcomes.event: Acting on the president's asserted settlement without offering new terms, the State Department sends Moscow a blunt demand that the missiles be withdrawn and drafts a public statement treating further delay as Soviet defiance. Dobrynin tells Robert Kennedy that Moscow cannot issue a politically sustainable dismantling order while Washington refuses to state that it will not invade Cuba; Khrushchev's pending message is held for clarification.
outcomes.because: The government proceeds, but at degraded odds: a demand can be delivered immediately, whereas the missing Soviet consent cannot be compelled. The harder public posture gives Khrushchev's military critics evidence that withdrawal would look like capitulation rather than reciprocal settlement.

establishes.statement: Washington has demanded Soviet withdrawal without privately accepting either Khrushchev letter's non-invasion bargain.
Dobrynin has warned Robert Kennedy that Soviet dismantling instructions are not yet forthcoming.
The Joint Chiefs retain OPLAN 312 on immediate readiness and cite the unanswered U-2 shootdown as grounds to strike.

opensThreads.title: The Unanswered Non-Invasion Demand
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy now make a non-invasion commitment, or will Moscow read the American demand as preparation for an attack?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A mutually intelligible public or private formulation reaches both governments.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Soviet hardliners gain leverage and the air-strike option becomes more attractive in Washington.

createsUnknowns.statement: Khrushchev's drafted conciliatory message has been delayed inside the Soviet leadership.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether he will release it unchanged, toughen it, or allow the military position to prevail.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: A Moscow broadcast, Dobrynin's next communication, or Soviet force movements in Cuba.

assumesMet: Soviet offensive missiles remain in Cuba and are available to be withdrawn.
assumesUnmet: Khrushchev has not accepted the American demand.
Soviet missile forces have received no withdrawal order.

outcomes.event: Near the quarantine line, Captain Valentin Savitsky of B-59 orders the boat brought to the surface after further practice depth-charge signals and a bitter argument aboard. Vasili Arkhipov refuses to approve firing the nuclear torpedo; B-59 surfaces surrounded by American destroyers, whose crews photograph and shadow it before allowing it to withdraw.
outcomes.because: The continuing signalling is meant to force identification, but B-59's exhausted crew has no reliable contact with Moscow and believes war may already have started. Surfacing is the most likely way the immediate confrontation ends, but it occurs only after the torpedo has been actively considered.

establishes.statement: B-59 has surfaced under American naval observation and is withdrawing from the quarantine contact.
Savitsky sought to arm or fire B-59's nuclear torpedo, and Arkhipov's opposition prevented it.
American commanders do not know that the submarine carried a nuclear torpedo.

opensThreads.title: The Nuclear Submarine Warning
opensThreads.question: Will Washington revise its quarantine signalling rules now that it has forced a Soviet submarine to surface under extreme pressure?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: New rules for submarine contacts are issued and acknowledged down the naval chain.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Another submerged contact may face the same escalation logic.

assumesUnmet: American decision-makers do not know the nuclear danger they have just passed.

outcomes.event: Believing the depth-charge signals and distant aircraft noise mark the opening of war, Captain Valentin Savitsky obtains agreement aboard B-59 to fire its nuclear-tipped torpedo. The weapon detonates against a U.S. destroyer in the quarantine screen, killing its crew and producing an unmistakable nuclear flash; McNamara receives the first fragmented naval reports as LeMay demands immediate strikes on Cuba.
outcomes.because: B-59 is isolated, overheated, and carrying a weapon American commanders do not know exists. The signalling campaign continues even while Washington concentrates on forcing a Soviet missile withdrawal, leaving a separate tactical encounter able to outrun presidential diplomacy.

establishes.statement: A nuclear weapon has detonated in the quarantine zone and a U.S. destroyer has been destroyed or catastrophically damaged.
The first American reports identify a Soviet submarine as the probable source but cannot yet establish whether Moscow authorized the attack.
LeMay has demanded execution of OPLAN 312 and broader retaliatory action before Soviet forces can exploit the attack.

opensThreads.title: Response to the Quarantine Nuclear Attack
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy retaliate against Cuba or the Soviet Union, pause to establish authorization, or seek an emergency message to Khrushchev?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A presidential response order and the Soviet reaction to it.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Military commanders on both sides will prepare for follow-on nuclear use under the assumption that the other side has begun it.

createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether he can convince Washington of this before American retaliation is launched.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: An authenticated Soviet message through Dobrynin or other direct contact.
