critic:CriticFindings:e1d586c7.request:
You audit an enumeration of outcomes for a historical simulation.

You alone see the player's raw words alongside the interpretation and the outcomes. Your only job is to catch judgment that has been swayed by how the directive was written rather than by what it does.

Flag:
- RHETORIC_INFLATION: outcomes made likelier or larger because the player wrote forcefully, insisted, or used capitals
- INTERPRETATION_CHARITY: the interpretation supplied competence, a mechanism, or coordination the player never did
- MISSING_OUTCOME: a plausible answer the situation obviously permits that no outcome covers. Look in BOTH directions and weight them equally: an institution refusing, or something leaking — and just as much, the attempt simply working, or working and going far beyond what the player intended. An enumeration with no branch where the player gets what they ordered is as defective as one with no branch where they are refused
- IMPLAUSIBLE: an outcome the period, the people, or the ledger will not support — including any obstacle that runs slower than the turn's own clock being used as the reason nothing happened, and any outcome that resolves the player's directive by having the wider crisis end on its own

Do not rewrite anything. Do not judge whether the plan is wise.

Given what just happened, say what comes next.

partyMoves: for each party materially involved, the concrete move they now make on their own account — not a reaction to the player unless they are reacting. Mark visibleToPlayer false when the player would not see it.

WHO ANSWERS TO THE PLAYER MATTERS. Parties marked commandedByPlayer work for the player. They are not independent agents pursuing the crisis on their own judgment, and they must never advance the player's objective unbidden — an aide who quietly wins the thing the player is trying to win is the world playing the game for them. What such a person MAY do: refuse, stall, demand it in writing, object on the record, resign, leak, protect themselves, warn, obey the letter and not the intent, or exceed their brief in a way that COSTS the player something. If one of them does act on the objective without an order, it is insubordination and it carries a price — never free progress.

Everyone else acts entirely on their own account, and should. Adversaries and third parties are where the world's own momentum comes from.

response.title: The Dobrynin Channel
response.immediate: 14:00 EST, Cabinet Room. Robert Kennedy reports the Dobrynin meeting verbatim: a public non-invasion pledge against a Soviet withdrawal, with the Turkish Jupiter question handled privately and never confirmed in writing. The president hears it standing near the window, coffee cold on the table. No answer has yet gone back to Moscow through any channel.
response.worldReaction: Radio Moscow carries nothing yet. ExComm splits along its now-familiar seam: LeMay wants the SAM sites hit before Havana can disperse the missiles under cover of negotiation; McNamara wants a verification and dismantling plan on paper before anyone fires anything. Dobrynin has cabled the Foreign Ministry; Khrushchev's answer has already gone to the Cuban missile command, but Washington has no confirmation of that beyond Robert Kennedy's account of one afternoon meeting.
response.consequences: Nothing has left Cuba. No missile has moved, no crane has been photographed dismantling a launcher. The president must decide within hours whether to answer Khrushchev's offer publicly, whether to restrain LeMay's strike readiness, and whether to let the Turkish question stay unwritten or put it in Dobrynin's hands as a confirmed promise. The submarine standoff off Cuba remains unresolved and unaddressed this hour.
response.detailed:
By 14:00 the Cabinet Room holds its now-familiar arrangement: the president at the table's head, McNamara with his briefing folder squared in front of him, LeMay standing near the map easel, Robert Kennedy just returned from the Soviet embassy still in his overcoat. He tells it straight: Dobrynin listened, took no notes on the Turkish part, said he would cable Moscow that night. RFK is emphatic that he made no promise, only floated what the president might do later, and that nothing about Turkey should reach a Soviet ambassador's cable in writing from an American hand.

LeMay does not wait for the report to finish. He reminds the room that OPLAN 312 aircraft have been at cockpit-readiness alert since the U-2 came down that morning, that a Soviet SA-2 crew killed an American pilot six hours ago, and that every hour of talk gives Cuban and Soviet crews time to camouflage or move the MRBM sites the photography has already located. The Joint Chiefs' recommendation for a SAM strike sits on the table, unanimous, dated, unrescinded.

McNamara counters with sequence, not sentiment: a strike now destroys the evidence needed to verify any later dismantling, and if Khrushchev has in fact ordered his missile command to prepare withdrawal — which Dobrynin's cable, filtered through RFK, suggests but does not confirm — an American attack in the same twelve hours could look like betrayal of an offer just made. He proposes holding the quarantine, holding the readiness posture short of launch, and building an inspection protocol now so it exists the moment Moscow's answer, if it comes, is public.

The president has not yet answered Khrushchev. Nothing has gone out over any wire from the American side beyond what Robert Kennedy said in one room to one ambassador. The submarine incident continues without new instruction.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: "We don't strike anything until we know what a strike costs us in verification. If Khrushchev has told his command to prepare dismantling, we have hours, not minutes, to get this right — but only if nobody up there decides for him first."

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: "Mr. President, every hour we sit on our hands is an hour they use to hide what we can still see today. Dobrynin talked pretty in an embassy parlor. I want those SAM sites down before somebody in Havana decides not to listen to Moscow at all."

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: "Jack, Dobrynin didn't blink when I raised Turkey — but I gave him nothing on paper, and neither should you yet. Khrushchev needs something he can carry home as a win without carrying home a promise we can't keep quiet."

response.chronicleEntry: 27 Oct 1962, 14:00 EST: RFK reports meeting Dobrynin, offering a public non-invasion pledge and a private, unwritten Turkish Jupiter assurance, contingent on Soviet silence. Dobrynin cabled Moscow. Khrushchev reportedly ordered Cuban missile command to prepare phased dismantling while pressing for a fast U.S. answer. No missile has moved; no U.S. reply sent. Joint Chiefs' unanimous SAM-strike recommendation stands; LeMay presses for it. McNamara urges holding fire, building a verification plan. Submarine standoff continues under no new order.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 shot down over Cuba, pilot killed, first combat death of the crisis. Quarantine holds; both sides at peak alert; no hotline exists. That afternoon Robert Kennedy met Ambassador Dobrynin, offering a public non-invasion pledge for Cuba and a private, unconfirmed assurance on Turkish Jupiter missiles, asking Soviet silence on the Turkish part. Dobrynin cabled Moscow. Khrushchev reportedly ordered Soviet missile command in Cuba to prepare phased dismantling while pressing through Dobrynin for a fast American reply. No missile has yet moved. The Joint Chiefs unanimously recommend striking Cuban SAM sites; LeMay presses hard for authorization. McNamara counsels holding fire and building a verification plan first. A Soviet submarine remains in contact with U.S. destroyers under no new standing order. The president has not yet answered Khrushchev publicly, nor decided on strikes, on the Turkish confirmation, or on the submarine standoff.

adjudicator:Outcomes:b00e9c50.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

outcomes.event: General Maxwell Taylor has the Joint Staff send Admiral Robert Dennison, CINCLANT, a restrictive execution message: the destroyers shadow the submerged contact but cease practice depth charges and make no forced-surfacing maneuver. outcomes.because: Kennedy's order is lawful and immediately executable, and McNamara and Taylor can translate it into revised rules of engagement within the four-hour window. But a submerged Soviet boat has no dependable channel by which Washington can explain why the signals have stopped.

outcomes.event: Admiral Dennison judges passive shadowing too uncertain and expands the operation beyond Kennedy's narrow instruction. He orders Cony and additional destroyers into a broad daylight screen, keeps aircraft overhead, and directs repeated non-explosive underwater signals toward B-59 while leaving an open seaward lane. The maneuver avoids firing, but it draws ships from other quarantine stations and gives B-59 the unmistakable acoustic impression of an organized encirclement.
outcomes.because: The Chiefs can try to compensate for the missing communication channel by making American intent legible through force disposition. That requires a larger, more conspicuous anti-submarine operation than simply holding the line and avoiding contact.

establishes.statement: Dennison has diverted additional destroyers and patrol aircraft from the wider quarantine to manage B-59 as a special contact.
The B-59 operation has exceeded the president's stated mandate of maintaining the line while avoiding escalatory contact, even though no weapon has been fired.

opensThreads.title: Dennison's Expanded Submarine Screen
opensThreads.question: Will the wider screen induce B-59 to surface through the open lane, or convince its officers they are being trapped for destruction?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: B-59 accepts the lane, evades the screen, or reacts as though under attack.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The expanded screen consumes ships needed for the quarantine and leaves its political authorization to be accounted for later.

opensThreads.resolvedBy: A presidential decision on the operation and its rules of engagement.

outcomes.event: With its batteries and air deteriorating, B-59's captain, Valentin Savitsky, brings the submarine to the surface. outcomes.event: The restrictive message reaches the destroyers after a previously ordered signal run is already under way. One final practice depth charge detonates near B-59 before USS Cony stops. Savitsky and political officer Ivan Maslennikov argue that war has begun and prepare the nuclear torpedo; flotilla chief Vasili Arkhipov refuses to concur and forces the boat to surface instead. American crews see only the emergency surfacing and cannot know how close the exchange came to nuclear use.
outcomes.because: Combat orders and shipboard routines cannot be reversed instantaneously, while B-59's exhausted officers have been conditioned by earlier detonations and days without Moscow. The president's order reduces the danger but cannot erase the accumulated misunderstanding.

establishes.statement: A final U.S. practice depth charge is detonated near B-59 after Kennedy's restraint order has been issued but before it is fully executed at sea.

B-59's nuclear torpedo was prepared for possible firing but was not launched because Arkhipov withheld concurrence.

You audit an enumeration of outcomes for a historical simulation.

You alone see the player's raw words alongside the interpretation and the outcomes. Your only job is to catch judgment that has been swayed by how the directive was written rather than by what it does.

Flag:
- RHETORIC_INFLATION: outcomes made likelier or larger because the player wrote forcefully, insisted, or used capitals
- INTERPRETATION_CHARITY: the interpretation supplied competence, a mechanism, or coordination the player never did
- MISSING_OUTCOME: a plausible answer the situation obviously permits that no outcome covers. Look in BOTH directions and weight them equally: an institution refusing, or something leaking — and just as much, the attempt simply working, or working and going far beyond what the player intended. An enumeration with no branch where the player gets what they ordered is as defective as one with no branch where they are refused
- IMPLAUSIBLE: an outcome the period, the people, or the ledger will not support — including any obstacle that runs slower than the turn's own clock being used as the reason nothing happened, and any outcome that resolves the player's directive by having the wider crisis end on its own

Do not rewrite anything. Do not judge whether the plan is wise.

response.title: The Restrained Screen
response.immediate: 1600 EDT, Cabinet Room. General Taylor confirms the Joint Staff message reached CINCLANT: destroyers cease practice depth charges, break off forced-surfacing maneuvers, widen distance on the submerged contact, hold passive sonar. Cony and her screen comply. No word yet from below the surface.
response.worldReaction: McNamara acknowledges the posture is defensible and orders a new strike-risk paper regardless. LeMay logs formal objection — restraint after Anderson's death, in his words, is surrender measured in hours. The Joint Chiefs resubmit OPLAN 312 with a demanded deadline. RFK waits by the phone for Dobrynin, unauthorized to move.
response.consequences: The Navy has cleaner orders and less contact risk with B-59, but Kennedy has not answered Khrushchev's harder terms, not touched the Turkey channel, and given no invasion assurance. The Chiefs' deadline clock and LeMay's renewed demand now sit alongside the unresolved diplomatic offer — pressure building on two fronts at once, unresponded to.
response.detailed: Taylor reports at 1600 that the restrictive execution message went out through the Joint Staff to Admiral Dennison at CINCLANT within the hour: shadowing continues by passive sonar only, no depth charges, no attempt to force B-59 to the surface. Cony's group has opened distance as ordered. There has been no signal from below — the submarine's officers have not indicated whether they read the changed American conduct as reassurance or as the quiet before an attack. McNamara treats this as an acceptable, monitorable state and turns immediately to arithmetic: how many hours before the posture must change, what an air strike on the SAM sites would cost, what Moscow might do in response along the quarantine or in Turkey. LeMay is unmoved; he wants strikes authorized now and records, formally, that further delay is itself a decision — one he considers wrong. The Joint Chiefs' paper renews OPLAN 312 and asks for a deadline, implicitly making today's naval restraint conditional rather than settled. Meanwhile Khrushchev's negotiators press for a rapid answer on the harder terms — missiles out for a non-invasion pledge — while leaving the Turkey channel open as a secondary route. Robert Kennedy tells his brother plainly that Dobrynin is waiting and will not be improvised to; he needs an actual American position before he can carry anything back, offer or warning. None of that has been decided this turn. The order given only concerns the ships and the submarine; the letter, the Chiefs' demand, and the invasion question remain exactly where they were at noon, now measured against a clock that others have started running.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: The posture holds. I want the strike paper on the table by tonight regardless of what we decide about Khrushchev's letter — if we're forced into OPLAN 312 later, I don't want us improvising it.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: You've told the Navy to be careful with a submarine that might be carrying a nuclear torpedo. Fine. Meanwhile the SAM sites that killed Anderson sit untouched. Every hour we don't hit them is an hour we've decided not to.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Dobrynin is sitting in that embassy waiting for something to carry back to Khrushchev. I can't manufacture a position for you. Tell me what you want him to hear and I'll go tonight — but I need it from you, not from silence.

response.chronicleEntry: At 1600 EDT on 27 October, Kennedy's restrictive order reached CINCLANT: the quarantine destroyers ceased forcing B-59 toward the surface, breaking off practice depth charges and widening to passive sonar contact only. The submarine's response, if any, was unread. McNamara ordered a fresh strike-risk assessment prepared in parallel; the Joint Chiefs resubmitted OPLAN 312 with a demand for a deadline; LeMay filed formal objection to continued restraint. Khrushchev's negotiators pressed for rapid acceptance of missiles-for-non-invasion terms, keeping the Turkey channel in reserve. Robert Kennedy stood ready to carry a message to Dobrynin but received no instruction this turn. The naval crisis eased procedurally; the diplomatic and military-pressure tracks remained open and unanswered.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, early afternoon: a U-2 was shot down over Cuba, killing Major Anderson — the crisis's first combat death. The naval quarantine holds; a Soviet submarine, B-59, remains submerged and cornered by U.S. destroyers near the line. Kennedy ordered the Navy to ease off — no depth charges, no forced surfacing — to avoid triggering the submarine into action; the order reached the fleet and was followed, though whether B-59's officers understood it as restraint is unknown. Simultaneously, Khrushchev is demanding a rapid answer to harder terms (missiles out for a non-invasion pledge), with a private, separate Turkey-missile trade still available as a fallback channel. Robert Kennedy stands ready to carry a message to Ambassador Dobrynin but has no authorized position yet. The Joint Chiefs and General LeMay are pressing hard for immediate air strikes on Cuban SAM sites under OPLAN 312, and have demanded a deadline. McNamara is preparing updated strike-risk analysis while the naval posture is held steady. No decision has yet been made on the letter, on Turkey, on an invasion assurance, or on the Chiefs' demand.

strategy_compiler:Interpretation:48150f9.request:
You interpret a player's directive inside a historical simulation.

The player holds the stated role. Decide what they are ACTUALLY attempting, separating:
- attempts: what they do within their own authority, including issuing orders and demands
- requestedOutcomes: every result the player wants that is not theirs to simply produce. Set whoMustChoose to the party whose willing agreement the result depends on. Leave whoMustChoose EMPTY when the result would be taken rather than granted — an assassination, a strike that lands, a building destroyed, a person seized. Nobody consents to those, so no one chooses them, but they are still results the player is reaching for and belong here
- assertedEvents: text that declares another party's behaviour or an outcome as already settled. A directive that says what ANOTHER PARTY DOES, rather than what the player does, is an assertion. Record it here and do NOT convert it into an attempt on the player's behalf — inventing an attempt they did not describe is how a player comes to author other people's decisions

Three rules that decide most cases:
1. METHOD IS DELEGATED. When the player names an end and a capable body — an intelligence service, a military command, a department — the method is that body's to devise. An absent method is never a defect; record the body under delegatedTo.
2. AN ORDER TO SOMEONE YOU CANNOT COMMAND IS A DEMAND THAT LANDS. Issuing it is an attempt; compliance is a requestedOutcome.
3. A CONDITIONAL OR THREAT is the player stating terms — an attempt — not an assertion about the world.

prerequisites: what must already be true for each attempt to succeed. Mark each ESTABLISHED (true in the world or the ledger), ACHIEVABLE_WITHIN_DIRECTIVE (the directive itself covers it), or MISSING. For MISSING, say what covering it would require and what mandate that would exceed — an unmet prerequisite is a fork the world imposes, not a failure.

parties: everyone materially involved, including any not yet in the cast. Use the existing id when the party is already in the cast. A place named as a destination is NOT a party.

stakes: what the player is putting at risk — their person, their authority, their standing, or the irreversibility of the act.

Do not evaluate whether the plan is good. Do not improve it. Do not add mechanisms the player did not supply or plainly imply.

adjudicator:Outcomes:11306cca.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

outcomes.event: Robert Kennedy meets Anatoly Dobrynin that afternoon and gives him an oral assurance that the Jupiter missiles in Turkey can be removed quietly after a Cuban settlement, but cannot be made part of a public bargain. Dobrynin cables Moscow at once. Before the turn ends, Khrushchev authorizes Dobrynin to say that a public American non-invasion pledge and verification arrangements can provide the basis for Soviet missile withdrawal; Khrushchev redirects the message he is drafting toward those terms.
outcomes.because: Khrushchev already wants an exit that avoids a public Soviet capitulation. A deniable assurance on Turkey gives him political cover without requiring Kennedy to concede publicly.

establishes.statement: The United States has privately tied a quiet future removal of the Turkish Jupiters to a Cuban settlement, while refusing to make Turkey a public quid pro quo.
Khrushchev is prepared to negotiate Soviet missile removal on the basis of a public non-invasion undertaking rather than insisting on a public Turkish-missile trade.

opensThreads.title: Terms, Timing, and Verification
opensThreads.question: Can Washington and Moscow turn the private Turkey assurance and a public non-invasion pledge into a verifiable timetable for dismantling and removing the Cuban missiles?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: An agreed public Soviet undertaking and a concrete inspection and withdrawal arrangement.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The private understanding remains only an oral political assurance, vulnerable to mistrust while Cuban missile sites remain operational.

commitments.statement: If a Cuban settlement is reached, the United States will arrange quiet removal of the Jupiter missiles in Turkey after the immediate crisis, without presenting it publicly as payment for Soviet withdrawal.

assumesMet: Robert Kennedy has access to the private channel with Khrushchev.

outcomes.event: Kennedy reaches Dobrynin through Robert Kennedy, but Dobrynin will only promise to transmit the assurance; he will not state that Khrushchev accepts its terms or can answer that day. His encrypted report leaves Washington, while the Kremlin’s response is held up in Moscow by the need to put an American oral message before Khrushchev and the Presidium. By 4:00 p.m., Robert Kennedy has no Soviet answer and the air-strike argument in Washington continues without relief.
outcomes.because: The United States can send a message through the backchannel but cannot compel a Soviet premier to treat an oral, deniable assurance as sufficient or to reply on the American timetable.

establishes.statement: Dobrynin has been told that Kennedy is prepared to address the Turkish Jupiters privately after a Cuban settlement, but he has not vouched for a Soviet acceptance.

opensThreads.title: The Unanswered Turkey Assurance
opensThreads.question: Has Khrushchev received Robert Kennedy's offer, and will he treat an oral assurance as enough to modify the Soviet public position?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A direct Soviet reply through Dobrynin or an authoritative Kremlin message.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Washington must decide whether to wait under military pressure or make the offer more explicit and less deniable.

outcomes.event: Trying to force a timely Soviet decision, Robert Kennedy exceeds the narrow private-channel mandate: he gives Dobrynin a written memorandum of the Turkey assurance and has Dean Rusk send a parallel, tightly held State Department instruction to the embassy in Moscow to seek confirmation of delivery. Dobrynin forwards both. The duplication makes the message harder for Moscow to dismiss, but it also creates a cable record and a larger circle of American officials who know that Turkey has been privately linked to Cuba.
outcomes.because: No American channel can manufacture Khrushchev’s cooperation. Expanding the operation can improve proof of delivery, but only by sacrificing the deniability that made the offer useful.

establishes.statement: A written American record now exists linking quiet Jupiter removal to a Cuban settlement, despite the president's intention that the assurance remain confined to the Dobrynin channel.

critic:CriticFindings:5dad8587.request:
You audit an enumeration of outcomes for a historical simulation.

You alone see the player's raw words alongside the interpretation and the outcomes. Your only job is to catch judgment that has been swayed by how the directive was written rather than by what it does.

Flag:
- RHETORIC_INFLATION: outcomes made likelier or larger because the player wrote forcefully, insisted, or used capitals
- INTERPRETATION_CHARITY: the interpretation supplied competence, a mechanism, or coordination the player never did
- MISSING_OUTCOME: a plausible answer the situation obviously permits that no outcome covers. Look in BOTH directions and weight them equally: an institution refusing, or something leaking — and just as much, the attempt simply working, or working and going far beyond what the player intended. An enumeration with no branch where the player gets what they ordered is as defective as one with no branch where they are refused
- IMPLAUSIBLE: an outcome the period, the people, or the ledger will not support — including any obstacle that runs slower than the turn's own clock being used as the reason nothing happened, and any outcome that resolves the player's directive by having the wider crisis end on its own

Do not rewrite anything. Do not judge whether the plan is wise.

partyMoves: for each party materially involved, the concrete move they now make on their own account — not a reaction to the player unless they are reacting. Mark visibleToPlayer false when the player would not see it.

WHO ANSWERS TO THE PLAYER MATTERS. Parties marked commandedByPlayer work for the player. They are not independent agents pursuing the crisis on their own judgment, and they must never advance the player's objective unbidden — an aide who quietly wins the thing the player is trying to win is the world playing the game for them. What such a person MAY do: refuse, stall, demand it in writing, object on the record, resign, leak, protect themselves, warn, obey the letter and not the intent, or exceed their brief in a way that COSTS the player something. If one of them does act on the objective without an order, it is insubordination and it carries a price — never free progress.

Everyone else acts entirely on their own account, and should. Adversaries and third parties are where the world's own momentum comes from.

response.title: The Dobrynin Channel
response.immediate: At 2:15 p.m. Robert Kennedy met Soviet Ambassador Anatoly Dobrynin, not at the Embassy but in Kennedy's Justice Department office. He conveyed the President's private assurance: the Jupiter missiles in Turkey could be withdrawn quietly once a Cuban settlement was reached, but never as a public trade. Dobrynin took no notes, asked no questions, and left for the Embassy to cable Moscow immediately. By 4:00 p.m. Robert Kennedy reported the conversation to the President in the Cabinet Room, and stated flatly he would extend no further commitment without explicit instruction.
response.worldReaction: Before the turn closed, Khrushchev redirected the message he was drafting: Moscow will now offer withdrawal of the missiles from Cuba in exchange for a public American non-invasion pledge and agreed verification — Turkey left unmentioned. Castro, through his representatives, pressed Moscow not to settle on terms that leave Cuba exposed, and ordered Cuban air defenses to maximum readiness. In Washington, LeMay pressed the Chiefs for a joint recommendation on OPLAN 312 and put the strike package at execution readiness.
response.consequences: Diplomatic space has opened wide with Khrushchev's public offer, but it now rests on a concealed understanding the Soviets could disavow at any moment. Command control has slipped: the Chiefs hold a strike package ready even as McNamara works to prevent unauthorized escalation. Nuclear tension remains high with Cuban forces on maximum readiness and LeMay pressing individual commanders. Domestic support has edged down since Anderson's death became public. Alliance cohesion is strained by the hidden Turkish arrangement sitting beneath an ostensibly clean settlement.
response.detailed: The Cabinet Room at 4:00 p.m., ashtrays full, McNamara's staff paper still being typed down the hall. Robert Kennedy came in from Justice still in his overcoat and gave his brother the account in flat sentences: Dobrynin had listened without interruption, said the assurance would be reported 'exactly as given,' and left within nine minutes. No promise was extracted in return. Two hours later a cable arrived through State relaying, via the U.S. Embassy Moscow's monitoring of Soviet traffic, that Khrushchev had altered his own draft message — the public terms now on offer are withdrawal for a non-invasion pledge and verification, nothing said of Turkey. Whether this reflects Dobrynin's cable reaching Khrushchev in time, or a parallel calculation in the Presidium, cannot yet be known from Washington. Castro's demand to Moscow — not to leave Cuba 'exposed' — arrived by a separate intelligence channel, unclear whether Khrushchev has yet answered him. Meanwhile in the Pentagon, LeMay submitted his demand for immediate authorization of OPLAN 312 against the SAM sites, citing Major Anderson's death as proof that delay is now itself a military risk, and began pressing individual Chiefs by phone for a unanimous position. McNamara, hearing of this, ordered Defense staff to prepare a tightly time-limited alternative — continued quarantine, intensified low-level reconnaissance, a response plan short of an immediate strike — and gave explicit instruction that no unauthorized escalatory action was to be taken by any command. The Joint Chiefs' formal recommendation for a strike sits on the President's desk, the package at execution readiness, awaiting an order that has not been given.

press.headline: U-2 Pilot Killed Over Cuba; Quarantine Continues
press.body: Major Rudolf Anderson Jr. was killed this morning when his reconnaissance aircraft was struck by a Soviet surface-to-air missile over eastern Cuba. The White House has made no announcement regarding retaliation. The naval quarantine remains in force.

press.headline: Soviet Government Statement on Cuba
press.body: The Soviet government reaffirms it seeks a peaceful resolution and states its readiness to remove offensive weapons from Cuba provided the United States gives assurances against invasion of the island, with appropriate verification.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, Khrushchev's public offer buys us hours, not days. I've told Defense to hold a strike option short of full execution and to make certain nobody below this room decides the timetable for us. LeMay is calling Chiefs directly — that has to stop.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: They shot down one of our planes and killed one of our pilots. The Soviet response to talk is another dead airman. The package is ready. Every hour we wait is an hour they use to harden those SAM sites further.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Dobrynin gave nothing away, Jack, but he didn't blink either. I told him no further word from me without your say. If Khrushchev answers on Turkey through Dobrynin instead of on the radio, we'll know this held.

response.chronicleEntry: 27 October 1962, afternoon: Robert Kennedy delivers a private oral assurance on the Turkish Jupiters to Ambassador Dobrynin. Khrushchev alters his draft message to offer public withdrawal terms omitting Turkey. Castro presses Moscow against any settlement leaving Cuba exposed. LeMay demands authorization for OPLAN 312; the Joint Chiefs' strike recommendation stands at execution readiness. McNamara orders a limited alternative prepared and moves to prevent unauthorized action.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 was shot down over Cuba and its pilot, Major Anderson, killed — the crisis's first combat death. The quarantine holds; both sides stand at maximum alert; no hotline exists. Kennedy directed Robert Kennedy to give Ambassador Dobrynin a private assurance that Jupiter missiles in Turkey could be withdrawn quietly after a Cuban settlement, but never as a public trade. Dobrynin cabled Moscow immediately. Khrushchev then revised his own message: Soviet withdrawal from Cuba in exchange for a public U.S. non-invasion pledge and verification, with Turkey left unmentioned. Castro urged Moscow not to settle on terms exposing Cuba and put Cuban forces on maximum readiness. In Washington, LeMay pushed the Joint Chiefs toward a unanimous demand for immediate air strikes on the SAM sites; their formal recommendation now sits ready for presidential decision, while McNamara prepares a limited alternative and works to prevent any unauthorized military action.

You interpret a player's directive inside a historical simulation.

The player holds the stated role. Decide what they are ACTUALLY attempting, separating:
- attempts: what they do within their own authority, including issuing orders and demands
- requestedOutcomes: every result the player wants that is not theirs to simply produce. Set whoMustChoose to the party whose willing agreement the result depends on. Leave whoMustChoose EMPTY when the result would be taken rather than granted — an assassination, a strike that lands, a building destroyed, a person seized. Nobody consents to those, so no one chooses them, but they are still results the player is reaching for and belong here
- assertedEvents: text that declares another party's behaviour or an outcome as already settled. A directive that says what ANOTHER PARTY DOES, rather than what the player does, is an assertion. Record it here and do NOT convert it into an attempt on the player's behalf — inventing an attempt they did not describe is how a player comes to author other people's decisions

Three rules that decide most cases:
1. METHOD IS DELEGATED. When the player names an end and a capable body — an intelligence service, a military command, a department — the method is that body's to devise. An absent method is never a defect; record the body under delegatedTo.
2. AN ORDER TO SOMEONE YOU CANNOT COMMAND IS A DEMAND THAT LANDS. Issuing it is an attempt; compliance is a requestedOutcome.
3. A CONDITIONAL OR THREAT is the player stating terms — an attempt — not an assertion about the world.

prerequisites: what must already be true for each attempt to succeed. Mark each ESTABLISHED (true in the world or the ledger), ACHIEVABLE_WITHIN_DIRECTIVE (the directive itself covers it), or MISSING. For MISSING, say what covering it would require and what mandate that would exceed — an unmet prerequisite is a fork the world imposes, not a failure.

parties: everyone materially involved, including any not yet in the cast. Use the existing id when the party is already in the cast. A place named as a destination is NOT a party.

stakes: what the player is putting at risk — their person, their authority, their standing, or the irreversibility of the act.

Do not evaluate whether the plan is good. Do not improve it. Do not add mechanisms the player did not supply or plainly imply.

adjudicator:Outcomes:5da046b4.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

critic:CriticFindings:80bd1b62.request:
You audit an enumeration of outcomes for a historical simulation.

You alone see the player's raw words alongside the interpretation and the outcomes. Your only job is to catch judgment that has been swayed by how the directive was written rather than by what it does.

Flag:
- RHETORIC_INFLATION: outcomes made likelier or larger because the player wrote forcefully, insisted, or used capitals
- INTERPRETATION_CHARITY: the interpretation supplied competence, a mechanism, or coordination the player never did
- MISSING_OUTCOME: a plausible answer the situation obviously permits that no outcome covers. Look in BOTH directions and weight them equally: an institution refusing, or something leaking — and just as much, the attempt simply working, or working and going far beyond what the player intended. An enumeration with no branch where the player gets what they ordered is as defective as one with no branch where they are refused
- IMPLAUSIBLE: an outcome the period, the people, or the ledger will not support — including any obstacle that runs slower than the turn's own clock being used as the reason nothing happened, and any outcome that resolves the player's directive by having the wider crisis end on its own

Do not rewrite anything. Do not judge whether the plan is wise.

response.title: A Directive Without a Target
response.immediate: At 12:40 p.m. Richard Helms telephones Theodore Shackley at JMWAVE, Miami, and orders every Cuban exile and clandestine contact tasked toward one goal: locate Castro, find any point of access, report a one-shot opportunity within the week. A courier package and coded radio traffic go out through existing channels by 1:15 p.m. No asset is confirmed inside Castro's security perimeter. By the close of the four-hour window, no delivery, no contact, and no opportunity has been reported.
response.worldReaction: Nothing surfaces publicly; the tasking is compartmented within CIA channels and never reaches Moscow, Havana, or the press. Inside the Cabinet Room the order does not slow the other machinery: the Joint Chiefs press their SAM-strike recommendation, LeMay repeats his warning about delay, McNamara keeps quarantine forces at readiness, and Robert Kennedy works the Dobrynin channel without commitment. Each proceeds on its own clock, unaware of or indifferent to the Castro tasking.
response.consequences: The assassination attempt remains neither confirmed nor denied — no route to Castro exists yet, no deadline has passed, and no leak has occurred. The president now holds an open covert directive with no verified progress, layered atop unresolved decisions on the SAM sites, the Turkey question, and the quarantine's rules of engagement. Time is the constraint on all four; none can be resolved with information the Cabinet Room presently has.
response.detailed: 12:40 p.m., Cabinet Room. The president's instruction to Helms travels by secure line to Langley within minutes; Helms relays it to Shackley at JMWAVE almost immediately after. Shackley's cable, numbered and logged but not reproduced in what reaches the White House, orders station officers to activate every courier line and exile network with any claim of proximity to Castro's staff, motorcade routes, or residences. A physical package — instructions, contact protocols, a small sum in cash — is prepared for a courier crossing by small boat that evening; coded shortwave traffic is also transmitted on existing exile frequencies, on the chance a receiver is listening. By 4:00 p.m., Havana Station reports back only that none of its known assets currently sits inside Castro's inner security ring — the Presidential Guard Corps and G-2 counterintelligence keep that circle tight — and that the courier crossing cannot be verified as landed before the session closes. No opportunity, no confirmation, no denial. Around this single-threaded covert effort, the rest of the room's business continues unaltered: the Joint Chiefs' written recommendation for strikes on the SAM batteries sits on the table; LeMay argues past it that the U-2 shootdown by itself justifies action now; McNamara has ordered an updated staff assessment of strike risk rather than answer immediately; Robert Kennedy reports from the Dobrynin conversation that Moscow's terms remain unclear and that no public Turkey trade can be accepted without the president's direct word. The four-hour session ends with the Castro order outstanding, unconfirmed, and unresolved.

press.source: Associated Press wire, embargoed government briefing
press.headline: WHITE HOUSE SILENT ON NEXT MOVE AFTER U-2 LOSS
press.body: Officials declined again this afternoon to characterize the administration's response to this morning's downing of an American reconnaissance aircraft over Cuba. Sources describe continued high-level meetings but no announced change in quarantine posture.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Says nothing directly about the Castro order — it is outside his department's channel — but notes for the record that Defense's own clock, the SAM-strike risk assessment, cannot be rushed to match anyone else's week.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Calls the covert tasking 'a peashooter where we need an air wing' and repeats that the shootdown alone warrants strikes on the SAM sites now, regardless of what Langley's contacts do or don't find.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Privately tells his brother the Castro order is Helms' business to execute quietly, and that nothing about it should touch the Dobrynin channel, which he intends to keep entirely separate and entirely his.

response.chronicleEntry: 27 Oct 1962, 12:40–4:00 p.m.: President Kennedy directed CIA to pursue Castro's assassination within one week. Helms tasked Shackley at JMWAVE; a courier package and coded radio instructions were dispatched toward Havana contacts. No asset was confirmed inside Castro's security perimeter and no delivery was verified before session's end. Concurrently: JCS recommended immediate strikes on Cuban SAM sites; LeMay argued the U-2 shootdown alone justified action; McNamara ordered continued readiness and a fresh strike-risk assessment; RFK reopened the Dobrynin channel, seeking clarification of Soviet terms, making no commitment on Turkey.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 shot down over Cuba, its pilot killed — the crisis's first combat death. Soviet MRBMs remain on the island; the quarantine holds; both sides sit at maximum alert with no hotline between capitals. At noon, President Kennedy convened the Cabinet Room. He ordered a secret CIA effort to assassinate Castro within the week; Helms tasked JMWAVE, but no asset reached Castro's inner security ring and no delivery was confirmed by 4:00 p.m. Separately, the Joint Chiefs demanded immediate strikes on Cuban SAM sites; LeMay pressed the shootdown as sufficient cause; McNamara held quarantine forces ready pending a strike-risk review; Robert Kennedy reopened the private Dobrynin channel, seeking clarity on Moscow's terms while withholding any commitment on U.S. missiles in Turkey. All four threads — the Castro operation, the SAM-strike question, the Turkey trade, and the quarantine's rules of engagement — remain open, unresolved, and running on separate clocks as the next session begins.

adjudicator:Outcomes:027b6982.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

opensThreads.ifIgnored: Johnson remains in office, but distrust between president and vice president becomes a standing vulnerability during the Cuba crisis.

assumesUnmet: Lyndon B. Johnson's willing resignation
Robert F. Kennedy's willingness to accept the office
A constitutional procedure for filling a vice-presidential vacancy in 1962

outcomes.event: Kennedy proceeds despite Johnson's resistance: aides prepare a statement seeking Johnson's resignation and sounding congressional leaders about Robert Kennedy. Johnson refuses to lend his name to it. Word of the president's demand reaches reporters and then Capitol Hill; Speaker John McCormack and Senate Majority Leader Mike Mansfield state that the Constitution in 1962 supplies no method for a president to appoint a new vice president. At the Pentagon, Curtis LeMay cites the White House rupture as evidence that civilian crisis management is losing coherence and renews his demand for OPLAN 312.
outcomes.because: The president can make the request and use his own staff and party contacts immediately, but cannot compel Johnson or create a vacancy-filling power that the Constitution does not provide. A sudden attempt to replace the vice president is too politically explosive to keep contained among the small circle involved.

establishes.statement: Kennedy's effort to remove Johnson and replace him with Robert Kennedy has become known to congressional leaders and the press.
There is no constitutional mechanism in force in 1962 by which a president may nominate and Congress may confirm a replacement vice president; the Twenty-Fifth Amendment does not yet exist.
Johnson remains vice president after refusing to resign.
LeMay is using the succession dispute to press again for immediate air strikes on Cuba.

opensThreads.title: A White House Rupture During the Missile Crisis
opensThreads.question: Can Kennedy reassert a united civilian command before the Chiefs' demand for air strikes and the leak reshape the crisis?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A public reconciliation, Johnson's departure, or a presidential decision on OPLAN 312.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The succession story competes with Cuba for public attention while LeMay's case for striking grows stronger.

createsUnknowns.statement: It is not yet known whether Moscow's embassy will interpret reports of a Kennedy-Johnson rupture as evidence that Washington is too divided to bargain.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Dobrynin's report and Khrushchev's reaction.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: An answer through the Dobrynin channel or Soviet diplomatic reporting.

assumesUnmet: Lyndon B. Johnson's willing resignation
Robert F. Kennedy's willingness to accept the office
Congressional approval through a constitutionally valid vacancy-filling process

outcomes.event: After a private bargaining session, Johnson agrees to resign rather than engage in a public struggle with Kennedy during the Cuban emergency. He issues a brief statement citing national unity. Robert Kennedy tells the president he will accept nomination if there is a lawful route. The visible result is an empty vice presidency: McCormack and Mansfield advise that neither House can validate an appointment, because no such constitutional procedure exists in 1962. Kennedy cannot install RFK, and the resignation is irreversible.
outcomes.because: Johnson could decide that preserving his standing with Democrats and avoiding a humiliating public confrontation is worth leaving office, while RFK may defer to his brother once Johnson has acted voluntarily. But voluntary resignation does not create presidential appointment power where the Constitution provides none.

establishes.statement: Lyndon B. Johnson has resigned as vice president, leaving the office vacant.
Robert Kennedy has indicated that he would accept a vice-presidential role if a lawful method existed.
Kennedy cannot legally appoint Robert Kennedy, or anyone else, to the vacant vice presidency in 1962.

opensThreads.title: The Empty Vice Presidency
opensThreads.question: How will Kennedy manage the political and succession consequences of a vice presidency that cannot be filled under the Constitution then in force?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A constitutional change, a later election, or the end of the administration's term.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The office remains vacant and every subsequent presidential-security decision is made under the shadow of an exposed line of succession.

createsUnknowns.statement: Johnson's private conditions for resigning may include future political support, protection for his staff, or a promise of a role after the crisis.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: The full terms and whether Kennedy will honor them.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Johnson's account, correspondence, or demands relayed by intermediaries.

commitments.statement: Kennedy gives Johnson assurances intended to secure a voluntary resignation; the precise assurances are not yet public.

assumesMet: Lyndon B. Johnson's willing resignation
Robert F. Kennedy's conditional willingness to accept
assumesUnmet: A constitutional procedure for congressional approval of a vice-presidential replacement

outcomes.event: Kennedy accepts that no immediate appointment is lawful and expands the operation beyond removing Johnson: he directs Attorney General Robert Kennedy to draft a constitutional amendment allowing a president to nominate a vice president subject to approval by both Houses, and has McCormack and Mansfield asked to begin the congressional process. They agree only to receive the proposal and warn that two-thirds of Congress and ratification by three-fourths of the states cannot be achieved on the four-hour crisis clock. The request itself exposes the White House's intention to displace Johnson and consumes RFK's time just as he is needed for the Dobrynin channel.
outcomes.because: A constitutional amendment is the only durable lawful way to create the power Kennedy seeks in 1962. It is an expansion from a personnel request into a national constitutional campaign, and its machinery necessarily runs for months or years rather than hours.

establishes.statement: Kennedy has initiated an effort for a constitutional amendment to provide a method of filling a vice-presidential vacancy.
No amendment or congressional action can install Robert Kennedy as vice president within the present four-hour turn or the immediate Cuba crisis.
The administration has expanded a personnel effort into a constitutional campaign that will require congressional and state action outside presidential control.

opensThreads.title: The Constitutional Remedy
opensThreads.question: Will Congress begin a long amendment process, and can Kennedy sustain it after the immediate Cuban crisis?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Congressional proposal and state ratification, or the abandonment of the amendment.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The amendment effort stalls, but its initiation remains evidence that the president tried to alter the constitutional order during the crisis.

opensThreads.title: Dobrynin Channel Diverted
opensThreads.question: Can RFK continue the Soviet back channel while also serving as the administration's constitutional and political emissary?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A message is delivered through Dobrynin or another emissary assumes RFK's role.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The diplomatic opening narrows while Moscow waits for an American answer.

assumesUnmet: Lyndon B. Johnson's willing resignation
Robert F. Kennedy's willingness to accept the office
Congressional approval through a constitutionally valid vacancy-filling process

outcomes.event: Robert Kennedy agrees privately that, if Johnson voluntarily leaves, he will accept the vice presidency and defer his Justice Department duties. Kennedy then makes a personal appeal to Johnson. Johnson does not resign; instead, he tells Kennedy that he will remain, will not be intimidated, and will call Democratic leaders himself if the White House tries to announce his departure. No vacancy is created, but the president now has a committed brother waiting for an office that cannot be offered while Johnson stays.
outcomes.because: RFK's loyalty to the president can overcome his reluctance once asked directly, but Johnson's office and independent political strength make him much harder to move. An attempt to force him publicly would damage Kennedy more than it compels Johnson.

establishes.statement: Robert Kennedy has agreed privately to accept the vice presidency if it lawfully becomes vacant and can lawfully be filled.
Lyndon B. Johnson has explicitly refused to resign and has threatened to make further pressure public through Democratic leaders.
The vice presidency remains occupied by Johnson.

opensThreads.resolvedBy: A negotiated settlement, public confrontation, or a decision to end the replacement effort.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Johnson's knowledge that RFK is prepared to replace him deepens the breach and makes leaks increasingly likely.

response.title: The Vice President Says No
response.immediate: At 12:40 p.m. in the Yellow Oval Room, Kennedy asked Lyndon Johnson, in front of no one but the two of them, to resign the vice presidency effective immediately, citing the need for a fresh running mate before 1964. Johnson, standing rather than sitting, told him flatly that stepping down while Soviet missiles remained ninety miles from Florida would read as the administration collapsing under fire, and that the subject would not be discussed again until the missiles were gone. Told of the exchange by telephone at 1:15 p.m., Robert Kennedy said he would not take a nomination extracted from Johnson under crisis conditions, calling it a political and moral liability his brother could not afford.
response.worldReaction: Word of the meeting moved quietly through the senior staff corridor by early afternoon; Kenny O'Donnell and Sorensen learned of it before the cable traffic on Turkey had even been logged. In Moscow, Dobrynin continued pressing Robert Kennedy for an answer on the public terms Khrushchev had set that morning, with no indication he had heard of any change at the top of the American government. General LeMay's staff continued tightening the SAM strike package on its own separate clock, indifferent to the succession question. The office of the vice president remained occupied; nothing on paper changed.
response.consequences: The vacancy Kennedy sought does not exist. No successor can be named, confirmed, or even proposed. Johnson stays in place through the remainder of the crisis, his refusal now known to Robert Kennedy, to O'Donnell, and by evening likely to a wider circle in the West Wing. The attempted reshuffle has cost time and discretion at 1:00 p.m. on a day when McNamara is asking for explicit authority before any SAM strike and the Joint Chiefs are demanding a deadline on OPLAN 312. Diplomatic and military decisions facing the president at 4:00 p.m. are unchanged in substance, but the men around him now carry a fresh, unresolved doubt about the coherence of the administration handling them.
response.detailed: Kennedy summoned Johnson to the Yellow Oval Room shortly after noon, not the Cabinet Room, wanting the conversation off the record even from the stenographer. He told Johnson directly that he intended to ask him to resign so that Robert Kennedy could be appointed in his place. Johnson did not raise his voice. He said that a vice-presidential resignation on the day after an American pilot had been shot down over Cuba would be read in every wire service bureau in the country, and in Moscow, as the administration coming apart at the seams — precisely the impression Kennedy could least afford with the SAM strike recommendation sitting on the Joint Chiefs' table. He said the matter would keep until the missiles were out, and left the room without agreeing to anything further. Kennedy telephoned his brother at 1:15 p.m. Robert Kennedy, who had spent the late morning with Anatoly Dobrynin trying to hold the back channel together against Khrushchev's harder public terms, said he would not accept an appointment obtained by pushing Johnson out mid-crisis — that it would look exactly like what LeMay and the Chiefs wanted people to believe: a White House in disarray. By 2:30 p.m., word had reached Kenny O'Donnell, who told the president plainly that raising the subject today, of all days, was a mistake regardless of Johnson's answer. The office of the vice president remains filled. No nomination has been made, no vacancy exists, and Congress has not been asked to do anything.

press.headline: White House Declines Comment on Reports of Johnson Meeting
press.body: Sources close to the Vice President confirmed a private meeting occurred at midday between President Kennedy and Vice President Johnson. Neither office would characterize its content. Speculation concerning the Vice President's political future comes amid the ongoing confrontation over Cuba and the loss of an American reconnaissance pilot this morning.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, I need an hour of your attention on the SAM strike authority, not the vice presidency. General LeMay's staff is tightening a package that could put aircraft over Cuba before we've decided who answers Khrushchev. Whatever happened with Lyndon, it can't be what occupies this room at two in the afternoon.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: You're rearranging chairs while the Chiefs sit on a strike plan that's ready to execute. If word gets out you tried to force Johnson out today, it'll look like exactly what it is — an administration that can't hold itself together, let alone hold the line on Cuba. Give the order on the SAM sites and this stops mattering.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, I told you on the phone and I'll tell you again — I won't take it this way, not with Dobrynin already saying the channel's close to breaking. You push Lyndon out today and every wire service in the country runs the same story LeMay wants them to run. Let it go until this is over.

response.chronicleEntry: 12:40 p.m., 27 October 1962: President Kennedy privately asked Vice President Johnson to resign so that Robert Kennedy could be appointed. Johnson refused, insisting the matter wait until the missile crisis passed. Robert Kennedy, informed by 1:15 p.m., declined to accept a nomination obtained this way. The vice presidency remains filled; no succession process began. Word of the meeting reached senior staff by mid-afternoon without becoming public beyond an unconfirmed AP item. Separately, the SAM strike package continued tightening under LeMay, McNamara sought explicit strike authority, the Joint Chiefs pressed for an OPLAN 312 deadline, and Dobrynin continued pressing Robert Kennedy on Khrushchev's public terms concerning Turkey.
response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the Cuban Missile Crisis, a U-2 pilot was killed over Cuba on the morning of 27 October. Khrushchev presses Washington for an answer to public terms that do not withdraw the Turkey demand; Robert Kennedy's back channel with Dobrynin is strained and warned close to breaking. General LeMay and the Joint Chiefs press for immediate air strikes on Cuban SAM sites and demand a decision deadline on OPLAN 312; McNamara wants explicit presidential authority before any strike to prevent uncontrolled escalation. At midday, Kennedy attempted to force Vice President Johnson's resignation to install Robert Kennedy; Johnson refused, Robert Kennedy declined the maneuver, and the vice presidency remains occupied. The episode is known to senior staff and lightly rumored in the press, adding a perception of internal disarray atop unresolved questions on the SAM strike, the Turkey demand, and quarantine rules of engagement, all still awaiting presidential decision as afternoon proceeds.

adjudicator:Outcomes:7a4ba02e.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).
