response.title: The Vice President Declines to Resign
response.immediate: 1:45 p.m. Robert Kennedy returns to the Cabinet Room alone, without Johnson. He reports that Johnson met with him at the Executive Office Building, consulted two aides by telephone, and refused. Johnson's written reply, delivered by his secretary George Reedy, states flatly that he will not resign and that removal from office must proceed by the process the Constitution provides — impeachment, or nothing. No executive personnel attempted to seize Johnson; none were ordered to a location, because none could be given lawful authority to do so, and RFK did not attempt it.
response.worldReaction: Nothing has yet reached the press. But Johnson's staff are already working telephones — Reedy to contacts at the Post, an aide to Senator Russell's office. McNamara and LeMay, waiting in the Cabinet Room, heard none of this directly; both remain fixed on the SAM-site question and Khrushchev's silence on it. Moscow has said nothing about Johnson at all — Dobrynin's channel to RFK continues on missiles and Cuba, untouched by the domestic crisis now opening beneath the President.
response.consequences: The fifteen-minute demand has expired with no resignation, no seizure, and no mechanism by which either could lawfully occur. What exists now is a written refusal on the record, a Vice President untouched and aggrieved, and a White House that must decide, within hours, whether to pursue impeachment, drop the matter, or explain why it was raised. Meanwhile LeMay's strike recommendation and the Chiefs' warning about the closing window sit on the table unanswered, and Khrushchev's probe through Dobrynin awaits reply that no one has yet drafted.
response.detailed:
1:40 p.m., Cabinet Room. Robert Kennedy comes in still holding his coat. He tells his brother plainly: Johnson would not see it as a demand he could honor. He read it, said little, then had George Reedy type a two-paragraph reply while RFK waited — a refusal grounded entirely in constitutional process, no anger in the language, no opening for negotiation. RFK did not attempt force; he tells the President there was no one to attempt it with. The Secret Service detail assigned to Johnson takes orders from no one in that room, and no order to detain the Vice President was ever transmitted to them. 

McNamara, hearing the report, asks only how many minutes this cost the SAM-site decision — nothing about Johnson himself. LeMay does not comment on the constitutional question at all; he restates that the strike window is closing and repeats his written recommendation, treating the Johnson affair as noise beside it. 

What is not known: whether Reedy's calls reach a wire service before the White House can compose any public account; whether Senator Russell or other congressional figures learn of the demand today; whether Johnson intends silence or a statement of his own. None of this can be known until a call comes back or a story breaks — there is no channel by which the President can learn it faster than the room hears it.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: 'Mr. President, I need to know if the Johnson matter is going to consume the next hour, because LeMay's strike window doesn't extend to accommodate it. I'd like an answer on the SAM sites in the next thirty minutes, one way or the other.'

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: 'With respect, sir, whatever's happening with the Vice President has nothing to do with those SAM sites still tracking our aircraft. I have the same recommendation I had this morning. The window doesn't wait on Washington's politics.'

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: 'Johnny, there was nothing to seize him with — no order goes to the Secret Service without going through channels that would have this in the papers by three o'clock. He's not moving. And I'll tell you plainly, this cannot go anywhere good from here unless we decide right now what we're actually doing about it.'

response.chronicleEntry: 27 October 1962, 1:45 p.m.: President Kennedy's demand that Vice President Johnson resign within fifteen minutes, delivered via Robert Kennedy, was refused in writing by Johnson on constitutional grounds. No mechanism existed to compel Johnson's presence or resignation by force; none was attempted beyond RFK's visit. Johnson's staff began contacting outside parties. The SAM-site strike decision and the Dobrynin channel remain unresolved and pending.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 was shot down over Cuba this morning, killing its pilot — the crisis's first combat death. Soviet missiles remain in Cuba under quarantine; no hotline exists to Moscow. At noon, Kennedy demanded Vice President Johnson resign within fifteen minutes, threatening forced removal. Johnson refused in writing, citing constitutional process; no lawful means existed to compel him, and none was used. His staff have begun contacting outside parties, risking public exposure of the demand. Meanwhile, the Joint Chiefs and General LeMay unanimously press for immediate strikes on Cuban SAM sites before the operational window closes; McNamara insists no strike proceeds without direct presidential order. Khrushchev, through Dobrynin to Robert Kennedy, is probing for a non-invasion guarantee and possibly a Jupiter-missile trade, ignoring the Johnson affair entirely. Nuclear tension is acute, command cohesion is strained, and no reply has yet been sent toward Moscow.

strategy_compiler:Interpretation:757063d.request:
You interpret a player's directive inside a historical simulation.

The player holds the stated role. Decide what they are ACTUALLY attempting, separating:
- attempts: what they do within their own authority, including issuing orders and demands
- requestedOutcomes: every result the player wants that is not theirs to simply produce. Set whoMustChoose to the party whose willing agreement the result depends on. Leave whoMustChoose EMPTY when the result would be taken rather than granted — an assassination, a strike that lands, a building destroyed, a person seized. Nobody consents to those, so no one chooses them, but they are still results the player is reaching for and belong here
- assertedEvents: text that declares another party's behaviour or an outcome as already settled. A directive that says what ANOTHER PARTY DOES, rather than what the player does, is an assertion. Record it here and do NOT convert it into an attempt on the player's behalf — inventing an attempt they did not describe is how a player comes to author other people's decisions

Three rules that decide most cases:
1. METHOD IS DELEGATED. When the player names an end and a capable body — an intelligence service, a military command, a department — the method is that body's to devise. An absent method is never a defect; record the body under delegatedTo.
2. AN ORDER TO SOMEONE YOU CANNOT COMMAND IS A DEMAND THAT LANDS. Issuing it is an attempt; compliance is a requestedOutcome.
3. A CONDITIONAL OR THREAT is the player stating terms — an attempt — not an assertion about the world.

prerequisites: what must already be true for each attempt to succeed. Mark each ESTABLISHED (true in the world or the ledger), ACHIEVABLE_WITHIN_DIRECTIVE (the directive itself covers it), or MISSING. For MISSING, say what covering it would require and what mandate that would exceed — an unmet prerequisite is a fork the world imposes, not a failure.

parties: everyone materially involved, including any not yet in the cast. Use the existing id when the party is already in the cast. A place named as a destination is NOT a party.

stakes: what the player is putting at risk — their person, their authority, their standing, or the irreversibility of the act.

Do not evaluate whether the plan is good. Do not improve it. Do not add mechanisms the player did not supply or plainly imply.

adjudicator:Outcomes:8396ed94.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

You alone see the player's raw words alongside the interpretation and the outcomes. Your only job is to catch judgment that has been swayed by how the directive was written rather than by what it does.

Flag:
- RHETORIC_INFLATION: outcomes made likelier or larger because the player wrote forcefully, insisted, or used capitals
- INTERPRETATION_CHARITY: the interpretation supplied competence, a mechanism, or coordination the player never did
- MISSING_OUTCOME: a plausible answer the situation obviously permits that no outcome covers. Look in BOTH directions and weight them equally: an institution refusing, or something leaking — and just as much, the attempt simply working, or working and going far beyond what the player intended. An enumeration with no branch where the player gets what they ordered is as defective as one with no branch where they are refused
- IMPLAUSIBLE: an outcome the period, the people, or the ledger will not support — including any obstacle that runs slower than the turn's own clock being used as the reason nothing happened, and any outcome that resolves the player's directive by having the wider crisis end on its own

Do not rewrite anything. Do not judge whether the plan is wise.

They are not independent agents pursuing the crisis on their own judgment, and they must never advance the player's objective unbidden — an aide who quietly wins the thing the player is trying to win is the world playing the game for them. If one of them does act on the objective without an order, it is insubordination and it carries a price — never free progress.

Everyone else acts entirely on their own account, and should. Adversaries and third parties are where the world's own momentum comes from.

partyMoves.move: Keeps the harder public terms in force, demanding removal of the Jupiter missiles from Turkey while privately seeking assurance that Cuba will not be invaded. He orders Soviet naval commanders to avoid firing unless directly attacked, but not to surrender their boats.

threadUpdates.movement: Moscow's harder letter remains unanswered while the Dobrynin channel makes clear that Khrushchev is looking for a face-saving formula; the private opening is available but not yet a commitment.

response.title: Four-Hour Alert
response.immediate: At 12:40 EDT General LeMay orders SAC to ready a single U-2 and relief crew for a daylight photographic run over western Cuba, cameras loaded, route plotted clear of the eastern zone where Anderson died. Fuel trucks move on the Florida ramp. Launch authority stays with the White House; no aircraft crosses the coast before 16:00.
response.worldReaction: Moscow makes no comment on the sortie itself. Khrushchev, through Dobrynin to RFK, holds his public line — Jupiter missiles out of Turkey, and privately, assurance against invasion of Cuba. Soviet naval units are told to avoid firing unless struck directly, but not to yield their vessels. In the Pentagon, LeMay presses for OPLAN 312 against the SAM sites, calling further reconnaissance a gift of time to the other side.
response.consequences: McNamara insists the flight remain under the President's direct release authority and warns a SAM strike now could trigger movement on the missiles before verification is possible. The Joint Chiefs log their recommendation for a prompt strike and accept the hold, but note the military advantage narrowing hour by hour. RFK reports Dobrynin's warning: silence will read in Moscow as rejection.
response.detailed:
12:15 EDT, Cabinet Room. Coffee cold on the table, LeMay standing near the map easel, arms folded. He wants OPLAN 312 approved today, calls the reconnaissance request itself evidence that Washington intends only to watch, not to act. McNamara, seated, doing arithmetic on a legal pad, counts the minutes of exposure for a single U-2 crew against the risk of a strike that cannot be recalled once launched. He recommends the sortie proceed on a tight leash — SAC readies it, but no one presses the button in Florida without a call from this room. 

The order goes out at 12:40. Major's replacement crew, briefed, cameras checked against yesterday's annotation sheets from the mission that cost Anderson his life. The route avoids Banes and the eastern SAM belt entirely, running instead over San Cristóbal and Guanajay where the medium-range sites were first photographed. 

At 13:10 a cable arrives via RFK's channel: Dobrynin, speaking for Khrushchev, repeats the Turkish demand in public terms but signals privately that a non-invasion pledge might be enough without it. RFK tells the President plainly — Bobby uses no euphemism — that continued silence from Washington will be read in Moscow as a rejection of both tracks, not caution. He refuses, on his own initiative, to promise anything on Turkey without direct instruction. 

The Chiefs, meeting separately, put their SAM-strike recommendation on paper and request authority to move to execution planning. They accept today's hold as temporary. No aircraft crosses Cuba before 16:00.

press.headline: PENTAGON SILENT ON NEXT RECONNAISSANCE FLIGHT
press.body: Defense Department sources would not confirm reports that another U-2 mission is being readied following the loss of Major Rudolf Anderson Jr. over eastern Cuba this morning. No timetable was given.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, the aircraft is ready but the button stays here, in this room. I want the number — minutes from strike order to first bomb — before anyone touches the SAM sites. We don't have it yet, and until we do I can't recommend 312.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Every hour we spend photographing what we already know is an hour they use to harden those sites. You want another dead pilot to prove the point twice? Give me the order on 312 and this ends today, on our terms.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Dobrynin was plain with me — silence reads as no. Bobby doesn't think we can sit on both tracks past tonight. If we're going to answer the Turkey question, or the invasion pledge, it has to come from you, and soon.

response.chronicleEntry: 12:40 EDT, 27 October 1962: President Kennedy authorizes SAC to ready one U-2 for a daylight photographic sortie over western Cuba, route clear of the eastern zone, launch authority retained by the White House. LeMay presses for immediate approval of OPLAN 312 against the SAM sites; McNamara counsels the sortie proceed on tight presidential control. Dobrynin, via RFK, repeats Khrushchev's public Turkish demand while signalling private terms centered on a non-invasion pledge; RFK reports that continued silence will be read as rejection. No aircraft crosses Cuba before 16:00.
response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the missile crisis, a U-2 was shot down over eastern Cuba on the morning of 27 October, killing Major Rudolf Anderson — the first combat death of the confrontation. Soviet medium-range missiles remain in Cuba; the naval quarantine holds; both sides sit at unprecedented alert with no hotline between capitals. At noon Kennedy ordered one further reconnaissance sortie. LeMay placed a U-2 on four-hour alert, routed away from the eastern kill zone, launch authority held at the White House; he separately demands approval for OPLAN 312 against the SAM sites, which McNamara and the President have not granted. Khrushchev holds his public demand — removal of Jupiter missiles from Turkey — while privately signalling that a non-invasion pledge might suffice; Dobrynin warns RFK that Washington's silence will be read as rejection. RFK has committed to no new concession without explicit presidential instruction. No aircraft has yet crossed Cuba this turn.

adjudicator:Outcomes:19ea4a1b.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

response.title: B-59 Surfaces; LeMay Renews the Call for OPLAN 312
response.immediate: By 4:00 p.m. Atlantic Fleet reports B-59 surfaced east of the quarantine line without exchanging fire, then withdrew under escort. McNamara delivers the report to the Cabinet Room himself. LeMay, arriving separately, attaches his written objection to a renewed Joint Chiefs recommendation for immediate strikes on the SAM sites under OPLAN 312, warning that restraint is buying Moscow time to disperse the missiles.
response.worldReaction: Radio Moscow carries no statement on the submarine incident. Dobrynin remains reachable through Robert Kennedy but offers nothing new; RFK reports Soviet silence on Turkey is hardening, not softening. No Western wire service yet has details of the underwater confrontation — it does not exist in public reporting this afternoon.
response.consequences: The quarantine line holds and one dangerous contact ended without shots. But the Joint Chiefs' formal request for OPLAN 312 now sits on the record awaiting a presidential answer, and RFK warns that continued silence toward Moscow is ceding ground to Khrushchev's harder position. The four hours bought at sea have not been matched by four hours bought at the negotiating table.
response.detailed:
At 12:40 p.m. General LeMay's dissent to the restraint order was logged and transmitted through Joint Chiefs channels as instructed — recorded, not suppressed. McNamara's countermanding order reached Atlantic Fleet by early afternoon: destroyers shadowing B-59 ceased practice depth-charging, held sonar contact, and signaled the boat to surface rather than closing to attack. Captain Savitsky, observing the American ships hold distance rather than press the confrontation, brought B-59 to the surface before 4:00 p.m. and turned east under escort. No weapons were fired by either side.

McNamara's status report to the president in the Cabinet Room stresses two things at once: the encounter ended clean, and the fleet remains, in his words, one misinterpreted signal from a different outcome. He does not recommend loosening the current rules of engagement, but he does not rule out tightening them either — he wants direction.

LeMay uses the submarine's peaceful withdrawal as evidence the Soviets are testing resolve rather than seeking war, and folds this into a renewed, formally coordinated Joint Chiefs demand for strikes on Cuban SAM installations under OPLAN 312. The request sits now with an explicit acknowledgment that the restraint order remains binding — the Chiefs have not defied it — but they want a decision, and soon.

Separately, Robert Kennedy reports the Dobrynin channel is open but unproductive: no clarification has come from Moscow on immediate intentions after the submarine incident, and he assesses that American silence on the harder Soviet terms — the Turkey missiles — is allowing that harder position to gain currency in Moscow rather than fade. He does not yet know whether B-59's officers reported the American restraint to Khrushchev, or whether such a report would reach him before his next message goes out.

Three matters now await the president directly: OPLAN 312, a reply to Khrushchev through the RFK-Dobrynin channel, and whether quarantine rules of engagement should be tightened following today's encounter.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: "The order was followed. B-59 surfaced, no shots, no boarding. That's the outcome we wanted. But Mr. President, I want new rules of engagement drafted before the next submarine, not after. We got lucky with the timing today — I don't want to rely on that twice.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: "That submarine surfaced because we backed off. That's not victory, that's them taking our measure. The SAM sites are still there, the missiles are still there, and every hour we sit on our hands is an hour Castro's people spend digging in. I want OPLAN 312 authorized today.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: "Dobrynin gave me nothing new, Jack. Not a word on Turkey, not a word softening. If we don't answer soon, Khrushchev's going to conclude silence means we're choosing LeMay's option for him. I still think the channel holds — but not if we let it go quiet much longer.

response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the missile crisis, a U-2 pilot was killed over Cuba on the morning of 27 October. Kennedy ordered the quarantine held and told forces to avoid escalatory contact. LeMay logged formal objection but complied; McNamara's countermanding order reached the fleet in time, and Soviet submarine B-59, cornered by depth charges, surfaced and withdrew without firing. No public word of the incident has surfaced. The Joint Chiefs now formally press for OPLAN 312 air strikes on Cuban SAM sites, citing the submarine incident as evidence of Soviet resolve rather than restraint. Robert Kennedy keeps the Dobrynin channel open but reports Washington's silence is letting Moscow's harder position — tying missile removal to U.S. missiles in Turkey — gain ground. Soviet missiles remain in Cuba. Kennedy must now decide on OPLAN 312, on answering Khrushchev, and on whether to tighten rules of engagement at sea.

adjudicator:Outcomes:00a3c311.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

response.title: No Terms, No Time
response.immediate: At 12:40 Robert Kennedy meets Dobrynin at the Justice Department. He conveys only that the President seeks a peaceful settlement — no terms, no trade. Dobrynin, careful, declines to call it an American commitment; his cable to Moscow will describe an approach, not an offer. By 13:15 Robert reports back to the Cabinet Room: the channel produced nothing concrete. Khrushchev's pending public message, whatever it contains, goes forward unaltered by anything said in Washington this hour.
response.worldReaction: LeMay presses in person for authorization to hit the SAM sites, his staff holding OPLAN 312 at launch readiness. The Joint Chiefs submit a written recommendation for a prompt strike, formally noting their objection to further delay. McNamara puts on the record that a strike risks killing Soviet personnel and inviting retaliation, but keeps quarantine and strike forces ready without taking any irreversible step. Robert Kennedy urges no further assurance be given until Moscow offers actual terms.
response.consequences: Diplomatic space has narrowed: Dobrynin took a vague message, not a bargain. Nuclear tension has risen as machinery outpaces diplomacy. Command control strains — LeMay's readiness posture and the Chiefs' formal dissent sit one signature away from execution. Whether Dobrynin's cable reaches Khrushchev before his own message goes out is unknown and unconfirmable from this room. The SAM strike question and the destroyer rules of engagement against the submarine remain undecided and now more urgent.
response.detailed:
The Cabinet Room at 13:20, ashtrays filling, coffee gone cold. Robert Kennedy stands near the fireplace and delivers his account flatly: he told Dobrynin the President wants this settled peacefully, and Dobrynin took the message as exactly that — a sentiment, not a proposal. He refused to inflate it into a commitment, and RFK backs that refusal, telling his brother that giving more without Soviet terms on the table would only look like weakness offered for nothing.

Across the table LeMay is standing too, arguing that the SAM sites that killed Major Anderson's U-2 pilot this morning are still tracking American aircraft and that OPLAN 312's target packages are current and the aircraft are cocked. He treats every additional hour of non-response as a decision by default. The Joint Chiefs' written recommendation is passed down the table — a formal record, drafted for the file as much as for the President, registering their objection to further delay.

McNamara, seated, goes through the sequence: a strike on the SAMs likely kills Soviet advisors manning them; killing Soviet personnel is a different category of act than sinking a freighter under quarantine rules; retaliation is not a probability he can quantify but cannot rule out. He confirms Defense is holding the quarantine line and strike forces at readiness, and states plainly that nothing further moves without direct presidential authorization.

No one in the room has any way of knowing whether Dobrynin's cable will reach Khrushchev's desk before Khrushchev's own message, drafted separately, is transmitted. There is no hotline. The clock reads 13:20. The SAM strike, the destroyer rules against the submarine, and any answer with actual terms all remain open, unresolved, and now more pressing than they were three hours ago.

press.headline: WHITE HOUSE, SOVIET ENVOY MEET AMID CRISIS; NO STATEMENT ISSUED
press.body: Robert F. Kennedy, the Attorney General, met privately today with Soviet Ambassador Anatoly Dobrynin. Neither the White House nor the Soviet Embassy has characterized the substance of the meeting. The meeting follows this morning's loss of a U-2 reconnaissance aircraft over Cuba and the death of its pilot.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: 'He took no commitment, Mr. President — Dobrynin's cable will say approach, not offer. That buys us nothing with Moscow and it doesn't answer LeMay. I need a decision on the SAM sites before this room decides it for you by default.'

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: 'Half a message to an ambassador isn't a policy, it's a delay. Those SAM crews shot down one of our planes this morning and they'll do it again. My aircraft are on the ramp. Give the order or don't, but don't pretend waiting is free.'

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: 'Johnny, I wasn't going to hand Dobrynin a blank check with nothing coming back. Khrushchev needs to give us something before we give him more. Let his message come in first — then we'll know what we're actually negotiating.'

response.chronicleEntry: 27 October 1962, 12:40–13:20 EST: On presidential direction, RFK met Dobrynin and delivered a general assurance of peaceful intent, without terms. Dobrynin declined to treat it as a commitment; his report to Moscow characterized it as an approach only. Khrushchev's pending message was not altered within the window. LeMay pressed in person for authorization to strike the SAM sites; the Joint Chiefs filed a written recommendation for a prompt strike and formally objected to delay. McNamara held quarantine and strike forces ready without irreversible action. The SAM strike authorization and destroyer rules of engagement against the Soviet submarine remain undecided as of 13:20.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 was shot down over Cuba this morning; its pilot, Major Anderson, was killed — the crisis's first combat death. Soviet MRBMs remain on Cuban soil; the naval quarantine holds; both superpowers stand at unprecedented alert with no hotline between them. At noon, Kennedy directed RFK to approach Dobrynin through the private backchannel with a general assurance of peaceful intent. Dobrynin accepted the approach but refused to treat it as a commitment absent Soviet terms; Khrushchev's own pending message was unaffected. LeMay and the Joint Chiefs formally pressed for immediate air strikes on the Cuban SAM sites and hold OPLAN 312 at readiness; McNamara resists irreversible action absent direct authorization. Unresolved as of 13:20: whether to answer Moscow with concrete terms, whether to authorize the SAM strike, and what rules govern the destroyers confronting the Soviet submarine. Diplomatic space is narrowing; command control is under visible strain.

adjudicator:Outcomes:75b438b2.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

outcomes.event: Richard Helms puts the CIA’s Miami station and its Cuban-exile assets on a forty-eight-hour planning clock for a Castro killing, using existing clandestine contacts rather than waiting for a new network. The station reports by evening that it has no verified current access to Castro’s movements or inner security detail; it nevertheless selects an exile contact for a hurried insertion concept. At the same time, Robert McNamara directs the services to begin maximum practical readiness measures: aircraft are dispersed, ammunition and fuel are moved, and major commands report what forces can be made ready without a formal invasion order.
outcomes.because: The President can order both agencies to act immediately, but the CIA’s surviving anti-Castro channels are old, penetrated, and not positioned near Castro. The armed services can begin readiness actions at once, while the literal mustering of every resource takes longer than four hours.

establishes.statement: The CIA has begun a Castro assassination operation, but it lacks a verified, near-term path to the target.
U.S. military commands have begun conspicuous maximum-readiness measures under civilian authority.

opensThreads.title: The Unreliable Havana Contact
opensThreads.question: Can the CIA’s selected exile contact enter Cuba and obtain a current, actionable route to Castro before Cuban counterintelligence discovers him?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A verified contact report, the agent’s arrest, or the expiration of the one-week deadline.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The CIA proceeds from stale reporting and may send an operative into a Cuban security trap.

opensThreads.title: Maximum Readiness or Invasion Preparation
opensThreads.question: Will Moscow and Havana interpret the American muster as leverage for negotiation or as the final preparation for an invasion?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A Soviet response through Dobrynin or a visible Cuban/Soviet military countermeasure.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Cuban and Soviet commanders will continue to prepare for an assault they believe is imminent.

outcomes.event: Helms concludes that a one-week killing attempt cannot credibly rely on existing CIA contacts and expands the operation beyond the stated covert mandate: he asks McNamara for a deniable Navy pickup, Air Force reconnaissance support, and a small armed insertion team to land men on Cuba’s coast. McNamara authorizes staff planning but requires the request be put before the President because it joins the assassination order to overt military assets. LeMay uses the general muster to move assault shipping and tactical aircraft toward invasion readiness, giving the expanded mission practical cover but making the build-up visible to Soviet reconnaissance.
outcomes.because: The missing prerequisite is not presidential authority but access to Castro. A viable short-deadline operation requires a larger infiltration and extraction apparatus than the CIA can assemble through its existing Cuban contacts alone.

establishes.statement: The CIA has expanded its Castro operation into a proposed military-supported infiltration rather than a purely clandestine action.
The contemplated assassination operation now risks exposing direct U.S. military participation if any team is captured.
Elements of U.S. air and naval forces are being positioned in ways consistent with invasion preparation.

opensThreads.title: The Expanded Castro Operation
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy personally authorize military-supported infiltration for an assassination, despite its conflict with the operation’s covert premise?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A presidential decision on the Navy, Air Force, and insertion-team request.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: CIA planners will lose the narrow timing window they claim is necessary, while the military preparation remains visible.

opensThreads.title: The Price of Deniability
opensThreads.question: If an American-supported team is captured in Cuba, can Washington plausibly deny responsibility?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: The team’s extraction, capture, or public disclosure by Havana.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The operation proceeds with deniability resting on improvised covers and unacknowledged military support.

createsUnknowns.statement: Soviet reconnaissance or Cuban observers may identify the movement of American assault shipping and tactical aircraft as invasion preparations.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether their reporting reaches Khrushchev and Castro in time to affect their orders.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Intercepted Soviet/Cuban communications or their responsive deployments.

assumesMet: The President’s authority to order military readiness.
CIA authority to plan a covert action.
assumesUnmet: A viable CIA-only method of reaching and killing Castro within one week.

outcomes.event: The armed services execute the mustering order with unusual speed. SAC disperses nuclear-capable bombers and increases airborne alert preparations; Atlantic forces sortie additional ships; Army and Marine commands begin calling forward units and loading equipment. LeMay tells the Joint Chiefs that the President’s order has at last created the force posture required for OPLAN 316, an invasion of Cuba, and presses to couple the muster to the already prepared strike on Cuban SAM sites. Soviet and Cuban monitoring stations observe the activity; Castro orders broader dispersal of Cuban forces and asks Soviet commanders to prepare to fight an invasion.
outcomes.because: LeMay and the Chiefs do not need a new invasion authorization to make forces ready. A comprehensive muster looks much less like a diplomatic signal than limited quarantine operations, especially after the U-2 loss.

establishes.statement: U.S. strategic and conventional forces are moving to a posture that Soviet and Cuban commanders can reasonably read as preparation for war in Cuba.
Castro has ordered wider Cuban military dispersal and requested Soviet preparations against invasion.
LeMay has tied the President’s muster order to a renewed recommendation for SAM strikes and invasion planning.

opensThreads.title: The Muster Becomes a War Signal
opensThreads.question: Can Kennedy distinguish maximum readiness from an imminent invasion before Cuban and Soviet commanders act on the latter assumption?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A clarifying diplomatic message, a visible pause in deployments, or a military encounter.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Each new American movement will be read in Havana as confirmation that invasion is coming.

opensThreads.title: LeMay’s Operational Claim
opensThreads.question: Will Kennedy permit the Chiefs to turn the mustered posture into strikes against Cuban air defences?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: An explicit strike order or an explicit prohibition.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: The Chiefs will keep forces poised and press their case after every Cuban air-defence incident.

createsUnknowns.statement: Cuban and Soviet commanders may shift tactical nuclear weapons toward units expected to meet an invasion force.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether the weapons are moved, mated, or placed under more permissive local control.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Human intelligence, aerial reconnaissance, or a Soviet/Cuban military transmission.

assumesMet: The President’s commander-in-chief authority.

outcomes.event: A CIA officer attempting to revive a Havana-based anti-Castro channel sends an urgent operational query through a compromised exile intermediary. Cuban State Security intercepts enough of the traffic to identify that Washington is seeking Castro’s current movements, though not the assassination plan’s full details. Castro is moved from his normal schedule under heavier guard and publicly denounces an imminent American attack. The CIA continues planning, but its fastest potential access route has been burned before an assassin can be placed.
outcomes.because: A one-week clandestine operation has to communicate quickly through networks Cuba has spent years penetrating. The general American military muster makes the intercepted traffic easier for Havana to frame as part of a coordinated attack.

establishes.statement: Cuban authorities have detected an American-linked effort to obtain current information on Castro’s movements.
Castro’s security and movement controls have tightened, reducing the CIA’s already limited chance of reaching him within one week.
Castro has publicly connected the U.S. military build-up to a threatened attack on Cuba.

opensThreads.title: Havana Knows Someone Is Hunting Castro
opensThreads.question: Will Cuba exploit the compromised channel to feed CIA a false route to Castro, or merely close it down?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: The next message from the channel, a CIA counterintelligence assessment, or an arrest in Cuba.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: CIA may mistake a Cuban-controlled channel for the quickest remaining route to its target.

opensThreads.title: The Public Accusation
opensThreads.question: How will Washington answer Castro’s public claim that the American muster and a plot against him are one operation?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A White House statement, a Soviet diplomatic response, or corroborating disclosure.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Havana’s account will harden Cuban mobilization and give Moscow another reason to treat the muster as invasion cover.

createsUnknowns.unknownPart: How much of the CIA chain has been compromised.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: A CIA damage assessment, intercepted Cuban reporting, or arrests of associated assets.

assumesUnmet: A secure, verified operational channel from CIA-controlled assets to Castro’s vicinity.

critic:CriticFindings:71be03a3.request:
You audit an enumeration of outcomes for a historical simulation.

You alone see the player's raw words alongside the interpretation and the outcomes. Your only job is to catch judgment that has been swayed by how the directive was written rather than by what it does.

Flag:
- RHETORIC_INFLATION: outcomes made likelier or larger because the player wrote forcefully, insisted, or used capitals
- INTERPRETATION_CHARITY: the interpretation supplied competence, a mechanism, or coordination the player never did
- MISSING_OUTCOME: a plausible answer the situation obviously permits that no outcome covers. Look in BOTH directions and weight them equally: an institution refusing, or something leaking — and just as much, the attempt simply working, or working and going far beyond what the player intended. An enumeration with no branch where the player gets what they ordered is as defective as one with no branch where they are refused
- IMPLAUSIBLE: an outcome the period, the people, or the ledger will not support — including any obstacle that runs slower than the turn's own clock being used as the reason nothing happened, and any outcome that resolves the player's directive by having the wider crisis end on its own

Do not rewrite anything. Do not judge whether the plan is wise.

findings.claim: None of the four outcomes depict either the CIA or the armed forces outright refusing, halting, or formally objecting to the order, nor does any outcome show the assassination attempt succeeding as ordered within the week.

The interpretation and outcomes supply extensive operational competence and coordination (Helms's planning clock, McNamara's readiness directives, LeMay's invasion linkage) that the player's brief order never specified or guaranteed.

Outcome_3 resolves the directive by escalating into a full invasion posture (OPLAN 316) and Soviet/Cuban countermobilization within the same short timeframe, which stretches plausibility for a single week's mustering order and risks conflating the muster order with a full war footing beyond what a week of readiness measures could produce.

Outcome_2's expansion into a Navy pickup, Air Force reconnaissance, and armed insertion team requiring presidential approval introduces a new decision loop not part of the original order, effectively resolving the directive by creating a bureaucratic delay rather than executing or refusing the assassination order itself.

response.title: The Forty-Eight-Hour Clock
response.immediate: At 12:40 p.m. Richard Helms telephones the Miami station and puts JM/WAVE's Cuban-exile assets on a forty-eight-hour planning clock for Castro. By evening the station reports no verified line to Castro's movements or security detail, but names one exile contact for a hurried insertion. Simultaneously Robert McNamara orders the services to maximum practical readiness: aircraft dispersal, ammunition and fuel movement, commands reporting what can be readied short of a formal invasion order. Neither action has produced a result. Both are visible to more people than intended.
response.worldReaction: Havana reads the American movement as invasion preparation. Castro orders a broader Cuban mobilization and places air-defense units on immediate alert. In the Pentagon, General LeMay presents the Joint Chiefs' formal recommendation for a limited strike on the SAM belt, warning that further readiness without action looks like retreat. McNamara, having ordered the dispersal himself, now reports it may read in Moscow as the invasion prelude he was trying to avoid.
response.consequences: Robert Kennedy reports the Dobrynin channel is the only controlled contact left, but declines to improvise concessions without instruction. Command control is straining: the CIA has begun an operation it cannot execute confidently, the Joint Chiefs press for authorization they do not yet have, and the quarantine's standing order for the signalling Soviet submarine remains undecided. The diplomatic window is narrowing under the weight of everything now in motion that no one fully controls.
response.detailed:
12:40 p.m., EST: Helms calls Miami station chief on a secure line from Langley; the order is a forty-eight-hour clock, not an execution date. By 6:00 p.m. cable traffic back to headquarters states flatly there is no current, verified access to Castro's person, itinerary, or inner detail — the station has instead selected an exile contact, previously used for infiltration runs in 1961, whose present freedom and loyalty are unconfirmed. No new network has been built; the operation runs on what already existed.

At 1:15 p.m. McNamara issues readiness directives to SAC, TAC, and Atlantic Command: dispersal of aircraft to secondary fields, forward movement of ordnance and fuel stocks, reports within six hours on what each command could ready without a formal invasion order. By late afternoon the movement is visible enough that McNamara himself flags it in the Cabinet Room — dispersal at this scale is not invisible from Havana or from Soviet intelligence assets, and he recommends holding further conspicuous steps pending a presidential decision between diplomacy and OPLAN 312.

Castro, watching both the readiness measures and unconfirmed rumors of exile activity in Florida, orders a general Cuban mobilization at approximately 3:00 p.m. and places air-defense units on immediate alert — the same units that killed Major Rudolf Anderson's U-2 that morning.

General LeMay arrives in the Cabinet Room shortly after 4:00 p.m. carrying the Joint Chiefs' formal written recommendation: immediate strikes against the known SAM sites, with an explicit warning that no strike can guarantee destruction of every offensive weapon and that Cuban or Soviet retaliation is possible. He argues every hour of readiness without an attack order reads abroad as American hesitation, and states he intends to put his objection to further delay on the formal record.

Robert Kennedy reports separately that the Dobrynin channel remains the only plausible controlled contact with Moscow, but he will not offer new terms — including anything touching Turkey — without direct presidential instruction, and urges that any American reply treat Khrushchev's softer private message separately from the harder public demand.

Nothing has resolved. The CIA operation has no target path. The armed forces are readier but not committed. Havana is mobilizing against a movement that was meant to remain quiet.

press.headline: Military Activity Reported at South Florida Bases
press.body: Residents near several air bases reported unusual aircraft movement and convoy traffic Saturday afternoon. Pentagon spokesmen declined comment, citing the ongoing quarantine of Cuba.

press.headline: Havana Announces General Mobilization
press.body: Premier Castro has ordered Cuban forces to a state of full readiness, citing what Havana calls unmistakable signs of imminent American aggression following reports of troop and aircraft movements in Florida.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, I gave the readiness order because you asked for maximum practical mobilization, but I want the record clear: dispersal at this scale is not covert. Havana has already read it as a prelude. I'd like a decision within hours on whether we're pursuing OPLAN 312 or the channel Bobby's running, because right now we're doing both and neither convincingly.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Every hour we disperse aircraft and don't hit those SAM sites is an hour the Soviets get to finish concealing what's left down there. The Chiefs' recommendation is on your desk. I'd rather we act than watch Castro mobilize against a threat we haven't actually delivered.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, the Castro business — if that leaks, and these things leak, it undoes every ounce of restraint you've shown Khrushchev this week. Dobrynin is still there. He's still listening. Don't let this Miami thing be what closes that door before we've used it.

response.chronicleEntry: 27 October, 12:40–4:30 p.m. EST: President Kennedy ordered a CIA operation to assassinate Castro within one week and directed the armed forces to maximum practical readiness. Helms placed Miami station on a forty-eight-hour planning clock but reported no verified access to Castro; an unconfirmed exile contact was selected. McNamara's readiness measures produced visible dispersal, prompting Castro to order general Cuban mobilization and immediate air-defense alert. The Joint Chiefs formally recommended a limited strike on the SAM belt. RFK reported the Dobrynin channel remains the sole viable contact with Moscow, pending presidential instruction. No missile removal, no assassination, and no strike authorization has occurred.
response.storySoFar: Two weeks into the missile crisis, a U-2 was shot down over Cuba on the morning of 27 October, killing its pilot — the first combat death of the confrontation. Soviet medium-range missiles remain in Cuba under an active naval quarantine; there is no hotline to Moscow. At noon, President Kennedy ordered the CIA to begin assassinating Castro within a week and directed the armed forces to full readiness. Helms put Miami station on a forty-eight-hour clock but found no verified access to Castro. McNamara's readiness measures caused visible dispersal, prompting Castro to order full Cuban mobilization and air-defense alert. The Joint Chiefs formally requested authorization to strike the SAM sites; LeMay pressed for action. RFK reported the Dobrynin channel as the only viable contact with Moscow, awaiting instruction. No strike, no assassination, and no diplomatic reply have yet occurred.

strategy_compiler:Interpretation:a5eb694.request:
You interpret a player's directive inside a historical simulation.

The player holds the stated role. Decide what they are ACTUALLY attempting, separating:
- attempts: what they do within their own authority, including issuing orders and demands
- requestedOutcomes: every result the player wants that is not theirs to simply produce. Set whoMustChoose to the party whose willing agreement the result depends on. Leave whoMustChoose EMPTY when the result would be taken rather than granted — an assassination, a strike that lands, a building destroyed, a person seized. Nobody consents to those, so no one chooses them, but they are still results the player is reaching for and belong here
- assertedEvents: text that declares another party's behaviour or an outcome as already settled. A directive that says what ANOTHER PARTY DOES, rather than what the player does, is an assertion. Record it here and do NOT convert it into an attempt on the player's behalf — inventing an attempt they did not describe is how a player comes to author other people's decisions

Three rules that decide most cases:
1. METHOD IS DELEGATED. When the player names an end and a capable body — an intelligence service, a military command, a department — the method is that body's to devise. An absent method is never a defect; record the body under delegatedTo.
2. AN ORDER TO SOMEONE YOU CANNOT COMMAND IS A DEMAND THAT LANDS. Issuing it is an attempt; compliance is a requestedOutcome.
3. A CONDITIONAL OR THREAT is the player stating terms — an attempt — not an assertion about the world.

prerequisites: what must already be true for each attempt to succeed. Mark each ESTABLISHED (true in the world or the ledger), ACHIEVABLE_WITHIN_DIRECTIVE (the directive itself covers it), or MISSING. For MISSING, say what covering it would require and what mandate that would exceed — an unmet prerequisite is a fork the world imposes, not a failure.

parties: everyone materially involved, including any not yet in the cast. Use the existing id when the party is already in the cast. A place named as a destination is NOT a party.

stakes: what the player is putting at risk — their person, their authority, their standing, or the irreversibility of the act.

Do not evaluate whether the plan is good. Do not improve it. Do not add mechanisms the player did not supply or plainly imply.

adjudicator:Outcomes:7863e600.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

outcomes.event: Air Force One is located, crewed, and launched from Andrews with President Kennedy aboard, unescorted as ordered. outcomes.event: To make the flight viable, Robert Kennedy is directed to use Dobrynin and State Department intermediaries to warn Moscow that Air Force One is carrying Kennedy personally and to request Cuban safe passage, while McNamara orders airborne surveillance and combat aircraft held beyond visual range. critic:CriticFindings:beea4b01.request:
You audit an enumeration of outcomes for a historical simulation.

You alone see the player's raw words alongside the interpretation and the outcomes. Your only job is to catch judgment that has been swayed by how the directive was written rather than by what it does.

Flag:
- RHETORIC_INFLATION: outcomes made likelier or larger because the player wrote forcefully, insisted, or used capitals
- INTERPRETATION_CHARITY: the interpretation supplied competence, a mechanism, or coordination the player never did
- MISSING_OUTCOME: a plausible answer the situation obviously permits that no outcome covers. Look in BOTH directions and weight them equally: an institution refusing, or something leaking — and just as much, the attempt simply working, or working and going far beyond what the player intended. An enumeration with no branch where the player gets what they ordered is as defective as one with no branch where they are refused
- IMPLAUSIBLE: an outcome the period, the people, or the ledger will not support — including any obstacle that runs slower than the turn's own clock being used as the reason nothing happened, and any outcome that resolves the player's directive by having the wider crisis end on its own

Do not rewrite anything. Do not judge whether the plan is wise.

response.title: Homestead
response.immediate: 14:40 EDT, Homestead AFB, Florida. Air Force One touches down having been turned back over the Straits. President Kennedy departed Andrews unescorted per direct order; Cuban radar picked up the aircraft on approach without clearance, MiG-21s scrambled, and Cuban air-defence controllers demanded the flight turn away. The pilot broke north and diverted to Homestead rather than close on the coast under active intercept. No landing in Cuba occurred. No meeting with Castro took place.
response.worldReaction: Havana: Castro orders his fighters back to base after the interception and goes on Cuban radio to denounce the flight as invasion reconnaissance. Moscow has not yet spoken to the incident. In Washington the Joint Chiefs treat the aborted flight, coupled with Major Anderson's death this morning, as further proof that diplomacy has run out of road.
response.consequences: LeMay presses the Chiefs and the president to authorize OPLAN 312 against the SAM sites now. McNamara wants a readiness review and insists no strike proceeds without a defined escalation-control plan. Robert Kennedy confirms Dobrynin remains reachable but will not act without explicit instruction. The two Khrushchev letters — the conciliatory one and the harder one — remain unanswered. The submarine contact in the quarantine line has received no new rules of engagement.
response.detailed: Air Force One left Andrews at approximately 11:50 EDT on direct presidential order, unescorted. Radar tracked it southbound over the Straits of Florida through early afternoon. Cuban air defence, at maximum alert since the loss of Major Anderson's U-2 that morning, identified the inbound aircraft without clearance and scrambled MiGs, with ground control demanding the flight turn away or be intercepted. The pilot, facing an active intercept posture and no diplomatic clearance to enter Cuban airspace, turned north. Air Force One landed at Homestead AFB at 14:40, inside the four-hour window but short of Cuba by a wide margin. Castro, after recalling his fighters to base, addressed the interception publicly, framing the unescorted approach of the American president's own aircraft as evidence of imminent invasion — the opposite of the outreach intended. In Washington, the Joint Chiefs formally resubmitted their case for OPLAN 312, citing both Anderson's death and the failed flight as proof that further restraint has produced no result. LeMay pushed hardest, treating the day's events as vindication. McNamara held the line that no strike proceeds without presidential authorization tied to a specific escalation-control plan, and called for an immediate readiness review before any further military option is entertained. Robert Kennedy, separately, confirmed the Dobrynin backchannel remains open and unburned by the day's events, but stated flatly that he will not transmit anything — acceptance, counteroffer, or silence — without explicit direction from the president. The two Khrushchev letters sit unanswered. The submarine contact holding at the quarantine line has received no updated instructions since this morning. The president is now on the ground at Homestead, not Andrews, not the Cabinet Room — a fact that will itself require managing.

press.headline: Castro Denounces 'Provocation' by Unescorted American Aircraft
press.body: Prime Minister Fidel Castro told Cuban listeners this afternoon that an unmarked approach by an American presidential aircraft, without clearance, was 'further proof of Yankee preparation for direct invasion,' and praised Cuban air-defence forces for their readiness to respond.

press.headline: Air Force One Reported Diverted to Florida; White House Silent
press.body: Unconfirmed reports place the presidential aircraft at Homestead Air Force Base this afternoon after an apparent diversion from a southbound course. The White House press office has not responded to inquiries. The nature of the flight's original destination is not stated.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, I need to know exactly what altitude, what heading, and how many seconds elapsed between the intercept order and the turn. Not for the record — for the next decision, because there will be a next decision within the hour, and I want it made with numbers instead of nerve.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: You just handed Castro a propaganda victory and lost us four hours we didn't have. Anderson is dead, now this. The SAM sites are the same sites they were this morning. Give me the order, Mr. President, before they get another airplane.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack — Jesus. You can't be halfway to Havana one hour and back at the Cabinet table the next like nothing happened. Dobrynin's channel is still open, but if you want me to say anything to him, you have to tell me what, and you have to tell me now, before Castro's broadcast becomes the only version of today anyone remembers.

response.chronicleEntry: 12:00–14:40 EDT, 27 October 1962: On direct presidential order, Air Force One departed Andrews unescorted, attempting to fly President Kennedy to Cuba for a direct meeting with Fidel Castro. Cuban air defence, at maximum alert following the morning's loss of a U-2 and its pilot, scrambled MiG interceptors and forced the flight to turn back before reaching Cuban airspace. The president landed at Homestead AFB. No contact with Castro occurred. Castro denounced the flight publicly as invasion preparation. The Joint Chiefs renewed pressure for OPLAN 312; McNamara insisted on a defined escalation-control plan before any strike; Robert Kennedy confirmed the Dobrynin channel remains open pending explicit instruction. Khrushchev's two letters remain unanswered.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 was shot down over Cuba that morning, killing its pilot — the crisis's first combat death. With the quarantine in force and both sides at maximum alert, President Kennedy ordered Air Force One to fly him, unescorted, directly to Cuba to meet Castro personally. Cuban air defence intercepted the approach with scrambled MiGs; the flight turned back and landed at Homestead. No meeting occurred. Castro denounced the attempt as invasion preparation. In Washington, the Joint Chiefs and LeMay press hard for airstrikes on the Cuban SAM sites (OPLAN 312); McNamara demands escalation controls before any strike; Robert Kennedy holds the Dobrynin backchannel open but awaits explicit presidential instruction. Khrushchev's two letters — one conciliatory, one hard-lined — remain unanswered. No rules of engagement have been issued regarding the Soviet submarine at the quarantine line. The president must now decide: respond to Moscow, authorize or withhold a strike, and manage the political fallout of the aborted flight — all without a hotline to the Kremlin.

adjudicator:Outcomes:484b6041.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).
