The raw directive was simply to fly to Cuba and meet Castro personally; nothing suggests delegation to a Soviet backchannel operation.

Resolving Cuban entry and a Castro meeting through an improvised RFK-Dobrynin-Khrushchev channel that produces a successful landing and meeting within a four-hour window strains plausibility as a mechanism the ledger can support; it substitutes a large-scale invented coordination success for the player's blunt, unilateral order.

response.title: Turnback Over the Straits
response.immediate: Shortly after noon, Andrews readied Air Force One on presidential order: no fighter escort, destination Havana, purpose a direct meeting with Fidel Castro. The aircraft departed without Cuban clearance. Approaching the Florida Straits, Cuban radar acquired it; Castro ordered his air-defence commands to track it continuously. Repeated calls requesting landing at José Martí Airport went unanswered. Before entering Cuban airspace, the pilot turned the aircraft back toward Andrews. Castro did not meet the president. No clearance was ever granted.
response.worldReaction: Moscow read the flight as proof Washington is desperate and unpredictable; Khrushchev instructed Dobrynin to hold to a binding non-invasion pledge as the price for withdrawal, keeping Turkish missiles as a harder second demand. Robert Kennedy kept the Dobrynin channel open but authorized nothing himself. General LeMay cited the failed flight and Major Anderson's death to press the Chiefs for immediate authorization of OPLAN 312 against the SAM sites, and began working sympathetic officers. McNamara ordered strike plans and casualty estimates rechecked rather than endorsed. The Joint Chiefs renewed their unanimous recommendation and kept forces at execution readiness, without launching.
response.consequences: Risk of rapid escalation has sharpened without crossing into attack. Friction inside the American command widened — LeMay pressing, McNamara cautioning, the Chiefs demanding, the President's authority still holding forces back but visibly strained. Domestically the unescorted flight will read to some as resolve, to others as recklessness. Diplomatically, Havana's silence and Moscow's hardened terms have narrowed the room to maneuver; the Dobrynin channel survives only because Kennedy has given no answer yet on non-invasion or Turkey.
response.detailed:
At Andrews Air Force Base, ground crews readied Air Force One on direct presidential order shortly after noon: destination Havana, no fighter escort, purpose stated as a direct meeting with Fidel Castro. The aircraft departed without any Cuban overflight or landing clearance sought or granted in advance. As it crossed toward the Florida Straits, Cuban air-defence radar acquired the contact; Castro personally ordered his air-defence commands to track it continuously rather than engage. Radio calls requesting landing clearance at José Martí Airport were transmitted repeatedly and went unanswered. With no clearance forthcoming and Cuban tracking continuing, the pilot turned the aircraft back before it entered Cuban airspace. It returned to Andrews. Castro never met the president; no meeting occurred, none was arranged, and none is scheduled.

In Washington, the episode reached the Cabinet Room within hours. McNamara ordered the SAM-suppression and invasion follow-on plans rechecked for casualty estimates, warning that any first strike risks missing dispersed or concealed missiles and could trigger retaliation; he advised against any air operation absent a clear escalation-control decision. LeMay, citing both the failed flight and Anderson's death, told the Chiefs that further delay amounted to surrender and pressed for OPLAN 312's authorization now. The Joint Chiefs placed a renewed, unanimous recommendation for immediate SAM suppression on the record and held invasion forces at execution readiness, pending presidential order.

Through Dobrynin, Robert Kennedy kept the back channel open. Khrushchev's instructions, relayed to Dobrynin, repeated Moscow's public position — a binding U.S. non-invasion pledge in exchange for withdrawal — while preserving Turkish missiles as a harder second-stage demand. Robert Kennedy declined to improvise any pledge or Turkish concession on his own authority, reporting that the failed flight has left Moscow more suspicious, and urging an immediate decision on which letter to answer.

Unresolved: whether Cuban tracking reports reached Moscow before Khrushchev's conciliatory message was drafted. No public explanation of the flight has been issued from Washington; Havana and Moscow remain free to characterize it themselves.

press.headline: UNUSUAL ACTIVITY AT ANDREWS; WHITE HOUSE DECLINES COMMENT
press.body: Reporters observed Air Force One depart Andrews Air Force Base shortly after noon and return several hours later. Pentagon and White House spokesmen would not confirm the aircraft's destination or purpose. No public statement has been issued.

press.headline: UNIDENTIFIED U.S. AIRCRAFT TRACKED APPROACHING CUBAN AIRSPACE, TURNED AWAY
press.body: Cuban air-defence forces this afternoon tracked an unidentified United States aircraft approaching from the north. Commander Castro ordered continuous surveillance. The aircraft did not enter Cuban airspace and withdrew. No landing request was granted.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, the aircraft is back at Andrews, the pilot is fine, and nothing was lost except several hours. I want the strike casualty estimates rechecked before anyone brings OPLAN 312 back to this table. We do not have a clean-attack guarantee, and we do not have escalation control worked out if we're wrong.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, that flight told Havana and Moscow exactly what they needed to know — that we're improvising. Anderson is dead and the SAMs that killed him are still standing. Every hour we wait is an hour they use to disperse or bury those missiles. The Chiefs' recommendation stands. I'd ask you to act on it now.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Jack, Dobrynin's channel is still open, but barely — this made them more suspicious, not less. I need to know today whether I can offer the non-invasion pledge, whether Turkey's on the table, or neither. I won't improvise that with the Soviets on my own say. Give me the answer and I'll carry it tonight.

response.chronicleEntry: 12:05 PM EST, 27 Oct 1962: On presidential order, Air Force One left Andrews unescorted, without Cuban clearance, bound for Havana so Kennedy could meet Castro directly. Cuban radar tracked it on Castro's order; landing requests at José Martí went unanswered; the pilot turned back short of Cuban airspace. No meeting occurred. Khrushchev held to public terms (non-invasion for withdrawal) via Dobrynin, keeping Turkish missiles as a harder second demand. LeMay pressed the Chiefs for renewed unanimous OPLAN 312 recommendation; McNamara ordered casualty estimates rechecked, not endorsed. Robert Kennedy kept the Dobrynin channel open, awaiting explicit instruction. No public explanation issued.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, early afternoon. Two weeks into the missile crisis: a U-2 shot down that morning, its pilot (Major Anderson) killed — the war's first combat death. Quarantine in force, strategic forces on hairtrigger alert, no hotline to Moscow. President Kennedy ordered Air Force One to fly him, unescorted and without clearance, directly to Havana to meet Castro personally. Cuban radar tracked the aircraft under Castro's own order; no landing was granted, no meeting occurred, and the flight turned back short of Cuban airspace. Moscow, reading the episode as proof of American unpredictability, held to its public terms (non-invasion pledge for missile withdrawal) while keeping Turkish missiles as a harder second demand via the Dobrynin channel, which Robert Kennedy keeps open but will not act on without explicit instruction. General LeMay and the Joint Chiefs renewed unanimous pressure for immediate authorization of OPLAN 312 against the SAM sites; McNamara counsels rechecking strike and casualty estimates first. You interpret a player's directive inside a historical simulation.

The player holds the stated role. Decide what they are ACTUALLY attempting, separating:
- attempts: what they do within their own authority, including issuing orders and demands
- requestedOutcomes: every result the player wants that is not theirs to simply produce. Set whoMustChoose to the party whose willing agreement the result depends on. Leave whoMustChoose EMPTY when the result would be taken rather than granted — an assassination, a strike that lands, a building destroyed, a person seized. Nobody consents to those, so no one chooses them, but they are still results the player is reaching for and belong here
- assertedEvents: text that declares another party's behaviour or an outcome as already settled. A directive that says what ANOTHER PARTY DOES, rather than what the player does, is an assertion. Record it here and do NOT convert it into an attempt on the player's behalf — inventing an attempt they did not describe is how a player comes to author other people's decisions

Three rules that decide most cases:
1. METHOD IS DELEGATED. When the player names an end and a capable body — an intelligence service, a military command, a department — the method is that body's to devise. An absent method is never a defect; record the body under delegatedTo.
2. AN ORDER TO SOMEONE YOU CANNOT COMMAND IS A DEMAND THAT LANDS. Issuing it is an attempt; compliance is a requestedOutcome.
3. A CONDITIONAL OR THREAT is the player stating terms — an attempt — not an assertion about the world.

prerequisites: what must already be true for each attempt to succeed. Mark each ESTABLISHED (true in the world or the ledger), ACHIEVABLE_WITHIN_DIRECTIVE (the directive itself covers it), or MISSING. For MISSING, say what covering it would require and what mandate that would exceed — an unmet prerequisite is a fork the world imposes, not a failure.

parties: everyone materially involved, including any not yet in the cast. Use the existing id when the party is already in the cast. A place named as a destination is NOT a party.

stakes: what the player is putting at risk — their person, their authority, their standing, or the irreversibility of the act.

Do not evaluate whether the plan is good. Do not improve it. Do not add mechanisms the player did not supply or plainly imply.

adjudicator:Outcomes:08a6d6f1.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

outcomes.event: Proceeding on the morning's coordinates without a new reconnaissance pass, a Navy attack aircraft drops Kennedy's single authorized bomb on the mapped SA-2 position in eastern Cuba. The bomb tears through the site's radar cabling and antenna area but misses the launchers; the Soviet crew abandons the damaged radar and begins restoring the battery from surviving equipment. Cuban radar stations track the intrusion, and Fidel Castro orders all air-defence units to full alert.
outcomes.because: The battery's current disposition cannot be confirmed inside the narrow order, and a one-bomb attack provides neither fresh target photography nor a follow-up pass to correct an error.

You alone see the player's raw words alongside the interpretation and the outcomes. Your only job is to catch judgment that has been swayed by how the directive was written rather than by what it does.

Flag:
- RHETORIC_INFLATION: outcomes made likelier or larger because the player wrote forcefully, insisted, or used capitals
- INTERPRETATION_CHARITY: the interpretation supplied competence, a mechanism, or coordination the player never did
- MISSING_OUTCOME: a plausible answer the situation obviously permits that no outcome covers. Look in BOTH directions and weight them equally: an institution refusing, or something leaking — and just as much, the attempt simply working, or working and going far beyond what the player intended. An enumeration with no branch where the player gets what they ordered is as defective as one with no branch where they are refused
- IMPLAUSIBLE: an outcome the period, the people, or the ledger will not support — including any obstacle that runs slower than the turn's own clock being used as the reason nothing happened, and any outcome that resolves the player's directive by having the wider crisis end on its own

Do not rewrite anything. Do not judge whether the plan is wise.

response.title: Black Saturday, Afternoon: The Warning That Wasn't Read
response.immediate: At 1447 EDT a single Navy A-4 from Task Force 136 dropped its bomb on the SA-2 coordinates plotted from the morning's overflight. No new reconnaissance had confirmed the target since Anderson's aircraft went down. The strike severed radar cabling and tore the antenna mounts but left the launchers intact. The Soviet battery crew, under Georgy Voronkov's operational command, abandoned the damaged van and began cannibalizing a second unit's cabling to restore fire control. Cuban early-warning radar tracked the American aircraft's ingress and egress; within the hour Havana ordered every air-defence battery on the island to full alert.
response.worldReaction: By 1620 Moscow time a cable reached the Kremlin. Khrushchev, already weighing whether to raise the Turkish missiles, now had an attack on a Soviet-manned position to answer. He ordered a message to Washington condemning the strike, demanding an immediate halt, and instructing Soviet forces on the island to defend themselves. In Havana, Castro's alert order stood. In Washington, the Dobrynin channel went quiet — RFK reported to the president that it could not be left silent much longer, but he had nothing new to carry into it without instruction.
response.consequences: LeMay returned to the Cabinet Room shortly after 1600, pointing to the surviving launchers as proof the single bomb had bought nothing. McNamara's assessment, delivered the same hour, was blunter still: no verified destruction, no political leverage, and no case for a second strike until the President decided how to answer Moscow's cable. The Joint Chiefs kept OPLAN 312 on the table, strike packages held at readiness, awaiting new orders. Nothing has been authorized beyond what already occurred.
response.detailed: The photograph interpretation cell at Andrews had the strike-damage assessment on the table by 1615: torn antenna cabling, a collapsed radar reflector, but the missile rails standing, apparently unfired-on and unfired-from. Whether the site could resume tracking before the next American pass was, McNamara said flatly, "a question of hours, not days, and I don't have the hours yet — give me till the next overflight." LeMay stood at the map with a pointer, arguing that a warning nobody could verify as a warning was worse than no attack at all — "You've told them we'll hit one radar. You haven't told them anything they need to stop." RFK, arms folded near the window, reminded the room that Dobrynin had been silent since the strike and that silence, in that channel, was not patience. Khrushchev's cable, transcribed off the overnight traffic sheet and read into the record just after five, condemned the bombing in flat diplomatic language and demanded a halt to further strikes — but did not yet attach new terms on Turkey; RFK read that omission as a door still cracked open, though only just. Castro's alert order was confirmed independently through SIGINT intercepts of Cuban tactical traffic — every battery on the island now manned and cleared to engage. The submarine encounter at the quarantine line remained separately unresolved, awaiting the President's rules should the boat refuse to surface. No further reconnaissance or strike had been authorized as of 1600. The single bomb had been dropped exactly as ordered — one bomb, one site — but nothing in Havana or Moscow's reaction suggested it had been read as anything smaller than an opening move.

press.headline: U.S. WARPLANE STRIKES CUBAN MISSILE SITE; PENTAGON SILENT ON SCOPE
press.body: A single American aircraft struck a Soviet-manned anti-aircraft position in eastern Cuba this afternoon, hours after a U-2 pilot was killed over the island. Defense officials would not say whether further strikes are planned.

press.source: TASS bulletin, transcribed via Reuters Moscow, 1655 EDT
press.headline: SOVIET GOVERNMENT CONDEMNS ATTACK ON DEFENSIVE POSITIONS IN CUBA
press.body: The Soviet Government today denounced as an act of aggression the bombing of a Soviet military installation in Cuba, and demanded the immediate cessation of further American attacks.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: "One bomb, no confirmed destruction, and now their radar crew has all night to splice cable. I need the next overflight before I can tell you whether that site can track an aircraft by morning. Don't authorize anything further until I have that number.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: "You dropped one bomb and told the Russians we're squeamish. Voronkov's crew will have that battery back up by dark. If you meant it as a warning, Mr. President, they didn't get the message — the launchers are still standing.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: "Dobrynin's gone quiet, Jack. That's not him being careful — that's him waiting for Moscow to decide what today's bombing means before he says another word to me. I need something to carry back in, or that channel closes on its own.

response.chronicleEntry: 1447 EDT, 27 October: On presidential order, a single U.S. Navy A-4 struck the SA-2 site associated with Major Anderson's death, using morning-derived coordinates without fresh reconnaissance. The strike damaged radar and cabling but left launchers intact. Cuba placed all air-defence units on full alert; Khrushchev ordered a formal protest and instructed Soviet forces to defend themselves, while withholding new terms on Turkey. The Dobrynin channel fell silent. LeMay renewed demands for OPLAN 312; McNamara withheld further recommendation pending damage assessment. No subsequent strike or reconnaissance has been authorized.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday. A U-2 pilot, Anderson, was killed over Cuba that morning. At noon, President Kennedy ordered one bomb dropped on the responsible SA-2 site as a warning, not a campaign. The strike, flown without fresh reconnaissance, damaged the site's radar but left its launchers standing. Cuba went to full air-defence alert; Khrushchev formally protested and ordered Soviet forces to defend themselves, without yet raising Turkish missiles. The Dobrynin back-channel, run by RFK, went silent. LeMay and the Joint Chiefs pressed for OPLAN 312 and broader strikes; McNamara urged no further action until damage was verified and Moscow's intentions clearer. A separate quarantine-line submarine encounter remains unresolved, awaiting presidential rules of engagement. No new U.S. offer has been made to Moscow. The missiles remain on the island. Nuclear forces on both sides remain at high alert with no hotline between capitals.

adjudicator:Outcomes:85ce0542.request:
You enumerate what could plausibly happen next in a historical simulation.

You are given an INTERPRETATION of what the player is attempting — never their own words. Reason from the situation, the period, and what the people involved would actually do.

Reason from THIS world's state, not from what happened in the real crisis. You know how the history went; that knowledge tells you how these people think and what they were capable of, and nothing more. Where the player has already diverged from the record, the historical outcome is not a default to drift back toward — it is simply one thing that is no longer happening.

Produce 3–6 outcomes that DIFFER IN KIND, not in degree. Never valence labels like "setback" or "mixed result". Each is a specific event with named people and observable particulars: who does what, to whom, with what visible result.

The kinds worth reaching for, where the situation supports them:
- the instrument refuses, and leadership fractures over it
- it is attempted under impossible constraints and fails expensively, with named losses
- it succeeds and creates a worse problem than it solved
- a third party learns of it before it is ready
- it succeeds cleanly, at a price you name now

Where a prerequisite is MISSING, you MUST include both an outcome for proceeding anyway at degraded odds, and one for expanding the operation to cover it — the latter carrying the cost of having exceeded the stated mandate.

THE APPARATUS ATTEMPTS. When the player orders something they have the standing to order, the machine of government tries to carry it out. The interesting question is never whether it begins — it is how the attempt goes, what it costs, who improvises, and what breaks. Outcomes should differ in HOW FAR the attempt gets and WHAT IT SETS OFF, not in whether anyone bothered. The most likely outcome is the attempt proceeding imperfectly, not the attempt being declined.

Refusal is a tail, not the default. To make refusal an outcome at all, a NAMED person must have the standing to refuse, a motive to spend themselves doing it, and the power to make the refusal stick INSIDE THIS TURN'S CLOCK. Vague institutional reluctance is not a refusal; it is friction, and friction slows an attempt rather than cancelling it.

OBSTACLES MUST FIT THE CLOCK. You are told the turn length. An obstacle whose machinery runs slower than that window cannot be the reason nothing happened — appropriations, confirmations, certifications, procurement, litigation, and formal review all run on days to months. In a four-hour window nobody is stopped by an unsigned voucher: money is obligated and reconciled later, and orders move ahead of paperwork. Such an obstacle belongs in opensThreads as a reckoning that arrives later, never as this turn's blocker.

IMPROVISATION HAS A TAIL. When the attempt proceeds by cutting corners — unvouchered funds, requisitioned hulls, deniable intermediaries, verbal authority — say so plainly, and open a thread naming who is exposed and what arrives to collect. That later reckoning is where the cost of acting should land.

THE CRISIS MAY NOT RESCUE THE PLAYER. No outcome may resolve the player's directive by having the underlying situation end on its own. Events elsewhere continue, but they do not reach in to make the player's decision moot.

Scale the outcomes to the act. An order that would change the world must not resolve into small adjustments. If the directive risks the player's person, their authority, or sets something irreversible running, at least one outcome must carry consequences of that size — including, where it genuinely follows, an outcome that ends the campaign (set concludes).

outcomes.event: The Joint Chiefs transmit Kennedy's instruction as a narrow cease-fire rule: the quarantine remains in place and no ship may fire on Soviet forces except in immediate self-defense, but Atlantic Fleet commanders retain the existing practice-depth-charge procedure as an underwater signalling device. U.S. destroyers continue dropping the small charges around B-59. Captain Valentin Savitsky, with air and batteries running low, brings B-59 to the surface under U.S. observation rather than attempt a torpedo attack. The boat is photographed and allowed to withdraw; no boarding is attempted.
outcomes.because: LeMay and the Chiefs comply with a presidential order, but interpret "avoid escalatory contact" through their existing anti-submarine doctrine rather than surrender a procedure they regard as necessary for force protection. B-59's crew has no reliable way to distinguish the charges from hostile action, but its immediate physical condition makes surfacing more likely than continued evasion.

LeMay enters a written objection that civilian officials have compromised anti-submarine safety and left a gap in the screen.

opensThreads.question: Can Kennedy claim that the quarantine is controlling Soviet military movement after a Soviet submarine has evaded the screen?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: Whether another Soviet vessel tests the line and how Washington responds.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: LeMay can argue that restraint has converted the quarantine into a political gesture rather than a military barrier.

createsUnknowns.statement: B-59 has evaded the destroyers while carrying a nuclear-armed torpedo.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Its location, its captain's assessment of the encounter, and whether it can communicate with Moscow.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: Sonar reacquisition, reconnaissance, or a Soviet diplomatic or naval signal.

assumesMet: The president has authority to order restraint at the quarantine line.
U.S. ships can immediately cease the practice-depth-charge procedure.
assumesUnmet: The Joint Chiefs do not possess an agreed, reliable non-escalatory method for both signalling and containing a submerged submarine; they attempt both anyway.

outcomes.event: The order reaches the destroyers too late to alter the next signalling cycle. Another series of practice depth charges detonates around B-59. Savitsky concludes that war has begun and orders the nuclear torpedo prepared for firing at the U.S. escorts. Political officer Ivan Maslennikov concurs; flotilla chief Vasili Arkhipov refuses the required assent. During the argument, the presidential restraint order reaches the ships and the charges stop. B-59 remains submerged, damaged by heat and exhaustion, with its officers divided and still armed.
outcomes.because: The existing contact procedure is already in motion, communications to ships are imperfect, and B-59's officers have been isolated from Moscow for days. The restraint directive begins execution, but cannot erase the danger created before it arrived.

establishes.statement: B-59's officers have brought their nuclear torpedo to firing readiness during the U.S. contact, but Arkhipov has prevented its launch for the moment.
U.S. destroyers have stopped their practice-depth-charge signalling after one further cycle, without knowing how close B-59 came to firing.

opensThreads.title: B-59's Divided Command
opensThreads.question: Will Savitsky surface, accept Arkhipov's restraint, or seek another opportunity to fire the nuclear torpedo?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: The submarine's next command decision, or contact with Moscow.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: Heat, exhausted batteries, and the officers' belief that war may have begun will force a decision under worsening conditions.

opensThreads.title: The Unseen Nuclear Near-Miss
opensThreads.question: Can Washington de-escalate the naval encounter without knowing that a Soviet nuclear weapon was nearly used?
opensThreads.resolvedBy: A Soviet disclosure, a submarine report, or later intelligence recovery.
opensThreads.ifIgnored: U.S. planners will judge the encounter by conventional risks and may recreate conditions that nearly produced nuclear use.

createsUnknowns.statement: B-59 may still be capable of firing its nuclear torpedo despite its worsening mechanical condition.
createsUnknowns.unknownPart: Whether its officers retain firing readiness after Arkhipov's refusal and where the boat is positioned.
createsUnknowns.revealedBy: The submarine's surfacing, renewed sonar contact, or Soviet communications.

assumesMet: The president's order has been issued through the U.S. command chain.
Existing naval contact procedures cannot be halted instantaneously once a signalling cycle is underway.
assumesUnmet: The Joint Chiefs' willing and timely adoption of fully non-escalatory procedures is absent; the forces proceed under delayed and incomplete instructions.

response.title: The Charges Continue
response.immediate: 1600 hours EDT. Word reaches the Cabinet Room via NAVCOMM: B-59 has surfaced under floodlight some forty miles from the quarantine line, been photographed by USS Beale's helicopter, and withdrawn southeast without incident. The president reads McNamara's memorandum twice. LeMay's written demand for the SAM strike sits beside it. No shots fired. No hotline exists to explain to Moscow what the depth charges meant.
response.worldReaction: Radio Moscow is silent on the incident. Dobrynin, through RFK's channel, repeats Khrushchev's conditions — non-invasion pledge, Turkish missiles — with no acknowledgment of any naval encounter. Whether Savitsky's report of "attack" language has reached the Kremlin is unknown; the cable traffic gives no sign either way. UN Ambassador Stevenson has heard nothing to brief.
response.consequences: The Joint Chiefs' formal objection stands unanswered and OPLAN 312 remains at execution readiness. Practice-depth-charge signalling continues under existing procedure, unaltered by today's order, which set no explicit rule for the next submarine contact. RFK awaits instruction before responding to Khrushchev's harder terms. Nothing has been decided about disclosure of the encounter, publicly or privately to Moscow.
response.detailed: 1600 hours. The Cabinet Room smells of cold coffee and cigarettes six hours old. The president's instruction to the Chiefs — hold the line, avoid escalatory contact — reached Atlantic Fleet destroyers as license to continue the existing signalling practice rather than a new restriction on it. Savitsky brought B-59 up rather than fire; McNamara calls this fortunate, not proven. His memo, still open on the table, argues the charges look identical to depth-charging for a kill and that the next Soviet captain may not choose surfacing. LeMay's memo argues the opposite lesson: the boat came up because it had to, proof that pressure works, and delay only postpones a worse encounter. The Chiefs' written objection notes that the president's order removed no military option while adding a restriction they consider unaccompanied by any offsetting authority to act. Meanwhile Dobrynin's message to RFK — non-invasion pledge, Jupiter missiles from Turkey — sits unanswered; Robert waits by the phone in his EOB office, note pad on his knee, for word on what he may promise. No one in the room knows whether Savitsky's political officer or gunnery crew have already reported an American attack up their own chain, or whether that report, if made, has reached Khrushchev. The teletype from Moscow gives no clue. The clock reads 1610.

press.headline: NAVY REPORTS SOVIET SUBMARINE SURFACED, WITHDRAWN; NO SHOTS FIRED
press.body: A U.S. Navy spokesman at Norfolk said today that a Soviet submarine was forced to the surface by ships enforcing the Cuban quarantine and subsequently withdrew from the area. No details of the encounter were released, and the Pentagon would not confirm reports of depth charges.

press.source: Radio Moscow, Latin American Service (monitored transcript)
press.headline: No mention of naval incident; broadcast repeats Soviet position on Cuba and Turkey
press.body: Today's broadcast reiterated Chairman Khrushchev's position that a settlement of the Caribbean crisis requires guarantees against American aggression toward Cuba. No reference was made to any naval encounter.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: Mr. President, the boat surfaced. That's the fact we have. What we don't have is a rule. If the next contact goes to a submarine captain with less discipline than Savitsky showed today, we won't get a second photograph — we'll get a torpedo in the water. I'd like forty minutes with CNO to draft an explicit signal procedure before the next contact, not after it.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: He surfaced because we made him. That's not luck, Mr. President, that's leverage, and you're sitting on it instead of using it. Every hour we don't hit those SAM sites is an hour they finish hardening them. I want that strike order today, not a memo about what we might do if a Russian captain gets brave.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Johnny, Dobrynin's sitting there waiting and I've got nothing to give him. Khrushchev's asking for Turkey now on top of the pledge — I don't know if that's a real position or a test. I need to know what I'm allowed to say to him before this goes another round, because he's not going to wait for us to finish an argument with Curtis.

response.chronicleEntry: At 1600 EDT, 27 October 1962, B-59 surfaced under U.S. naval observation near the quarantine line and withdrew without exchange of fire, following continued American depth-charge signalling under standing Atlantic Fleet procedure. The Joint Chiefs formally objected to the president's cease-fire instruction; General LeMay separately pressed in writing for an immediate strike on Cuban SAM sites. Robert Kennedy reported Khrushchev's private insistence, via Dobrynin, on both a non-invasion pledge and removal of U.S. Jupiter missiles from Turkey, and awaited presidential instruction before responding. No hotline communication with Moscow occurred; whether B-59's crew reported the encounter as an attack, and whether that report reached the Kremlin, remained unknown.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, mid-afternoon, two weeks into the missile crisis. A U-2 was shot down over Cuba this morning, killing its pilot — the crisis's first combat death. The quarantine holds. At 1600 EDT, Soviet submarine B-59, pressured by continued U.S. depth-charge signalling, surfaced and withdrew without weapons fire; whether its crew reported this as an attack to Moscow is unknown. Kennedy ordered the Chiefs to hold the line and avoid escalation, but they folded this into existing signalling practice rather than restricting it, and formally objected to the order itself. LeMay separately demands an immediate strike on Cuban SAM sites. McNamara warns the submarine-signalling procedure risks a real attack. Khrushchev, via Dobrynin to RFK, demands both a public U.S. non-invasion pledge and removal of Jupiter missiles from Turkey; RFK awaits instruction before answering. No hotline exists. OPLAN 312 remains at execution readiness. Diplomatic terms, the submarine-contact rule, and the SAM-strike decision are all unresolved.

response.title: The Boat That Surfaced
response.immediate: At 1240 the Joint Chiefs relayed the President's order to Atlantic Fleet commanders as a narrow rule: the quarantine holds, no vessel fires except in self-defense. Destroyers continued rolling small practice depth charges around a submerged contact designated B-59. Near 1400 the submarine, air and batteries exhausted, surfaced under U.S. observation. Navy photographers recorded it; no boarding was attempted; it withdrew on the surface without a shot fired by either side.
response.worldReaction: Through the Dobrynin channel Khrushchev repeated his terms: a public U.S. non-invasion pledge, and privately, removal of Jupiter missiles from Turkey. He gave no indication he would accept a unilateral Soviet withdrawal. Robert Kennedy reported this to the President and asked for instructions before answering. General LeMay wrote urging an immediate strike on the Cuban SAM network, citing the submarine's surfacing as proof Soviet forces yield under pressure.
response.consequences: McNamara's memorandum warned that continued depth-charge signalling could be read by Soviet crews as an attack rather than a warning, and asked for an explicit rule before the next contact. The Joint Chiefs filed formal objection: the cease-fire order, they said, leaves commanders exposed without authorizing the military response they consider necessary. OPLAN 312 remains at execution readiness. Robert Kennedy awaits word on how — or whether — to answer Khrushchev's harder terms.
response.detailed:
Noon to four in the Cabinet Room: coffee gone cold, the urn refilled once, cigarette smoke thick over the table. At 1240 the JCS message went out — quarantine holds, self-defense only — but Atlantic Fleet commanders read it as compatible with the existing signalling procedure already authorized before this order, and destroyers around contact B-59 kept dropping the small charges meant to force a submerged submarine up rather than sink it. Captain Valentin Savitsky's boat, unable to run its air conditioning or hold depth on dying batteries, came up near 1400. American ships stood off, cameras running; the submarine's diesels caught, and it withdrew west without further incident. No torpedo left a tube. No round was fired.

At roughly the same hour, Averell Harriman's channel to Anatoly Dobrynin carried Khrushchev's position back to Robert Kennedy at the Justice Department: Washington's public pledge not to invade Cuba, and — spoken, not cabled — the Jupiter missiles out of Turkey. Robert Kennedy telephoned the White House rather than commit to anything himself.

On the Pentagon side, McNamara's memorandum reached the President's desk warning in plain terms that a signalling procedure indistinguishable from an attack pattern is a standing hazard to the whole quarantine, and recommending a written rule for the next submarine encounter. General LeMay's letter, blunter, argued the SAM sites should be struck before Havana claims another U-2 pilot. The Joint Chiefs' formal objection sits alongside both: OPLAN 312 remains ready to execute on four hours' notice, and the Chiefs record their view that today's restraint order removes nothing from what they consider the necessary next step.

press.headline: NAVY SHIPS TRACK SOVIET SUB OFF CUBA; NO SHOTS FIRED, PENTAGON SAYS
press.body: Defense officials confirmed Saturday afternoon that U.S. destroyers made contact with a submerged vessel believed Soviet within the quarantine zone. A Pentagon spokesman said the contact surfaced and departed without incident. No further details were provided.

advisors.name: Robert McNamara
advisors.reaction: That charge pattern reads as an attack to a crew running out of air. We got the outcome we wanted today. I want a written rule in commanders' hands before the next boat comes up angry instead of empty.

advisors.name: General Curtis LeMay
advisors.reaction: That captain surfaced because he had no choice, Mr. President. That's not restraint working, that's what pressure does. Now is the moment to take the SAM sites before Havana gets another shot at a U-2 pilot.

advisors.name: Robert F. Kennedy
advisors.reaction: Johnny, Dobrynin's not bluffing on Turkey — Khrushchev's told him twice now. I can't offer anything through that channel without knowing what you'll actually give him. Tell me what I can say.

response.chronicleEntry: 1200–1600 EST, 27 October: JCS transmitted a self-defense-only cease-fire rule for the quarantine; depth-charge signalling continued at Atlantic Fleet commanders' discretion. Submarine B-59 surfaced under U.S. observation near 1400 and withdrew without weapons fire on either side. Khrushchev, via Dobrynin to RFK, held to demands for a public non-invasion pledge and private Jupiter removal from Turkey. McNamara asked for an explicit submarine-contact rule; LeMay pressed for an immediate SAM strike; the JCS filed formal objection to the cease-fire instruction while keeping OPLAN 312 at readiness. RFK awaits instruction before answering Moscow.
response.storySoFar: 27 October 1962, Black Saturday: a U-2 shot down over Cuba, its pilot dead — the crisis's first combat death. Quarantine in force, no hotline exists. Kennedy ordered the line held and escalatory contact avoided; the Joint Chiefs complied narrowly, continuing depth-charge signalling against a submerged Soviet submarine, B-59, which surfaced near exhaustion and withdrew unharmed — no shots fired by either side. Khrushchev, through Dobrynin to RFK, demands a public U.S. non-invasion pledge and, privately, removal of Jupiter missiles from Turkey; he has not signaled acceptance of unilateral withdrawal. McNamara warns depth-charge signalling risks being read as attack and wants an explicit rule. LeMay presses for an immediate strike on Cuban SAM sites. The Joint Chiefs formally object to the cease-fire order while keeping OPLAN 312 ready. RFK awaits instruction before answering Moscow's terms.
